CYCLE 19 — STAGE 5: CROSS-DOMAIN CONVERGENCE SCAN
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

ENTERING STATE: C01-C124 convergence findings cumulative
NEW FINDINGS THIS CYCLE: C125-C132
SOURCE DOMAINS: 177-186 (DLP, Security Metrics, Cyber Insurance, Critical Infrastructure,
                Mobile Security, Physical/Cyber Convergence, Legal/Regulatory, Secure Coding,
                PETs, Defender OPSEC)
PATTERNS FEEDING THIS SCAN: 19.1 (Goodhart/Compliance), 19.2 (Insurance Moral Hazard),
                             19.3 (SIM Swapping), 19.4 (PETs vs. Monitoring)

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
C125: GOODHART'S LAW AS UNIVERSAL SECURITY METRIC FAILURE MECHANISM
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
CONVERGENCE DOMAINS: Security Metrics (Domain 178) x Organizational Behavior x
                     Economics (Campbell's Law) x Control Theory
FINDING: Goodhart's Law ("when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good
measure") is not a quirk of compliance — it is the universal failure mode of all
quantitative security programs. Security metrics (CVE count, patch cadence, mean
time to detect, phishing click rate) all degrade as targets. Organizations optimize
the metric rather than the security property the metric was intended to proxy.
Patch cadence becomes a patch-count theater. MTTD becomes alert triage speed that
closes tickets without investigating them. This is Campbell's Law (1979) applied
to security: the more any quantitative social indicator is used for social decision-
making, the more subject it will be to corruption pressures. The convergence
establishes: no security metric survives sustained pressure as a management KPI
intact. Defense requires rotating metrics before they corrupt, using lagging
indicators that are harder to game, and triangulating across uncorrelated proxies.
CROSS-DOMAIN LINK: Pattern 19.1 (Goodhart). Root R01 (boundary — the boundary
between measuring security and gaming security is not enforced by any mechanism).
CONFIDENCE: HIGH. Documented across every domain where measurement meets incentives.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
C126: ACTUARIAL SCIENCE COLLISION WITH ADVERSARIAL ENVIRONMENTS
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
CONVERGENCE DOMAINS: Cyber Insurance (Domain 179) x Actuarial Science x Game Theory
                     x Adversarial ML
FINDING: Classical actuarial science assumes independent risk events drawn from stable
distributions. Cyber insurance violates both assumptions simultaneously. Adversaries
actively study what insured organizations look like and target the insured population
(adverse selection without historical precedent). Ransomware operators have demonstrated
awareness of policy limits — ransom demands cluster just below known policy ceilings.
The insured population's behavior changes once insured (moral hazard). And catastrophic
correlation events (single vulnerability → thousands of orgs simultaneously) produce
correlated loss events that break the law of large numbers underwriting depends on.
Insurance mathematics built for actuarial independence fails in adversarial adaptive
environments. This is a fundamental mathematical incompatibility, not a pricing problem.
The convergence predicts: cyber insurance as currently structured cannot be stable
unless it fundamentally restructures either risk selection, policy terms, or its
mathematical model. Game-theoretic insurance design (where adversaries are modeled
as agents, not as weather) is an open field.
CROSS-DOMAIN LINK: Pattern 19.2 (Moral Hazard). Root R03 (trust without verification —
insurers trusting self-reported security postures). Root R07 (temporal — yesterday's
loss models misapplied to tomorrow's adversaries).
CONFIDENCE: HIGH. Actuarial literature on correlated risk + documented ransomware
policy-aware behavior.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
C127: INFORMATION THEORY LIMITS ON DATA LOSS PREVENTION
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
CONVERGENCE DOMAINS: DLP (Domain 177) x Information Theory x Steganography x
                     Compression Theory
FINDING: Shannon's information theory establishes that the semantic content of data
is independent of its physical representation. DLP systems detect data by pattern
matching physical representations (file signatures, regex patterns, keyword lists,
checksums). Any transformation that preserves semantic content while altering physical
representation defeats signature-based DLP. This is not an implementation gap —
it is an information-theoretic impossibility: no pattern-matching DLP system can
detect all semantically equivalent representations of protected data without solving
the halting problem (determining whether an arbitrary program output contains specific
semantic content is undecidable). Steganography, encoding, compression, paraphrasing,
translation, and reformatting all exploit this. The convergence establishes: effective
DLP requires either semantic analysis (AI-based, imperfect, expensive, false-positive
prone) or egress control (block channels entirely, remove the problem by removing
the path). Pattern-matching DLP is a partial control that provides compliance theater
more reliably than actual data loss prevention.
CROSS-DOMAIN LINK: Pattern 19.4 (PETs vs. Monitoring). Root R02 (data/instruction
conflation — pattern matching conflates data syntax with data semantics).
CONFIDENCE: HIGH. Directly derivable from information theory first principles.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
C128: RADIO FREQUENCY PHYSICS AS MOBILE SECURITY CONSTRAINT
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
CONVERGENCE DOMAINS: Mobile Security (Domain 181) x RF Engineering x Signal Processing
                     x Physical Layer Security
FINDING: Mobile device security is fundamentally constrained by RF physics. GSM/UMTS/LTE
downlink-only authentication (base station never proves identity to handset until late
protocol versions) is not a protocol design choice — it reflects real engineering tradeoffs
between RF spectrum efficiency and mutual authentication overhead. IMSI catchers exploit
this physics. Rogue base stations win because a legitimate base station and a rogue one
are RF-indistinguishable to a device that has not yet authenticated. Signal strength
spoofing (fake GPS via stronger signal than actual satellites) is likewise physics —
the receiver cannot verify source identity from signal properties alone. 5G SA (standalone)
addresses some of this via SUCI (subscription concealed identifier) and mutual auth,
but the physical layer remains attackable via jamming, downgrade to legacy radio,
and proximity attacks that exploit the physical necessity of broadcasting identity.
The convergence establishes: mobile security cannot be solved at protocol layer alone
because the RF physics constrains what the protocol can verify before committing to
a channel. Physical layer security research is a separate engineering discipline with
direct security implications.
CROSS-DOMAIN LINK: Root R08 (physical embodiment as attack surface). Root R03 (trust —
device trusts signal strength as base station legitimacy proxy).
CONFIDENCE: HIGH. RF physics is not disputed; IMSI catcher attacks are documented.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
C129: BEHAVIORAL PSYCHOLOGY OF PHYSICAL SECURITY BYPASS
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
CONVERGENCE DOMAINS: Physical/Cyber Convergence (Domain 182) x Social Psychology x
                     Behavioral Economics x Human Factors Engineering
FINDING: Physical security failures are systematically predictable from behavioral
psychology. Tailgating succeeds because humans are wired for social reciprocity —
holding a door for someone carrying boxes overrides security training through deeply
embedded social scripts. Pretexting succeeds because authority compliance (Milgram),
social proof, urgency, and liking are cognitive shortcuts that bypass analytical
processing. Visitor badge bypasses succeed because humans pattern-match on proxies
(badge shape, lanyard color, confident body language) rather than performing actual
verification. These are not training failures — they are properties of human cognitive
architecture. Security training that attempts to override instinctual social responses
has documented low retention and transfer rates. The convergence establishes: physical
security design must be architecturally resistant to human social psychology, not
dependent on humans overriding their social instincts. Mantrap engineering, credential
readers that require both a card and a PIN in sequence, visitor escort policies that
remove the decision from a single human — these work because they remove the social
bypass vector from the critical path.
CROSS-DOMAIN LINK: Root R06 (confused deputy — the compliant employee as confused
deputy for the attacker). Root R03 (trust without verification — humans trust social
signals as identity proxies). Pattern 19.3 (SIM Swapping — same social engineering
root).
CONFIDENCE: HIGH. Social engineering literature and behavioral psychology literature
converge directly.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
C130: INTERNATIONAL RELATIONS THEORY AND CYBER NORMS FAILURE
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
CONVERGENCE DOMAINS: Legal/Regulatory (Domain 183) x International Relations x
                     Game Theory x Deterrence Theory
FINDING: The failure of international cyber norms follows directly from IR theory
on enforcement problems in anarchic systems. Classical deterrence (MAD, retaliation
threats) requires attribution certainty, proportionality norms, and credible commitment
to retaliate. Cyber operations undermine all three simultaneously: attribution is
contested and deniable by design; proportionality in cross-domain retaliation (cyber
attack → kinetic response?) lacks established norms; commitment credibility is low
because cyber retaliation exposes the retaliating party's own offensive capabilities.
The result is the security dilemma translated to cyberspace: nations build offensive
cyber capabilities defensively (to deter), which creates offensive capability that
adversaries must respond to, which drives the arms race. The Tallinn Manual process
attempts to apply existing IHL to cyber but faces the same attribution and proportionality
problems at the treaty interpretation level. The convergence establishes: cyber norms
will not emerge from good-faith negotiation alone because the structural incentives
of the system prevent binding commitments. Technical norms (vulnerability disclosure,
critical infrastructure off-limits agreements) are more tractable than attribution-
dependent deterrence frameworks because they do not require resolving the attribution
problem first.
CROSS-DOMAIN LINK: Root R03 (trust without verification — treaty regimes without
verification mechanisms). Root R07 (temporal — deterrence models from nuclear era
misapplied to cyber era with different attribution and reversibility properties).
CONFIDENCE: MEDIUM-HIGH. IR theory is well established; cyber application is contested
but the structural analysis is sound.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
C131: PRIVACY-ENHANCING TECHNOLOGIES AND THE CRYPTOGRAPHIC COMPLEXITY FRONTIER
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
CONVERGENCE DOMAINS: PETs (Domain 185) x Cryptography x Complexity Theory x
                     Practical Engineering
FINDING: PETs (homomorphic encryption, secure multi-party computation, zero-knowledge
proofs, differential privacy) are grounded in complexity theory — their security
derives from the assumed computational hardness of specific problems (LWE, factoring,
discrete log). This is the same foundation quantum computing threatens. Additionally,
PETs impose computational overhead that is polynomial-to-exponential relative to
plaintext operations — fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) is currently 10^4 to 10^6x
slower than equivalent plaintext computation. The convergence creates a three-way
tension: PETs provide mathematical privacy guarantees that no other approach matches;
PETs are computationally expensive enough to be impractical for most real-time
applications; and PETs' security assumptions are subject to the same cryptographic
future risk as conventional encryption. The practical deployment frontier for PETs
is therefore applications where: (a) the data sensitivity justifies computational
cost, (b) operations are batched rather than real-time, (c) the operations required
map to PET-efficient primitives. Federated learning with differential privacy is the
current practical PET deployment model — it sacrifices some of FHE's guarantees for
orders-of-magnitude computational feasibility.
CROSS-DOMAIN LINK: Pattern 19.4 (PETs vs. Monitoring). Root R07 (temporal — current
complexity assumptions violated by future quantum capability).
CONFIDENCE: HIGH. Computational complexity bounds are mathematically established;
practical overhead figures are empirically measured.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
C132: MILITARY OPSEC DOCTRINE AND DEFENDER OPERATIONAL SECURITY
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
CONVERGENCE DOMAINS: Defender OPSEC (Domain 186) x Military Doctrine x Information
                     Theory x Intelligence Analysis
FINDING: US DoD OPSEC doctrine (originated in Vietnam-era PURPLE DRAGON study) follows
a five-step process: identify critical information → analyze threats → analyze
vulnerabilities → assess risk → apply countermeasures. This maps directly to defender
OPSEC but is rarely applied systematically. The critical information concept (what
does the adversary need to know about our defenses to defeat them?) is underused in
enterprise security. Defenders routinely expose: detection logic (through tool choice
visible to adversaries who've been in the network), response playbooks (through
consistent patterns that adversaries study during dwell time), team composition and
tooling (through job postings, conference talks, LinkedIn), and infrastructure details
(through DNS, certificate transparency logs, Shodan-visible assets). The convergence
establishes: defenders need their own intelligence collection → analysis → protection
cycle targeting their own operations. Threat actors conduct defender reconnaissance
systematically; defenders do not apply equivalent rigor to protecting their own
operational details. Military OPSEC doctrine, translated to enterprise context, provides
the framework that security OPSEC practice currently lacks.
CROSS-DOMAIN LINK: Root R03 (trust — defenders trust that their operational details
are not being collected by adversaries inside the network). Root R05 (TOCTOU — defenders
assume their countermeasures are unknown between check and action; adversary dwell
time violates this).
CONFIDENCE: HIGH. OPSEC doctrine is well-documented; defender reconnaissance exposure
is empirically confirmed in threat intelligence literature.

CONVERGENCE FINDINGS CUMULATIVE: 132

CYCLE 19 GAP ADDITIONS: G105-G112
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

G105: NO STANDARD FRAMEWORK FOR SECURITY METRIC ROTATION
Domain: Security Metrics (178)
Finding: Goodhart's Law (C125) implies metrics must be rotated before they corrupt.
No standard framework exists specifying when a security metric has become too gamed
to retain signal, how to detect metric corruption, or how to select rotation replacements
without immediately corrupting the replacement. CISOs operate by intuition or not
at all. Gap: a formal metric integrity framework with corruption detection and
rotation protocols.

G106: ACTUARIALLY SOUND CYBER INSURANCE MODEL DOES NOT EXIST
Domain: Cyber Insurance (179)
Finding: C126 established that classical actuarial independence assumptions are
violated in cyber. No published actuarial model exists that incorporates adversarial
adaptation, correlated catastrophic events, and moral hazard simultaneously in a
stable pricing model. Insurance products are priced on inadequate models. Gap: a
game-theoretic actuarial framework for adversarially adaptive risk environments.

G107: SEMANTIC DLP IS AN OPEN PROBLEM
Domain: DLP (177)
Finding: C127 established that pattern-matching DLP cannot detect all semantically
equivalent representations of protected data. Semantic DLP (AI-based content
understanding) is imperfect, expensive, and produces unacceptable false-positive
rates at scale. No deployed system reliably distinguishes intentional exfiltration
from legitimate data use across all content types. Gap: semantic data loss prevention
that is computationally feasible at enterprise egress volumes.

G108: PHYSICAL LAYER MOBILE SECURITY AUTHENTICATION UNSOLVED
Domain: Mobile Security (181)
Finding: C128 established that RF physics constraints prevent base station authentication
before channel commitment in legacy protocols. 5G SA partially addresses this but
deployment is incomplete globally. Billions of devices remain on 2G/3G/4G networks
with no cryptographic base station authentication. Gap: backwards-compatible physical
layer authentication that does not require full 5G SA infrastructure.

G109: BEHAVIORAL ARCHITECTURE STANDARDS FOR PHYSICAL SECURITY ABSENT
Domain: Physical/Cyber Convergence (182)
Finding: C129 established that physical security must be architected to be resistant
to human social psychology, not dependent on overriding it. No building security
standard incorporates behavioral psychology research into architectural requirements.
Security standards address technology and procedure, not the human social bypass
vectors that dominate physical intrusion events. Gap: behavioral-psychology-informed
physical security architecture standards.

G110: CYBER NORMS VERIFICATION MECHANISM IS UNSOLVED
Domain: Legal/Regulatory (183)
Finding: C130 established that international cyber norms require attribution certainty
that does not exist. No technical mechanism reliably provides legally defensible
attribution for state-sponsored cyber operations. Without attribution verification,
deterrence commitments are not credible and norms are not enforceable. Gap: a
technical attribution methodology that meets evidentiary standards for international
law and cannot be systematically defeated by nation-state actors.

G111: PET DEPLOYMENT ENGINEERING PLAYBOOK DOES NOT EXIST
Domain: PETs (185)
Finding: C131 established the three-way tension between PET mathematical guarantees,
computational overhead, and quantum threat. No deployed organization has published
a decision framework for: when to use FHE vs. MPC vs. ZKP vs. differential privacy,
what computational overhead is acceptable for what data sensitivity level, and how
to transition PET-protected systems when underlying complexity assumptions are broken.
Gap: a practical PET deployment engineering playbook with computational cost/benefit
analysis and quantum transition planning.

G112: DEFENDER OPSEC DISCIPLINE DOES NOT EXIST AS A FORMAL PRACTICE
Domain: Defender OPSEC (186)
Finding: C132 established that military OPSEC doctrine maps directly to defender
operational security but is not practiced systematically in enterprise security.
No professional certification, no published standard, no organizational framework
exists for applying OPSEC discipline to the defender's own operations, tooling,
playbooks, and personnel. Security teams protect client data; they do not protect
their own operational details. Gap: a formal defender OPSEC discipline with doctrine,
training, and organizational practice standards.

CYCLE 20 — STAGE 1: DOMAIN INVENTORY AND EXPANSION

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
DOMAIN 187: CYBER DECEPTION AND ACTIVE DEFENSE
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Core concept: Using deception offensively within the defender's own environment
to detect, delay, and study attackers. Distinct from Domain 110 (honeypots) in
scope — active defense spans honeypots, honeytokens, honeynets, canary tokens,
decoy credentials, fake data, moving target defense, and legally-bounded counter-
operations.
Sub-domains: Honeytoken deployment and management; decoy credential strategies;
canary token ecosystems (web bugs, DNS canaries, file-based triggers); moving
target defense (IP rotation, port randomization, OS fingerprint randomization);
deception orchestration platforms; attacker behavioral study during deception
engagement; legal boundaries of active defense; cyber counterstrike debate; breadcrumb
trails and attacker misdirection; deception-fed threat intelligence.
Intersection with previously catalogued domains: Domain 110 (honeypots), Domain
113 (threat intelligence), Domain 114 (deception technologies), Domain 120 (red
team/blue team). NOTE: Domain 114 was catalogued in Cycle 18; this domain deepens
the active defense component and the legal/ethical dimension.
Status: UNDER-DEVELOPED in prior cycles relative to its strategic importance.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
DOMAIN 188: SECURITY DATA SCIENCE AND ML OPERATIONS
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Core concept: Application of data science methodology and ML engineering practices
specifically to security data pipelines, model development, deployment, and operations.
Distinct from "AI in security" (Domain 135) in focusing on the engineering and
operational discipline of running ML in production security environments.
Sub-domains: Security data pipeline engineering; feature engineering for security
signals; model training on imbalanced security datasets (rare event problem); model
evaluation metrics appropriate for security (precision-recall tradeoffs at SOC scale);
model drift detection in adversarial environments; adversarial ML specific to deployed
security models; MLOps for security models; explainability requirements for security
AI; data poisoning defenses in security ML pipelines; federated learning for security
data that cannot be centralized.
Key tension: Security data is often sensitive, sparse, labeled poorly, and adversarially
generated. Standard ML best practices break down in these conditions.

DOMAIN 189: HARDWARE SECURITY AND FIRMWARE INTEGRITY

Sub-domains: BIOS/UEFI security and SecureBoot; BMC and iDRAC attack surface;

Note: Previously thin in this catalog relative to its foundational importance —
every software security control runs on hardware whose integrity is assumed.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PATTERN 20.1: THE DECEPTION PARADOX
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

FORM A:
Finding: Active deception defense (honeypots, honeytokens, decoys) works by exploiting
the information asymmetry between attacker and defender — the defender knows which
assets are real and which are fake; the attacker does not. This paradox holds: the
more sophisticated the attacker, the more valuable the deception (advanced attackers
do careful reconnaissance that hits decoys); but also the more likely the attacker
is to identify and avoid deception (sophisticated actors actively sweep for honeypots
before lateral movement). The deception paradox is that deception scales in value
with adversary sophistication up to the point where adversary sophistication enables
deception detection, at which point effectiveness drops.
Confidence: HIGH
Timeline:
  Historical (pre-2000): Clifford Stoll's "Cuckoo's Egg" (1986) — first documented
    systematic use of attacker monitoring through a deceptive environment
  Consolidation (2000-2015): Commercial honeypot products; Symantec Deception; early
    academic literature on deception game theory
  Escalation (2015-2022): Honeytoken ecosystems (CanaryTokens); enterprise deception
    platforms (Illusive, Attivo); attacker anti-deception tools (honeypot detection
    scripts); high-interaction deception at scale
  Current (2022-present): AI-generated deceptive environments; attacker ML to
    distinguish real from fake assets; deception as a service; moving target defense
    integration with deception

FORM B:
Research prompt: Under what conditions does attacker sophistication enhance vs. defeat
deception effectiveness? What is the optimal deception density (ratio of fake to real
assets) as a function of expected attacker sophistication level? Is there a Nash
equilibrium between defender deception investment and attacker anti-deception investment?
How does AI-generated realistic deception change the equilibrium?

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PATTERN 20.2: THE HARDWARE TRUST ANCHOR PROBLEM
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

FORM A:
Finding: Every software security control — encryption, authentication, access control,
integrity checking — ultimately depends on hardware whose integrity is assumed but
not verified at runtime. The trust anchor must terminate somewhere in physical silicon.
TPMs, HSMs, and Secure Enclaves (Intel SGX, ARM TrustZone) attempt to provide
hardware roots of trust, but they introduce their own attack surface: TPM2 vulnerabilities,
SGX side-channel attacks (Spectre/Meltdown derivative), TrustZone firmware attacks.
The pattern: every hardware root of trust that is software-configurable or firmware-
updateable can be attacked through that update mechanism. True hardware roots of trust
(read-only, burned at manufacture) are inflexible. Flexible hardware security is an
oxymoron: flexibility requires code, code has vulnerabilities.
Confidence: HIGH
Timeline:
  Historical (pre-2000): DES hardware implementations; physical tamper protection
    in early HSMs; smartcard attack research beginning
  Consolidation (2000-2010): TPM 1.2 standard; smartcard fault injection attacks;
    cold boot attacks (Halderman et al., 2008)
  Escalation (2010-2018): Intel SGX launch; ARM TrustZone widespread deployment;
    Rowhammer (2014); Spectre/Meltdown (disclosed 2018) — fundamental hardware trust
    assumption broken
  Current (2018-present): SGX deprecation by Intel for consumer platforms; persistent
    BMC vulnerabilities (iDRAC, iLO); supply chain hardware trojan research; TPM
    vulnerabilities (TPM-FAIL, 2019); hardware-based ransomware (theoretical but
    advancing)

FORM B:
Research prompt: Where exactly does the hardware root of trust terminate in modern
computing architecture, and what is the attack surface at that termination point?
Can a software-visible hardware security boundary be verified without trusting
additional software? Is there a regress problem (who verifies the verifier) that
terminates in silicon, and what is the threat model at the silicon level?

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PATTERN 20.3: ML MODEL DRIFT IN ADVERSARIAL SECURITY ENVIRONMENTS
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

FORM A:
Finding: ML models deployed for security detection degrade against adversaries who
actively probe and adapt to them. Standard MLOps tracks distribution shift (data
drift, concept drift) in stationary or slowly shifting environments. Security
adversaries produce adversarial drift: deliberate, targeted modification of their
behavior to push model inputs toward decision boundaries or into regions where the
model has low confidence or wrong predictions. This is not stochastic drift —
it is adversarial gradient descent against the deployed model's decision surface.
Security ML models must be treated as targets, not just tools: once deployed, an
adversary who can query the model (directly or via black-box behavioral inference)
can systematically find evasion inputs. The pattern: security ML models have an
effective life that ends when adversaries have had sufficient time to characterize
and evade the model, which is a function of adversary sophistication and black-box
query budget, not time elapsed.
Confidence: HIGH
Timeline:
  Historical (pre-2010): Spam filter evasion (adversarial text modification to avoid
    keyword filters) — earliest documented adversarial ML in security context
  Consolidation (2010-2017): Academic adversarial ML literature (Szegedy et al. 2013,
    Goodfellow et al. 2014); AV/EDR ML evasion tools emerge
  Escalation (2017-2022): Systematic ML model evasion as a penetration testing
    discipline; adversarial ML frameworks (Foolbox, ART); security ML model hardening
    research; model inversion and membership inference attacks against security models
  Current (2022-present): LLM-assisted adversarial example generation; automated
    evasion of EDR ML; real-time adaptive malware using feedback from deployed model
    responses; adversarial robustness as a required security ML property

FORM B:
Research prompt: What is the expected effective life of a deployed security ML model
against a sophisticated adversary who can perform black-box queries? What retraining
cadence is required to maintain a security ML model's detection rate against adaptive
adversaries? Is there a fundamental bound on security ML model robustness against
adversaries who can observe model outputs?

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PATTERN 20.4: THE SECURITY ECONOMICS MARKET FAILURE CLUSTER
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

FORM A:
Finding: Information security markets exhibit a cluster of simultaneous market failures
that individually would each impair security outcomes; collectively they produce
systematic underinvestment in security across the economy. The failures: (1) information
asymmetry — buyers cannot evaluate security product quality before purchase (Akerlof
lemons problem); (2) negative externalities — an organization's poor security imposes
costs on third parties who have no contract with it and no mechanism to require
improvement; (3) public goods — some security (e.g., internet protocol security
improvements) is non-excludable and therefore underproduced; (4) moral hazard —
cyber insurance reduces incentive to invest in security (C126); (5) network effects
in vulnerability — monoculture creates systemic risk that no individual has incentive
to correct. Each failure individually justifies market intervention; the cluster
makes voluntary market correction essentially impossible without regulatory or
structural mechanism changes.
Confidence: HIGH
Timeline:
  Historical (pre-2005): Ross Anderson's "Why Information Security is Hard — An
    Economic Perspective" (2001) — foundational; Schneier on security economics
  Consolidation (2005-2015): Academic security economics field established; Patch
    adoption economics studied; software liability debates
  Escalation (2015-2022): GDPR and mandatory breach disclosure as externality
    correction mechanisms; FTC security enforcement; SEC cyber disclosure rules
  Current (2022-present): EU Cyber Resilience Act (product security liability);
    US Secure by Design initiative; software bill of materials (SBOM) as information
    asymmetry correction; cyber insurance reform discussions

FORM B:
Research prompt: Which of the five security market failures identified is most tractable
to policy correction, and what mechanism (liability, disclosure, mandatory standards,
insurance mandates) most efficiently addresses it without creating new perverse
incentives? Can all five be addressed simultaneously, or do corrections for one
exacerbate others?

CYCLE 20 — STAGE 3: LAYERED PATTERN ANATOMY
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

ANATOMY 20.A — THE HARDWARE TRUST ANCHOR PROBLEM (Pattern 20.2)

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ LAYER 1: PHYSICS                                                              │
│ Electrons flow through transistors. Transistor state (on/off) encodes bits.   │
│ Physical phenomena → observable: power draw, EM radiation, heat, timing.     │
│ Silicon fabrication introduces structures invisible to post-fab inspection.    │
│ Quantum tunneling at nanometer scale introduces stochastic behavior in RNGs.  │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
         ↓
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ LAYER 2: MECHANISM                                                            │
│ Hardware security mechanisms: TPM (discrete chip holding keys, performing      │
│ measurements), HSM (dedicated cryptographic processor), Secure Enclave (CPU-  │
│ integrated isolated execution environment), Secure Boot (firmware signature   │
│ chain from silicon to OS). Each creates an isolation boundary within hardware.│
│ Attack surface = every interface crossing that boundary: firmware update path, │
│ bus communication (SPI, I2C, PCIe), physical probe access, EM/power side-     │
│ channel, microarchitectural state shared with untrusted code (SGX kills here). │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
         ↓
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ LAYER 3: FAILURE MODE                                                         │
│ The regress problem: hardware roots of trust are verified by other hardware or │
│ firmware. Every non-ROM component in the chain can be attacked at its update   │
│ or configuration interface. Spectre/Meltdown demonstrated that microarchitec- │
│ tural state shared between trust domains (SGX enclave and OS) leaks through    │
│ cache timing. The failure mode: isolation that is logically enforced by code   │
│ running on the same physical substrate as the attacker cannot be guaranteed    │
│ against an attacker who controls the physical environment or the microarch.    │
│ Supply chain: malicious hardware trojan inserted at wafer, package, or board   │
│ level is undetectable by software and persists through all software controls.  │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
         ↓
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ LAYER 4: HISTORICAL INSTANCE SET                                              │
│ 1. Cold boot attack (Halderman et al., 2008) — DRAM retains contents after   │
│    power loss; hardware assumed volatility violated; disk encryption keys      │
│    extracted from "off" machines.                                              │
│ 2. Spectre/Meltdown (2018) — CPU speculative execution shared microarch state │
│    between trust domains; SGX memory isolation defeated by cache timing.       │
│ 3. TPM-FAIL (2019) — timing side-channel in TPM firmware implementation       │
│    allows private key recovery from TPM2; trust anchor itself was the channel.  │
│ 4. BMC vulnerabilities (iDRAC, iLO) — ongoing; baseboard management           │
│    controllers with full out-of-band access to hardware are themselves         │
│    firmware systems with persistent vulnerabilities.                           │
│ 5. Bloomberg Supermicro report (2018, disputed) — alleged hardware trojan on  │
│    server motherboards; dispute itself illustrates that supply chain hardware  │
│    trojans are not publicly verifiable with current inspection methods.        │
│ 6. Rowhammer (2014) — DRAM bit flipping via repeated memory access; hardware  │
│    physics (charge leakage) exploited to bypass software memory isolation.     │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
         ↓
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ LAYER 5: DEFENSE SURFACE AND OPEN PROBLEM                                    │
│ Current best practice: hardware attestation chains (TPM + UEFI Secure Boot +  │
│ measured boot); HSM for key operations; physical access controls; supply chain │
│ verification (NIST SP 800-161); SBOM extended to hardware (HBOM concept).     │
│ Open problems: (1) hardware trojan detection without destructive analysis;    │
│ (2) attestation of attestation infrastructure (infinite regress);             │
│ (3) microarchitectural side-channel mitigations impose 5-30% performance cost │
│    with incomplete coverage; (4) BMC/firmware update integrity at cloud scale; │
│ (5) silicon-level trust for COTS hardware procured through commercial channels.│
│ Root mechanic: R04 (computation produces observable physical effects) and R08  │
│ (physical embodiment as attack surface) combine here permanently.             │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

ANATOMY 20.B — ML MODEL DRIFT IN ADVERSARIAL SECURITY ENVIRONMENTS (Pattern 20.3)

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ LAYER 1: PHYSICS                                                              │
│ ML models define a decision boundary in feature space. Features are           │
│ mathematical representations of observable data. The decision boundary is     │
│ determined by training data distribution. The boundary is fixed after         │
│ training unless retrained. Adversarial inputs are points in feature space     │
│ near the decision boundary in the malicious region that have been perturbed   │
│ toward the benign region. Perturbations can be in feature space (change the   │
│ mathematical representation) or in input space (change the actual artifact    │
│ — malware bytes, network packets) such that the feature representation moves. │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
         ↓
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ LAYER 2: MECHANISM                                                            │
│ Adversary attack chain: (1) probe deployed model via black-box queries         │
│ (submit samples, observe benign/malicious classification);                    │
│ (2) build surrogate model approximating decision boundary from observations;  │
│ (3) generate adversarial examples against surrogate (transferability means    │
│ these often work against target model too);                                   │
│ (4) verify against target; (5) deploy evasion at scale.                       │
│ White-box variant: if adversary knows model architecture/weights (possible    │
│ via model extraction attacks or insider access), gradient-based adversarial   │
│ example generation is direct and efficient.                                   │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
         ↓
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ LAYER 3: FAILURE MODE                                                         │
│ The arms race is asymmetric in one critical way: the defender must retrain     │
│ and redeploy to respond; the adversary only needs to generate new evasion      │
│ examples. Retraining requires: new labeled data (hard to get for novel         │
│ adversarial examples), compute, validation time, and deployment. The adversary │
│ generates examples in seconds to hours. This creates a temporal asymmetry:    │
│ the adversary can sustain pressure faster than the defender can adapt.         │
│ Additionally, including adversarial examples in training (adversarial          │
│ training) reduces clean-data performance and is not guaranteed to generalize   │
│ to novel adversarial perturbation strategies.                                  │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
         ↓
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ LAYER 4: HISTORICAL INSTANCE SET                                              │
│ 1. Spam filter evasion (2000s) — Bayesian spam filters defeated by including  │
│    random dictionary words to shift word frequency distributions.              │
│ 2. AV ML evasion (2016-present) — tools like MalwareGym, Ember, and           │
│    adversarial malware generators systematically evade ML-based AV.            │
│ 3. Network IDS ML evasion — adversarial packet crafting to evade ML-based      │
│    anomaly detection while preserving attack functionality.                    │
│ 4. Phishing detection evasion — adversarial URL and page generation that       │
│    scores as benign to ML classifiers while delivering phishing content.       │
│ 5. Model extraction attacks (Tramer et al., 2016) — reconstructing proprietary │
│    model parameters from black-box API queries; enables white-box attacks.     │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
         ↓
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ LAYER 5: DEFENSE SURFACE AND OPEN PROBLEM                                    │
│ Current defenses: adversarial training; ensemble models; input preprocessing  │
│ to remove adversarial perturbations; certified defenses (provable robustness  │
│ within L-p norm bounds); rate-limiting model queries; model output             │
│ monitoring for anomalous query patterns.                                       │
│ Open problems: (1) No defense simultaneously provides high clean accuracy,    │
│ high adversarial accuracy, and computational feasibility — robustness-         │
│ accuracy tradeoff is fundamental; (2) certified defenses provide bounds only  │
│ within specific perturbation sets; (3) adversarial training requires knowledge │
│ of adversary's perturbation strategy; (4) novel perturbation strategies not   │
│ in training set break all current defenses; (5) no general solution to        │
│ adversarial ML in the security domain is known.                               │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

ANATOMY 20.C — THE SECURITY ECONOMICS MARKET FAILURE CLUSTER (Pattern 20.4)

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ LAYER 1: PHYSICS                                                              │
│ Markets are information processing systems. Market failures are conditions     │
│ where the price mechanism does not aggregate information correctly or produce  │
│ efficient outcomes. Information asymmetry (one party knows more than the other)│
│ and externalities (effects borne by parties not in the transaction) are the   │
│ two most fundamental market failure types. Security exhibits both              │
│ simultaneously and irreducibly: the security of a product is inherently hard  │
│ to observe pre-purchase (asymmetry), and poor security creates risks for       │
│ people not party to the sale (externality). These are structural, not          │
│ correctable by better negotiation or more careful purchasing.                  │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
         ↓
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ LAYER 2: MECHANISM                                                            │
│ Five simultaneous failure mechanisms:                                         │
│ (1) Lemons: buyers cannot distinguish secure from insecure products; market   │
│     price reflects average quality; secure vendors cannot command premium;     │
│     market converges toward insecure products.                                 │
│ (2) Externality: insecure vendor/user imposes costs on unrelated third         │
│     parties (botnet victims, breach notification costs, systemic risk);        │
│     no mechanism to internalize these costs to the party generating them.     │
│ (3) Public goods: network security improvements (BGP security, DNS security)  │
│     are non-excludable; free-rider problem leads to underinvestment.           │
│ (4) Moral hazard: insurance reduces marginal value of security investment.    │
│ (5) Network effects in vulnerability: software monoculture creates correlated │
│     risk; no individual has incentive to move off the dominant platform.       │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
         ↓
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ LAYER 3: FAILURE MODE                                                         │
│ Each failure reinforces the others. Lemons market → no premium for security  │
│ → vendors underinvest → more insecure products → more externalities → more   │
│ pressure for regulation → compliance theater (Goodhart, C125) → metrics game  │
→ security theater certified as compliant. Insurance corrects underinvestment   │
│ partially but introduces moral hazard that reduces it again. Public good       │
│ investments (BGP security, RPKI adoption) stall because any single large       │
│ player's investment benefits all players but costs only them. The system       │
│ equilibrates at a level of security below what would be efficient because the  │
│ private incentives are systematically misaligned with social optimum.          │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
         ↓
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ LAYER 4: HISTORICAL INSTANCE SET                                              │
│ 1. SSL certificate authority failures (DigiNotar 2011, Comodo 2011) — market  │
│    pressure on CAs to compete on price produced race to bottom on vetting;    │
│    lemons dynamic in CA market.                                                │
│ 2. BGP hijacking persistence — RPKI (Resource Public Key Infrastructure)      │
│    deployed since 2008; adoption still partial in 2026 due to public goods     │
│    problem — each ASN that adopts it pays costs; benefits are network-wide.   │
│ 3. Software monoculture (Windows dominance 2000s) — network effect lock-in    │
│    created correlated vulnerability across global computing; no individual     │
│    incentive to diversify.                                                     │
│ 4. IoT security poverty line — low-margin device manufacturers externalize     │
│    security costs onto consumers and botnet victims; Mirai and successors.     │
│ 5. EU Cyber Resilience Act (2024) — attempt to correct lemons and externality │
│    failures via mandatory security requirements for connected products.        │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
         ↓
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ LAYER 5: DEFENSE SURFACE AND OPEN PROBLEM                                    │
│ Regulatory interventions in progress: EU CRA, SEC cyber disclosure, FTC        │
│ enforcement, US SBOM mandates for government procurement. These address        │
│ lemons (mandatory disclosure, certification) and externalities (liability).   │
│ Open problems: (1) liability framework for software vendors remains           │
│ underdeveloped — no established legal standard for what constitutes           │
│ "reasonably secure" software; (2) public goods problem for protocol security  │
│ not addressed by current regulation; (3) moral hazard from insurance not       │
│ corrected by any current market mechanism; (4) network effect lock-in         │
│ creating monoculture risk has no current policy remedy; (5) global regulatory │
│ fragmentation means a product can comply with one jurisdiction's requirements  │
│ while remaining insecure by another's, and global markets arbitrage to the    │
│ lowest standard.                                                               │

CYCLE 20 — STAGE 4: FULL ATTACK AND DEFENSE TAXONOMY
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

ENTERING STATE: A01-A168 (168 attacks) | D01-D172 (172 defenses) cumulative
NEW ATTACKS THIS CYCLE: A169-A176
NEW DEFENSES THIS CYCLE: D173-D188

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ATTACKS: A169-A176
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A169: HONEYTOKEN DETECTION AND EVASION
Domain: Cyber Deception (187)
Mechanism: Adversary systematically identifies and avoids honeytoken resources
(fake credentials, canary files, decoy accounts) before using legitimate resources.
Detection methods include: testing credentials against rate-limited endpoints (if
the account triggers an alert, it was a canary); identifying canary documents by
metadata patterns; avoiding files with suspicious names; cross-referencing credential
structure against known canary formats. Sophisticated actors perform deception
sweeps before any lateral movement.
Root mechanic: R03 (trust — deception works because attacker initially trusts
decoys as legitimate; evasion removes that trust assumption)
Historical: Documented in threat intelligence reports on APT groups; Fancy Bear
and Cozy Bear operational security includes deception detection steps
Temporal layer: Escalation-Current

A170: BMC/IPMI REMOTE ACCESS EXPLOIT
Domain: Hardware Security (189)
Mechanism: Exploitation of Baseboard Management Controller (BMC) or Intelligent
Platform Management Interface (IPMI) interfaces for persistent, out-of-band access
to servers. BMC operates independently of the main OS, has network access, can
power-cycle the host, and survives OS reinstallation. Vulnerabilities include: IPMI
cipher zero authentication bypass, BMC web interface vulnerabilities, default
credentials, unpatched firmware. A compromised BMC provides attacker persistence
that survives full OS remediation.
Root mechanic: R08 (physical embodiment — BMC is physically separate from OS,
attackers who control it control the hardware beneath the OS)
Historical: IPMI cipher zero (2013); iDRAC vulnerabilities (multiple, ongoing);
Supermicro BMC vulnerabilities; Eclypsium research (2018-present)
Temporal layer: Escalation-Current

A171: BROWSER EXTENSION SUPPLY CHAIN COMPROMISE
Domain: Enterprise Browser Security (190)
Mechanism: Compromising browser extensions through acquisition, developer account
takeover, or malicious update injection. Installed extensions have elevated browser
privileges (access to all page content, cookies, credentials, browsing history).
Extension updates install silently and automatically in most browsers. An extension
with 100,000 users that is acquired and weaponized instantly reaches all users.
Root mechanic: R03 (trust — users and organizations trust extensions they have
installed; supply chain attack exploits that established trust)
Historical: DataSpii campaign (2019) — multiple extensions collecting browsing data;
Great Suspender compromise (2021); multiple extension takeovers documented 2020-2024
Temporal layer: Escalation-Current

A172: MODEL INVERSION AND TRAINING DATA EXTRACTION
Domain: Security Data Science (188)
Mechanism: Extracting information about training data from a deployed ML model.
Model inversion: given model access and a target class, reconstruct inputs that
the model would classify as that class (leaks what training examples looked like).
Membership inference: determine whether a specific data point was in the training
set (privacy violation when training data is sensitive). Training data extraction
from LLMs: prompt the model to reproduce memorized training data verbatim (documented
for GPT-2, GPT-3, and other large models).
Root mechanic: R02 (data/instruction conflation — model weights encode training
data in ways that allow reconstruction; the data is embedded in the parameters)
Historical: Fredrikson et al. (2015) first model inversion; Carlini et al. (2021)
training data extraction from GPT-2; membership inference attacks (Shokri et al. 2017)
Temporal layer: Escalation-Current

A173: SECURE ENCLAVE SIDE-CHANNEL ATTACK
Domain: Hardware Security (189)
Mechanism: Extracting secrets from Intel SGX or ARM TrustZone enclaves via
microarchitectural side-channels. The enclave and the attacking process share
physical resources (CPU cache, branch predictor, memory bus). Cache-timing attacks
(Flush+Reload, Prime+Probe) measure cache state to infer enclave memory access
patterns, recovering cryptographic keys or other secrets. SGX does not protect
against these attacks because the untrusted OS controls cache flushing.
Root mechanic: R04 (computation produces observable physical effects — cache
timing is the observable effect of enclave computation)
Historical: SGX-Step (2017); Foreshadow/L1TF (2018) — extracted SGX secrets via
L1 cache filling; CacheOut (2020); multiple SGX attacks leading Intel to deprecate
SGX on consumer platforms
Temporal layer: Escalation-Current

A174: THREAT HUNT HYPOTHESIS POISONING
Domain: Threat Hunting (193)
Mechanism: Adversary who has intelligence on defender hunting methodology shapes
their activity to avoid generating evidence that matches hunt hypotheses. If the
defender hunts for lateral movement via PsExec, the adversary uses WMI. If the
defender hunts for PowerShell, the adversary uses LOLBins. Sophisticated adversaries
with persistent access conduct counter-intelligence operations against defender
tooling, reading EDR agent configuration files, monitoring for hunting activity,
and adapting TTPs to below the hunt hypothesis threshold.
Root mechanic: R03 (trust — defender trusts that adversary is unaware of hunting
methodology; adversary's dwell time invalidates this assumption)
Historical: APT groups documented to adapt TTPs based on public reporting of
defender hunt techniques; Mandiant M-Trends reports note adversary TTP shifts
following public disclosure
Temporal layer: Escalation-Current

A175: RED TEAM DECONFLICTION ABUSE
Domain: Adversarial Simulation (196)
Mechanism: External adversary who discovers a concurrent red team engagement uses
the red team's presence as cover. The SOC, seeing alerts consistent with red team
activity, attributes malicious activity to the authorized test. Or, the adversary
mimics red team tool signatures (known red team tools like Cobalt Strike, Metasploit)
to blend into existing authorized activity. Deconfliction breakdowns (where real
attacks are dismissed as red team noise) have been documented in actual incidents.
Root mechanic: R06 (confused deputy — the SOC is confused deputy for the attacker
who impersonates the authorized red team)
Historical: Multiple documented cases of real attackers using Cobalt Strike (an
offensive security tool) making detection harder when red teams also use it; Capital
One breach (2019) partly attributed to detection failures related to tool confusion
Temporal layer: Escalation-Current

A176: SECURITY ECONOMICS ADVERSARIAL FRAMING (INFLUENCE OPERATION)
Domain: Security Economics (195)
Mechanism: Adversarial actors — including nation-state threat actors — deliberately
shape the security economics narrative to maximize attacker advantage. This includes:
lobbying against liability for software vendors (keeps externality unpriced); funding
research that frames security as a cost center (suppresses investment); seeding
narratives that breach disclosure harms victims (undermines transparency requirements);
opposing insurance-mandated security practices (prevents moral hazard correction).
The market failure cluster (Pattern 20.4) is not self-correcting; adversaries benefit
from preventing correction and have resources to do so.
Root mechanic: R03 (trust — defenders trust that security policy debates are
conducted in good faith; sophisticated adversaries exploit that trust)
Historical: Documented foreign influence in cybersecurity policy debates; vendor
lobbying against liability; FTC enforcement opposed by industry coalitions
Temporal layer: Current

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
DEFENSES: D173-D188
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

D173: DECEPTION DIVERSITY AND ROTATION
Domain: Cyber Deception (187)
Mechanism: Rotating honeytoken types, structures, and placement patterns to prevent
adversary characterization. If honeytokens always have the same metadata pattern,
adversaries learn to identify them. Diversity in token type, generation method,
naming convention, and placement location raises the cost of deception detection.
Rotation (replacing detected or aged tokens) prevents the adversary from maintaining
a stable list of known decoys.
Addresses: A169 (honeytoken detection and evasion)
Maturity: MEDIUM — deception diversity is practiced by mature security programs;
systematic rotation is less common

D174: SECURE BOOT AND MEASURED BOOT WITH REMOTE ATTESTATION
Domain: Hardware Security (189)
Mechanism: Chain of trust from firmware through bootloader through OS verified
cryptographically at each stage. Measured boot records the hash of each boot
component into TPM PCRs. Remote attestation allows a remote party to verify the
boot chain matches known-good values before trusting the machine. Detects firmware
and bootloader tampering.
Addresses: A170 (BMC exploitation) partially; hardware trojan risk partially
Maturity: HIGH — Secure Boot is standard; measured boot and remote attestation
deployment is less universal

D175: BMC NETWORK ISOLATION AND HARDENING
Domain: Hardware Security (189)
Mechanism: Isolating BMC management interfaces on a separate management VLAN not
reachable from production networks or the internet. Disabling IPMI over LAN if
not required. Patching BMC firmware on a defined cadence. Changing default credentials.
Enabling BMC authentication logging. Monitoring for anomalous BMC activity.
Addresses: A170 (BMC/IPMI exploitation)
Maturity: MEDIUM-LOW — many organizations deploy servers without addressing BMC
attack surface due to lack of awareness

D176: ENTERPRISE BROWSER EXTENSION GOVERNANCE
Domain: Enterprise Browser Security (190)
Mechanism: Allowlisting permitted browser extensions, blocking installation of
unapproved extensions, monitoring extension updates for permission escalation,
vetting extensions against known malicious registries, and using enterprise browser
products that enforce extension policies at the browser level (not just by policy
that can be bypassed).
Addresses: A171 (browser extension supply chain)
Maturity: LOW — most enterprises do not formally govern browser extensions despite
the attack surface

D177: ML MODEL MONITORING AND DRIFT DETECTION IN SECURITY CONTEXT
Domain: Security Data Science (188)
Mechanism: Monitoring deployed security ML models for performance degradation,
distribution shift in model inputs, and anomalous query patterns (potential adversarial
probing). Setting detection rate baselines and alerting when rates drop unexpectedly.
Monitoring for model inversion / extraction attack signatures (repeated systematic
queries exploring decision boundaries). Treating model performance as a security
control that requires continuous monitoring.
Addresses: A172 (model inversion), A169 (pattern — adversarial model probing)
Maturity: LOW — most security ML deployments lack production monitoring for
adversarial degradation

D178: MICROARCHITECTURAL SIDE-CHANNEL MITIGATIONS
Domain: Hardware Security (189)
Mechanism: OS-level and hypervisor-level mitigations for Spectre/Meltdown and
related attacks. KPTI (kernel page-table isolation), retpoline (return trampoline
for indirect branch mitigation), IBRS/IBPB/STIBP for speculative execution
containment, L1TF mitigations via L1D cache flushing on VM context switches.
Performance cost: 5-30% in workloads with high kernel call frequency.
Addresses: A173 (secure enclave side-channel)
Maturity: HIGH — deployed at OS level; performance overhead is accepted cost

D179: SGX DEPRECATION MIGRATION PLANNING
Domain: Hardware Security (189)
Mechanism: Intel deprecated SGX on consumer platforms due to unresolvable side-channel
attack surface. Organizations relying on SGX for confidential computing must migrate
to AMD SEV (Secure Encrypted Virtualization) or Intel TDX (Trust Domain Extensions),
which provide VM-level memory encryption as an alternative isolation model with
different threat model. Migration requires threat model reassessment.
Addresses: A173 (secure enclave side-channel) — architectural response
Maturity: ACTIVE TRANSITION — organizations must plan migration timelines

D180: THREAT HUNT METHODOLOGY COMPARTMENTALIZATION
Domain: Threat Hunting (193)
Mechanism: Limiting disclosure of active hunt hypotheses, hunting data sources,
and hunting schedules to need-to-know. Treating hunt methodology as operationally
sensitive. Varying hunt cadence and technique to prevent adversary characterization
of hunting blind spots. Using deceptive telemetry to mislead adversaries about
which data sources defenders are monitoring.
Addresses: A174 (threat hunt hypothesis poisoning)
Maturity: LOW — most hunt programs do not apply OPSEC discipline to hunt methodology

D181: RED TEAM DECONFLICTION CONTROLS
Domain: Adversarial Simulation (196)
Mechanism: Strict operational security for concurrent red team engagements. Real-time
deconfliction logs showing all red team actions with timestamps, source IPs, and
techniques. SOC alert review process that checks deconfliction log before closing
any security alert. Out-of-band deconfliction channel not accessible to adversaries
who may be on the network. Kill-switch protocol for pausing red team if a suspicious
event cannot be confirmed as authorized.
Addresses: A175 (red team deconfliction abuse)
Maturity: MEDIUM — formal deconfliction exists in mature programs; real-time
deconfliction with SOC integration is less common

D182: SECURITY ECONOMICS ENGAGEMENT AND POLICY ADVOCACY
Domain: Security Economics (195)
Mechanism: Defenders and security community engaging in policy processes that shape
security economics — supporting liability frameworks, mandatory disclosure, security
standards requirements. Treating security economics policy as a defense-in-depth
layer. Monitoring and countering influence operations that frame security policy
debate in attacker-favorable directions.
Addresses: A176 (adversarial economics framing)
Maturity: NASCENT — security community policy engagement is increasing but not
organized as a defense discipline

D183: HARDWARE BILL OF MATERIALS (HBOM)
Domain: Hardware Security (189)
Mechanism: Documentation of hardware components (chips, firmware, sub-assemblies)
in a product, analogous to SBOM for software. Enables tracking of hardware component
vulnerabilities, identifying affected systems when a component vulnerability is
disclosed, and verifying supply chain integrity against expected component list.
HBOM standards development is early-stage (2023-present).
Addresses: Hardware supply chain risk; A170 (BMC)
Maturity: VERY LOW — HBOM concept is defined; tooling and adoption are nascent

D184: DECEPTION INTEGRATION WITH THREAT INTELLIGENCE
Domain: Cyber Deception (187)
Mechanism: Feeding attacker behavior observed in deception environments into threat
intelligence workflows. When an attacker interacts with a honeytoken or decoy system,
the interaction data (TTPs, tooling, infrastructure, timing patterns) becomes threat
intelligence. Deception systems become active intelligence collection platforms
rather than passive alert tripwires. This closes the loop: deception detects, and
the detection generates intelligence that improves other defenses.
Addresses: A169 (deception evasion) — improves intelligence on adversaries who
interact with deception before evading it
Maturity: MEDIUM — practiced by mature threat intelligence programs; integration
with deception platforms is emerging

D185: BROWSER ISOLATION (REMOTE BROWSER ISOLATION)
Domain: Enterprise Browser Security (190)
Mechanism: Executing browser rendering in an isolated environment (cloud, container,
VM) and transmitting only a visual stream or safe document representation to the
user's device. Malicious content executes in the isolated environment and never
reaches the endpoint. Effective against browser exploits, drive-by downloads, and
malicious extension behavior. Performance tradeoff: latency increases, some web
functionality breaks.
Addresses: A171 (browser extension supply chain); browser-based exploitation generally
Maturity: MEDIUM — products exist (Menlo, Zscaler RBI, Cloudflare Browser Isolation);
adoption limited by cost and performance impact

D186: HUNT PROGRAM FEEDBACK TO DETECTION ENGINEERING
Domain: Threat Hunting (193)
Mechanism: Formalizing the pipeline from threat hunting findings to detection engineering
outputs. When a hunt surfaces a TTP that lacks automated detection coverage, the
hunt finding triggers a detection rule development workflow. Hunt programs measure
their effectiveness partially by the number of new detections generated. This converts
hunt findings (manual, one-time) into permanent detection coverage (automated, ongoing).
Addresses: A174 (hunt hypothesis poisoning) — by building detection coverage hunters
find, adaptive adversaries face a moving detection surface
Maturity: MEDIUM — best practice known; systematic pipeline is less universally implemented

D187: ADVERSARIAL ROBUSTNESS REQUIREMENTS FOR SECURITY ML
Domain: Security Data Science (188)
Mechanism: Requiring that security ML models meet adversarial robustness standards
before deployment. Robustness testing using adversarial example generation frameworks
(Foolbox, Adversarial Robustness Toolbox). Certifying models against specific
perturbation norms where computationally feasible. Treating adversarial robustness
as a required property alongside accuracy and latency.
Addresses: A172 (model inversion); A164 (adversarial ML evasion — from prior cycle)
Maturity: LOW-MEDIUM — adversarial robustness is a research area; production
deployment requirements are not standardized

D188: SECURITY ECONOMICS LABELING AND CERTIFICATION
Domain: Security Economics (195)
Mechanism: Government-backed security labeling programs (analogous to energy efficiency
labels) that reduce information asymmetry for buyers. US Cyber Trust Mark (2024),
EU CE marking for connected products under CRA. Allows buyers to distinguish secure
from insecure products without deep technical expertise. Addresses lemons problem
partially by providing a certified proxy for security quality.
Addresses: A176 (economics framing); market failure cluster (Pattern 20.4) — lemons
failure specifically
Maturity: NASCENT — programs exist (US Cyber Trust Mark, EU CRA); adoption and
consumer awareness are early-stage
