═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
STAGE 2 — FULL 5-LAYER ANATOMY: LAWS L104–L107
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
L104 — FIXED POINT THEOREM
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

LAYER 1 — SURFACE
any continuous mapping from a compact convex set back to itself has at least one
fixed point — a point the function maps to itself. equilibria exist not because
of specific circumstances but because of the geometry of the space.

LAYER 2 — TECHNICAL
Brouwer fixed point theorem (1911): every continuous f: Dⁿ → Dⁿ (where Dⁿ is the
  closed n-dimensional ball) has at least one x* with f(x*) = x*
Kakutani fixed point theorem (1941): extends to set-valued (correspondence) functions
  → used in Nash equilibrium existence proof: every finite game has a Nash equilibrium
  because the best-response correspondence satisfies Kakutani's conditions
Banach fixed point theorem (contraction mapping): any contraction mapping on a complete
  metric space has a unique fixed point, and iterations converge to it
  → condition: ||f(x) − f(y)|| ≤ k||x − y|| with k < 1
  → iteration: xₙ₊₁ = f(xₙ) converges to x* exponentially
Tarski fixed point theorem: any monotone function on a complete lattice has a fixed point
  → used in logic (Kleene fixed point), type theory, and program semantics

LAYER 3 — STRUCTURAL
the structural claim: equilibrium is geometrically necessary, not contingent.
if a system maps a compact convex domain to itself continuously, it must have at least
one resting point. the existence of equilibrium does not require perfect rationality,
perfect information, or any specific mechanism — only continuity and bounded space.
architecture: compact convex domain + continuous self-mapping → fixed point existence
  → what determines equilibrium location: system-specific dynamics
  → what determines equilibrium existence: geometry alone
this separates existence (geometry: always guaranteed under conditions) from uniqueness
(depends on system) and stability (depends on dynamics).
implication: looking for equilibria is always justified in compact continuous systems.
the question is never "does equilibrium exist?" but "which one, and is it stable?"

LAYER 4 — CROSS-DOMAIN
→ economics: Nash equilibrium existence (von Neumann-Morgenstern, Nash) rests entirely
  on Kakutani. equilibrium in competitive markets, auctions, and games is geometrically
  necessary given the assumptions.
→ computer science: iterative algorithms converge (by Banach) if they are contractions.
  numerical methods (Newton-Raphson, gradient descent) are fixed-point iterations.
→ machine learning: training convergence is a fixed-point problem. a model has "converged"
  when its parameters are a fixed point of the gradient update step.
→ biology: homeostasis is a fixed point of physiological feedback systems. body temperature,
  pH, blood glucose are fixed points of closed-loop regulatory systems.
→ organizational: stable power structures are fixed points of social influence dynamics.
  the structure that persists is the one where each actor's strategy is their best response
  to everyone else's (Nash/Kakutani applied to organizations).

LAYER 5 — ROOT
the root: stability is a geometric property.
the universe's equilibria are not designed — they are the fixed points of its dynamics.
any system that continuously maps itself back to itself will settle.
this is why stability is ubiquitous and why disruption requires breaking the self-mapping —
changing the domain (expansion), the function (innovation), or the continuity (shock).

BUILD APPLICATION
→ algorithm design: cast computational problems as fixed-point problems. if you can
  define f such that the solution is f(x*) = x*, iterating f will converge (if it's a contraction).
  EM algorithm, PageRank, value iteration in RL — all fixed-point iterations.
→ organizational design: stable team structures are fixed points. to change the structure,
  change the reward function (f), not just the current state. the old f will converge back.
→ product equilibria: a product's market position is a fixed point of competitive dynamics.
  to shift it, change the competitive mapping — enter new distribution, change pricing geometry.
→ control systems: design controllers by finding the fixed point of the closed-loop system.
  a stable controller is one where the controlled state is the fixed point of the combined
  plant-controller dynamics.

───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
L105 — EXTREME VALUE THEOREM
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

LAYER 1 — SURFACE
a continuous function on a closed bounded domain attains both its maximum and minimum
somewhere on that domain. every optimization problem on a compact domain has a solution.
you are guaranteed a best answer exists — the question is only finding it.

LAYER 2 — TECHNICAL
extreme value theorem (Weierstrass 1861): if f: [a,b] → ℝ is continuous, then
  ∃ x_max, x_min ∈ [a,b] such that f(x_min) ≤ f(x) ≤ f(x_max) for all x ∈ [a,b]
  → both maximum and minimum are attained (not just approached)
generalizes to: f continuous on compact K ⊆ ℝⁿ → f attains its sup and inf on K
why compactness is required:
  f(x) = x on (0,1) — open interval, no maximum (approaches 1 but never attains it)
  f(x) = 1/x on [1,∞) — unbounded domain, no minimum (approaches 0, never attains it)
connection to optimization: the existence of optima is guaranteed only on compact domains.
  unconstrained optimization on unbounded domains may have no solution.
  constrained optimization (which restricts to a compact feasible set) always has a solution.

LAYER 3 — STRUCTURAL
the structural claim: well-posed optimization requires bounded domains.
unbounded problems may be ill-posed — there may be no optimal solution, only asymptotic approach.
the architecture: continuous objective + compact domain → extreme values attained
implications:
  (a) every engineering design problem (bounded parameters) has an optimal design
  (b) every biological organism (bounded energy, bounded lifespan) has an optimal strategy
      within its constraints — the question is finding it
  (c) every constrained resource allocation (budget, time, capacity) has an optimal allocation
the theorem doesn't find the optimum — it guarantees the optimum exists.
it converts the question from "is there a solution?" to "which of possibly many solutions
is the right one?" — a fundamental philosophical shift.

LAYER 4 — CROSS-DOMAIN
→ product design: any product with bounded constraints (cost, size, weight, power) has an
  optimal design. the design process is the search; the theorem guarantees the search is not futile.
→ financial portfolio optimization: Markowitz mean-variance optimization on a bounded
  feasible set (sum of weights = 1, weights ≥ 0) is guaranteed to have a solution by EVT.
→ biology: species in bounded environments (food, space, mates) have optimal life history
  strategies. evolution finds them via selection; EVT guarantees they exist.
→ machine learning: training loss minimization on a compact parameter space has a global
  minimum. the challenge is finding it (non-convexity, local minima) — not that it exists.

LAYER 5 — ROOT
the root: finite worlds have solutions.
the universe's constraints — bounded energy, bounded space, bounded time — guarantee
that every optimization problem within the universe has an answer.
the question is always "which optimum?" never "is there one?"
this is the universe's implicit guarantee: every well-posed problem on a bounded domain is solvable.

BUILD APPLICATION
→ project scoping: any project with bounded resources has an optimal solution.
  the manager's job is not to determine if a solution exists (it does) but to search for it.
→ ML training: ensure parameter spaces are implicitly compact (weight decay, clipping).
  without compactness, training may diverge to unbounded parameters with no solution.
→ resource allocation: frame all allocation problems with explicit bounds.
  unconstrained problems (no budget ceiling, no timeline) are ill-posed by EVT.
  explicit constraints are not limitations — they are the condition that guarantees a solution exists.


───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
L106 — LYAPUNOV STABILITY LAW
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

LAYER 1 — SURFACE
a system is stable if you can find a function that decreases over time along every
trajectory. you don't need to solve the equations of motion. if a decreasing function
exists, the system won't blow up. this is the certificate of stability.

LAYER 2 — TECHNICAL
Lyapunov's direct method (1892):
  a function V(x) is a Lyapunov function for ẋ = f(x) if:
    (1) V(x) > 0 for x ≠ 0 (positive definite)
    (2) V(0) = 0
    (3) dV/dt = ∇V · f(x) ≤ 0 along trajectories (non-increasing)
    → if (3): stable equilibrium
    → if dV/dt < 0 (strictly decreasing): asymptotically stable (perturbations decay)
    → if dV/dt > 0 somewhere: unstable
  V plays the role of generalized energy — any quantity that decreases over time
  serves as a Lyapunov function
  LaSalle's invariance principle: extends asymptotic stability to cases where dV/dt = 0
  on a non-trivial set (orbit analysis)
  stochastic Lyapunov: extends to stochastic systems (Itô calculus version)
  → confirms stability in systems with noise

LAYER 3 — STRUCTURAL
the structural claim: stability can be certified without simulation.
the architecture: find V → check V̇ ≤ 0 → conclude stability
  → this separates proof of stability from computation of trajectories
  → Lyapunov functions are stability certificates — they prove the system is safe
this is the mathematical version of "trust but verify" — you don't need to follow
every trajectory to know the system is stable. you need one function that decreases.
implication: designing stable systems = designing Lyapunov functions.
  the system is designed around the certificate, not discovered by simulation.

LAYER 4 — CROSS-DOMAIN
→ control engineering: all modern control design (PID, LQR, MPC, H-infinity) constructs
  Lyapunov functions implicitly. the quadratic form V = xᵀPx (LQR) is the Lyapunov
  function that certifies stability of the closed-loop system.
→ machine learning: loss functions are Lyapunov candidates for training stability.
  if the loss decreases monotonically (V̇ < 0), training is asymptotically stable.
  gradient clipping is a Lyapunov intervention — preventing loss explosions.
→ economic stability: a social welfare function that decreases over time in a market
  is a Lyapunov function certifying market stability. the Lyapunov condition for
  tâtonnement (Walrasian price adjustment) is the stability condition for competitive markets.
→ organizational health: a metric that decreases when the organization is unhealthy
  and increases toward health (e.g., employee satisfaction, decision speed) is a
  Lyapunov function for organizational stability.

LAYER 5 — ROOT
the root: decreasing energy certificates stability.
every stable thing in the universe has something that decreases along its trajectories.
thermodynamic equilibrium: entropy decreases free energy. ecosystem stability: population
variance decreases around the attractor. cognitive stability: prediction error decreases
with learning. the Lyapunov function is the universe's stability receipt.

BUILD APPLICATION
→ system design: before deploying a complex system, construct a Lyapunov function for it.
  what quantity should be decreasing if the system is healthy? monitor that quantity.
  if it starts increasing, the system is Lyapunov-unstable — intervene before blowup.
→ model stability: neural network training has Lyapunov structure.
  design training so that a certificate exists (bounded gradients, decreasing loss envelope).
  systems without a Lyapunov certificate (gradient explosions, reward divergence) are unstable.
→ organizational indicators: define a Lyapunov function for your organization —
  a composite metric that should decrease (dysfunction, cost) or increase (health, capacity)
  monotonically if the system is stable. track it. if it reverses, the equilibrium is lost.

───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
L107 — FLUCTUATION-DISSIPATION THEOREM
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

LAYER 1 — SURFACE
in any system at thermal equilibrium, the forces that cause dissipation (friction, resistance)
are the same forces that cause random fluctuations (noise, brownian motion).
you cannot have one without the other. a perfectly smooth (zero-friction) medium produces
no thermal noise. a noisy medium always dissipates. noise and friction are two faces of the same phenomenon.

LAYER 2 — TECHNICAL
fluctuation-dissipation theorem (Callen-Welton 1951, built on Nyquist 1928):
  S(ω) = (4kT/ω) · Im[χ(ω)]
  where:
    S(ω) = power spectral density of fluctuations at frequency ω
    χ(ω) = generalized susceptibility (response to perturbation)
    Im[χ(ω)] = imaginary part = dissipative response
    kT = thermal energy
  → Johnson-Nyquist noise: voltage noise in resistor: S_V = 4kTR (Nyquist 1928)
    noise power proportional to resistance — cannot have resistance without noise
  → Einstein relation (1905): D = kT/γ
    diffusion coefficient D linked to friction γ — same microscopic interactions
  → Brownian motion: velocity autocorrelation function related to friction via FDT
  → Green-Kubo relations: transport coefficients (viscosity, thermal conductivity)
    expressed as time integrals of equilibrium fluctuation correlations
    → viscosity = (1/kT) ∫₀^∞ ⟨σₓᵧ(t)σₓᵧ(0)⟩ dt (where σ = stress tensor)

LAYER 3 — STRUCTURAL
the structural claim: dissipation and fluctuation are not independent — they are dual.
the architecture: microscopic reversibility (detailed balance at equilibrium) →
  fluctuations and response are related by time-reversal symmetry →
  FDT as exact consequence
implication: you cannot design a system with dissipation and no noise, or noise and no dissipation.
  reducing noise requires reducing dissipation (resistance). reducing dissipation generates noise.
  this is a fundamental trade-off built into thermodynamics, not a design failure.
the generalized FDT (non-equilibrium): extensions exist for systems near equilibrium
  (linear response theory) — the relationship holds to first order in perturbation strength.

LAYER 4 — CROSS-DOMAIN
→ electronics: amplifier noise (thermal + shot noise) is irreducible.
  the noise figure of any amplifier is bounded below by FDT.
  quantum amplifiers operate near this limit (SQUID amplifiers, parametric amplifiers).
→ financial markets: market impact (price slippage = dissipation) and price volatility
  (fluctuation) are related by a financial FDT. markets with high impact also have
  high volatility — they are dual. attempts to reduce volatility by removing liquidity
  increase impact (the other face of the same phenomenon).
→ organizational systems: the cost of making decisions (dissipation) is related to
  the uncertainty in outcomes (fluctuations). organizations that try to reduce outcome
  uncertainty must increase deliberation cost. FDT analog: you pay for certainty with process.
→ biology: receptor sensitivity (response to signal) is related to receptor noise
  (spontaneous activation) by FDT. maximally sensitive receptors are maximally noisy.
  this explains why highly sensitive sensory systems (e.g., rod photoreceptors, hair cells)
  operate at the quantum noise limit.

LAYER 5 — ROOT
the root: response and noise are the same coin.
the universe cannot create a system that responds to perturbations without producing fluctuations.
to be responsive is to be noisy. to be resistant is to fluctuate.
this is the universe's statement about sensitivity: you pay for it with noise.
perfect signal-to-noise ratio is achievable only by T = 0 — absolute zero, no fluctuations,
no response, death of dynamics. life, intelligence, and sensitivity require accepting the noise.

BUILD APPLICATION
→ signal processing: design signal chains knowing that low-noise amplification requires
  low-dissipation (cryogenic amplifiers, superconducting circuits). there is no free lunch.
  the noise floor is set by the FDT for the operating temperature.
→ market design: understanding that liquidity provision (reducing friction/impact) and
  volatility are linked. market makers who provide liquidity are taking on the volatility
  that their presence reduces. the FDT quantifies the exchange rate between them.
→ decision design: build explicit tolerance for outcome variance into high-responsiveness
  systems. a fast-responding, highly-sensitive decision process will be noisier than
  a slow, deliberate one. optimize for the right trade-off, not for eliminating the trade-off.
→ sensor design: operating near the FDT limit requires cryogenic cooling or quantum sensing
  methods. for room-temperature sensing, the FDT sets the irreducible noise floor —
  measure it, acknowledge it, design around it rather than pretending it can be eliminated.

  functions), Noether's theorem implies a conserved quantity — economic "energy."
  in equilibrium economics: the sum of consumer and producer surplus is conserved
  under small perturbations that preserve the market's time symmetry.
  breaking time symmetry (technological change, preference shifts, regulation) destroys
  conservation — surplus is created or destroyed, entropy of value distribution changes.
  together: every market conservation law corresponds to a market symmetry.
  the "invisible hand" conserves total surplus because of the market's temporal symmetry.
  markets with broken symmetry (monopoly, externalities) violate this conservation.
WHY NEITHER ALONE PREDICTS IT: Noether links symmetry to conservation. supply/demand gives
  market dynamics. entropy gives value distribution. together: market equilibrium
  is a conservation law consequence — and market failures are symmetry-breaking events.
DOMAIN: welfare economics, market design, antitrust theory, monetary policy

S69 — PERCOLATION-PHASE-UNIVERSALITY
NAME: percolation-phase-universality
LAWS: L102 (percolation threshold) × L15 (phase transition) × L96 (scale-dependent coupling)
EMERGENT BEHAVIOR: percolation transitions and thermodynamic phase transitions are
  in the same universality class — their critical exponents are the same.
  water boiling (3D Ising model) and network percolation (Erdős-Rényi) have different
  microscopic mechanisms but identical macroscopic critical behavior near the threshold.
  this is the renormalization group's deepest result: the critical behavior is determined
  by dimension and symmetry, not by microscopic details.
  together: all phase transitions — physical, social, network — are in universality classes
  determined only by dimensionality and symmetry. the coupling constants run to the
  same fixed point regardless of starting conditions.
WHY NEITHER ALONE PREDICTS IT: percolation gives network transitions. phase transitions
  give thermodynamic transitions. scale-dependent coupling gives universality classes.
  together: percolation IS a phase transition. both are in the same universality class.
  the same critical exponents describe both — the microscopic mechanism is irrelevant.
DOMAIN: physics, network science, social science, financial markets

S70 — FIXED-POINT-LANGUAGE-GRAMMAR
NAME: fixed-point language grammar
LAWS: L104 (fixed point theorem) × L55 (Gödel incompleteness) × L100 (Zipf)
EMERGENT BEHAVIOR: natural language grammar is a fixed point of linguistic evolution —
  the grammatical structure that, once established, speakers preserve because they
  learned it from others who learned it from others.
  Gödel: every sufficiently expressive language contains sentences it cannot parse
  according to its own grammar (garden-path sentences, self-referential paradoxes).
  Zipf: word frequencies are the fixed-point distribution of lexical evolution.
  together: language is a Gödel-incomplete, Zipf-distributed, fixed-point system —
  self-consistent (fixed point), inevitably containing unparseable structures (Gödel),
  with power-law word distribution (Zipf emerging from preferential attachment in lexical space).
WHY NEITHER ALONE PREDICTS IT: fixed point gives stability. Gödel gives incompleteness.
  Zipf gives distribution. together: language is a stable, power-law-distributed system
  that cannot express all of its own semantic content — an incomplete fixed point.
DOMAIN: linguistics, natural language processing, AI language models, communication design

organized by domain for maximal practical utility.

───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
DOMAIN: SOFTWARE — EXPANDED COVERAGE
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

L1 (zeroth law / thermodynamic equilibrium):
  → eventual consistency in distributed systems: databases that achieve eventual
    consistency are implementing the zeroth law — they wait for thermal equilibrium
    between all replicas. design for eventual equilibrium, not instant consistency,
    unless the cost of inconsistency exceeds the cost of synchronization.

L2 (second law / entropy):
  → code entropy: every codebase increases in entropy over time (more coupling, more
    dead code, more debt). entropy decrease requires energy (refactoring sprints).
    measure entropy metrics: cyclomatic complexity, coupling, duplication. track the
    derivative. if dEntropy/dt > 0 unchecked, the codebase will reach heat death.

L5 (conservation of energy):
  → compute conservation: energy-in = energy-out + heat. GPU training energy is
    conserved — it exits as model weights, heat, and carbon. account for all three.
    sustainable ML requires energy auditing across the full chain.

L10 (Noether / symmetry → conservation):
  → API versioning as symmetry: backward-compatible changes preserve the symmetry of
    the API contract. breaking changes destroy the symmetry → conservation law broken →
    downstream breakage. semantic versioning is a symmetry classification scheme.

L11 (Shannon information):
  → compression as intelligence: the ability to compress data is a direct measure of
    understanding. an ML model that perfectly predicts the next token is a perfect compressor.
    test understanding by measuring compression ratio — better models = better compressors.

L12 (Kolmogorov complexity):
  → code complexity audit: functions with high Kolmogorov complexity (hard to compress,
    no pattern) are algorithmic accidents — they should be replaced with explicit logic
    or generated from a simpler rule. complexity without pattern is technical debt.

L13 (emergence):
  → microservice emergence: distributed system behavior emerges from service interactions —
    it cannot be predicted from individual service specs. test system-level behavior explicitly;
    unit tests on individual services do not catch emergent failures.

L15 (phase transitions):
  → system capacity planning: don't model capacity linearly. identify the phase transition
    thresholds (connection pool exhaustion, GC pressure, lock contention) and engineer
    explicit buffers below them. post-transition behavior is qualitatively different —
    plan for it separately.

L17 (feedback loops):
  → feature flag feedback: a/b tests create feedback loops — user behavior changes
    the metric, which changes the feature, which changes user behavior.
    design feedback loops explicitly with settling time and convergence criteria.

L18 (power law):
  → cache hit rate follows power law: 80% of requests hit 20% of cached content.
    design caches for the Zipf distribution — tiered caching with hot/warm/cold tiers
    matching the power law tail.

L21 (Heisenberg uncertainty):
  → performance measurement uncertainty: measuring performance (profiling) changes
    performance (observer overhead). production profiling always underestimates overhead.
    design measurement systems that minimize perturbation (sampling profilers, not instrumenting profilers).

L22 (observer effect):
  → logging overhead: adding logging changes system behavior (timing, memory, I/O).
    structured logging with sampling rates manages the observer effect — log at 1%
    in production to measure without perturbing.

L25 (quantum entanglement / non-locality):
  → distributed transaction consistency: entangled distributed state (two services that
    must agree) requires explicit synchronization. there is no "spooky action at a distance"
    in software — consistency requires communication. design the communication protocol
    explicitly; pretending entanglement comes free is how distributed systems fail.

L26 (Pauli exclusion):
  → resource lock exclusion: two threads cannot occupy the same mutex — Pauli exclusion
    at the software level. deadlock is the violation of this principle when two locks
    are mutually required. design lock ordering to enforce a consistent Pauli structure.

L29 (natural selection):
  → A/B testing as evolution: features compete for user engagement. selection (metric)
    determines which variants survive. design the selection metric carefully —
    it determines what "fitness" means in your feature evolution.

L33 (Lotka-Volterra):
  → microservice dependency cycles: services in a mutual dependency cycle exhibit
    Lotka-Volterra dynamics — oscillating failures. break cycles; design acyclic
    service dependency graphs to eliminate the predator-prey oscillation.

L35 (small world):
  → six degrees in software: any function in a well-designed codebase should be reachable
    in O(log N) imports. small-world architecture (few hubs, many direct connections)
    minimizes import depth.

L38 (Metcalfe's law):
  → platform API network effects: API value scales as N². design APIs to be connectable —
    webhooks, event streams, and standard formats maximize the connections each integration
    can form.

L40 (Braess's paradox):
  → adding cache can slow the system: adding a cache between components can increase
    latency by creating a chokepoint. test system performance after every optimization —
    Braess says counterintuitive degradations are structurally possible.

L41 (Weber-Fechner):
  → log scales for user metrics: display performance metrics on log scales, not linear.
    human perception of "2× as fast" is proportional — 10ms→5ms feels similar to 1s→500ms.
    design performance goals in Weber-Fechner space (log scale), not absolute space.

L47 (supply and demand):
  → request queuing: request rate (supply) vs. processing capacity (demand).
    when supply exceeds demand, queue depth grows (price rises in elastic queues =
    increased latency). design systems with explicit back-pressure mechanisms
    (the market-clearing price for compute is latency; design the price correctly).

L50 (Nash equilibrium):
  → API design as game theory: API consumers will choose their strategies based on
    what they believe other consumers will do. design rate limits and quotas as
    mechanism design — the Nash equilibrium of all consumers acting optimally
    should be acceptable for the provider. if not, the mechanism is wrong.

L55 (Gödel incompleteness):
  → no complete test suite: no finite test suite can prove a program correct for all inputs
    (Gödel applied to formal verification). formal verification is only complete within
    a bounded model. design with explicit undecidable-region awareness; test for
    classes of behavior rather than all behaviors.

L57 (central limit theorem):
  → microservice latency distributions: aggregate latency of N independent service calls
    converges to Gaussian by CLT. but individual service latencies may be fat-tailed.
    tail latency (p99, p99.9) is determined by the fat tail of individual services,
    not the CLT-converged mean. optimize the tail, not the mean.

L58 (Bayesian updating):
  → feature flag gradual rollout: treat feature rollout as Bayesian updating.
    start with prior (expected conversion rate). roll out to 1%, update posterior,
    increase if posterior justifies. this is optimal sample-efficient feature validation.


───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
DOMAIN: PRODUCT — EXPANDED COVERAGE
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

L2 (entropy): products accumulate entropy — features, options, edge cases pile up.
  → periodic entropy reduction: schedule "simplification sprints" as energy investments
    in product entropy reduction. products that never reduce entropy reach unusability.

L13 (emergence): product behavior emerges from user interaction patterns.
  → emergent use cases: monitor how users actually use the product (not how you designed it).
    emergent usage patterns are signals that users are finding higher-value applications
    than you designed for. follow the emergence.

L15 (phase transitions): user behavior has tipping points.
  → onboarding cliff: most users experience a phase transition in their relationship
    with a product — from "trying it" to "dependent on it." identify the actions that
    trigger this transition (the "aha moment") and optimize for that specific threshold.

L17 (feedback loops): product improvements create feedback loops.
  → compound improvement: each product improvement generates user feedback that reveals
    the next improvement. design product development as a tight feedback loop —
    weekly releases generate weekly feedback generates weekly improvements.

L18 (power law): user value contribution is power-law distributed.
  → community power users: the top 1% of users generate ~50% of community value (content,
    support, referrals). design explicit programs for power users that acknowledge their
    disproportionate contribution and deepen their engagement.

L21 (Heisenberg uncertainty): you cannot simultaneously measure all aspects of user experience.
  → measurement trade-offs: quantitative metrics (measuring everything) change user behavior.
    qualitative research (disturbs less) misses scale. design a portfolio: high-volume
    behavioral data + low-sample qualitative depth. neither alone is complete.

L29 (natural selection): product features evolve by competitive fitness.
  → ruthless deprecation: features that don't have users are evolutionary dead ends.
    select against them. deprecate features with <X% adoption after Y months.
    product fitness = engagement density, not feature count.

L35 (small world): product discovery follows small-world network dynamics.
  → referral network design: viral loops should be built on existing social networks
    (small world property — any user is ~6 links from any other user).
    the marginal cost of viral growth is low because the network topology is already small-world.

L36 (preferential attachment): early traction compounds.
  → seed market strategy: the first 100 users matter more than the next 10,000 because
    preferential attachment means early users attract later users.
    choose the first 100 users deliberately — they set the Zipf baseline.

L41 (Weber-Fechner): user perception of product value is logarithmic.
  → pricing anchoring: the perceived value of a price reduction from $100→$80 equals
    $10→$8 in Weber-Fechner space (same proportion). design pricing tiers with equal
    proportional steps, not equal absolute steps.

L42 (Hick's law): decision time increases with choice count.
  → pricing page: no more than 3 pricing tiers (Hick predicts decision paralysis above 3).
    feature comparison tables should highlight the recommended choice to short-circuit
    the logarithmic decision time increase.

L43 (Fitts's law): interaction time scales with target size and distance.
  → CTA design: primary calls to action should be large and close to natural eye/cursor
    resting position. Fitts's law is the quantitative foundation of button size design.
    double the button area → cut acquisition time by ~40%.

L50 (Nash equilibrium): multi-sided platform design is a Nash equilibrium problem.
  → platform pricing: the prices charged to each side of the market should be the Nash
    equilibrium where both sides find participation profitable. single-side pricing
    often destroys the equilibrium by making one side's participation irrational.

L55 (Gödel incompleteness): no product specification is complete.
  → spec humility: every product spec is Gödel-incomplete — there are valid user needs
    it cannot express. ship fast, observe emergent usage, update the spec from reality.
    the spec is a starting model, not the complete truth.

L57 (CLT): aggregate user metrics converge to Gaussian.
  → metric aggregation: mean and standard deviation are valid statistics for large-scale
    user metrics (CLT applies). but individual user behavior is often non-Gaussian.
    segment by cohort before applying CLT — pooling non-comparable populations
    violates the CLT independence assumption.

L58 (Bayesian updating): product roadmap is a belief system.
  → Bayesian roadmap: treat each roadmap item as a hypothesis with a prior probability
    of success. user research and analytics are evidence that updates the posterior.
    ship the highest expected-value item (highest posterior × payoff), not just the
    highest-confidence item.

───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
DOMAIN: RESEARCH — EXPANDED COVERAGE
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

L2 (entropy): information has thermodynamic cost.
  → data collection cost: every measurement creates entropy (observer-system entanglement).
    design experiments to minimize entropy production while maximizing information gain.
    entropy-efficient experiments: maximum information per measurement perturbation.

L5 (conservation of energy): energy balance in experiments.
  → energy audit: any experiment that appears to create energy (perpetual motion-type results)
    violates L5. the first check for anomalous results: does the energy balance close?
    if not, find the hidden energy source before publishing.

L10 (Noether): every experimental symmetry is a conservation law.
  → symmetry-based experimental design: if your experiment has a symmetry (same result
    when left/right swapped, same result at different times), the corresponding conserved
    quantity is a check on experimental accuracy. verify conservation laws as consistency checks.

L11 (Shannon): information theory for experimental design.
  → maximum entropy experimental design: choose experiments that maximize information gain
    (maximize entropy reduction in the hypothesis space). this is the formal basis of
    active learning and sequential experimental design (D-optimal, A-optimal designs).

L15 (phase transitions): scientific paradigms have phase transitions.
  → paradigm shift detection: monitor the critical slowing down near paradigm shifts —
    anomalies accumulate, variance increases, the existing framework requires more epicycles.
    these are the statistical signatures of an approaching phase transition in the field.

L17 (feedback loops): citation networks create feedback.
  → citation inflation: highly-cited papers attract more citations (preferential attachment).
    the h-index is a measure of the fixed point of your citation feedback loop.
    design research programs to accelerate the feedback loop rather than waiting for it.

L18 (power law): scientific impact follows power law.
  → publication strategy: a small number of highly-cited papers produce most scientific impact.
    one influential paper in a high-impact venue > ten average papers.
    power law impact means concentration of effort in the highest-value work dominates the strategy.

L21 (Heisenberg): measurement limits in physics experiments.
  → uncertainty-limited experiments: identify the Heisenberg limit for your measurement.
    quantum metrology (using entangled states) can beat the standard quantum limit by
    1/√N → 1/N (Heisenberg limit). for precision measurement experiments, this matters.

L29 (natural selection): scientific ideas evolve by selection.
  → idea fitness: scientific ideas compete for adoption by the community.
    fitness criteria: predictive accuracy, simplicity, generalizability, reproducibility.
    design research to score high on all four fitness dimensions, not just accuracy.

L36 (preferential attachment): early results define a research program.
  → first-mover citation advantage: the first paper to clearly articulate a phenomenon
    accumulates citations by preferential attachment even if subsequent papers are better.
    clear articulation early in a research program is strategically critical.

L41 (Weber-Fechner): statistical effect sizes are perceived logarithmically.
  → effect size reporting: report effect sizes in natural log units where applicable
    (Cohen's d = 0.2 vs. 0.8 should be understood as a logarithmic scale difference in impact).
    researchers systematically underestimate small effect sizes and overestimate large ones
    due to Weber-Fechner perception.

L50 (Nash equilibrium): academic incentive structures produce Nash equilibria.
  → publication incentive game: the academic game (publish or perish, h-index optimization)
    has a Nash equilibrium that is not the optimal science equilibrium.
    strategies: find the local Nash of the current incentive system; optimize within it.
    better: design institutional mechanisms that move the Nash equilibrium toward better science.

L55 (Gödel incompleteness): science cannot be complete.
  → research horizon awareness: every scientific field has Gödel-incomplete regions —
    questions that cannot be answered within the field's current axiomatic framework.
    identify these questions explicitly. they mark where the field needs expansion, not more depth.

L57 (CLT): statistical inference relies on CLT.
  → sample size planning: CLT converges for N > 30 (rough rule). for non-Gaussian distributions,
    convergence requires larger N. use simulation to determine required N for your specific
    distribution before running the experiment.

L58 (Bayesian updating): hypothesis testing should be Bayesian.
  → p-values vs. Bayes factors: p-values do not measure evidence for a hypothesis.
    Bayes factors do. the replication crisis is partly a p-value misuse crisis.
    report Bayes factors alongside p-values for correct evidence interpretation.
