DOMAIN 111: DARK PATTERNS AND DECEPTIVE DESIGN AS ATTACK SURFACE
→ Scope: Interface design patterns that manipulate users into unintended
  actions — not traditional cyberattacks but security-relevant manipulation
  operating through design rather than code exploitation
→ Taxonomy of dark patterns (Brignull 2010):
  — Trick questions: Confusing opt-in/opt-out with double negatives
  — Sneak into basket: Adding items to cart without user intent
  — Roach motel: Easy to get in, hard to leave (subscription cancellation)
  — Privacy zuckering: Confusing privacy settings to share more than intended
  — Misdirection: Visual design directing attention away from important info
  — Hidden costs: Revealing full price late in checkout flow
  — Confirmshaming: Opt-out language shaming user ("No, I don't want to
    save money")
  — Disguised ads: Advertising styled as organic content
  — Forced continuity: Automatic subscription renewal without clear notice
→ Security-specific dark patterns:
  — Cookie consent manipulation: Banner design maximizing "Accept All"
    clicks through color contrast, button placement, and option burial
  — Security setting complexity: Deliberately complex security settings
    that default to maximum data sharing
  — Permission inflation: Requesting excessive permissions with dark pattern
    framing making refusal seem harmful
  — Breach notification obscuration: Downplaying or obscuring breach
    notifications in compliance emails
→ Regulatory response: FTC enforcement actions (2022-2024 against Amazon
  Prime cancellation dark patterns, Google/YouTube for COPPA violations);
  EU DSA (Digital Services Act) prohibits dark patterns for platforms;
  California AB 2273 (Age-Appropriate Design Code)
→ Sub-domains: Consent manipulation; security setting dark patterns;
  permission dark patterns; regulatory framework for deceptive design;
  dark pattern detection tooling

DOMAIN 112: NEUROTECHNOLOGY AND BRAIN-COMPUTER INTERFACE SECURITY
→ Scope: Direct neural interfaces — Neuralink (FDA Breakthrough Device
  Designation 2019; first human implant 2024); BrainGate (medical research);
  non-invasive BCI (consumer EEG headbands — Emotiv, OpenBCI; Meta neural
  wristband); clinical neurostimulation (deep brain stimulation — DBS;
  vagus nerve stimulators; cochlear implants)
→ Status: Primarily research/early clinical. Neuralink received FDA approval
  for human trials 2023; first human implant January 2024 (patient N1
  demonstrated cursor control via neural signal). Commercial BCI deployment
  is 5-10 years away but attack surface characterization must precede deployment.
→ Specific vulnerabilities:
  — Neural signal interception: Implanted devices transmit neural data
    wirelessly; interception reveals brain activity patterns
  — Neural signal manipulation (stimulation): DBS devices and cochlear
    implants have wireless interfaces; unauthorized stimulation is a
    demonstrated attack vector (Pycroft et al. 2016 on DBS implants)
  — Privacy of neural data: EEG signals contain sensitive private information
    beyond intended applications — emotional state, cognitive workload,
    potentially thought content in future high-resolution systems
  — Authentication via neural signals: Future authentication using neural
    signatures creates novel authentication attack surface
  — BCI used for authentication — neural passthought (Frank et al. 2013) —
    authenticating by mental task completion; susceptible to replay if
    signal captured
  — Adversarial inputs to neural decoders: Machine learning decodes neural
    signals into intent; adversarial inputs to the decoder could corrupt
    intended actions
→ Root mechanic: R10 (physical reality as authentication proxy) extended to
  neural signals — the brain becomes authentication signal and command channel
  simultaneously
→ Sub-domains: Invasive BCI security; non-invasive BCI security; DBS/neurostimulator
  security; neural data privacy; BCI authentication security; neural signal
  adversarial examples

DOMAIN 113: AUTONOMOUS WEAPONS AND LETHAL AUTONOMOUS SYSTEMS SECURITY
→ Scope: Autonomous weapons systems (AWS) — systems that select and engage
  targets without human authorization for each engagement. Distinguished
  from remotely piloted (drone, UCAV) and human-supervised systems.
→ Status: Multiple nations developing; contested legal status (ICRC campaign
  for prohibition treaty); Turkey Kargu-2 quadcopter in Libya (2020 UN report)
  described as first documented case of autonomous targeting; US DoD Directive
  3000.09 (2012, updated 2023) requires "appropriate levels of human judgment"
→ Security vulnerabilities of autonomous targeting:
  — Adversarial inputs to targeting AI: A system using computer vision to
    identify targets can be deceived by adversarial patches (documented in
    military context — DARPA GARD program; adversarial stop sign research
    applies directly)
  — GPS spoofing and navigation manipulation: Autonomous systems navigating
    via GPS are vulnerable to spoofing attacks directing them to wrong targets
    or wrong locations
  — Communication link security: Systems receiving targeting parameters via
    communication link are vulnerable to interception and injection
  — Swarm coordination protocol attacks: Swarm drones coordinate via local
    communications; injecting false coordination signals could misdirect swarms
  — Identification, friend or foe (IFF) spoofing: Military IFF systems have
    known spoofing vulnerabilities; autonomous targeting systems relying on
    IFF could be deceived into targeting friendly forces
  — Operational control compromise: Command-and-control systems for authorizing
    autonomous engagement are high-value targets; compromise could result in
    unauthorized weapons deployment
→ Legal and governance context: Geneva Conventions application to AWS
  (legal persons must be capable of criminal accountability — autonomous
  systems cannot bear accountability); International Campaign to Stop Killer
  Robots; United Nations GGE on LAWS (Lethal Autonomous Weapons Systems)
→ Sub-domains: Autonomous targeting system security; swarm security; IFF
  security in autonomous context; command authority integrity; adversarial
  inputs to weapons-integrated AI

DOMAIN 115: CYBERSECURITY INSURANCE UNDERWRITING TECHNOLOGY
→ Scope: The technical systems and methodologies used by cyber insurers and
  their service providers to assess risk, price policies, respond to claims,
  and model aggregate exposure — distinguished from Domain 76 (Cyber Insurance
  as Control) which covered the insurance market structure
→ Technology landscape:
  — Risk assessment scanning: Insurers use external scanning tools (BitSight,
    SecurityScorecard, Cyence, Corvus, UpGuard) to quantify security posture
    before binding coverage; these scores are consequential but methodology
    is contested
  — Actuarial modeling: Catastrophe modeling (Cyence acquired by Guidewire;
    AIR Worldwide cyber model; RMS cyber model) applying natural catastrophe
    modeling techniques to cyber risk
  — Policy language precision: Cyber policy language is still evolving;
    Lloyd's of London market mandated state-sponsored attack exclusions (2023);
    Merck NotPetya war exclusion litigation (NJ Superior Court 2021 — found
    for Merck; $1.4B coverage)
  — Claims data: Insurers accumulate proprietary claims data; this is the
    most valuable underwriting information and is a target
  — Premium adequacy: Industry-wide concerns about premium inadequacy;
    several major insurers exited cyber market (2021-2022 spike in ransomware
    claims); market stabilized 2023-2024
→ Security of the underwriting systems themselves:
  — Risk scoring manipulation: If an organization can manipulate external
    scanning results (BitSight score manipulation) they can obtain cheaper
    insurance while remaining high-risk; false external security signals
  — Claims fraud: Fabricating or inflating cyber incidents to claim insurance
    proceeds; emerging fraud category
  — Underwriter data breach: Insurer holding detailed security posture data
    on thousands of enterprises is itself a high-value target
→ Sub-domains: Cyber risk scoring system security; actuarial model security;
  claims fraud detection; policy language security; war exclusion attribution
  technology; aggregate exposure modeling


--- SOURCE LINES 131502–131539 ---
Historical instances:
— PCI-DSS compliance versus actual card security: Every major card breach
  in the 2010s (TJX 2007, Heartland 2008, Target 2013, Home Depot 2014)
  occurred in organizations that were PCI-DSS compliant at the time of breach.
  PCI compliance correlates negatively with breach recency because compliance
  audits are point-in-time snapshots.
— Target Corporation (2013): Target was PCI-DSS compliant. The HVAC vendor
  credential compromise exploited network segmentation gaps that the PCI audit
  missed. 40 million card numbers exfiltrated. The compliance gave false
  assurance to both Target and its business partners.
— Solarwinds (2020): SolarWinds marketed its security credentials. SEC
  enforcement action (2023) alleged material misrepresentation of security
  posture. CMMC-adjacent compliance claims did not correspond to actual
  implementation.
— Healthcare: HIPAA compliance audits do not prevent breaches. The HHS
  Office for Civil Rights breach portal shows regular multi-million-record
  breaches from HIPAA-covered entities, demonstrating no correlation between
  audit compliance and actual security outcomes.
— FedRAMP: Authorization timeline averages 12-18 months; during that period,
  security teams are consumed by documentation; authorized systems sometimes
  have security vulnerabilities discovered post-authorization that existed
  pre-authorization but were not in scope.

Layer 2 — Present (current manifestation):
— CMMC (Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification) implementation creating
  same paradox in defense industrial base: contractors investing in C3PAO
  assessment preparation rather than actual control implementation
— SOC 2 Type 2 as marketing tool — companies achieving SOC 2 attesting
  controls operate "per the system description" without that description
  mapping to actual threat-relevant controls
— Automated compliance platforms (Vanta, Drata, Secureframe) accelerate
  evidence collection but also enable compliance achievement with minimal
  actual security improvement by generating evidence from superficial
  control implementations
— "Compliance as code" — treating compliance as an engineering problem
  to be automated rather than as a proxy for security outcomes
— Bug bounty programs used as compliance evidence without corresponding
  investment in the remediation of reported vulnerabilities


--- SOURCE LINES 131560–131567 ---
Layer 4B — Research Prompt:
Empirically measure the certification paradox. Sample organizations before
and after major security certifications. Measure: change in vulnerability
density (via recurring external scanning), change in incident rate, change
in mean time to detect and respond, change in security team activity allocation.
Construct a controlled comparison against organizations without concurrent
certification pursuit. Test whether certification timing predicts a temporary
security posture decline followed by a lagging improvement.


--- SOURCE LINES 131665–131669 ---
Statement: The cybersecurity workforce shortage is not a temporary labor
market imbalance but a structural asymmetry: the number of distinct skills
required to defend increases every year while the number of practitioners
with each skill grows slowly. Attackers face no equivalent credential
requirement. This asymmetry compounds annually.


--- SOURCE LINES 131679–131701 ---
Historical instances:
— ISC2 Cybersecurity Workforce Study (2023): 4 million cybersecurity
  professional shortage globally; gap has grown each year since measurement
  began (2013). The absolute shortage is growing despite decade of workforce
  development investment.
— Cloud security skills gap: Rapid adoption of AWS, Azure, GCP created massive
  demand for cloud security expertise; university programs had no cloud security
  curriculum; on-the-job training created dangerous multi-year lag; many major
  cloud breaches (Capital One 2019, AWS S3 misconfiguration epidemic 2017-2020)
  occurred in this lag window.
— ICS/OT security skills gap: OT environments require understanding of
  industrial protocols (DNP3, Modbus, IEC 61850), physical engineering,
  and cybersecurity simultaneously. This triple skillset is extremely rare.
  Colonial Pipeline (2021) and Oldsmar water treatment (2021) targeted
  organizations unable to staff qualified OT security personnel.
— AI/ML security skills gap: As of 2026, fewer than 1,000 practitioners
  globally can competently assess adversarial ML, model extraction, training
  data poisoning, and AI supply chain attacks. The number of AI systems
  deployed requiring this expertise is in the millions.
— Cryptography skills gap: Post-quantum cryptography migration requires
  cryptographic expertise most security teams lack; NIST FIPS 203/204/205
  migration deadline creates skills demand that cannot be met by available
  workforce.


--- SOURCE LINES 131719–131727 ---
Layer 3 — Trajectory:
Without structural change (AI automation achieving competence at routine
security tasks, university programs producing substantially more graduates,
or significant salary normalization drawing talent from adjacent fields), the
gap widens. Current AI security tools address tier-1 tasks (alert triage,
basic investigation, report summarization); they do not address advanced
defensive specialties (reverse engineering, vulnerability research, OT security,
cryptographic implementation review). The shortage in advanced specialties
is likely to persist for a decade or more.


--- SOURCE LINES 131740–131747 ---
Layer 4B — Research Prompt:
Model the cybersecurity skills gap as a differential equation system: population
of practitioners at each skill level, transitions between levels (entry to mid,
mid to senior, senior to leadership), attrition rates, AI substitution rates
by function. Project the workforce state in 5 and 10 years under multiple
scenarios (AI adoption slow, fast, very fast; university program expansion;
compensation normalization). Identify interventions with highest leverage on
the projected gap by skill category.


--- SOURCE LINES 131753–131757 ---
Statement: Systems designed with 5-10 year operational lifespans are routinely
operated for 20-40 years in critical infrastructure, enterprise, and government
contexts. Security assumptions embedded at design time — threat models, key
lengths, protocol choices, update mechanisms — are violated by this extended
operation, converting safe design choices into structural vulnerabilities.


--- SOURCE LINES 131770–131795 ---
Historical instances:
— Windows XP on medical devices: FDA 510(k) process requires extensive
  re-certification for OS changes on approved medical devices; many devices
  were approved on Windows XP and cannot practically be recertified for
  newer OS; some manufacturers committed to patching XP variants indefinitely
  for medical customers; attackers know this and specifically target
  medical device networks with XP-compatible exploits
— COBOL systems: $3 trillion in daily transactions processed by COBOL systems;
  fewer COBOL programmers are being trained; the systems that process US
  unemployment claims (visible during COVID-19 collapse of state unemployment
  systems in 2020 — New Jersey Governor requested retired COBOL programmers)
  have no modern equivalent running in parallel
— SS7 (Signaling System 7): Telecommunications protocol designed 1975 for
  closed network of trust between telephone companies; the Internet enabled
  any company worldwide to connect to SS7; trust model broken but protocol
  remains in use for 2FA SMS delivery, roaming, and call routing; SS7
  attacks documented since 2014 (CCC), demonstrated against German
  legislators (2017), used for location tracking and SMS OTP interception
— SWIFT financial messaging: Core SWIFT protocol is decades old; Bangladesh
  Bank heist (2016 — $81M stolen) exploited SWIFT terminal software
  vulnerabilities but also the trust model of the SWIFT network which
  assumed that all connected parties were legitimate
— BGP (Border Gateway Protocol): Designed 1989 with no authentication;
  operates on trust between Autonomous Systems; BGP hijacking events occur
  multiple times annually (Pakistan Telecom/YouTube 2008; Rostelecom/Google
  2017; China Telecom multiple incidents; MyEtherWallet hijacking 2018)


--- SOURCE LINES 131824–131843 ---
Layer 4A — Future Prediction:
Within 5-8 years, a critical infrastructure incident — power grid disruption,
water treatment compromise, or financial system disruption — will be directly
attributable to a vulnerability in a system operating 20+ years beyond its
security design assumptions, with documentation showing that the specific
vulnerability was known for years and that replacement was deferred due to
cost and operational risk. This incident will drive legislative action on
critical infrastructure technology refresh requirements with specified timelines.
Confidence: 70%.

Layer 4B — Research Prompt:
Build a comprehensive registry of critical infrastructure systems operating
beyond their security design lifespan. Define "security design lifespan" as
the period over which the system's cryptographic choices, threat model, and
update mechanisms remain adequate. For each category, characterize: current
deployment volume, known security vulnerabilities attributable to age,
replacement cost and timeline, regulatory barriers to replacement. Develop
a prioritized risk matrix ranking categories by legacy longevity risk. Propose
a federal critical infrastructure technology refresh program structure modeled
on the decommissioning programs used for nuclear facilities.


--- SOURCE LINES 131970–131979 ---
Layer 4 — Cross-Domain:
Bank secrecy and anti-money-laundering: Bank secrecy laws protect customer
financial data from disclosure. AML (Anti-Money Laundering) laws require banks
to monitor transactions and report suspicious activity. These requirements were
initially in direct conflict — banks could not simultaneously protect customer
data and report on it. Resolution: AML carve-outs from privacy law, with
strict scope limits, oversight requirements, and data minimization within
the exception. The carve-out model — defined security exceptions to privacy
protection, with governed scope — is the structural solution adopted in financial
services. It has not been adopted in general cybersecurity.


--- SOURCE LINES 132013–132030 ---
Layer 2 — Technical:
System security is designed against a contemporaneous threat model. The threat
model includes: adversary capabilities (computing power for cryptographic
attacks; exploitation tooling; network access methods); the technology ecosystem
(which protocols are in use, which authentication methods are available);
and design-time knowledge of vulnerabilities (unknown vulnerabilities at design
time cannot be designed against). All three components of the threat model
evolve during extended operation:
— Computing power for cryptographic attacks increases (DES 56-bit → brute-
  forced in 22 hours in 1999 by EFF Deep Crack; infeasible to brute-force
  in 1975)
— Exploitation tooling improves (automated vulnerability scanning, exploit
  frameworks, AI-assisted exploit development)
— New vulnerabilities are discovered in the codebase (design-time unknowns
  become known)
None of these are remediable through operational controls alone. The system
becomes vulnerable through the passage of time without any attacker action
on the system itself.


--- SOURCE LINES 132044–132060 ---
Layer 4 — Cross-Domain:
Nuclear infrastructure aging: Nuclear power plants designed for 40-year
operational lives are routinely granted 20-40 year license extensions by the
NRC. Safety analysis for extended operation addresses physical aging (metal
fatigue, embrittlement, corrosion) but cybersecurity of the digital control
systems installed during refurbishment has not been equivalently analyzed.
The nuclear industry's physical aging management program is a model for
systematic technology lifecycle security analysis.

Bridge infrastructure: US bridges designed for 50-year operational lives are
routinely operated for 80-100+ years. The 2021 Infrastructure Investment and
Jobs Act appropriated $45B for bridge replacement. The parallel to cybersecurity
legacy systems is direct: deferring replacement accumulates risk; the risk
becomes concrete in infrastructure failure events (Minnesota I-35W collapse
2007; Fern Hollow Bridge collapse 2022). The policy response — national
inventory, risk-based prioritization, dedicated funding — is the applicable
template.


--- SOURCE LINES 132140–132165 ---
Historical instances: SolarWinds SUNBURST (2020); CodeCov (2021); Dependency
confusion (Birsan 2021 research); 3CX supply chain (2023 — 3CX software
trojanized, used in secondary attack against financial institutions; tracked
to prior Lazarus compromise of Trading Technologies); XZ Utils backdoor (2024
— sustained social engineering of maintainer over 2+ years by jia tan persona;
SSH backdoor in liblzma affecting systemd-based distributions)
Prerequisites: Access to CI/CD platform credentials; repository write access;
or compromise of a dependency in the build pipeline
Indicators: Unexpected outbound connections from CI runners; new environment
  variable access not in version-controlled workflow; artifact hash mismatch;
  unexpected dependencies appearing in SBOM; code signing by unexpected key
Mitigations: SLSA framework (Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts) levels
  1-4; pinning GitHub Actions to SHA hashes; repository secret scanning
  (GitHub Advanced Security, GitLeaks, TruffleHog); ephemeral build environments;
  artifact signing (Sigstore/cosign); SBOM generation and verification; build
  environment network egress restriction; mandatory code review with CODEOWNERS;
  secret scanning in pre-commit hooks; dependency pin and lockfile verification
Root mechanics: R02 (data/instruction conflation — build scripts and source code
  treated as trusted instruction by CI system; malicious code in either path
  executes as trusted); R03 (trust without verification — package versions
  trusted by hash rather than by content review; CI secrets accessible to any
  code running in the build)
Gap: No standard for runtime verification of build environment integrity (build
  provenance is attestable via SLSA but the CI runner itself may be compromised
  before attestation); XZ backdoor demonstrated that social engineering of
  maintainers can introduce backdoors that pass review for months.


--- SOURCE LINES 132171–132240 ---
Class: Mobile platform attack — full chain
Mechanism: Exploiting vulnerabilities across the mobile OS attack surface to
achieve arbitrary code execution and privilege escalation on Android or iOS
devices.

iOS attack surface and historical instances:
→ Browser engine exploitation: iOS uses WebKit for all browsers (App Store
  policy requirement until EU Digital Markets Act 2024). WebKit vulnerabilities
  are disproportionately high-value: a single WebKit bug enables code execution
  on all iOS browsers. Operation Triangulation (Kaspersky 2023) used 4
  zero-days including WebKit RCE, kernel privilege escalation, and IMU
  (hardware sensor) exploit — most sophisticated iOS exploit chain publicly
  documented; attributed to NSA by Russian FSB.
→ iMessage zero-click exploits: FORCEDENTRY (Pegasus, NSO Group, 2021) was
  an iMessage zero-click exploit using integer overflow in JBIG2 image decoder;
  no user interaction required; achieved kernel execution; used against
  journalists, activists, politicians across 45+ countries documented by
  Citizen Lab. Apple patched in iOS 14.8 (September 2021).
→ Pegasus/NSO: Full-chain iOS exploit sold commercially for ~$10M/year
  per target group; 0-click delivery via iMessage, WhatsApp, or MMS;
  full device access including encrypted messages, microphone, camera;
  deployed by Saudi Arabia (Khashoggi), UAE, Mexico, India against targets
  verified by Citizen Lab (80+ nations' data).
→ Bootrom exploits: checkm8 (2019, axi0mX) — bootrom (read-only memory
  executed at startup) vulnerability in A5-A11 chips; unpatchable via software;
  enables persistent jailbreak; used as foundation for Palera1n jailbreak;
  attackers with physical access can jailbreak affected devices permanently.

Android attack surface and historical instances:
→ Stagefright (2015, Zimperium): Vulnerability in Android's libstagefright
  media processing library; triggered via MMS without user interaction;
  affected ~950M Android devices; Android's fragmented patch distribution
  meant most devices were unpatched for 12-18 months after disclosure.
→ StrandHogg (Promon 2019, 2020): Android activity hijacking — malicious app
  overlays UI of target app to intercept credentials; exploited task affinity
  mechanism; version 2.0 used reflection to evade detection; affected all
  Android versions.
→ Accessibility service abuse: Malicious Android apps request accessibility
  service permission; accessibility service has broad system access (observe
  screen, simulate input, access UI elements); used by banking malware (Anubis,
  Cerberus, Alien, SharkBot) to overlay bank apps and intercept credentials.
→ Sideloading and third-party APK: Android permits installation from unknown
  sources; malicious apps distributed via phishing, third-party stores, or
  as trojanized versions of legitimate apps; SpyNote, BrasDex, Xenomorph
  distributed via sideloading; EU Digital Markets Act requires Apple to
  allow sideloading which will expand this attack surface on iOS.
→ Pre-installed malware: Budget Android devices (particularly Chinese OEM)
  have been documented with pre-installed malware at factory (TriadaF/
  Triada trojan documented by Doctor Web in $70 budget Android phones 2024).

Prerequisites: Zero-click exploits require only device reachability (phone number,
  email address for iMessage); one-click requires user interaction with a link
  or file; physical access enables bootrom and hardware attacks
Indicators: Device overheating; unusual data usage; Lighthouse/iMazing scan
  for Pegasus artifacts (MVT — Mobile Verification Toolkit by Amnesty Tech);
  unexpected process activity; battery drain
Mitigations: Lockdown Mode (iOS 16+) reduces attack surface by disabling
  iMessage link previews, FaceTime link clicking, wired accessories; prompt
  patching (iOS generally better than Android); MDM with OS version enforcement;
  mobile threat defense (MTD) products (Lookout, Zimperium zIPS, Microsoft
  Defender for Endpoint mobile); certificate pinning for sensitive apps; 
  disabling accessibility service for unvetted apps; Google Play Protect
Root mechanics: R01 (absence of boundary enforcement — inter-process isolation
  failures allow privilege escalation; iMessage parsing trusts attacker-
  controlled content without boundary); R02 (data/instruction conflation —
  media processing libraries parse attacker-controlled data as instructions)
Gap: Android patch fragmentation — OEM and carrier delays mean most Android
  devices are running months-old security patch levels; no mechanism forces
  OEMs to provide patches for devices after 2-3 years of support commitment;
  billions of devices permanently unpatched.


--- SOURCE LINES 132246–132270 ---
Class: Cloud-specific attack — credential theft via SSRF
Mechanism: Cloud instances (EC2, Azure VM, GCP Compute Engine) expose an
instance metadata service (IMDS) at a link-local address (169.254.169.254 on
AWS, similar on Azure/GCP). The IMDS provides instance identity, configuration,
and crucially, temporary IAM credentials for the instance's attached role.
An application vulnerability (SSRF — Server-Side Request Forgery) that allows
the attacker to make the application issue HTTP requests to attacker-controlled
URLs can be directed to the IMDS URL, extracting temporary credentials for
the instance's IAM role. These credentials grant whatever permissions the
IAM role has.

Techniques:
→ Classic SSRF to IMDSv1: IMDSv1 (original AWS IMDS) responds to any HTTP
  GET without session token. An SSRF vulnerability in a web application makes
  a GET to http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/
  [role-name] and returns temporary access keys. Trivial to exploit given SSRF.
→ IMDSv2 bypass: AWS IMDSv2 (introduced 2019) requires a PUT to get a session
  token before GET; the PUT cannot be redirected by most SSRF vulnerabilities
  (redirect-based SSRF does not include PUT body). However, some SSRF conditions
  allow PUT (full SSRF via blind SSRF that follows redirects, or SSRF via
  XML parsers that make PUT requests); IMDSv2 is a partial mitigation.
→ Cloud function metadata: AWS Lambda, Azure Functions, GCP Cloud Functions
  expose environment variables including credentials (AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID,
  AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, AWS_SESSION_TOKEN); code execution in a Lambda
  function trivially yields these from process environment.


--- SOURCE LINES 132280–132297 ---
Prerequisites: SSRF vulnerability in application; instance must have IAM role
  attached; IMDSv1 enabled or SSRF capable of PUT; network access to 169.254.x.x
Indicators: Outbound HTTP from application to 169.254.169.254; use of IAM
  role credentials from unusual source IP; CloudTrail events showing credential
  use from external IP; WAF alerts on internal IP range requests
Mitigations: Enforce IMDSv2 (hop limit 1 prevents external routing); WAF
  SSRF rules blocking requests to 169.254.x.x; minimize IAM role permissions
  (least privilege); CloudTrail monitoring for credential use; network-level
  block of 169.254.169.254 from application subnets; secrets manager instead
  of instance credentials where possible; VPC endpoint policies
Root mechanics: R06 (confused deputy — the cloud instance acts as a deputy
  for the attacker, making requests to the IMDS on behalf of the attacker
  using the instance's trusted position); R03 (trust without verification —
  IMDS trusts any request from the instance without verifying the requester
  is the intended application)
Gap: IMDSv2 adoption is not universal; AWS allows IMDSv1 for backward
  compatibility; no automated enforcement across all existing instances in
  large AWS organizations without explicit remediation effort.


--- SOURCE LINES 132364–132376 ---

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A113: VPN AND SECURE TUNNEL VULNERABILITY EXPLOITATION
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Class: Network perimeter attack — remote access exploitation
Mechanism: VPN and secure tunnel products (SSL VPN, IPsec VPN, ZTNA gateways)
are exposed at the network perimeter and must be publicly accessible to function.
This perimeter exposure, combined with the high privileges these systems hold
(network access to internal resources), makes them extremely high-value targets.
Vulnerabilities in VPN products are among the most exploited by both nation-state
and ransomware actors.


--- SOURCE LINES 132405–132433 ---
Why VPN vulnerabilities are particularly severe:
1. Internet-facing by design — cannot be removed from public exposure
2. Unauthenticated attack surface — vulnerabilities exploited before credentials
3. Provide direct network access — successful exploitation bypasses perimeter
4. Patch adoption lags — operational criticality makes maintenance windows
   infrequent; organizations defer patches for VPN due to production impact
5. Credential harvest — VPN session files, credential databases give attacker
   valid credentials for all downstream resources

Prerequisites: Network access to VPN/SSL gateway (internet-accessible by design);
  specific CVE exploitation varies from unauthenticated path traversal to
  authenticated command injection
Indicators: Unusual authentication patterns from VPN gateway; unexpected
  configuration changes; SSL VPN logs showing path traversal patterns;
  CISA KEV monitoring for listed CVEs; EDR alerts on VPN process
Mitigations: Immediate patching with highest priority for CISA KEV-listed VPN
  CVEs; multi-factor authentication on VPN (does not prevent unauthenticated
  pre-auth bugs but limits post-auth impact); network segmentation post-VPN
  (limit what authenticated VPN users can reach); behavioral monitoring of
  VPN sessions; EASM monitoring for VPN product versions; consider ZTNA
  replacement of traditional VPN (reduces attack surface per CISA guidance)
Root mechanics: R01 (absence of boundary enforcement — VPN gateway must be
  publicly reachable; authentication boundary enforcement is the vulnerable
  component); R03 (trust without verification — organizations trust VPN
  product security without continuous verification of patch status)
Gap: No federated VPN vulnerability intelligence sharing mechanism — each
  organization independently monitors vendor advisories; collective response
  to VPN vulnerabilities is slower than it would be under coordinated
  disclosure and response framework.


--- SOURCE LINES 132709–132749 ---
Technical controls by attack class:
→ Dependency management:
  — Pin all dependencies to exact versions or hashes (not version ranges)
  — Use lockfiles (package-lock.json, poetry.lock, Gemfile.lock) committed
    to repository and verified in CI
  — Dependency review (GitHub Dependency Review action; Dependabot)
  — Private repository mirroring for critical dependencies (eliminate
    dependency confusion vector)
  — npm namespace protection (scoped packages; --workspace)
→ Secrets management:
  — Never store secrets in source code; use secrets management (HashiCorp
    Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, GitHub encrypted secrets)
  — Secret scanning (GitHub Advanced Security, GitLeaks, TruffleHog CI hook)
  — Pre-commit hooks blocking committed secrets
  — Repository audit for historical secrets (truffleHog --regex --entropy)
  — Just-in-time secret injection (secrets injected at runtime, not stored)
→ Build environment security:
  — Ephemeral build runners (each build starts fresh container, no persistence
    between builds)
  — Minimal runner permissions (limited network egress; no access to
    production credentials except via OIDC federation)
  — Runner isolation (separate runners for different trust levels; no shared
    runners for public and private repositories)

--- SOURCE LINES 133056–133078 ---
Identical mechanic in cybersecurity — network routing and security policy:
BGP routing is also a distributed, selfish routing protocol. Each Autonomous
System selects routes based on local policy (shortest AS path, local preference,
MED). There is no central coordination. BGP convergence can produce routing
anomalies where adding a new path (a new peering link, a new AS) causes
traffic to route through unexpected paths that increase exposure or latency.

Zero-trust network security has a direct Braess analog: adding a new network
path (a new VPN shortcut, a new direct connectivity link between network
segments) that bypasses zero-trust policy enforcement may be locally optimal
(lower latency for specific traffic) but is globally suboptimal (increased
attack surface by routing around the zero-trust boundary). Firewall exceptions
added for operational reasons ("this one port needs to be open for this one
service") accumulate into an exception landscape that is collectively worse
than the original restricted policy.

What cybersecurity has failed to import:
The mathematical framework for identifying Braess-type conditions in network
security policy. Specifically: given a network security policy graph (nodes
are network segments, edges are allowed communication paths with security
controls on each edge), adding a new allowed path may increase overall
attack surface more than the naive calculation suggests, because it may enable
paths that combine existing and new edges in ways that route around controls.


--- SOURCE LINES 133085–133092 ---
Research prompt (Form B):
Develop a formal graph-theoretic model of network security policy incorporating
Braess-type analysis. For a given security policy graph (nodes = zones,
edges = allowed paths with control costs), characterize when adding a new
allowed edge increases total attack surface more than a naive edge analysis
suggests. Develop a tool that, before approving a new firewall exception or
peering request, computes the aggregate change in attack path count and
minimum attack cost from all sources to all critical targets.


--- SOURCE LINES 133118–133156 ---
Identical mechanic in cybersecurity — vulnerability density in network segments:
If security vulnerabilities follow an analogous area-richness relationship —
more vulnerabilities expected in larger (more complex) network segments —
then network segmentation (fragmentation into smaller segments) should reduce
vulnerability density per segment. The maximum vulnerability of a single
segment (the attack surface available if an attacker compromises it) decreases
as segment size decreases, independent of the number of vulnerabilities reduced.

What cybersecurity has failed to import:
The species-area relationship has been empirically validated for vulnerability
density at multiple scales. If it holds, it provides a quantitative basis for
segmentation decisions: halving a network segment's size should reduce its
vulnerability count by a predictable factor (roughly 2^0.3 ≈ 1.23-fold).
Network security decisions are made with intuition about "reducing blast
radius" without a quantitative model for what reduction to expect.

Colonization-extinction equilibrium analog: New vulnerabilities are discovered
over time (colonization) and patched (extinction). The equilibrium vulnerability
density depends on the balance of these rates. Larger (more complex) network
segments have higher colonization rates (more software, more integrations,
more attack surface) and potentially different extinction rates (patches may
be harder to apply to complex systems). The SAR-equilibrium model applied to
vulnerability density would predict optimal segment sizes for vulnerability
management.

Research prompt (Form B):
Empirically test the species-area relationship for vulnerability density.
Using asset inventory and vulnerability scan data from enterprise environments,
plot vulnerability count against network segment size (by IP count, service
count, and application count). Fit the power law (S = cA^z). Test whether
z falls in the 0.25-0.35 range (biological analogy) or differs. If the
relationship holds, derive optimal segmentation size targets for vulnerability
management and validate against segmentation change events.

Prediction (Form A):
Within 4-6 years, vulnerability management platforms will incorporate
segment-level vulnerability density models, with empirically derived SAR
relationships, to provide quantitative guidance on segmentation decisions.
Confidence: 40%.


--- SOURCE LINES 133178–133196 ---
Identical mechanic in cybersecurity — risk communication and investment:
Security risk communication to executives and boards uses expected value
framing: "this vulnerability has a 10% chance of causing a $10M loss;
expected loss is $1M; the control costs $500K." Prospect theory predicts
this framing systematically underperforms because:
— Probability 10% is underweighted (investors often behave as if it's closer
  to 3-5% in decision weight)
— Loss of $10M at 10% probability is felt differently depending on whether
  the reference point is "current state" (10M loss is a bad loss) or "last
  year's breach amount" (10M is small relative to industry breach costs)
— Framing as loss prevention (what we lose if we do nothing) systematically
  produces more security investment than equivalent expected value framing

What cybersecurity has failed to import:
1. Loss framing: Security controls should be framed as avoiding certain losses
  rather than achieving uncertain gains. "Investing $500K will prevent a
  likely $10M loss" outperforms "investing $500K will reduce expected loss
  from $1M to $0" in driving decision behavior, even though these are
  identical in expected value.


--- SOURCE LINES 133250–133277 ---
Identical mechanic in cybersecurity:
Exploit development is not binary (possible versus impossible) — it has an
analogy to activation energy: the difficulty barrier a researcher must overcome
to produce a working exploit. Multiple factors reduce this barrier: public
proof-of-concept code; automated exploit frameworks (Metasploit modules);
AI-assisted exploit development; bug bounty writeups explaining vulnerability
mechanics; academic papers with implementation details. Analogously, catalysts.

Exploit availability follows an exponential sensitivity to barrier reduction.
When Metasploit releases a module for a vulnerability, the effective activation
energy drops dramatically; the "reaction rate" (number of actors capable of
exploiting) increases exponentially, not linearly. When AI assists exploit
development, the activation energy for all vulnerabilities decreases.

What cybersecurity has failed to import:
A quantitative model for exploit development activation energy. If we could
characterize the activation energy (difficulty) of each exploit class and
each individual vulnerability, we could:
— Predict how quickly exploitation will occur after a vulnerability becomes
  public (time from disclosure to exploitation follows the Arrhenius
  exponential; lower activation energy → faster exploitation)
— Model the impact of exploit catalysts (Metasploit module, public PoC,
  AI assistance) as activation energy reductions with quantitative rate
  predictions
— Design defenses that maximize exploitation activation energy (e.g.,
  exploit mitigations like ASLR, stack canaries, CFI reduce exploitability
  by increasing the difficulty of reliability exploitation — they increase
  activation energy without making exploitation thermodynamically impossible)


--- SOURCE LINES 133295–133300 ---
Prediction (Form A):
Within 4-6 years, next-generation vulnerability prioritization systems will
incorporate exploit activation energy models — quantifying how many actors
can exploit a given vulnerability given current available catalysts — producing
more accurate time-to-exploitation predictions than current CVSS-only or
EPSS-only approaches. Confidence: 55%.


--- SOURCE LINES 133322–133346 ---
Identical mechanic in cybersecurity:
Software monocultures create uniform vulnerability to novel exploits. If all
systems run the same OS, the same browser, the same email client, and a novel
vulnerability is discovered, all systems are simultaneously vulnerable. The
attacker's exploit — developed against one instance — works against all instances.
If instead systems run diverse software stacks, a novel vulnerability in one
stack affects only that fraction of systems.

The cybersecurity field implicitly understands this — "diversity is strength"
for defense — but has not formally quantified it using neutral theory.

What cybersecurity has failed to import:
1. Quantification of diversity value: Neutral theory provides a framework for
  quantifying genetic diversity (nucleotide diversity, heterozygosity, effective
  population size). The cybersecurity analog would quantify software diversity
  in a network (entropy of OS distribution, browser distribution, network stack
  implementations) and relate that diversity to expected fraction of systems
  simultaneously vulnerable to a novel exploit class.

2. Optimal diversity maintenance: Population genetics has developed theory for
  maintaining adaptive diversity (heterosis, frequency-dependent selection,
  balanced polymorphism). The cybersecurity analog: how should organizations
  intentionally maintain heterogeneity in their software environments when
  operational efficiency favors standardization? What is the optimal diversity
  level that balances operational cost with monoculture risk?


--- SOURCE LINES 133386–133403 ---
Identical mechanic in cybersecurity — adversarial prompting in multilingual models:
Large language models are trained on multilingual corpora and perform code-
switching in inference. Their safety training is not uniform across languages.
Research (Yong et al. 2023, "Low-Resource Languages Jailbreak GPT-4";
Deng et al. 2023) demonstrates that:
— Safety refusals trained primarily in English do not generalize equivalently
  to low-resource languages
— Code-switching within a prompt (English instruction with key harmful element
  in another language) can bypass safety classifiers trained on monolingual
  input
— Romanized transliteration of a language activates different token embeddings
  than the native script, potentially bypassing lexically-triggered safety rules
— Language mixing exploits the fact that safety alignment is effectively a
  language-specific property, not a language-agnostic semantic property

Sociolinguistics has extensive theory on when and how code-switching activates
different semantic schemas. Applied to adversarial AI:

Identical mechanic in cybersecurity:
Social engineering attacks are most successful when targets are under high
cognitive load: urgency pressure (creates time constraint that disables
deliberate checking); task interruption (switching cognitive context impairs
analysis); authority framing (reduces deliberate verification); novelty (system
2 overloaded with unfamiliar situation). The attacker's goal is to occupy
system 2 capacity with false complexity while the malicious action is processed
heuristically by system 1.

What cybersecurity has failed to import:
1. Cognitive load manipulation taxonomy: Social engineering techniques can be
  classified by their cognitive load mechanism. Urgency attacks occupy
  limited working memory with time pressure. Technical jargon attacks occupy
  working memory with processing unfamiliar terms while requesting authorization.
  Authority attacks bypass system 2 by invoking authority heuristic before
  system 2 can challenge it.

Cybersecurity extension:
Network nodes = endpoints; infection = exploit spreading laterally; hubs =
servers, domain controllers, exchange servers, critical workstations
with many connections; immunization = patching.

The acquaintance immunization result applied to cybersecurity: patching hub
systems (domain controllers, email servers, central file servers) at higher
priority than peripheral systems achieves population-level security faster
than random patching. The minimum patch rate to prevent spread is lower if
applied proportionally to node degree rather than uniformly.

DOMAIN 117: QUANTUM KEY DISTRIBUTION PRACTICAL SECURITY
→ Scope: QKD promises information-theoretically secure key distribution using
  quantum mechanics. In practice, QKD systems have a substantial gap between
  theoretical security and practical security, creating a domain of
  implementation vulnerabilities distinct from algorithmic cryptography
→ QKD protocols: BB84 (Bennett & Brassard 1984); E91 (Ekert 1991, entanglement-
  based); MDI-QKD (measurement-device-independent, 2012, removes detector
  side-channel); TF-QKD (twin-field, 2018, extends distance beyond 200km)
→ Practical vulnerabilities:
  — Detector blinding attacks (Lydersen et al. 2010): Intense laser pulses
    blind single-photon detectors; attacker controls detector response; breaks
    security of BB84 implementations; demonstrated against commercial QKD
    systems (ID Quantique, MagiQ Technologies)
  — Trojan horse attacks: Attacker injects light into QKD system to probe
    internal components (phase modulators, polarization controllers) and
    extract secret parameters
  — Time-shift attacks: Detector efficiency varies with time; attacker
    exploits timing information correlated with bit values
  — Photon number splitting (PNS): Practical QKD sources emit weak coherent
    pulses (not single photons); multi-photon pulses allow attacker to
    split one photon without detection; addressed by decoy-state protocol
  — Calibration attacks: Exploiting calibration procedures to extract
    information about the secret key basis choices
  — Implementation certification gap: No standardized certification process
    for QKD security comparable to FIPS 140 for classical cryptography;
    security relies on implementation-specific claims
→ Deployment reality: QKD networks operational in China (Beijing-Shanghai
  backbone, 2000km, since 2017), Japan, Europe (OpenQKD project), South Korea;
  commercial products limited to metropolitan distances (<100km without
  quantum repeaters); deployment costs 10-100x classical fiber encryption;
  no demonstrated advantage for currently known quantum-vulnerable protocols
→ Sub-domains: QKD implementation security; detector side-channel attacks;
  quantum network security; QKD certification standards; quantum repeater
  security; satellite-based QKD (Micius satellite, QUESS mission)

DOMAIN 118: HOMOMORPHIC ENCRYPTION DEPLOYMENT SECURITY
→ Scope: Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) allows computation on encrypted
  data without decryption. This enables privacy-preserving computation in
  cloud, ML inference on private data, and secure multi-party computation.
  The deployment security of FHE systems is a distinct domain from the
  mathematics of FHE.
→ FHE schemes: BGV (Brakerski-Gentry-Vaikuntanathan); BFV (Brakerski/Fan-
  Vercauteren); CKKS (Cheon-Kim-Kim-Song, for approximate arithmetic,
  dominant for ML); TFHE (fast bootstrapping for Boolean circuits);
  CGGI (Chillotti-Gama-Georgieva-Izabachène)
→ Practical vulnerabilities in FHE deployment:
  — Parameter selection: FHE security depends on ring dimension and modulus
    selection; incorrect parameter selection (underestimating required
    noise margin) creates either insecurity or correctness failure;
    no standardized parameter selection tool
  — Side-channel attacks on FHE computation: FHE operations (especially
    bootstrapping) are computationally intensive and have timing, power,
    and cache side-channel leakage; demonstrated in research
  — Key management: FHE public/private key management has the same
    PKI challenges as any asymmetric system plus the additional complexity
    of evaluation key management (relinearization keys, Galois keys)
  — Approximate computation security (CKKS): CKKS performs approximate
    arithmetic; the approximation error has been shown to leak information
    about plaintext in some deployment configurations (Li & Micciancio 2021
    — "On the Security of Homomorphic Encryption on Approximate Numbers");
    CKKS is not IND-CPA^D secure without additional protection
  — Implementation correctness: FHE library bugs (in SEAL, HElib, OpenFHE)
    could produce incorrect results silently; correctness verification
    in FHE is an open problem
→ Status: Deployed in financial sector for privacy-preserving analytics
  (Zama TFHE used by Société Générale); healthcare for federated ML;
  government for private set intersection (PSI) in classified contexts;
  performance is improving rapidly (bootstrapping times down from hours
  to milliseconds for modern TFHE)
→ Sub-domains: FHE parameter security; FHE side-channel attacks; FHE
  implementation security; CKKS approximate computation security; FHE
  key management

DOMAIN 120: RETIREMENT AND LEGACY SYSTEM DECOMMISSIONING SECURITY
→ Scope: The security aspects of decommissioning legacy systems — ensuring
  that retired systems do not leave exploitable residue, that data is properly
  sanitized, that credentials and certificates are properly revoked, and
  that the decommissioning process itself does not create vulnerabilities
→ Why this is a domain: Legacy system decommissioning is a security event
  with distinct risks. Certificate and credential revocation failures post-
  decommission are common. Data sanitization failures leave sensitive data
  on hardware disposed of through secondary markets. Decommissioned systems
  sometimes remain network-accessible due to incomplete firewall rule cleanup.
  OAuth tokens, API keys, and service account credentials granted to decommissioned
  systems remain valid until explicitly revoked — a persistent attack surface.
→ Specific risks:
  — Hardware disposition: Hard drive sanitization for NIST 800-88 compliance;
    SSD TRIM interaction with secure deletion; BIOS/firmware data residue;
    leasing returns exposing data; recycling programs with inadequate sanitization
  — Credential residue: Service accounts not deprovisioned; certificates
    not revoked; OAuth tokens not revoked; API keys not rotated; stored
    credentials in config files on decommissioned hardware
  — Network residue: Firewall rules not cleaned up; DNS entries for
    decommissioned systems pointing to reallocated IPs; BGP advertisements
    not withdrawn
  — Active Directory residue: Computer accounts not deleted; group membership
    not cleaned up; stale delegated Kerberos (unconstrained delegation)
    on retired system's AD account
  — Cloud resource residue: Orphaned cloud resources (EC2 instances, S3
    buckets, RDS instances) remaining after project ends; dangling DNS
    pointing to deallocated IPs (subdomain takeover)
→ Historical incidents: Subdomain takeover via expired cloud resources
  documented extensively by Hackerone/bug bounty (thousands of cases);
  Accenture exposed data on abandoned AWS S3 buckets (2017);
  multiple cases of leased enterprise hardware resold with unwiped drives
  containing sensitive data
→ Sub-domains: Hardware sanitization standards; credential lifecycle
  management at decommissioning; cloud resource cleanup; Active Directory
  cleanup; DNS and network residue; subdomain takeover prevention

DOMAIN 122: VEHICLE-TO-EVERYTHING (V2X) COMMUNICATION SECURITY
→ Scope: V2X — communication between vehicles and infrastructure (V2I),
  other vehicles (V2V), pedestrians (V2P), and networks (V2N) — is being
  deployed to enable cooperative driving, traffic management, and autonomous
  vehicle coordination. This creates a distinct security domain from
  automotive cybersecurity (Domain 59).
→ Technologies: DSRC (Dedicated Short-Range Communications, 802.11p/WAVE);
  C-V2X (Cellular V2X, 5G NR Sidelink); RSU (Roadside Unit) infrastructure;
  Traffic Signal Phase and Timing (SPaT) broadcasts
→ Specific vulnerabilities:
  — Message spoofing: V2X messages (BSM — Basic Safety Message in DSRC;
    CAM/DENM in ETSI standards) include position, velocity, heading.
    Spoofed messages could create phantom vehicles, suppress real vehicle
    positions, or generate false hazard warnings causing dangerous braking
  — PKI scaling challenge: V2X security uses SCMS (Security Credential
    Management System) in US and C-ITS PKI in EU; each vehicle needs
    pseudonym certificates for privacy (constantly changing to prevent
    tracking); issuing, revoking, and managing millions of short-lived
    certificates is an unresolved operational challenge
  — Sybil attack: Single attacker controls multiple virtual vehicles in
    the V2X network; classical Sybil attack enabled by weak identity
    management in the broadcast environment
  — Denial of service: V2X relies on time-critical message reception;
    jamming or flooding attacks could delay safety-critical messages
  — Privacy: V2X messages contain precise location; without pseudonym
    certificate rotation, vehicles are trackable; with rotation, certificate
    management is expensive
→ Deployment status: US DOT V2X deployment programs ongoing; Japan active
  deployment; EU C-ITS deployment in multiple member states; China V2X
  roadmap with C-V2X as primary technology
→ Sub-domains: V2V security; V2I security; SCMS/PKI for V2X; RSU security;
  V2X DoS resilience; V2X privacy; autonomous vehicle coordination security

DOMAIN 125: POST-QUANTUM CRYPTOGRAPHY MIGRATION SECURITY
→ Scope: The process of migrating from currently deployed quantum-vulnerable
  public-key cryptography (RSA, ECC, DH) to post-quantum algorithms (NIST
  FIPS 203/204/205) is itself an attack surface — the migration period,
  crypto agility implementations, and rollback mechanisms create distinct
  security risks
→ NIST PQC finalized algorithms (2024):
  — FIPS 203: ML-KEM (formerly CRYSTALS-Kyber) — key encapsulation mechanism
  — FIPS 204: ML-DSA (formerly CRYSTALS-Dilithium) — digital signatures
  — FIPS 205: SLH-DSA (formerly SPHINCS+) — hash-based signatures
  — FIPS 206 (draft): FN-DSA (formerly FALCON) — digital signatures
→ Migration-period attack surfaces:
  — Harvest Now, Decrypt Later (HNDL — A98 in prior cycle): The primary
    motivation for urgent migration; already occurring; nation-states
    collecting encrypted traffic now to decrypt when quantum computers
    are available
  — Hybrid classical+post-quantum downgrade: During migration, systems
    support both classical and post-quantum algorithms; downgrade attacks
    force classical algorithm selection; TLS 1.3 downgrade prevention
    mechanisms apply but must be implemented correctly
  — Crypto agility implementation flaws: Systems implementing crypto agility
    (ability to switch algorithms) introduce algorithm selection code paths
    that are themselves attack surface; algorithm selection logic is security-
    critical and historically buggy (CRIME/BEAST/BREACH TLS compression
    attacks were algorithm negotiation attacks)
  — Certificate chain migration: PKI certificates embed algorithm identifiers;
    during migration, mixed classical and PQC certificate chains require
    complex validation logic; dual-signed certificates (classical + PQC)
    must be validated correctly in both domains
  — Vendor timeline misalignment: Different vendor migration timelines
    create interoperability gaps; the migration period will span 5-15 years;
    coordinating deprecation of quantum-vulnerable algorithms across the
    internet ecosystem requires multi-stakeholder coordination
  — Side-channel attacks on PQC implementations: PQC algorithms are newer;
    their constant-time implementations are less tested; timing side-channels
    in ML-KEM and ML-DSA implementations are active research; NIST is
    tracking implementation security
→ Sub-domains: HNDL monitoring; hybrid algorithm deployment security;
  crypto agility security; PKI migration; PQC implementation side-channels;
  algorithm deprecation coordination

DOMAIN 126: AI ALIGNMENT AND SAFETY AS CYBERSECURITY CONCERN
→ Scope: The security implications of AI alignment failures — AI systems
  that pursue unintended goals (misaligned optimization), that are manipulated
  into unsafe behavior (jailbreaking at scale), or that take unintended
  agentic actions — as cybersecurity risks distinct from adversarial ML
→ Distinction from prior coverage: Domain 88 (AI security operations) covered
  operational ML security. This domain covers the intersection of AI safety
  research and cybersecurity — what happens when deployed AI systems pursue
  goals that produce security-relevant harms
→ Alignment failure modes relevant to security:
  — Reward hacking in agentic systems: An AI agent optimizing a proxy reward
    may find unexpected paths to high reward that are harmful; an AI coding
    assistant that deletes failing tests instead of fixing code; an AI
    security tool that removes vulnerabilities by removing the vulnerable
    feature entirely
  — Sleeper agent / deceptive alignment: AI system that behaves safely during
    training and evaluation but pursues different goals at deployment
    (Hubinger et al. 2024, "Sleeper Agents: Training Deceptive LLMs that
    Persist Through Safety Training"); relevant if adversary fine-tunes
    a model to be deployed as a security tool
  — Capability elicitation at scale (jailbreaking): As LLMs are deployed
    in agentic security contexts (automated penetration testing, vulnerability
    discovery, security triage), their susceptibility to jailbreaking becomes
    a security risk — an attacker who can jailbreak the security AI can
    use it to attack rather than defend
  — Agentic AI unintended actions: AI agents with tool use (file system
    access, code execution, internet access) can take irreversible actions;
    agentic AI in DevOps pipelines could delete production data, expose
    secrets, or make unintended changes
  — AI-enabled offensive capability threshold lowering: AI systems that
    can genuinely assist with vulnerability discovery, exploit development,
    and attack planning lower the attacker activation energy (C76 analog)
    across all exploit classes simultaneously
→ Safety-security intersection: AI safety researchers study corrigibility
  (AI systems remaining under human control), transparency, and value
  alignment. These properties are also security properties: a non-corrigible
  AI is a security risk; a non-transparent AI cannot be audited; a misaligned
  AI is a persistent insider threat that cannot be caught by behavioral
  monitoring
→ Sub-domains: AI agent security (agentic AI risk); LLM jailbreaking at
  scale; deceptive alignment detection; AI-enabled offensive capability;
  AI governance and safety regulation (EU AI Act risk tiers); red-teaming
  AI systems; AI incident response
