CONVERGENCE FINDING 268 — PATTERN 36.2 (MANDATE SPLIT) AS UNIVERSAL TRANSITION PATTERN
Pattern 36.2 (confirmed 3 instances) predicts a universal transition structure
for any safety-critical domain that receives a cybersecurity mandate:
  Phase 1: Vulnerability class identified; research/red team disclosure
  Phase 2: Regulatory awareness; guidance issued (non-binding initially)
  Phase 3: Mandate issued for new production (binding)
  Phase 4: Transition window (new = mandated; existing = unprotected)
  Phase 5: Full transition (one equipment lifecycle; 15-30 years)
  The attack surface shrinks at the retirement rate of legacy equipment;
  in no documented domain has the transition been accelerated by recall
  or mandatory retrofit except for: (a) life-critical recalls with
  demonstrated patient harm (rare); (b) recall-equivalent UEFI DBX update
  (software only; no hardware; effectively zero cost to deploy)
  New domain predictions (not yet at Phase 3):
    Satellite bus systems: software-defined radios on satellite;
    groundstation uplink authentication varies; no mandate yet
    AI/ML model inference hardware: speculative execution analogs;
    no security mandate for AI accelerators
    Medical imaging devices (MRI, CT): DICOM protocol; minimal auth;
    not yet mandated beyond general FDA 2023 guidance
  Pattern 36.2: CONFIRMED (3 instances); predictive framework established

  Domains adopting memory-safe languages:
    Android kernel drivers: Rust in Linux kernel (v6.1 Rust support 2022)
    Windows: Microsoft building Rust components in Windows (2023)
    Chrome: Chromium Rust components; memory-safe browsers
    Embedded: Rust-embedded working group; automotive (Ferrocene Rust)
  Effect: memory safety vulnerabilities eliminated in new code;
  existing C/C++ codebase remains vulnerability source for decades
  Pattern 36.2 instance (candidate): new code mandate (memory-safe) +
  legacy C/C++ codebase exempt; transition will require one full rewrite
  cycle; estimated 20-30 years for critical infrastructure

--- SOURCE LINES 171524–171530 ---
Memory corruption vulnerabilities — buffer overflows, use-after-free, double-
free, integer overflow leading to incorrect size, type confusion — are the
implementation-layer substrate beneath many higher-level attacks:
  Browser exploitation: heap spray + UAF → code execution → sandbox escape
  Kernel exploitation: stack overflow in syscall handler → privilege escalation
  Parser attacks: malformed input → heap buffer overflow in parser → RCE
  ICS: memory corruption in HMI software → attacker control of HMI


--- SOURCE LINES 171537–171558 ---
Google Project Zero / Microsoft MSRC data:
  ~70% of critical vulnerabilities in large C/C++ codebases are memory safety
  class; consistent across Chrome, Windows, Android, iOS, Firefox
  This is not a decreasing trend in absolute terms (total critical vulns
  increasing with codebase size); memory-safe language adoption reduces
  new code contribution but legacy C/C++ remains the dominant source

Memory corruption exploit primitives:
  ASLR (Address Space Layout Randomization): randomizes base addresses;
    defeated by information leak vulnerability (read primitive → leak
    heap/stack address → defeat ASLR → control flow hijack)
  DEP/NX (Data Execution Prevention): marks data pages non-executable;
    defeated by ROP (Return-Oriented Programming) — chains existing
    code gadgets without injecting new code
  CFI (Control Flow Integrity): limits valid call/return targets;
    defeated by partial CFI implementations, type confusion, shadow stack
    bypass via info leak + overwrite
  Stack canaries: random value on stack; overflow detection;
    defeated by info leak (read canary value; reproduce in overflow)
  Pattern: each memory safety mitigation creates a corresponding bypass
  technique; mitigations narrow the exploit path but do not eliminate it
  Only memory-safe language eliminates the class in new code

CONVERGENCE FINDING 269 — R10.5 COUNTER-EXAMPLE CYCLE 3: TIMING ORACLE
Candidate: Timing oracle in RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 (Bleichenbacher 1998)
  Mechanism: RSA decryption oracle returns timing difference between
  'invalid padding' and 'valid padding with wrong MAC'; adaptive chosen-
  ciphertext attack recovers plaintext in O(million) queries
  R10.5 fit check:
    Performance optimization? RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 padding check is not
    a performance optimization; it is a correctness check; timing
    difference arises from early exit on invalid padding (early-exit
    IS a performance optimization: stop processing as soon as error detected)
    BUT: the fundamental vulnerability is the oracle itself (returning
    distinguishable error), not the timing side-channel specifically;
    timing is one channel; error codes are another; this is more R10.1
    (specification ambiguity in how errors should be signaled) or a
    distinct class
  Classification verdict:
    Bleichenbacher: RSA padding oracle = specification did not mandate
    constant-time error handling; implementations that exit early on
    padding error create distinguishable timing; this combines:
    R10.1 (spec ambiguity: PKCS#1 v1.5 does not mandate constant-time)
    R10.5a (optimization leakage: early-exit timing is optimization)
    Dual classification is possible: R10.1 ∩ R10.5a
    Does not require R10.6: fits within existing taxonomy
  R10.5 counter-example: NOT FOUND (cycle 3 of 5; taxonomy holds)


--- SOURCE LINES 172113–172136 ---
CONVERGENCE FINDING 271 — GPS AS UNIVERSAL TIME/POSITION SUBSTRATE
GPS spoofing (Pattern 37.3) reveals GPS as the universal substrate for
position and time in modern infrastructure. The attack surface is:
  Position: navigation, AIS, ADS-B, V2X, vehicle tracking, emergency dispatch
  Time: financial timestamps, LTE base stations, power grid synchronization,
    NTP hierarchy, distributed system consensus, PTP (IEEE 1588)
A single GPS spoofing capability attacks ALL these systems simultaneously.
The unifying property: all these systems trusted civilian GPS (L1 C/A)
because it was the only available precision time/position source when
designed; there was no alternative; authentication was not available.
This is R01 at infrastructure level: ambient authority granted to any
signal on the GPS L1 frequency with sufficient power.
LAW-1 application:
  Civilian GPS L1 is unauthenticated; OSNMA (Galileo) is emerging but
  not deployed; GPS M-code is authenticated but not civilian-accessible;
  infrastructure depending on civilian GPS cannot be migrated without
  hardware receiver replacement across all affected systems.
  The coordinated receiver upgrade timeline (NTP servers, financial systems,
  power grid relays, V2X) is decades; GPS spoofing is a LAW-1 class problem
  for the dependent civilian infrastructure.
  Note: this is a LAW-1 extension — the protocol (GPS L1) is secure-at-design
  in military application (P(Y) code, M-code) but the civilian version was
  intentionally downgraded (Selective Availability era); the vulnerability
  is deliberate civilian signal design, not oversight.


--- SOURCE LINES 172161–172176 ---
CONVERGENCE FINDING 273 — AI/ML AS BOTH ATTACK SURFACE AND DEFENSE TOOL
The AI/ML security domain (D329) exhibits a bidirectional property:
  ML as defense: anomaly detection, malware classification, NLP for
  phishing detection, face recognition for access control
  ML as attack surface: adversarial examples evade ML defenses;
  model supply chain poisoning undermines ML classifier integrity;
  prompt injection exploits LLM agents; model theft extracts IP
  LAW-2 extended: ML detection is a new perimeter; adversarial techniques
  cross it; but ML also creates new attack primitives (deepfakes, AI-generated
  phishing, automated vulnerability discovery); the dynamic is bidirectional,
  not merely defensive
  Finding: ML is the first security technology class that simultaneously
  generates new defense layers AND new attack primitives at approximately
  equal rates. Prior technologies (firewalls, PKI, MFA) primarily added
  defense; attackers adapted. ML generates novel attack classes (not just
  adaptations of prior attacks).

--- SOURCE LINES 172428–172436 ---
The quantum-safe migration is structurally different from normal vulnerability
patching in one critical way: the window to act is measured in years, the
scope is global, and the consequence of failure is retroactive (HNDL data
collected NOW becomes decryptable in the future even if migration occurs later).
This creates a different urgency calculus than typical patching:
  Normal patch: vulnerability discovered → exploit available NOW → patch NOW
  PQC migration: threat arrives in ~2030 → migrate before 2030 → data
    collected before migration and retained by adversary is retroactively exposed
  The urgency is measured by HNDL storage horizon, not exploit availability

--- SOURCE LINES 172917–172932 ---
  Alternative new class candidate: R10.6 — FEATURE-SECURITY CONTEXT MISMATCH
    A feature designed for trusted context is deployed in untrusted context;
    the feature's capabilities (code execution, network access, dynamic loading)
    become vulnerabilities when input comes from adversary
    Instances:
      Pickle: object serialization with code execution; safe in trusted context
      JNDI in Log4j: directory service lookup; safe in trusted context;
        attacker-controlled log content = untrusted context
      XXE: external entity resolution; safe in trusted context;
        user-supplied XML = untrusted context
      SSRF: URL fetching by server; safe for internal use; external user
        controlling URL = untrusted context
      eval() in JavaScript: safe for trusted code; user input to eval = disaster
    This is conceptually distinct from R10.1 (spec ambiguity) and R10.2
    (implementation divergence): the spec is clear; the implementation is
    correct; the security error is deploying a powerful feature in wrong context

D336 — Zero-Knowledge Proofs in Security
  Description: ZKP (Zero-Knowledge Proof) — cryptographic primitive allowing
  prover to convince verifier of statement's truth without revealing why
  it's true; interactive (sigma protocols) and non-interactive (zk-SNARKs,
  zk-STARKs, Bulletproofs)
  Security applications:
    Anonymous authentication: prove you hold a valid credential without
      revealing which credential (Anonimity in V2X — approach 2 from G215)
    Privacy-preserving audit: prove computation was performed correctly
      without revealing inputs (regulatory compliance without data disclosure)
    Cross-chain bridges (blockchain): prove state from one chain to another
    Passport/identity: prove age without revealing birthdate (selective disclosure)
  Security of ZKP systems:
    Trusted setup: zk-SNARKs require trusted setup ceremony; if ceremony
      compromised (toxic waste not destroyed), prover can forge proofs;
      Zcash powers-of-tau ceremony (2018); Groth16 trusted setup vulnerability
      if ceremony fails
    Soundness: if cryptographic assumptions (discrete log, hash collision
      resistance) broken, ZKP soundness fails; PQC ZKP systems exist
      (zk-STARKs: hash-based; quantum-resistant)
    Implementation bugs: ZKP library vulnerabilities can break soundness
      (Circom underconstrained circuits — specific ZKP language bugs allowing
      prover to cheat verifier without breaking crypto)

ANATOMY G241 [NEW]: EXPLOIT MARKET vs. CVD ECOSYSTEM
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUBJECT: Vulnerability disclosure ecosystem — coordinated disclosure vs.
         commercial exploit brokerage
DOMAIN: Vulnerability economics / threat intelligence
ROOT MECHANICS: R02 (attack economics), R07 (disclosure coordination)

LAYER 1 — CVD (COORDINATED VULNERABILITY DISCLOSURE) MODEL:
  Discoverer reports to vendor. Vendor patches. Public disclosure after patch
  (typically 90-day deadline from Google Project Zero). CVEs assigned via CNA
  (CVE Numbering Authority) network. CVSS scoring provides severity metric.
  Bug bounty programs (HackerOne, Bugcrowd) incentivize researchers: $500-$1M
  depending on platform and severity.


--- SOURCE LINES 173537–173562 ---
LAYER 4 — SYSTEMIC EFFECT:
  [A] Vulnerability retention: critical vulnerabilities sold to Zerodium may
      remain unpatched for 12-36 months while used operationally.
  [B] Weaponization diffusion: NSA EternalBlue retained for ~5 years (est.) before
      Shadow Brokers leak (2017). Vulnerability then weaponized in WannaCry,
      NotPetya within weeks. Classic HNDL-analog for exploits.
  [C] CVD ecosystem erosion: researchers with high-value finds increasingly bypass
      CVD entirely. Vendor visibility into critical vulnerability landscape degrades.
  [D] Patch timeline distortion: vendor cannot patch what it doesn't know. MTTR
      (mean time to remediation) becomes undefined for retained 0-days.

LAYER 5 — GOVERNANCE RESPONSE:
  EU Cyber Resilience Act (2024): imposes vulnerability disclosure requirements
  on product manufacturers. ENISA receives reports. Does not regulate researcher
  behavior or restrict commercial market.
  US CISA: Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog. No authority over
  commercial exploit sales. First Amendment constraints (US) limit regulation
  of security research publication.
  Wassenaar Arrangement: attempted to control 'intrusion software' exports (2013);
  revised 2017 after security community pushback. Partial export controls only.

LAYER 6 — STRUCTURAL ASYMMETRY:
  Defenders: must patch all known vulnerabilities across entire estate, continuously.
  Attackers: need only one unpatched vulnerability per target, from retained pool.
  Commercial exploit market widens this asymmetry by extending the window during
  which high-value vulnerabilities remain unknown to defenders.

[CF278] ACARS/ADS-B structural isomorphism
  Two independent aviation systems (ACARS: datalink messaging; ADS-B: position
  broadcast) share identical attack surface architecture: RF broadcast,
  unauthenticated, safety-critical, massive installed base, decade-scale

  designed in the pre-adversarial era of civil aviation (1970s-1990s) when the
  threat model was equipment failure, not deliberate injection.

  Implication: any aviation communication or navigation system designed in this
  era requires adversarial re-examination. ATC radar (ATCRBS Mode C): also
  unauthenticated. ILS glide slope: RF spoofable. Pattern is systemic.

[CF280] R10.6 refinement — action-enabling vs. information-only threshold
  TCP timestamps (CE-5, G236 cycle 1) vs. pickle/Log4j JNDI/SSRF: the former
  produces only information leakage (uptime, OS fingerprint) without enabling
  attacker action in isolation. The latter enable direct code execution or
  credential theft. Proposed R10.6 refinement:
    R10.6-THRESHOLD: feature-security context mismatch produces exploitable
    vulnerability at scale IFF the mismatch enables attacker ACTION (code
    execution, authentication bypass, data exfiltration) not merely information
    leakage. Information-only mismatches are self-limiting (low CVSSv3 impact
    scores; mitigated at kernel level without protocol change).
  This refinement does not falsify R10.6; it defines a sub-class boundary.
  Status: DRAFT refinement; 4 counter-example cycles remain for R10.6 proper.


--- SOURCE LINES 173771–173780 ---
[CF282] CVD ecosystem as distributed early warning system — and its failure mode
  CVD, when functioning, provides defenders with: (1) patch before exploit
  weaponization; (2) CVSS severity for patch prioritization; (3) public
  disclosure drives awareness. Commercial exploit market degrades all three:
  (1) patches cannot exist for retained vulnerabilities; (2) CVSS undefined
  for unknown vulnerabilities; (3) awareness zero until Shadow Brokers-type
  event. CVD failure mode is not random — it tracks economic incentive differential.
  Where exploit market payout > bug bounty payout, CVD degrades systematically.
  Currently: iOS/Android critical 0-click; Chrome full chain; Exchange RCE.
  These are exactly the highest-impact platforms. Correlation is not coincidence.

R10.5 COUNTER-EXAMPLE STATUS UPDATE (cycle 5 of 5 — FINAL):
  R10.5 hypothesis: hardware timing/power side channels via compiler/microarch
  optimizations that create observable timing differentials not present in the
  abstract algorithm.
  Cycles 1-4: no falsifying counter-example found. Spectre/Meltdown, PRIME+PROBE,
  FLUSH+RELOAD, Bleichenbacher — all confirmed R10.5 (or R10.1∩R10.5a).
  Cycle 5 (this cycle): final scan for counter-example.
  CANDIDATE: constant-time cryptographic implementations (e.g., OpenSSL's
  BN_BLINDING, BEARSSL's constant-time AES, libsodium).
  Assessment: these are DEFENSES against R10.5, not counter-examples. Their
  existence confirms R10.5 is real (we need constant-time specifically because
  non-constant-time creates vulnerabilities). A defense is not a falsification.
  CANDIDATE: formally verified timing properties (e.g., CT-Verif, binsec/haunted).
  Assessment: formal verification can confirm a specific implementation is
  constant-time. This eliminates R10.5 for that implementation. But R10.5
  taxonomy is about the substrate class (hardware/compiler timing side channels);
  individual constant-time implementations don't falsify the substrate class.
  DECISION: R10.5 CLOSED — NOT FALSIFIED. 5 counter-example cycles complete.
  No instance found where the optimization-creates-timing-observable mechanism
  failed to produce exploitable vulnerability across all examined instances.
  R10.5 elevated from DRAFT to CONFIRMED sub-taxonomy.

  [D346] Memory safety vulnerability class

  [D347] Rust memory safety model
    Ownership system: each value has exactly one owner. Borrowing: references
    (shared &T or exclusive &mut T) with lifetime guarantees. No use-after-free:
    compiler enforces lifetime; borrow checker prevents dangling references.
    No data races: &mut T is exclusive. No buffer overflows: Vec/slice indexing
    bounds-checked at runtime (panic, not UB). unsafe blocks: explicit opt-out,
    auditable.
  [D348] Memory-safe migration in critical software
    Linux kernel: Rust support merged in 6.1 (Dec 2022). First Rust drivers in
    mainline. Android: 0 memory safety vulnerabilities in Rust code (Google 2024
    data). Windows: Microsoft Rust adoption in kernel components. Chrome: Rust
    in Chromium (select components). NSA guidance (2022): recommends memory-safe
    languages (Rust, Go, Java, Swift, C#, Python) over C/C++.
  [D349] Go memory model and garbage collection tradeoffs
    Go: garbage-collected; no manual free. Memory safe by default. Tradeoffs:
    GC pauses (latency-sensitive applications); no RAII; CGO reintroduces
    unsafe. Go is memory-safe for pure Go code; CGO interaction is escape hatch.
  [D350] Java/JVM memory safety and deserialization
    JVM provides memory safety (no raw pointers). Deserialization (ObjectInputStream):
    Java gadget chains allow RCE despite memory safety. Apache Commons Collections,
    Spring, Jackson gadgets. Memory safety does not prevent logic vulnerabilities.
    Contrast with Rust: Rust prevents memory unsafety but does not prevent
    logic errors in safe code.

DOMAIN BLOCK 40.E: HARDWARE SECURITY PRIMITIVES
  [D359] Trusted Platform Module (TPM)
    TPM 2.0 (ISO/IEC 11889): hardware security chip. Functions: secure key storage
    (RSA, ECC, symmetric); attestation (TPM quote: sign platform state with TPM
    key); sealing (encrypt data to PCR state: only accessible if platform
    configuration matches). Used by: BitLocker (PCR-based disk encryption),
    Secure Boot measurement, UEFI attestation, Windows Hello (key storage).
  [D360] TPM attacks
    Physical attacks: TPM bus sniffing (LPC bus on older systems): BitLocker key
    extractable if TPM communicates without encryption. CVE-2023-1017/1018: TPM2.0
    library buffer overflow. Spectre-class attacks against TPM context: indirect.
    Design limit: TPM proves hardware state, not software correctness. A compromised
    OS that can measure itself into PCRs (rollback attack) defeats sealing.
  [D361] Intel SGX (Software Guard Extensions)
    Hardware enclave: isolated memory region (EPC). Code and data encrypted by CPU;
    not accessible to OS, hypervisor, or other processes even with ring-0 access.
    Remote attestation: CPU produces signed report of enclave measurement.
    Attacks: Foreshadow (CVE-2018-3615): L1TF extracts SGX enclave data.
    SGXPectre: Spectre variant targeting SGX. Plundervolt: voltage glitching
    corrupts SGX computations. Intel deprecated SGX on consumer CPUs (2021 11th gen).
  [D362] ARM TrustZone
    Two execution worlds: Normal World (rich OS: Android, Linux) and Secure World
    (Trusted Execution Environment: TEE). Secure monitor mode (EL3) mediates.
    Keymaster/Keymint: Android TEE component for key storage. Attacks: TZAR,
    TrustKit, TZBot: vulnerabilities in TEE implementations (Samsung, Qualcomm,
    Huawei) allowing Normal World breakout into Secure World. TEE implementation
    security is highly variable across vendors.

  GAP: G261 [NEW] — ARM TrustZone vulnerability history across vendor implementations

PATTERN ANALYSIS — NEW DOMAINS (Cycle 40):

[P40.1] Supply chain as R06.ARCH ultimate form
  R06.ARCH: system architecture encodes implicit trust that attackers leverage.
  Supply chain attacks exploit the deepest architectural trust: the build
  process itself. SolarWinds SUNBURST: the update trust (customers trust signed
  updates from their vendor) is the attack vector. XZ Utils: the contribution
  trust (maintainers trust well-established contributors) is the attack vector.
  Dependency confusion: the package resolution trust (package manager trusts
  semantic versioning to select highest version) is the attack vector.
  PATTERN 40.1: SUPPLY CHAIN AS TRUST INVERSION — the more trusted a software
  delivery channel, the higher its value as an attack vector and the lower
  the per-delivery inspection rate.
  Instances: SolarWinds (update channel), XZ Utils (contributor trust),
  dependency confusion (version resolution trust), CI/CD pipeline (build system
  trust), npm typosquatting (package name trust).
  Root: R06.ARCH (trust architecture), R07 (institutional trust)
  Relationship to LAW-1: supply chain attack surface is LAW-1 because the
  installed base of dependent software cannot be audited or replaced on security
  timescales.

[P40.2] Memory safety migration as LAW-1 attacker transition
  ~70% of critical CVEs (Chrome, Android, Windows) are memory safety bugs in C/C++.
  Rust eliminates this class at the language level (borrow checker). Migration
  trajectory: Linux 6.1 (2022), Android zero memory safety CVEs in Rust code (2024),
  Windows kernel Rust adoption. PATTERN 40.2: MEMORY SAFETY LANGUAGE MIGRATION IS
  LAW-1 ON THE DEFENDER SIDE — the existing C/C++ codebase (billions of lines)
  cannot be rewritten on security timescales; migration is incremental (new code
  in Rust, existing code remains). Attackers will shift to: (a) remaining C/C++
  components; (b) logic vulnerabilities in memory-safe code (deserialization,
  injection, auth bypass); (c) Rust unsafe blocks.
  This mirrors Pattern 33.3 (defense layer creates new perimeter): Rust
  creates a new perimeter; attacker finds the gap (unsafe blocks, C/C++ interface
  via FFI, CGO, JNI).

  liblzma. Binary analysis: found IFUNC hook. Reported to oss-security mailing

  Mechanism: attacker compromises build server (CI/CD, TeamCity, Jenkins, Azure

--- SOURCE LINES 174526–174535 ---
[CF286] Memory safety migration as generational security debt reduction
  ~70% of critical vulnerabilities in C/C++ codebases are memory safety bugs.
  Rust eliminates this class entirely for safe code. The transition is generational:
  new code written in Rust accumulates safety debt at near-zero rate; existing
  C/C++ code continues to accumulate. Net effect over 20 years: as Rust fraction
  grows, the proportion of memory safety CVEs drops. This is the slowest possible
  remediation (rewrite-as-you-go) but the only feasible one given LAW-1 (existing
  codebase size). Android data (Google 2024): 0 memory safety CVEs in Rust
  components vs. ongoing CVEs in C/C++ components — empirical confirmation of
  the model.


--- SOURCE LINES 174559–174599 ---
[CF289] TLS 1.3 as proof of concept for 'eliminate, don't remediate'
  Pattern: when a class of vulnerabilities (POODLE, BEAST, DROWN, LOGJAM, FREAK)
  all stem from the same root (legacy cipher suite retention for compatibility),
  the correct response is to eliminate the root, not to add countermeasures.
  TLS 1.3 removes 492 cipher suites; retains 5. Removes RSA key exchange entirely.
  Removes CBC mode entirely. Result: the entire downgrade attack class is closed.
  This is in contrast to the dominant practice: patch individual CVEs within
  a broken-by-design system (TLS 1.0/1.1 had dozens of individual CVEs while
  the root cause — legacy cipher retention — remained).
  Contrast with memory safety: Rust eliminates the class; C/C++ patches individual
  CVEs. Same meta-pattern in two domains.
  PATTERN 40.6 (NEW): CLASS ELIMINATION IS MORE EFFECTIVE THAN INSTANCE REMEDIATION.
  Instances: TLS 1.3 (cipher class elimination), Rust (memory corruption class
  elimination), FIDO2 (phishing class elimination), ASLR+DEP (exploit reliability
  class reduction).

[CF290] Hardware TEE attack surface as meta-pattern
  Every hardware security primitive introduces its own attack surface:
    TPM: bus sniffing (LPC), rollback attacks, firmware bugs (CVE-2023-1017)
    SGX: Foreshadow, SGXPectre, Plundervolt, CacheOut
    TrustZone: vendor implementation bugs (Samsung, Qualcomm, Huawei TEEs)
    TPM+Secure Boot: measured boot proves configuration, not correctness; attacker
      who can modify measurements defeats sealing.
  META-PATTERN: every security primitive that provides a new guarantee creates
  a new attack surface targeting that guarantee. The primitive is not a solution;
  it shifts the attack target. Defense-in-depth requires that no single primitive
  is the sole trust anchor.

[CF291] Pattern 33.3 — 8th instance assessment (Rust/unsafe)
  Pattern 33.3: each new defense layer creates a new perimeter that becomes
  the attack target. Rust memory safety adoption candidate for 8th instance.
  Evidence needed: adversarial exploitation of Rust unsafe blocks or FFI boundaries
  at meaningful scale. Current state (2024-2026): Rust unsafe CVEs exist
  (e.g., CVE-2022-21658 in std::fs::remove_dir_all on Windows — race condition
  in safe API with unsafe internals); Rust soundness bugs tracked separately.
  But: systematic attacker targeting of Rust unsafe specifically (as opposed
  to finding bugs in Rust code that happen to use unsafe) is not yet documented
  at the same scale as prior Pattern 33.3 instances.
  STATUS: Pattern 33.3 instance 8 remains PROVISIONAL. Not yet CONFIRMED.
  Confirmation criterion: documented attacker tooling or exploit specifically
  targeting Rust unsafe blocks or Rust FFI boundaries as primary attack surface.

DOMAIN BLOCK 41.A: IDENTITY AND ACCESS — OAUTH/OIDC ATTACK SURFACE
  [D363] OAuth 2.0 authorization code interception
    PKCE bypass: servers that don't enforce PKCE allow authorization code theft.
    Attacker registers custom URI scheme or intercepting redirect URI. Auth code
    captured before client. RFC 9700 (OAuth 2.1): PKCE mandatory for all flows.
  [D364] Authorization code injection
    Victim clicks attacker-controlled link; attacker-controlled auth code injected
    into victim's session at redirect. Requires code_challenge binding missing.
    Defense: PKCE; state parameter; nonce in OIDC.
  [D365] OAuth token leakage via Referer header
    Access token in redirect URI fragment (implicit flow). Browser sends token
    in Referer header to third-party resources on the page.
    Defense: authorization code flow; token binding; strict Referer policy.
  [D366] OIDC provider confusion / issuer mismatch
    Multi-tenant OIDC: application accepts tokens from correct issuer but doesn't
    validate 'aud' claim. Attacker registers in same OIDC provider; obtains token
    for their own client_id; token valid for same issuer. Missing 'aud' validation
    = authentication bypass.
  [D367] OAuth SSRF via redirect_uri
    redirect_uri validation insufficient; attacker supplies internal URL. After
    auth flow, authorization server POSTs auth code to internal endpoint.
    Variant of SSRF via trusted server.

DOMAIN BLOCK 41.D: NETWORK ATTACK SURFACE — BGP AND ROUTING
  [D378] BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) hijacking
    BGP: inter-AS routing protocol. Routers trust route announcements from peers.
    No cryptographic validation in base protocol.
    Attack: AS announces more-specific prefix than legitimate AS (more specific
    wins in route selection). Traffic hijacked to attacker AS.
    Historical incidents: Pakistan Telecom hijacking YouTube (2008, 30 minutes);
    Russian BGP hijack of Twitch/AWS (2020); Rostelecom hijacking >8000 prefixes
    (2020). China Telecom repeated incidents (Renesys/Dyn research).
  [D379] BGP route leak (unintentional hijack)
    BGP misconfiguration causes AS to announce routes it should not. Large AS
    (Cloudflare Incident 2019: Level 3 misconfiguration caused major outages).
    Google (2018): misconfigured BGP route via Nigeria caused rerouting of
    Google traffic through Russia/Nigeria (not intentional but real impact).
  [D380] RPKI (Resource Public Key Infrastructure)
    Cryptographic attestation of IP prefix ownership. Route Origin Authorization
    (ROA): resource holder signs which AS can announce their prefix. Routers
    with RPKI-validating mode: reject INVALID routes (wrong AS for prefix).
    Adoption (2024): ~50% of global BGP prefixes have ROAs; ~40% of routers
    validate. Major providers (AT&T, NTT, ARIN, RIPE): RPKI enforced.
    Limitation: ROAs prevent origin hijacks; do not prevent AS path manipulation.
    BGPsec: full AS path signing; not widely deployed (performance concerns).
  [D381] BGP as critical infrastructure substrate
    All internet routing depends on BGP. A sufficiently large BGP hijack can
    intercept traffic destined for: certificate authority OCSP endpoints (bypass
    revocation), software update servers (inject malicious updates), financial
    clearing systems. BGP hijack + MITM + certificate misissuance = powerful
    combination. Demonstrated: 2018 BGP hijack of Let's Encrypt validation
    requests to obtain fraudulent certificates (MyEtherWallet incident).

PATTERN ANALYSIS — NEW DOMAINS (Cycle 41):

[P41.1] BGP as unauthenticated routing substrate — LAW-1 + R04
  BGP was designed for cooperative routing between trusted ASes (1989). No
  authentication of route announcements in base protocol (R04: authentication
  absent by design). The installed base of BGP-speaking routers (hundreds of
  thousands of ASes worldwide) cannot be migrated to a new routing protocol
  on security timescales (LAW-1). RPKI is the retrofit: adds cryptographic
  ROA verification without replacing BGP. Adoption after 15+ years of RPKI
  availability: ~50% prefix coverage, ~40% router enforcement. This is the
  standard LAW-1 retrofit trajectory. BGPsec (full path signing): even slower
  adoption due to performance overhead.
  Pattern: BGP/RPKI is structurally identical to DNS/DNSSEC — both are
  unauthenticated broadcast protocols with cryptographic retrofit. Both show
  slow, incomplete adoption. R01 sub-class candidate: R01.ROUTING (unauthenticated
  routing announcements as broadcast vulnerability class).


--- SOURCE LINES 174896–174905 ---
[P41.5] HTTP request smuggling as parsing discrepancy attack class
  HTTP/1.1 spec (RFC 7230) allows ambiguity: Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding
  coexist; different implementations resolve the ambiguity differently.
  Attack: craft request that exploits this discrepancy between two deployed
  implementations in sequence (front-end proxy + back-end server).
  ROOT: R10.3 (interaction between two correct implementations). Both the front-end
  and back-end implement the spec; the vulnerability is in their interaction.
  This is a canonical R10.3 instance. Prior R10.3 examples: TLS session resumption
  across implementations; CSRF across browser+server. HTTP request smuggling adds
  a particularly severe web-tier R10.3 with cross-user impact.


--- SOURCE LINES 175119–175126 ---
CONVERGENCE:
  Canonical R10.3: both implementations are RFC-compliant; vulnerability in
    interaction. The spec allows the ambiguity; different resolution creates gap.
  Pattern 40.6 (eliminate > remediate): HTTP/2 binary framing eliminates
    the ambiguity class entirely within HTTP/2. H2.H1 desync shows that
    partial migration (H2 front-end, H1.1 back-end) recreates the vulnerability.
    Full migration to H2 end-to-end is the class-eliminating fix.

--- SOURCE LINES 175160–175171 ---
[A332] DNS rebinding attack
  Mechanism: attacker registers domain with short TTL; phase 1: IP = public
  attacker server (user visits, JS loaded). Phase 2: DNS TTL expires, rebinds
  to internal IP (192.168.1.1). User's browser now sends requests to internal
  IP via attacker's script — same-origin allows since domain hasn't changed.
  Can access: internal admin interfaces, IoT devices, development servers on
  localhost. Extract data, modify configuration.
  Prerequisites: attacker controls DNS for their domain; target has valuable
  internal HTTP services.
  Impact: bypass same-origin policy without SOP vulnerability; access internal
  network from victim's browser.
  Root: R10.3 (browser same-origin enforcement vs. DNS rebinding reality)


--- SOURCE LINES 175306–175329 ---
[CF293] RowHammer as hardware physics intruding into software security model
  Software security model fundamental assumption: memory contents are determined
  by software writes; physical hardware faithfully executes the abstract machine.
  RowHammer violates this: software-accessible operation (repeated memory read)
  causes bit flips without any software 'write' operation. This breaks the
  abstraction boundary between hardware physics and the software trust model.
  Consequence: software-layer security guarantees (page table integrity, privilege
  separation, sandboxing) can be violated by hardware physics without any
  software vulnerability being present. R10.5b is the sub-taxonomy for this
  class: attacker uses software to access hardware physics, bypassing software
  abstraction. The 'implementation' (DRAM cell isolation) is faithful to the spec;
  the spec assumed higher isolation than the physics provides at modern densities
  (R10.2 component).

[CF294] DNS rebinding as same-origin policy architectural bypass
  Same-origin policy: browser isolates JavaScript by origin (scheme + host + port).
  DNS rebinding does not exploit a bug in SOP; it exploits the gap between
  the assumption underlying SOP ('host' is stable during a session) and the
  reality (DNS can change the IP behind a host at any time after TTL expiry).
  SOP is correct; DNS TTL resolution is correct; the vulnerability is their
  interaction (R10.3). The browser cannot easily distinguish 'this is still the
  same host' from 'the IP changed and this is now an internal address' because
  DNS has no such concept. This is a design gap at the intersection of two
  correct systems.

--- SOURCE LINES 175437–175543 ---
DOMAIN BLOCK 42.A: CRYPTOGRAPHY — SIDE CHANNEL IN IMPLEMENTATIONS
  [D386] RSA timing attack (Kocher 1996)
    Paul Kocher: timing measurements of RSA decryption reveal private key bits.
    Modular exponentiation using square-and-multiply: extra multiplication step
    when bit is 1 vs. 0 is observable via timing. 1000 measurements sufficient
    to extract 512-bit key. Foundation of side-channel cryptanalysis field.
  [D387] AES cache-timing attacks (BERNSTEIN 2005)
    AES lookup table implementation: table lookup timing depends on cache state
    (L1 hit vs. miss). Cache state depends on key bytes and plaintext. Attacker
    observes timing variations; recovers AES key in ~2^20 encryptions.
    Defense: AES-NI hardware instruction (constant time, no table lookups);
    bitsliced AES implementation. AES-NI: virtually universal on modern x86.
  [D388] Elliptic curve scalar multiplication timing
    Point multiplication (Q = kP): timing reveals scalar k (private key).
    Montgomery ladder: constant-time scalar multiplication — same operations
    regardless of bit value. Most modern EC implementations use Montgomery ladder
    or equivalent. OpenSSL: constant-time since 2003 (after Brumley-Boneh paper).
  [D389] ECDSA nonce reuse vulnerability
    ECDSA: signature (r, s) where s = k^-1 * (z + r*d) mod n. If same nonce k
    used for two signatures (s1, s2) on messages (z1, z2): k and private key d
    recoverable from two equations with two unknowns. PlayStation 3 (2010): same
    k for all signatures. Bitcoin: several wallets reused k; coins stolen.
    Sony developer used rand() with fixed seed — not random. Defense: RFC 6979
    (deterministic ECDSA: k derived from hash(private_key || message)).
  [D390] Post-quantum signature timing
    ML-DSA (FIPS 204): derived from CRYSTALS-Dilithium. Constant-time requirement
    in spec. Early implementations had timing leaks (Dilithium rejection sampling
    path variance). Formal verification needed for constant-time compliance.
    Lesson: new algorithm does not guarantee constant-time implementation.

  GAP: G272 [NEW] — Formal verification tools for constant-time code (ct-verif, Frama-C)
  GAP: G273 [NEW] — RFC 6979 adoption in modern crypto libraries

DOMAIN BLOCK 42.B: PHYSICAL SECURITY AND TAMPER RESISTANCE
  [D391] Common Criteria evaluation and secure element certification
    Common Criteria: international standard (ISO 15408) for security product
    evaluation. Evaluation Assurance Levels: EAL1 (lowest) to EAL7 (highest).
    Secure elements (payment chips, HSMs, government smart cards): typically
    EAL4+ to EAL7. Evaluation: vulnerability analysis, functional testing, source
    code review (EAL5+), formal mathematical proof (EAL7). Smart card certification:
    EMVCo requires CC EAL4+. SIM cards: EAL4+.
  [D392] Anti-tamper mechanisms in secure elements
    Physical protections: active mesh (conductive layer; opens circuit if layer
    breached); light sensors (detect decapsulation attempt); temperature sensors;
    voltage monitors (detect glitching); random clock jitter (complicates timing);
    memory scrambling; bus encryption between functional blocks.
    Dual-rail logic: logic designed to consume equal power for both 0 and 1 —
    eliminates power side-channel. Cost: area doubles; only in highest-assurance devices.
  [D393] Hardware Security Modules (HSMs)
    Dedicated hardware for cryptographic key storage and operations. FIPS 140-3
    (current standard): security levels 1-4. Level 4: physical tamper evidence;
    active tamper response (zeroize keys on detected intrusion). Examples:
    Thales Luna, Entrust nShield, AWS CloudHSM, Azure Dedicated HSM.
    Used for: CA private keys (root CAs use Level 4), payment HSMs (bank PINs),
    code signing keys, PQC key storage (new generation).
  [D394] Cold boot attack specifics
    DRAM remanence: DRAM bit persistence time after power loss:
      at room temp: 2-30 seconds
      at 0°C: minutes
      at -50°C (compressed air spray): up to 10 minutes
      at liquid nitrogen: potentially hours
    Attack kit: USB bootable tool (msramdump, Cold Boot Toolkit); target PC
    powered off; RAM removed (or system cooled in-place); booted from USB;
    memory dump analyzed offline. BitLocker key (AES-128): findable in 2-30GB
    dump if not yet scrubbed. findaes tool: locates AES key schedule in raw dump.
    Defense: require PIN on BitLocker (not just TPM-only); encrypted RAM (AMD
    SME/SEV; Intel MKTME for VMs); TRESOR (key in x86 debug registers, not DRAM).

  GAP: G274 [NEW] — FIPS 140-3 vs FIPS 140-2 transition status (current state)
  GAP: G275 [NEW] — AMD SEV/SME and Intel TDX adoption in cloud providers

DOMAIN BLOCK 42.C: WIRELESS SECURITY DEPTH
  [D395] WPA3 and Wi-Fi security evolution
    WPA2 (CCMP/AES): replaced WEP/TKIP. 4-way handshake: PMKID attack (Jens Steube
    2018): capture PMKID from single beacon; offline brute-force SSID+password.
    WPA3-Personal (SAE): Dragonfly key exchange; resistant to offline dictionary
    attack; no PMKID offline attack possible. WPA3-Enterprise: 192-bit security
    mode (ECC with CNSA suite). Adoption: required for Wi-Fi CERTIFIED since 2020.
  [D396] KRACK attack (WPA2 4-way handshake key reinstallation)
    Mathy Vanhoef 2017: CVE-2017-13077. 4-way handshake state machine: if ACK
    for message 3 lost, AP retransmits. Client accepts retransmit; reinstalls
    PTK with nonce reset to 0. Nonce reuse in CCMP enables decryption/injection.
    CVSS 8.1. Affected all WPA2 implementations. Patched via OS updates.
    WPA3 SAE: not vulnerable to KRACK class (different handshake design).
  [D397] Dragonblood attacks on WPA3
    Mathy Vanhoef 2019: timing and cache side-channels in SAE (Dragonfly)
    implementation enable partial password recovery. Also: denial of service via
    SAE Commit frame replay. IEEE 802.11 amended; countermeasures added to SAE.
    Illustrates Pattern 33.3: WPA3 (new defense layer) creates new attack target
    (SAE implementation side-channels).
  [D398] LTE/5G IMSI catchers (IMSI stingrays)
    IMSI: unique subscriber identifier. 2G: IMSI sent in plaintext on identity
    request. 3G/LTE: base station authentication still asymmetric (network not
    authenticated to UE in all cases). IMSI catcher: rogue base station requests
    IMSI before authentication; UE responds with IMSI.
    5G (NR): SUPI (Subscriber Permanent Identifier) sent as SUCI (Subscriber
    Concealed Identifier) using home network public key. Prevents passive IMSI
    collection. Active IMSI catchers: force 4G/3G/2G fallback (if supported);
    extract IMSI from older protocol.
  [D399] Bluetooth security attack surface
    BLE (Bluetooth Low Energy): LE legacy pairing — no authentication for 'Just Works';
    key exchanged in cleartext; eavesdrop and impersonate.
    BIAS (Bluetooth Impersonation AttackS, Bluetooth Classic 2020): legacy
    authentication allows role switch after partial auth; impersonate paired device.
    BLUFFS (2023): six Bluetooth exploits for session establishment weaknesses.
    Bluetooth Classic BR/EDR: widely deployed; security model has accumulated
    known weaknesses.


--- SOURCE LINES 175624–175637 ---
PATTERN ANALYSIS — NEW DOMAINS (Cycle 42):

[P42.1] LOLBin evasion as architectural trust exploitation (R06.ARCH)
  LOLBins: system tools signed by the OS vendor, trusted by application allowlists,
  present on every endpoint, performing legitimate functions. Attackers repurpose
  these tools for: download, execution, persistence, lateral movement, exfiltration.
  The attacker doesn't bring tools — they use the defender's tools against them.
  This is R06.ARCH at the endpoint level: the OS architecture trusts signed binaries
  as a categorical rule (necessary for function); this categorical trust is the
  attack surface. No individual LOLBin has a vulnerability; the vulnerability is
  the architectural decision to trust all signed binaries unconditionally.
  PATTERN: identical to Supply Chain Trust Inversion (P40.1) at a different layer.
  P40.1 targets the delivery channel; P42.1 targets the execution layer post-delivery.
  Both exploit categorical trust rather than individual vulnerability.


--- SOURCE LINES 175652–175673 ---
[P42.3] WPA3 Dragonblood as Pattern 33.3 (new protocol, new attack surface)
  WPA3 SAE (Dragonfly): designed to fix WPA2 offline dictionary attack.
  Dragonblood (2019): SAE implementation has side-channel in Dragonfly hunting-and-
  pecking algorithm (timing depends on password length) and cache-timing (depends
  on password characters). New protocol creates new attack surface at implementation
  level. This is Pattern 33.3 instance candidate: WPA3 as the new defense layer;
  SAE implementation timing as the new perimeter.
  STATUS: CONFIRMED Pattern 33.3 instance 8 (replacing Rust unsafe, which remains
  PROVISIONAL). Criteria: new defense layer (WPA3) creates new attack target
  (Dragonfly side-channel). Adversarial exploitation demonstrated (Dragonblood).

[P42.4] C2 domain fronting as LAW-1 defender tool turned weapon
  CDNs (Cloudflare, AWS CloudFront): designed to route traffic to origin servers
  while appearing to communicate with the CDN. Domain fronting: attacker C2 server
  appears as traffic to legitimate CDN domain (e.g., allowed.cdn.com) while
  actual HTTPS Host header routes to attacker's domain. Defender's allowlist
  (allow CDN domains for legitimate traffic) becomes the attack surface.
  Pattern: every time defenders add CDN/cloud providers to allowlists to enable
  business functionality, they create an evasion path for attackers using those
  same providers. CDN restrictions (2018+) forced C2 operators to different
  evasion methods (direct HTTPS to compromised hosts, DGA, DNS C2).
  This is R06.ARCH: the CDN routing architecture creates the evasion mechanism.

--- SOURCE LINES 176041–176052 ---
[CF297] RFC 6979 / EdDSA as the cleanest Pattern 40.6 instance
  Pattern 40.6: class elimination > instance remediation. RFC 6979 and EdDSA
  exemplify this at the cryptographic protocol level. The 'instance' approach
  to nonce reuse would be: better RNG recommendations, developer education, RNG
  testing requirements. All of these still leave the fundamental vulnerability
  (security depends on caller-supplied randomness) intact. RFC 6979 eliminates
  the class by removing the dependency: k is now derived deterministically, and
  no caller-supplied randomness can cause nonce reuse. EdDSA goes further: the
  algorithm has no exposed nonce parameter at all. The class does not exist in
  EdDSA's design space.
  This progression (ECDSA -> RFC 6979 ECDSA -> EdDSA) is the ideal form of
  Pattern 40.6: remove the problematic construct entirely at each iteration.


--- SOURCE LINES 176069–176083 ---
[CF299] DNS C2 as architecture-respecting evasion
  DNS C2 does not exploit a DNS vulnerability. DNS resolution is working correctly:
  any process can query for any domain; responses are returned by the authoritative
  DNS server; recursive resolvers forward queries through organizational boundaries.
  The C2 channel is the feature, not a bug. Defender cannot simply 'block DNS
  C2' without breaking DNS (which breaks nearly all internet connectivity).
  Defense must be: behavioral (anomaly in query volume, subdomain length, entropy),
  intelligence-based (block known C2 domains), or architectural (DNS firewall with
  threat intelligence). All three are imperfect and bypassable.
  This is R06.ARCH at the network architecture level: the design decision that
  DNS recursion crosses organizational boundaries (necessary for internet) creates
  the evasion channel. Compare: HTTP/S C2, ICMP C2, SMTP C2 — all the same
  structural pattern. Every protocol that legitimately crosses firewall boundaries
  becomes a C2 candidate. Perimeter defense cannot solve this; only endpoint
  detection and zero-trust can.


--- SOURCE LINES 176108–176135 ---
[CF301] Convergence finding: LAW-3 CANDIDATE
  Observation from CF300 and the full loop history: defensive security measures
  do not reduce the attack surface; they transform it. Each new layer:
  (a) closes the previous attack class at that layer
  (b) opens a new attack class at the next layer (Pattern 33.3)
  (c) creates a production/legacy split for the previous layer's technology (Pattern 36.2)
  (d) retains the previous layer as a downgrade path (R10.4)
  This is a system-level property, not a local failure. It holds across:
  cryptography (WEP -> WPA2 -> WPA3; each generation + downgrade), networking
  (SMTP+SPF+DKIM+DMARC+ARC; each addition + bypass), endpoint (AV+HIPS+EDR+XDR;
  each layer + LOLBin), protocol (SSL+TLS+TLS1.3; each version + downgrade),
  authentication (password+MFA+FIDO2; each strength + attack on the weaker).

  CANDIDATE LAW-3: SECURITY MEASURES TRANSFORM ATTACK SURFACE; THEY DO NOT
  REDUCE IT. THE TOTAL VOLUME OF EXPLOITABLE ATTACK SURFACE ACROSS ALL LAYERS
  IS APPROXIMATELY CONSERVED ACROSS DEFENSIVE GENERATIONS.

  Status: DRAFT. This is a stronger claim than LAW-1 or LAW-2. Requires:
  (a) counter-example search (is there a domain where total attack surface
      reduced, not just transformed?), and (b) formal definition of 'attack
      surface volume' as a comparable quantity across different domains/layers.
  Candidate counter-example: post-quantum cryptography transition. If PQC
    replaces RSA/ECC and harvest-now attacks are prevented, and if PQC has no
    equivalent of RSA timing/nonce vulnerabilities — then total cryptographic
    attack surface decreases. But: PQC introduces new attack surface
    (implementation side-channels, trusted setup in some schemes, lattice
    reduction advances). Pending: whether PQC net attack surface is smaller.
  LAW-3 STATUS: DRAFT. Counter-example cycle begins next cycle.

--- SOURCE LINES 176216–176291 ---
DOMAIN BLOCK 43.A: VIRTUALIZATION AND CLOUD SECURITY DEPTH
  [D406] Hypervisor security and VM escape
    Hypervisor (VMM): Type 1 (bare-metal: Hyper-V, Xen, KVM, ESXi) or Type 2
    (hosted: VMware Workstation, VirtualBox). Isolation: each VM has own address
    space, IOMMU for device isolation.
    VM escape vulnerabilities: CVE-2018-3646 (Foreshadow/L1TF): L1 cache data
    from another VM readable via speculative execution. CVE-2021-21985 (VMware
    vCenter RCE via vSAN Health Check plugin — not VM escape but hypervisor
    management plane). VENOM (CVE-2015-3456): virtual floppy disk controller
    buffer overflow; guest-to-host escape in QEMU/KVM, Xen, VirtualBox.
    Ghost (CVE-2023-20887): VMware vCenter pre-auth RCE (not escape).
  [D407] AWS Nitro Enclave and confidential computing
    AWS Nitro: custom hypervisor with hardware attestation. Nitro Enclaves:
    isolated execution environment with no persistent storage, no interactive
    access, cryptographic attestation of code identity. Attested with AWS KMS.
    Designed for: processing sensitive data (PII, cryptographic operations)
    without host system visibility.
    GCP Confidential VMs: AMD SEV-SNP encrypted VM memory. Azure Confidential
    Computing: Intel TDX/SGX-based VMs.
  [D408] Container vs. VM isolation comparison
    VMs: hardware-enforced boundary (hypervisor + IOMMU). Kernel not shared.
    Containers: software isolation (Linux namespaces + cgroups). Kernel shared
    with host. Security: VM escape requires hypervisor vulnerability; container
    escape requires namespace vulnerability + kernel vulnerability. VMs: stronger
    isolation, higher overhead. Containers: weaker isolation, lower overhead.
    Kata Containers: container API + VM isolation (microVM per container).
  [D409] Cloud shared responsibility model
    Provider responsibility: physical security, hypervisor, network infrastructure,
    managed service security. Customer responsibility: OS configuration, application
    security, identity/access, data encryption, network ACLs. Common
    misunderstanding: RDS is a managed database but SQL injection is still customer
    responsibility. S3 is managed storage but bucket policies are customer
    responsibility. Misconfigurations cause majority of cloud data breaches.
  [D410] Kubernetes security (extended)
    Cluster security model: etcd (cluster state, secrets) at highest risk.
    Lateral movement paths: RBAC misconfiguration -> service account privilege;
    hostPath volume mount -> host filesystem access; hostNetwork: true -> access
    to host network stack; privileged container -> host root.
    Hardening: Pod Security Standards (PSS: baseline, restricted); OPA/Gatekeeper
    for custom policies; network policies (Calico, Cilium); etcd encryption at rest
    (kube-apiserver --encryption-provider-config).

  GAP: G282 [NEW] — VENOM and VM escape vulnerability history; hypervisor CVE taxonomy
  GAP: G283 [NEW] — AMD SEV-SNP attestation mechanism; TDX vs. SGX comparison
  GAP: G284 [NEW] — Kubernetes etcd encryption adoption rates

DOMAIN BLOCK 43.B: WEB3 AND SMART CONTRACT SECURITY
  [D411] Smart contract vulnerability classes
    Reentrancy: contract calls external contract; external contract calls back
    before state update. The DAO hack (2016): $60M ETH. SWC-107.
    Integer overflow/underflow: Solidity < 0.8.0 has no built-in overflow checks.
    access control: missing modifier; arbitrary tx.origin check instead of msg.sender.
    Front-running: transactions visible in mempool before mining; attacker submits
    same tx with higher gas (sandwich attack on DEX). Flashloan attack: borrow
    large amount within one transaction; manipulate oracle; profit; repay.
  [D412] Ethereum EVM security model
    EVM: deterministic state machine. All state on-chain. Smart contract code is
    immutable (by default). Proxy pattern: upgradeable contracts via delegatecall.
    Delegatecall vulnerability: DELEGATECALL in target's storage context; storage
    slot collision between proxy and implementation.
    Oracle manipulation: price oracle reads single DEX price; attacker flashloans
    to manipulate price; protocol takes action based on manipulated oracle.
  [D413] Bridge security and cross-chain attacks
    Blockchain bridges: lock assets on chain A; mint equivalent on chain B.
    Signature verification on bridge smart contract. Ronin bridge (2022): $625M
    stolen. Attacker compromised 5 of 9 validator private keys (social engineering
    + weak key management). Threshold signature scheme — compromising k-of-n.
    Wormhole bridge (2022): $320M. Signature verification bypass (guardian set
    initialization state).
  [D414] MEV (Maximal Extractable Value)
    MEV: profit miners/validators can extract by reordering, inserting, or
    censoring transactions in a block. Sandwich attack: front-run user swap +
    back-run for profit. JIT (Just-in-Time) liquidity: provide liquidity exactly
    when needed; remove immediately after. MEV-Boost (Ethereum): PBS (Proposer-
    Builder Separation) separates block building from proposing. Flashbots:
    private transaction mempool to reduce MEV competition gas wars.


--- SOURCE LINES 176456–176491 ---
LAW-3 COUNTER-EXAMPLE SEARCH (Cycle 1 of 5):
  Hypothesis: security measures transform attack surface; total exploitable
  volume is approximately conserved across defensive generations.
  CANDIDATE COUNTER-EXAMPLE CE-A: IPv6 and ICMPv6 security
    IPv4: many attack classes (broadcast amplification, ICMP redirect exploitation,
    ARP poisoning). IPv6: eliminates broadcast (uses multicast); NDP replaces ARP.
    Did IPv6 reduce total attack surface vs. IPv4?
    ASSESSMENT: IPv6 introduced new attack classes: NDP flooding, SLAAC attacks,
    IPv6 extension header evasion (firewalls that don't parse extension headers),
    Teredo/6to4 tunnel evasion, dual-stack complexity. IPv4 broadcast attacks
    eliminated; IPv6 multicast attacks introduced. NET CHANGE: roughly neutral,
    possibly increased due to dual-stack complexity.
    VERDICT: not a counter-example. Attack surface transformed, not reduced.
  CANDIDATE CE-B: TLS 1.3
    TLS 1.3 eliminates: 492 cipher suites, RSA key exchange, CBC mode, RC4,
    MD5, SHA-1, export ciphers, renegotiation, compression. Closed: POODLE,
    BEAST, DROWN, LOGJAM, FREAK, CRIME (compression). New: TLS 1.3 implementation
    bugs (e.g., CVE-2020-1967 OpenSSL NULL pointer, CVE-2021-3711 SM2 buffer
    overflow), H2.H1 desync with TLS 1.3 front-ends, new cipher suite
    implementation side-channels (AES-GCM nonce reuse in some implementations).
    NET CHANGE: significantly fewer attack classes in the protocol layer;
    some new implementation bugs. TLS 1.3 IS a net reduction in the cryptographic
    attack surface within TLS. This is potentially a LAW-3 counter-example.
    ASSESSMENT: TLS 1.3 reduced protocol-layer attack surface significantly.
    BUT: the total web security attack surface includes application layer
    (IDOR, injection, broken auth), which TLS does not address at all.
    If LAW-3 is claimed about TOTAL security (all layers), TLS 1.3 doesn't
    falsify it (application layer unchanged). If LAW-3 is claimed only about
    the specific protocol layer it addresses, TLS 1.3 IS a counter-example
    for that layer. This requires LAW-3 scope clarification.

LAW-3 CE CYCLE 1 RESULT: CE-A (IPv6) not counter-example. CE-B (TLS 1.3):
  partial counter-example at layer scope; not falsifying if LAW-3 is total-system.
  LAW-3 SCOPE REFINEMENT: claims apply to total-system attack surface, not
  individual-layer isolated analysis. In total-system scope, no counter-example
  found in cycle 1. 4 cycles remain.

C43.C3: Flashloan as R02 economic barrier complete removal
  Traditional finance attacks require capital proportional to target size.
  Flash loans (Aave, dYdX) allow uncollateralized loans within single block —
  borrow $100M, attack, repay, net profit. Beanstalk ($182M, 2022): attacker
  flash-loaned $1B, bought governance majority, passed malicious proposal,
  drained treasury, repaid loan in one transaction. This is not a novel
  vulnerability class. It is the complete elimination of R02 (economic barrier)
  as an attack deterrent. R02.DEFI sub-class CANDIDATE: economic barriers
  eliminated by atomic flash-loan composability.

C43.C4: ML supply chain as P40.1 extension (training data poisoning)
  P40.1 (supply chain trust inversion) extends to ML domain. HuggingFace model
  poisoning: attacker uploads model with embedded backdoor (specific input
  triggers malicious output). Trust inversion: users trust model repositories
  as trusted supply chains; repositories have no equivalent of code signing +
  reproducible builds for model weights. The attack surface is the weight
  space — 100 billion float32 values that cannot be manually audited. P43.3
  = P40.1 instantiated in ML weight supply chain. Pattern 40.6 CANDIDATE
  instance 7: class elimination required (cryptographic weight signing +
  reproducible training) rather than instance scanning.

── CONVERGENCE BLOCK C43.2: LAW-3 COUNTER-EXAMPLE CYCLE 2 ───────────────────

LAW-3 DRAFT: SECURITY MEASURES TRANSFORM ATTACK SURFACE; TOTAL VOLUME
APPROXIMATELY CONSERVED.

CE CYCLE 2 OF 5: PROPOSED COUNTER-EXAMPLE — MEMORY-SAFE LANGUAGES

Claim: Rust eliminates entire attack surface classes (buffer overflow, use-
after-free, data race). Total attack surface is not conserved — it is reduced.

Analysis:
  Surface eliminated: ~70% of CVEs in memory-unsafe code are memory safety
  issues. If codebase migrated to Rust, this 70% disappears.
  
  Surface created: 
    (a) Unsafe blocks. Every Rust codebase has unsafe blocks for FFI, hardware
        access, performance. These blocks inherit all C-class vulnerabilities.
    (b) Logic errors. Memory safety does not prevent algorithmic bugs, integer
        overflow in arithmetic, business logic errors, cryptographic misuse.
    (c) Dependency supply chain. Rust crates introduce supply chain attack
        surface (Pattern 33.3 instance 9 + P40.1).
    (d) Serialization layer. Rust code parsing untrusted input (JSON, binary
        protocols) creates parsing attack surface.

LAW-3-THRESHOLD question: does volume of (b)+(c)+(d)+(e) approximately equal
volume of memory safety surface eliminated?

Assessment: This is the hardest CE candidate so far. Memory safety elimination
is quantifiable (~70% of CVEs). Logic error + supply chain surface is harder
to quantify. However:
  - Android's migration to Rust: memory safety vulnerabilities dropped from
    ~76% to ~35% of security bugs over 4 years. Total vulnerability count
    also dropped (~40% reduction in total CVEs).
  - This would falsify LAW-3 if total volume decreases, not merely transforms.

Verdict: NOT FALSIFIED but SCOPE REFINEMENT REQUIRED.
  Android data suggests total volume reduction is possible during class
  elimination phase. LAW-3 may hold only in steady-state (mature attack surface)
  not during architectural transition. Refinement: LAW-3 may be a long-run
  steady-state law, not a transition law. During class elimination (Pattern 40.6
  events), temporary volume reduction can occur before new surface is discovered.

  This is a new dimension that existing root mechanics don't fully capture.

G297 ANATOMY: SGX/TEE side-channel attacks
  Surface: Intel SGX enclave execution model
  Mechanism (cache-timing variant):
    Layer 1 — Enclave co-location: attacker process runs on same physical CPU
    Layer 2 — Cache observation: monitor cache state during enclave execution
    Layer 3 — Access pattern recovery: deduce secret-dependent memory accesses
    Layer 4 — Key recovery: reconstruct private key from access pattern
  Mechanism (page fault variant, Controlled-Channel Attack):
    Layer 1 — OS controls page tables (SGX does not protect against OS)
    Layer 2 — Page fault timing: OS induces page faults and observes which
      pages are accessed in what order
    Layer 3 — Secret recovery: page access sequence reveals algorithm path
  Root mechanics: R10.5a (passive side-channel: cache timing, page faults),
    R06.ARCH (SGX threat model excludes OS as adversary; real deployments
    have untrusted OS), R10.6 (SGX evaluated assuming OS is trusted or
    that memory encryption suffices; side-channel context not fully addressed)
  Defense: constant-time code within enclave, oblivious RAM (ORAM) for
    memory access pattern hiding, hardware mitigations (CLFLUSH restrictions)
  G297 STATUS: CLOSED

G310 ANATOMY: NTP amplification + time confusion attacks
  Surface: NTP protocol (UDP, unauthenticated in base RFC 958 / RFC 5905)
  Mechanism (amplification DDoS):
    Layer 1 — Reflection: attacker sends monlist request to NTP servers

C44.C4: LAW-3 COUNTER-EXAMPLE CYCLE 3 — PROPOSED CE: SANDBOXING

  Claim: Modern OS sandboxing (macOS sandbox, Android SELinux, Chrome renderer
  isolation) eliminates attack surface classes. Volume not conserved — reduced.

  Analysis:
    Surface eliminated: post-compromise impact reduced (attacker must chain
    sandbox escape; direct code execution no longer gives OS-level access)
    Surface created:
      (a) Sandbox escape vulnerabilities (new class; CVE-dense; Chrome sandbox
          escapes: ~15-20 critical CVEs per year)
      (b) IPC attack surface: sandboxed process must communicate via IPC to
          less-privileged API broker; broker becomes attack surface
          (e.g., XMPC, mach messages in macOS sandbox: historically CVE-rich)
      (c) Privilege escalation chains: attacker now needs exploit chain
          (renderer bug + sandbox escape + privilege escalation vs. just one
          exploit). Market price: a Chrome full chain is ~$2-3M (ZDI/Zerodium).
          A Chrome renderer-only RCE is ~$500K.
    
    Volume assessment:
      - Sandbox escape CVEs replace some fraction of post-exploitation CVEs
      - IPC broker attack surface is new surface with real CVE density
      - Total attack surface: likely ~conserved (different distribution, not
        reduced). The $2-3M full chain vs. $500K partial confirms that the
        added surface (sandbox escape) has market-validated difficulty premium
        but does not disappear — it is priced.

  Verdict: NOT FALSIFIED. Sandboxing transforms attack surface distribution
  (forces attacker to chain exploits) without eliminating total volume.
  The market pricing directly measures the added difficulty (sandbox escape
  commands premium) — this is not conservation of attack surface volume
  exactly, but conservation of attack SURFACE existence. LAW-3 scope:
  attack surfaces are not eliminated, merely transformed.

PATTERN 45.4 DRAFT: PERMISSIVE DEFAULT CONFIGURATION AS VULNERABILITY CLASS
  Platform defaults are designed for ease of use, not security. Operators
  accept defaults without understanding security implications. The platform's
  security posture depends entirely on operators overriding defaults — but most
  don't, either from ignorance or operational pressure.
  Instances:
    1. AWS S3 public ACL (default was public until 2023 when Amazon changed it)
    2. AWS IAM AdministratorAccess wildcard (still default for convenience)
    3. Docker daemon root access (default behavior exposes host)
    4. Kubernetes default ServiceAccount token (auto-mounted, full API access)
    5. MongoDB no-auth default (2017 ransomware wave: 27,000 open MongoDB instances)
    6. Redis no-auth default (2016+: mass exploitation of internet-facing Redis)
  Count: 6. Status: DRAFT. Counter-example: if platform changes defaults to
  secure, does this pattern end? Yes — this pattern is partially contingent
  on platform design choices. Pattern 45.4 identifies where the gap exists
  in current ecosystem, not a timeless structural law.

G262 ANATOMY: WebAuthn/FIDO2 implementation vulnerabilities
  Surface: WebAuthn authenticator-to-relying-party protocol
  Mechanism:
    Layer 1 — Registration: authenticator creates credential bound to origin +
      rpId; private key in authenticator hardware (security key, TPM, secure enclave)
    Layer 2 — Authentication: authenticator signs challenge with private key;
      relying party verifies signature + origin binding
  Attack surfaces:
    (a) Clone detection bypass: FIDO2 signature counter increments on each use;
      cloned authenticator has same counter; RP must detect non-monotonic counter
      and reject. Implementation gap: many RPs don't enforce counter validation.
    (b) Origin binding bypass: rpId must match effective domain; subdomain
      takeover on relying party allows attacker to register credential on
      attacker-controlled subdomain with same rpId
    (c) Attestation verification gaps: RP doesn't verify attestation cert chain;
      attacker registers unverified authenticator as "hardware-bound"
    (d) Backup-eligible credentials (passkeys): credential synced across devices;
      cloud backup provider compromise recovers all passkeys
  Root mechanics: R06.ARCH (optional counter validation is architectural choice),
    R05 (trust model: RP trusts attestation without verification),
    P40.1 for passkeys (sync provider becomes supply chain for credential security)
  Pattern 40.6 instance: FIDO2 class-level defense degrades to instance-level
    vulnerability when RP implementation is incomplete
  G262 STATUS: CLOSED

G265 ANATOMY: Container escape via cgroup/namespace vulnerabilities
  Surface: Linux kernel isolation primitives used by container runtimes
  Mechanism (CVE-2022-0492: cgroup v1 release_agent escape):
    Layer 1 — Container has CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE or runs as root inside container
    Layer 2 — Mount cgroup v1 filesystem inside container (allowed if privileged)
    Layer 3 — Write to release_agent file (executed by host kernel when cgroup
      is released with no processes remaining)
    Layer 4 — Container exits; host kernel executes attacker-controlled command
      as root on host
  Mechanism (runc CVE-2019-5736: runc binary overwrite):
    Layer 1 — Attacker controls container image
    Layer 2 — Container image references /proc/self/exe to overwrite runc binary
      when container exec opens it
    Layer 3 — Next runc execution on host executes attacker code
  Root mechanics: R06.ARCH (container isolation uses kernel primitives that
    were not designed as security boundaries; they are resource isolation
    mechanisms; true security isolation requires VM-level boundaries or
    gVisor/Kata containers), R05 (container trust model: container assumed
    to not have kernel capabilities; privileged containers break this)
  Lesson: container != VM; container isolation is a software boundary;
    VM isolation is a hardware boundary. Security properties differ fundamentally.
  G265 STATUS: CLOSED

G272 ANATOMY: Hardware Security Module (HSM) attack surface
  Surface: Tamper-evident/tamper-resistant hardware device storing crypto keys
  Mechanism (logical attacks):
    Layer 1 — HSM API attack: HSM exposes API for crypto operations; API has
      attack surface if keys are extractable through crafted operation sequences
      (e.g., PKCS#11 attribute manipulation: import key with wrong template;
      export key marked non-exportable by manipulating attributes at import)
    Layer 2 — Oracle attacks: HSM used as decryption oracle; repeated queries
      with different ciphertexts extract key information (Bleichenbacher attack
      on RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 via HSM oracle)
  Mechanism (physical attacks on lower-grade HSMs):
    Layer 1 — Decapsulation: remove epoxy, expose die
    Layer 2 — Microprobing: probe memory buses, extract key material
    Layer 3 — Side-channel: power analysis on HSM crypto operations
  Root mechanics: R10.5a (passive side-channel on HSM power trace),
    R06.ARCH (PKCS#11 API design allows attribute manipulation that bypasses
    non-exportable flag in some implementations),
    R05 (HSM trust model: HSM trusted to enforce non-exportability; API attack
    exploits gap between intended trust model and implementation)
  G272 STATUS: CLOSED

G283 ANATOMY: Zero-knowledge proof systems (zk-SNARK/zk-STARK)
  Surface: cryptographic proof systems used in privacy coins and ZK rollups
  Mechanism (trusted setup vulnerability, zk-SNARKs):
    Layer 1 — zk-SNARK requires trusted setup: generates Common Reference
      String (CRS) with toxic waste (secret randomness)
    Layer 2 — If toxic waste is not destroyed, holder can generate false proofs
    Layer 3 — "Trusted setup ceremony" distributes trust across multiple parties;
      security holds if at least one party destroys their randomness
    Attack: if all ceremony participants collude or are compromised, false proofs
      can be generated — attacker can mint arbitrary cryptocurrency
  Mechanism (constraint system bugs):
    Layer 1 — ZK circuit must encode correct constraints for the statement
    Layer 2 — Underconstrained circuit: proof is valid for statement AND for
      other unintended statements
    Layer 3 — Attacker crafts proof for false statement that satisfies
      underconstrained verification
    Example: Zcash Sapling (2019): underconstrained circuit would have allowed
      infinite Zcash inflation (discovered before exploitation, fixed)
  Root mechanics: R06.ARCH (trusted setup architectural assumption; circuit
    correctness is the architectural constraint that must be verified formally),
    R05 (trust model: verifier trusts circuit encodes the right statement;
    circuit bugs violate this)
  Note: zk-STARKs eliminate trusted setup (transparent) but are larger proofs;
    circuit correctness problem remains for both
  G283 STATUS: CLOSED

── CONVERGENCE BLOCK C45.1: COGNITIVE LAYER AS FINAL ATTACK SURFACE ─────────

C45.C1: Human cognitive layer is the terminal attack surface that technical
  controls cannot fully eliminate.

  Technical stack attack surfaces:
    Hardware → firmware → OS kernel → libraries → applications → network →
    human operator.

  Each layer has technical defenses. The human layer has:
    - Training (reduces but does not eliminate vulnerability)
    - Procedural controls (callback verification, dual authorization)
    - Technical assists (anti-phishing toolbars, DMARC, visual indicators)
    None eliminates the fundamental vulnerability: humans make trust
    decisions based on incomplete information under time pressure.

  Each class has different trust inversion mechanism but shares root P40.1
  structure. The attack surface is wherever trust is assumed without verification.
  LAW-1 applies to all: verification at supply chain scale is computationally
  and economically infeasible at current depths (100+ transitive dependencies,
  millions of lines of build toolchain code).


--- SOURCE LINES 178839–178850 ---
  Bluetooth LE introduced privacy features (random address rotation) to prevent
  tracking. Was tracking risk evaluated at BLE design time?

  Analysis:
    BLE Core Spec 4.0 (2010): advertising packets from fixed MAC address.
    Tracking problem documented in academic literature by 2012.
    BLE Core Spec 4.2 (2014): LE Privacy feature added — resolvable private
    addresses (RPA), randomized every few minutes.
    Security context: tracking by passive scanner was not fully evaluated
    at BLE 4.0 design; BLE was designed for low-energy device communication.
    The privacy attack surface (passive tracking of physical location via
    fixed BLE MAC) was unanticipated at design time.


--- SOURCE LINES 178876–178914 ---
── CONVERGENCE BLOCK C45.2: LAW-3 COUNTER-EXAMPLE CYCLE 4 ─────────────────

LAW-3 DRAFT: SECURITY MEASURES TRANSFORM ATTACK SURFACE; TOTAL VOLUME
APPROXIMATELY CONSERVED.

CE CYCLE 4 OF 5: PROPOSED CE — REMOVING ATTACK SURFACE CLASS ENTIRELY

  Specific case: Physical USB attack surface. USB attacks (BadUSB, HID
  injection, USB rubber ducky) require physical access + USB port.
  Defense: disable all USB ports physically or via policy.

  Analysis:
    If USB ports are physically removed/disabled, the entire USB attack
    surface class is eliminated. There is no USB attack surface when there
    are no USB ports.
    
    New surface created: removable media alternatives must exist (network
    transfer, provisioning process). Network provisioning creates network
    attack surface. If network is also air-gapped, humans become the attack
    surface (social engineering for physical access, malicious insider).
    
    Is this conservation? The surface transforms: USB attack surface →
    network transfer surface + human bridging surface. For true air-gap
    with no network and no USB: the attack surface compresses to physical
    access + physics-layer covert channels (R01, radiation emissions).
    This is genuinely smaller than a full-connectivity surface.

  Verdict: NOT FALSIFIED but SCOPE REFINEMENT CONFIRMED.
  LAW-3 holds in network-connected systems. In physically isolated systems
  (true air-gap), total surface volume can be significantly reduced through
  physical elimination of attack surface classes. The residual (physics-layer
  covert channels + insider threat + supply chain) is smaller than the
  original connected surface.

  LAW-3 SCOPE FINAL: holds for network-connected systems in steady state.
  Physically isolated systems can achieve genuine surface reduction at the
  cost of operational friction (cannot receive software updates via network,
  requires human-mediated supply chain for any update — which creates its
  own supply chain attack surface).

--- SOURCE LINES 179294–179319 ---
── ANATOMY BATCH 46.A: CARRIED + NEW PRIORITY GAPS ──────────────────

G267 ANATOMY: ARM Memory Tagging Extension (MTE) and hardware memory safety
  Surface: Hardware-assisted memory safety (ARM MTE, SPARC ADI, CHERI)
  Mechanism:
    Layer 1 — Tag allocation: each 16-byte memory granule has a 4-bit tag;
      pointer carries corresponding tag in top-byte ignore (TBI) bits
    Layer 2 — Tag check: on memory access, hardware compares pointer tag
      with memory tag; mismatch = fault (SIGSEGV or asynchronous report)
    Layer 3 — Attack surface: temporal safety (use-after-free) defeated if
      freed region gets new tag; spatial safety (buffer overflow) defeated
      if adjacent allocation has different tag
  Attack surface of MTE itself:
    (a) Tag brute force: 4-bit tag = 1/16 chance of guess; 16 attempts
      statistically gets one through. Async mode (default for performance)
      doesn't kill process on tag fault — allows brute force iteration.
    (b) Information leaks: if attacker can read tag value, defeats protection
    (c) Heap spray: if attacker can control heap layout, can ensure dangling
      pointer tag matches reallocated region tag (tag reuse)
  Root mechanics: Pattern 40.6 (class-level defense) vs. residual attack
    surface. MTE eliminates naive heap overflow/UAF but creates new sub-attack
    surface (tag inference, brute force in async mode). Pattern 33.3 CANDIDATE:

--- SOURCE LINES 179415–179435 ---
G342 ANATOMY: Return-oriented programming (ROP) bypass of DEP/NX
  Surface: DEP/NX (Data Execution Prevention / No-Execute) memory protection
  Mechanism:
    Layer 1 — DEP prevents injecting shellcode and jumping to it: data pages
      are non-executable
    Layer 2 — ROP: instead of injecting code, attacker chains existing code
      gadgets (short instruction sequences ending in RET)
    Layer 3 — Stack overflow or other memory corruption controls stack
    Layer 4 — Return address chain: each gadget executes and returns to next
      gadget; chain implements arbitrary computation from existing code
    Layer 5 — Full bypass: attacker achieves arbitrary code execution without
      injecting any new code; only existing (executable) code is used
  Root mechanics: LAW-2 (DEP thought strong barrier; ROP discovered within
    ~2 years of widespread DEP deployment), LAW-3 (DEP transforms attack
    surface from code injection → code reuse; volume approximately conserved),
    Pattern 33.3 (DEP security layer creates ROP as new attack perimeter;
    B = executable/non-executable boundary; T = ROP chain compilers)
  Note: Pattern 33.3 instance CONFIRMED: DEP → ROP surface. This is one
    of the strongest instances in the corpus: the security measure (DEP)
    directly created the attack technique (ROP) that bypasses it.
  G342 STATUS: CLOSED

--- SOURCE LINES 180072–180086 ---
── PATTERN IDENTIFICATION BLOCK 47.A ────────────────────────────────────────

PATTERN 47.1 DRAFT: CLASS-LEVEL DEFENSE ERASURE BY FINE-TUNING
  Safety training in LLMs is a class-level defense (alignment training
  prevents harmful outputs). Fine-tuning can erase class-level safety
  training, creating instance-level vulnerability. This is the inverse of
  Pattern 40.6: instead of class elimination providing security, class-level
  security is erased by localized modification. Mechanism: LoRA fine-tuning
  on adversarial examples; catastrophic forgetting of safety training when
  fine-tuned on targeted domain.
  Instances:
    1. LLM safety bypass via fine-tuning (Qi et al., 2023): 100 adversarial
       examples sufficient to significantly degrade safety alignment
    2. Concept erasure via fine-tuning (inverse of gradient-based unlearning)
  Count: 2. Status: DRAFT. Counter-example cycle pending.
