────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A631: SERVER-SIDE TEMPLATE INJECTION TO REMOTE CODE EXECUTION
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Domain: SSTI (D1599)
Class: Injection / remote code execution
Layer stack:
  L1 — Template engine mechanics: templates execute expressions embedded in
         markup (Jinja2: {{expr}}, Twig: {{expr}}, Freemarker: ${expr}).
         Expressions are evaluated server-side; evaluated result replaces tag.
  L2 — Vulnerable pattern: user input concatenated directly into template string
         before rendering. Distinguishable from XSS: injection executes server-side,
         not client-side.
  L3 — Jinja2 RCE chain (Python): {{config.__class__.__init__.__globals__
         ['os'].popen('id').read()}} traverses Python object model from template
         context to os module. Alternative: {{lipsum.__globals__.os.popen('id')}}
  L4 — Freemarker RCE (Java): <#assign ex="freemarker.template.utility
         .Execute"?new()> ${ex("id")} invokes arbitrary Java class execution.
         CVE-2015-5223 (Alfresco), CVE-2019-3396 (Confluence Server).
  L5 — Detection: inject {{7*7}}, expect 49 in response (arithmetic evaluation);
         engine fingerprinting by error messages; tplmap automates probing.
  L6 — Defense: never render user input as template; use template engine
         sandbox mode (Jinja2 SandboxedEnvironment); pass user data as
         template variables, not as template text; WAF rules for template
         expression patterns as defense-in-depth.
  L7 — Real-world: Uber bug bounty (Jinja2 SSTI, 2016); Shopify bug bounty
         (Handlebars SSTI); HackerOne Top 25 vulnerability classes include SSTI.
  Root mechanics: R06 (complexity), R05 (attacker tooling).


--- SOURCE LINES 254853–254879 ---
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A635: FILE UPLOAD WEB SHELL VIA EXTENSION MISMATCH
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Domain: File upload vulnerabilities (D1609)
Class: Remote code execution / web shell
Layer stack:
  L1 — Attack objective: upload PHP/ASP/JSP web shell to web-accessible directory;
         trigger execution via HTTP request; achieve server-side RCE.
  L2 — Extension bypass techniques:
         (a) Double extension: shell.php.jpg — server validates .jpg, web server
         misconfiguration executes .php files regardless of secondary extension.
         (b) Null byte: shell.php%00.jpg (historic, patched in modern PHP).
         (c) MIME type mismatch: send Content-Type: image/jpeg with PHP content;
         validation checks MIME type from client, not content.
         (d) Case variation: shell.PHP on case-insensitive filesystem.
  L3 — ImageTragick (CVE-2016-3714): upload image file; server processes with
         ImageMagick; crafted filename or header triggers delegate execution;
         RCE without requiring script execution. Pattern: server-side processing
         of uploaded files as additional attack surface beyond script execution.
  L4 — Storage location attack: uploaded files stored in web root vs. outside
         web root. Web root storage + execution = RCE. Outside web root storage
         + serving via script eliminates direct execution path.
  L5 — Defense: store uploads outside web root; serve via controller that
         sets Content-Type from allowlist, never user-supplied; validate file
         content (magic bytes) not just extension; use CDN/separate domain
         for user content serving (eliminates same-origin execution).
  Root mechanics: R06 (complexity), R05 (attacker bypass tooling).


--- SOURCE LINES 254963–255019 ---
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A639: AWS IMDSV1 SSRF TO CROSS-ACCOUNT PRIVILEGE ESCALATION
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Domain: AWS security architecture (D1598)
Class: Cloud SSRF / credential theft / privilege escalation
Layer stack:
  L1 — IMDSv1 vulnerability: EC2 Instance Metadata Service v1 responds to any
         HTTP request without authentication. SSRF vulnerability in application
         allows attacker to make server-side request to 169.254.169.254.
  L2 — Credential retrieval: GET 169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-
         credentials/<role-name> returns temporary IAM credentials.
         Capital One breach (2019): Paige Thompson exploited SSRF in WAF EC2
         instance to obtain role credentials with S3 GetObject permissions.
  L3 — Cross-account escalation chain: stolen role credentials used to call
         sts:AssumeRole on cross-account role that trusts the compromised account.
         Cross-account trust relationships not visible in original account;
         attacker enumerates via sts:GetCallerIdentity and role assumption attempts.
  L4 — Blast radius amplification: single SSRF + IMDSv1 vulnerability in one
         account may provide access to multiple accounts via cross-account trust
         relationships. Organization-wide impact from single application SSRF.
  L5 — Defense: enforce IMDSv2 (hop limit 1, token-required) via Instance
         Metadata Options; restrict EC2 instance roles to minimum required
         permissions; monitor for unusual sts:AssumeRole across accounts;
         SCP blocking cross-account assumptions from application roles.
  Root mechanics: R06 (cloud complexity), R11 (IMDS as ambient credential source).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A640: KEY MANAGEMENT ESCROW COMPROMISE FOR BULK DECRYPTION
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Domain: Encryption key management lifecycle (D1606)
Class: Cryptographic infrastructure attack
Layer stack:
  L1 — Key escrow context: organization stores copies of encryption keys with
         escrow agent (for regulatory compliance, recovery purposes, lawful
         access requirements). Escrow agent holds keys for multiple customers.
  L2 — Escrow as attack target: compromising escrow agent provides bulk access
         to all escrowed keys. Single attack target enables decryption of data
         from all customers whose keys are escrowed.
  L3 — Law enforcement escrow: CALEA and international lawful access proposals
         require key escrow or exceptional access mechanisms. Such mechanisms
         create centralized key repositories as high-value attack targets.
         NSA/NIST Dual_EC_DRBG backdoor (2006-2014) is the documented case
         of centralized key generation parameter compromise.
  L4 — Cloud KMS escrow analogy: cloud KMS (AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, GCP Cloud KMS)
         holds customer encryption keys. CSP compromise or insider threat
         provides access to customer keys. BYOK/HYOK models reduce but
         do not eliminate CSP key access depending on implementation.
  L5 — Split key custodianship: m-of-n key sharing (Shamir Secret Sharing)
         requires compromising m custodians. Reduces single-point risk;
         does not eliminate if m custodians can be simultaneously compromised
         (supply chain, coercion, social engineering of custodians).
  L6 — Defense: HYOK for highest sensitivity data; HSM with physical security
         controls; key usage audit with independent oversight; minimize escrowed
         key count; prefer key derivation from protected root key over escrow
         of individual data keys.
  Root mechanics: R07 (scale — escrow compromise scales), R09 (regulatory
  mandate creating attack surface), R06 (key lifecycle complexity).

A1337: NODE.JS PROTOTYPE POLLUTION VIA JSON MERGE RCE
Domain: Prototype pollution (A632 anatomy)
Mechanism: Express.js API endpoint accepts JSON body; passes to merge function
(lodash.merge, deepmerge). Attacker sends {"__proto__":{"shell":true,"env":
{"NODE_OPTIONS":"--require /dev/stdin"}}} in body. Subsequent child_process.spawn
call inherits polluted options; attacker-controlled code executes.
Evidence: CVE-2019-10744 (lodash); multiple express.js HackerOne RCE reports;
widespread lodash usage makes this a high-prevalence vulnerability class.
Impact: RCE on any Node.js application using vulnerable merge libraries
with attacker-controlled JSON input.

A1340: FILE UPLOAD POLYGLOT WEB SHELL BYPASS
Domain: File upload vulnerabilities (A635 anatomy)
Mechanism: Attacker creates polyglot file: valid JPEG image header (FFD8FF)
followed by PHP web shell code. File passes MIME type validation (image/jpeg),
magic byte validation (JPEG header), and extension validation (.jpg).
Server-side processing by PHP interprets file as script due to .php reference
in server configuration or backup filename rename vulnerability.
Evidence: Polyglot file techniques documented in OWASP File Upload testing guide;
multiple HackerOne reports; ImageTragick class demonstrates server-side processing
as alternative execution vector.
Impact: Web shell upload bypassing multiple validation layers; RCE without
requiring server misconfiguration in some PHP deployment scenarios.

A1347: SUPPLY CHAIN ATTACK VIA COMPROMISED VULN DATABASE ENRICHMENT
Domain: Vulnerability management (D1594)
Mechanism: Attacker compromises NVD data provider or NVD enrichment tool
to modify CVSS score and description for a specific CVE. Lowers CVSS score
from 9.8 to 5.3 for a critical vulnerability in widely-deployed software.
Organizations using automated CVSS-based patching defer the vulnerability
to standard patch cycle. Attacker exploits it during extended remediation window.
Evidence: NVD processing delays documented (NVD backlog crisis 2024: NIST paused
enrichment for thousands of CVEs); enrichment toolchain complexity creates
manipulation surface; specific manipulation not publicly documented but NVD
data quality issues confirmed.
Impact: Vulnerability prioritization infrastructure itself becomes attack target;
single score change across entire NVD consumer ecosystem simultaneously.

Domain: Board governance / SEC disclosure (D1602)

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A641: ICS/SCADA Historian Exploitation for Lateral Movement
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Layer 1 — Surface: Attackers pivot from IT network to OT historian servers
  that aggregate process data, using them as dual-homed bridge nodes.
Layer 2 — Mechanism: Industrial historians (OSIsoft PI, Aspentech IP.21,
  Honeywell PHD) run on Windows with SQL backends and DCOM interfaces.
  Historian sits on both IT (reporting) and OT (data collection) VLANs.
  Compromise via IT-side vulnerability grants OT network adjacency.
Layer 3 — Structural driver: Operational requirement for cross-network data
  flow creates permanent dual-homed exposure; segmentation cannot fully
  isolate without breaking business reporting function.
Layer 4 — Detection gap: OT network lacks EDR coverage; IT SIEM does not
  receive OT telemetry; historian process anomalies not baselined.
Layer 5 — Exploitation chain: IT phish → IT foothold → historian lateral
  → OT network adjacency → engineering workstation → PLC program modification.
  Industroyer/CRASHOVERRIDE used historian-adjacent paths.
Layer 6 — Defense leverage: Unidirectional gateways (Waterfall, OWL) on
  historian OT interface; historian process integrity monitoring; OT-specific
  NDR (Claroty, Dragos, Nozomi) for lateral movement detection.
Gap closure: partial (G-C102-01 — OT consequence mapping unresolved).


--- SOURCE LINES 256124–256148 ---
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A646: Deepfake Detector Evasion via Adversarial Perturbation
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Layer 1 — Surface: Deepfake generation pipeline incorporates adversarial
  perturbation to defeat deployed detection models.
Layer 2 — Mechanism: Deepfake detectors (CNN-based, frequency-domain)
  are themselves neural classifiers vulnerable to adversarial examples.
  Neekhara et al. (2021) demonstrated universal adversarial perturbations
  degrading detector accuracy from >90% to <10% without visible image
  degradation. Perturbation magnitude constrained by L-inf norm to remain
  imperceptible. Arms race: detector trained on perturbed fakes; new
  perturbation defeats updated detector.
Layer 3 — Structural driver: Detector brittleness is fundamental to gradient-
  based models; perceptual similarity does not imply adversarial robustness;
  same structural vulnerability as image classifiers in adversarial ML.
Layer 4 — Detection gap: Perturbed deepfake is visually indistinguishable
  from authentic; detector returns false-negative; human judgment is the
  only remaining signal (and is itself manipulable under time pressure).
Layer 5 — Exploitation chain: Train surrogate detector → compute universal
  perturbation via PGD on surrogate → apply to deepfake generation output
  → deploy in targeted campaign → target org's detector returns benign.
Layer 6 — Defense leverage: Ensemble detectors with diverse architectures;
  provenance-based authentication (C2PA); frequency-domain artifacts
  analysis; adversarial training of detectors.
Gap closure: partial (G-C102-06 generalization benchmark open; P93 context).


--- SOURCE LINES 256229–256253 ---
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A650: Tabletop Exercise Gap Recurrence via Untracked Finding Closure
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Layer 1 — Surface: Gaps identified in tabletop exercises recur in subsequent
  exercises because findings are not tracked to verified closure.
Layer 2 — Mechanism: Tabletop exercise identifies decision-making gap
  (e.g., no defined authority for ransom payment decision). After-action
  report documents gap. Remediation assigned to CISO. 12 months later,
  next exercise: same gap present. No tracking system verified policy
  was actually updated; CISO turnover lost context. Pattern documented
  in FEMA HSEEP after-action follow-up guidance as endemic problem.
Layer 3 — Structural driver: Tabletop exercises are episodic events, not
  continuous improvement programs; findings registers not integrated into
  security program management; no accountability for closure verification.
Layer 4 — Detection gap: There is no detection failure here — the gap
  is a program management failure. The attack surface created: real
  incident exploits unresolved decision authority gap identified in
  exercise but never remediated.
Layer 5 — Exploitation chain: Real incident triggers scenario identical
  to unresolved tabletop gap → decision paralysis from undefined authority
  → delayed response → attacker achieves objective during paralysis window.
Layer 6 — Defense leverage: Integrated findings register with owner, due
  date, verification criteria; pre-exercise review of prior open findings;
  G-C102-10 closure tracking standard partially addresses.
Gap closure: partial (G-C102-10 tracking standard open).

--- SOURCE LINES 256866–256894 ---
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A655: UEFI BootKit Persistence via Secure Boot Bypass
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Layer 1 — Surface: Attacker installs bootkit in UEFI firmware to achieve
  persistence that survives OS reinstall and antivirus.
Layer 2 — Mechanism: Secure Boot verifies boot chain via signature chain
  (UEFI → bootloader → OS kernel). Bypass vectors: (1) Signed UEFI driver
  with exploitable vulnerability (BlackLotus, 2023 — used CVE-2022-21894
  Baton Drop signed bootloader); (2) UEFI firmware vulnerability allowing
  unsigned code execution before Secure Boot initialization; (3) MOKList
  manipulation on Linux (adding attacker key to Machine Owner Key list).
  BlackLotus: first in-the-wild UEFI bootkit bypassing fully-patched Windows.
Layer 3 — Structural driver: Secure Boot chain of trust depends on signature
  revocation (DBX list); revocation requires firmware update; firmware
  updates are slow (OEM dependency); revocation of widely-deployed bootloaders
  risks breaking existing installations.
Layer 4 — Detection gap: Bootkit executes before OS; EDR loads after OS;
  bootkit can patch EDR drivers or OS kernel before EDR initialization;
  detection requires pre-OS measurement (TPM PCR values, UEFI integrity
  measurement).
Layer 5 — Exploitation chain: Obtain admin/physical access → deploy signed
  vulnerable bootloader → execute UEFI exploit → install bootkit in EFI
  System Partition or firmware → persistence through OS reinstall;
  patch EDR on each boot.
Layer 6 — Defense leverage: UEFI DBX updates (KEK revocation); Secure
  Boot Custom Mode monitoring; CHIPSEC firmware integrity scanning;
  measured boot with TPM attestation (Trusted Boot); hardware-enforced
  BIOS write protection.
Gap closure: partial (G-C103-05 firmware disclosure timeline open).


--- SOURCE LINES 256926–256951 ---
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A657: Government Equity Process Exploitation via Disclosure Embargo Extension
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Layer 1 — Surface: State actor exploits vulnerability during extended
  government coordinated disclosure embargo that delays public patch.
Layer 2 — Mechanism: Vendor discovers vulnerability; notifies CISA/NSA
  under CVD process; government equity process (VEP) evaluates offensive
  utility; determines to retain for offensive use; extends embargo beyond
  90-day norm. Adversary independently discovers same vulnerability during
  embargo window; exploits unpatched systems. Or: government retains vuln,
  offensive tooling is stolen (EternalBlue/WannaCry: NSA exploit leaked by
  Shadow Brokers; used in WannaCry before patch cycle complete).
Layer 3 — Structural driver: Government offensive equities create retention
  incentive; VEP process opaque; vendor and public unaware of extended
  embargo; zero-day market creates parallel discovery incentive for
  adversaries; patch gap window proportional to embargo length.
Layer 4 — Detection gap: Victim has no knowledge of vulnerability existence
  during embargo; cannot patch; cannot detect exploitation of unknown vuln;
  anomaly detection is only mitigation.
Layer 5 — Exploitation chain: Vuln discovered → reported to government
  → VEP retains → adversary discovers independently → exploits globally
  before patch available → mass compromise during embargo window.
Layer 6 — Defense leverage: VEP transparency reporting (annual aggregate);
  embargo duration caps with exception process; vendor notification
  even under retention decision; G-C103-07 multi-party CVD standard.
Gap closure: partial (G-C103-07 embargo duration standard open).

A667: M&A Target Company Breach via Known Acquired Vulnerability
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Layer 1 — Surface: Attacker exploits security debt in acquired company
  before integration security remediation completes.
Layer 2 — Mechanism: M&A announcement is public. Attacker identifies
  acquisition target → conducts external attack surface mapping of target
  (Shodan, certificate transparency, Censys) → identifies known
  vulnerabilities in target's exposed infrastructure → exploits before
  integration team remediates. Acquired company: smaller security team,
  known technical debt, ongoing organizational disruption reduces
  response capacity. Yahoo breach: disclosed during acquisition by Verizon,
  reduced deal value by $350M. Integration period: typically 18-36 months;
  attack surface during this window is acquirer's liability.
Layer 3 — Structural driver: M&A announcement creates known high-risk
  window; integration security work cannot be compressed below minimum
  feasible timeline; target company security state is independent of
  acquirer's security posture during due diligence.
Layer 4 — Detection gap: Acquirer's SOC may not yet have visibility into
  acquired company's infrastructure during transition; SIEM integration
  and tool deployment lag behind acquisition close.
Layer 5 — Exploitation chain: M&A announcement → attacker scans target
  external attack surface → identifies vulnerable service (unpatched
  VPN, exposed RDP) → establishes foothold before integration security
  remediation → operates during integration disruption period.
Layer 6 — Defense leverage: Day-1 integration security checklist (MFA
  enforcement, critical vulnerability remediation, SIEM integration);
  pre-close security assessment; G-C104-08 M&A due diligence standard;
  communication blackout on security tool deployment timing.
Gap closure: partial (G-C104-08 M&A due diligence standard open).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A668: Compliance Control Mapping Gaming via Evidence Fabrication
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Layer 1 — Surface: Organization fabricates or manipulates audit evidence
  to demonstrate compliance with control requirements without actual
  implementation.
Layer 2 — Mechanism: Point-in-time compliance assessment creates gaming
  opportunity. Vulnerability scan run day before audit: suppresses
  findings not yet remediated by marking as 'accepted risk' temporarily;
  then re-enables after audit. Access review: bulk-approve without
  actual review. Pen test remediation: document as 'mitigated' without
  actual fix; re-assess as false positive. Theranos analogy in healthcare.
  Equifax PCI DSS compliance before 2017 breach: passed audit while
  vulnerable Apache Struts unpatched. Structural: auditor has limited
  time, sampled evidence, no continuous visibility.
Layer 3 — Structural driver: Point-in-time audit creates temporal gaming
  window; compliance cost/benefit incentivizes evidence optimization;
  auditor independence limited by client relationship; G-C104-09
  continuous monitoring coverage gap enables gaming.
Layer 4 — Detection gap: Auditor: sees snapshot, not continuous state.
  Regulator: relies on auditor. Board: relies on CISO report. Gap:
  no independent continuous verification of control implementation.
Layer 5 — Impact: Organization appears compliant; actual vulnerability
  persists; breach occurs; regulatory liability despite audit pass;
  audit pass provides false assurance to board and insurers.
Layer 6 — Defense leverage: Continuous compliance monitoring (GRC platforms
  with API integration); evidence immutability (append-only log for
  compliance evidence); surprise audit component; G-C104-09 coverage
  standard for continuous monitoring completeness.
Gap closure: partial (G-C104-09 continuous monitoring coverage open).

Status: CONFIRMED at C103. Extended application this cycle:
P97×A666 (honey token deception arms race): The honey token / canary
  evasion arms race (Layer 4 of A666) is structurally isomorphic to P97.
  Deploy deception → attacker tooling adds detection → update deception

  detection mechanism that an adversary can probe and train against.

  but is particularly acute in ML due to gradient accessibility and
  formally characterized in the adversarial ML literature.
  P97 scope note added: applies to any gradient-accessible or probe-able
  detection mechanism; acute instance in adversarial ML; structural instance
  in deception technology.

── New Pattern Candidate: P98 ───────────────────────────────────────────────
P98 candidate: Point-in-Time Assessment Temporal Gaming Pattern
  Observation: Multiple distinct attack categories exploit the temporal
  gap between point-in-time security assessment and actual continuous
  security state:
  - Compliance gaming (A668, A1388): vulnerability suppression before audit
  - Deceptive evidence (A668): documentation of remediation without fix
  - Penetration test scope gaming (A620, prior cycle): clean state during
    test, return to vulnerable after
  - Due diligence gaming (A1388 context): M&A target presents cleaned-up
    state during due diligence window
  Proposed pattern: Organizations subject to point-in-time security
  assessments systematically optimize for assessment performance rather
  than continuous security posture, creating temporal security theater.
  Structural cause: assessment incentive (pass/fail at point in time)
  misaligned with security objective (continuous posture). Rational
  individual response (optimize for assessment) produces collective
  degradation (assessment loses signal value).
  Note: This pattern intersects with LAW-9 structure (individual rational
  gaming → collective assessment validity degradation). Evaluate as
  LAW-9 candidate in addition to P98 candidate.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A677: Secure Coding Training Transfer Failure to Production Defects
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Layer 1 — Surface: Organizations invest in secure coding training;
  production code defect rate does not decrease proportionally;
  training does not transfer to behavior under real development conditions.
Layer 2 — Mechanism: Secure coding training (OWASP Top 10, SANS
  Secure Coding) improves knowledge test scores but not production
  behavior. Causes: (1) Time pressure overrides security behavior
  (sprint velocity pressure); (2) Training covers isolated examples
  without complex real-world context; (3) Developer lacks security
  feedback loop (SAST findings not reviewed; PR security comments
  not mandatory); (4) Security is not part of definition of done.
  A612 (C99S3) covered awareness training transfer failure; A677
  focuses specifically on developer secure coding training.
  BSIMM data: organizations with security champions show lower
  defect density; training alone insufficient without embedded feedback.
Layer 3 — Structural driver: Training optimizes for knowledge acquisition,
  not behavioral transfer; development incentive systems reward velocity,
  not security; security knowledge without structural feedback loop
  does not change behavior under pressure.
Layer 4 — Detection gap: Not applicable (this is a program effectiveness
  gap, not an attack). Security defect production rate is the outcome
  metric; G-C105-09 security champion effectiveness measurement open.
Layer 5 — Downstream attack surface: SQL injection, XSS, deserialization
  vulnerabilities persist in production code despite training investment;
  attack surface does not shrink; training ROI unmeasured.
Layer 6 — Defense leverage: Security embedded in development feedback
  (SAST in CI pipeline with mandatory triage); security in definition
  of done; security champion with code review responsibility; threat
  modeling in sprint planning; G-C105-09 measurement standard.
Gap closure: partial (G-C105-09 effectiveness measurement open).

A682: EDR Kernel Driver Exploitation for Privilege Escalation
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Layer 1 — Surface: Attacker exploits vulnerability in EDR kernel driver
  to gain SYSTEM-level privileges or disable EDR from kernel context.
Layer 2 — Mechanism: EDR agents run privileged kernel drivers for deep
  visibility (process injection detection, kernel callbacks, minifilter
  drivers). Kernel driver vulnerabilities: IOCTL interface bugs
  (input validation failures), race conditions in callback handlers,
  use-after-free in driver memory management. Exploitation achieves
  kernel-level code execution: can unload EDR driver, patch detection
  logic in kernel, or escalate to SYSTEM. CVE-2022-23960 (CrowdStrike),
  multiple Sophos kernel driver CVEs. BYOVd (Bring Your Own Vulnerable
  Driver): load known-vulnerable legitimate signed driver → exploit
  to achieve kernel execution without requiring EDR driver vuln.
Layer 3 — Structural driver: EDR kernel presence is necessary for
  detection capability; kernel exposure is unavoidable attack surface;
  signed driver requirement (DSE) addressed by BYOVd attack (legitimate
  vulnerable signed driver).
Layer 4 — Detection gap: Kernel-level attacker can blind EDR before
  alert is generated; BYOVd using legitimate signed driver may not
  trigger software vendor blocklist; HVCI can prevent unsigned driver
  loading but not all BYOVd vectors.
Layer 5 — Exploitation chain: Identify vulnerable signed driver in
  BYOVd database (loldrivers.io) → load driver with admin privileges
  → exploit driver to achieve kernel execution → unload EDR driver
  or patch callbacks → proceed undetected.
Layer 6 — Defense leverage: HVCI (Hypervisor-Protected Code Integrity)
  blocking unsigned/vulnerable drivers; Windows vulnerable driver
  blocklist (updated); Microsoft WHCP driver signing with extended
  security review; G-C106-02 EDR coverage standard.
Gap closure: partial (G-C106-02 EDR evasion benchmark open).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A684: AI Red Team Jailbreak via Prompt Injection Cascade
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Layer 1 — Surface: Attacker circumvents AI model safety controls
  via multi-step prompt injection that exploits context window
  accumulation to bypass safety filters.
Layer 2 — Mechanism: Direct jailbreaks (DAN, 'ignore previous
  instructions') are filtered by RLHF-trained safety classifiers.
  Cascade approach: (1) Establish benign context over multiple turns;
  (2) Gradually shift framing (hypothetical, fictional, roleplay);
  (3) Use many-shot jailbreaking (Anthropic research, 2024): provide
  many examples of model complying with similar requests in context
  window — model in-context learns to comply; (4) Crescendo attack
  (Microsoft Research, 2024): incrementally escalate from benign to
  harmful request over multiple turns. Context window length enables
  multi-turn context accumulation that overwhelms safety training.
Layer 3 — Structural driver: Safety training is finite; in-context
  learning from many examples can override safety training (many-shot);
  multi-turn context creates state that safety classifiers may not
  fully consider; model objective (be helpful) can be exploited by
  framing harmful requests as helpful.
Layer 4 — Detection gap: Individual turns appear benign; full context
  needed to detect crescendo pattern; safety classifier applied per
  response, not to full conversation arc; context window growth
  increases attack surface with model capability improvement.
Layer 5 — Exploitation chain: Start benign conversation → establish
  fictional/hypothetical framing → introduce many compliant examples
  (many-shot) → escalate request toward harmful content → model
  complies due to context-window-scale safety bypass.
Layer 6 — Defense leverage: Conversation-level safety monitoring
  (not just per-response); many-shot jailbreak detection via context
  pattern analysis; constitutional AI refusal reinforcement; red team
  testing with multi-turn attack protocols; G-C106-07 benchmark.
Gap closure: partial (G-C106-07 AI red team benchmark open; P97 context).

A685: ARM TrustZone Trusted Execution Environment Escape
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Layer 1 — Surface: Attacker exploits vulnerability in TrustZone Trusted
  Application (TA) or TEE OS to break TEE isolation and access secure
  world secrets from normal world.
Layer 2 — Mechanism: ARM TrustZone divides processor into Secure World
  (TEE) and Normal World (REE). TEE runs trusted applications (key
  storage, DRM, biometric matching); Normal World runs Android/Linux.
  Attack surface: (1) SMC (Secure Monitor Call) interface: vulnerable
  parameter validation in TA; (2) Shared memory interface: TOCTOU
  (time-of-check-time-of-use) attacks on shared buffers; (3) TEE OS
  (OP-TEE, Qualcomm QSEE) kernel vulnerabilities. CVEs: Qualcomm
  QSEE multiple CVEs (CVE-2015-6639, CVE-2016-2431); MediaTek TEE
  CVEs. Consequence: private key extraction from secure storage;
  DRM bypass; biometric template theft.
Layer 3 — Structural driver: TEE software complexity (OS + multiple
  TAs) creates large attack surface; TA code quality varies by vendor;
  SMC interface is high-privilege attack surface required for TEE
  functionality.
Layer 4 — Detection gap: Normal World OS cannot observe Secure World;
  TEE exploit execution invisible to Android security stack; TEE
  logging may not be available to Normal World monitoring.
Layer 5 — Exploitation chain: Gain Normal World code execution
  (Android app or OS vulnerability) → craft malicious SMC call →
  exploit TA parameter validation vulnerability → arbitrary code
  execution in Secure World → extract private keys or DRM secrets.
Layer 6 — Defense leverage: TA code review and fuzzing (Fuzzing TAs
  via SMC interface); TA minimal surface design; TOCTOU mitigation
  (copy parameters before use); periodic TA CVE patching (OEM
  firmware update); G-C106-08 PUF reliability standard context.
Gap closure: none (embedded hardware domain; no new gap directly).

A690: Security Debt Accumulation via Untracked Exception Approval
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Layer 1 — Surface: Security policy exceptions approved individually
  accumulate into organizational security debt that is not tracked,
  prioritized, or remediated, creating growing unmanaged risk.
Layer 2 — Mechanism: Security exception process: application team
  requests exception to security policy (e.g., allow HTTP instead
  of HTTPS for internal service; delay patching by 90 days; exempt
  from MFA for legacy system). Exception approved with compensating
  control and expiration date. In practice: expiration dates not
  enforced; compensating controls not verified; exception register
  not linked to vulnerability management or risk register. 500
  approved exceptions represent 500 untracked risk items. When a
  breach occurs via an excepted control, insurance and regulatory
  exposure is amplified by documented awareness of risk.
Layer 3 — Structural driver: Exception management is manual and
  process-heavy; expiration tracking requires operational discipline
  not typical of security teams; exception register grows without
  pruning; G-C106-05 security debt quantification standard open.
Layer 4 — Detection gap: Exception register is a known-risk register;
  'detection' here means risk materialization — the excepted
  vulnerability is exploited; no technical detection gap for the
  exception mechanism itself.
Layer 5 — Attack surface: Attacker who obtains exception register
  (via insider, leaked document, or discovery request in litigation)
  has a prioritized list of unmitigated vulnerabilities with documented
  organizational awareness. Exception register = prioritized attack
  roadmap for informed attacker. R11.AMBIENT candidate.
Layer 6 — Defense leverage: Exception register linked to vulnerability
  management with automated expiration enforcement; compensating control
  verification cadence; exception risk scoring for prioritization;
  exception register access restricted to need-to-know; G-C106-05.
Gap closure: partial (G-C106-05 security debt quantification open).
R11.AMBIENT candidate: exception register as ambient attack roadmap.

G-C107-02 — INDUSTRIAL ROBOTICS SECURITY ASSESSMENT METHODOLOGY
DOMAIN: D1719 (Industrial Robotics Security)
GAP: No published penetration testing or security assessment methodology specific to robotic systems. Generic ICS/OT assessment frameworks (IEC 62443, NIST SP 800-82) do not address ROS architecture, teach pendant attack surface, motion control protocol security, or physical consequence modeling of cyber-triggered robot behavior. Result: robotics deployments evaluated against inapplicable generic controls; safety-critical robot misbehavior attack paths systematically under-assessed.


--- SOURCE LINES 259784–259790 ---
G-C107-04 — FORMAL VERIFICATION COVERAGE FOR DEPLOYED CRYPTOGRAPHIC IMPLEMENTATIONS
DOMAIN: D1721 (Formal Methods in Security)
GAP: Formal verification of cryptographic protocols (ProVerif, Tamarin) verifies mathematical models, not implementations. Gap between verified protocol and deployed library code is not systematically measured. OpenSSL, BoringSSL, libsodium — no published formal verification coverage percentage for their implementations. Heartbleed, Lucky13, and similar vulnerabilities occurred in implementations of formally verified protocols. No standard for asserting implementation-level verification coverage.

G-C107-05 — ATTORNEY-CLIENT PRIVILEGE SCOPE FOR BREACH INVESTIGATION FINDINGS
DOMAIN: D1722 (Legal Discovery and Cybersecurity Evidence)
GAP: No consistent legal standard across jurisdictions for whether breach investigation reports prepared by outside counsel/forensic firms qualify for attorney-client privilege or work-product protection. Capital One (2022, 4th Circuit), Dittman v. UPMC, and Wengui v. Clark Hill have produced conflicting rulings. Organizations cannot reliably plan for investigation confidentiality. Result: inconsistent post-breach investigation structuring, some organizations structurally over-asserting privilege in ways courts reject.


--- SOURCE LINES 259796–259810 ---
G-C107-07 — AIS SPOOFING DETECTION STANDARD FOR MARITIME SECURITY
DOMAIN: D1736 (Maritime and Shipping Cybersecurity)
GAP: No published standard for detecting AIS (Automatic Identification System) position spoofing. AIS is unauthenticated, unencrypted VHF broadcast — trivially spoofable with ~$400 software-defined radio. Known use for vessel location falsification (sanctions evasion, DPRK fuel transfers, Iranian oil shipping). Existing detection approaches (SkyTruth, Windward, UN Panel of Experts analysis) are proprietary/ad hoc with no published methodology or detection rate benchmarks. IMO has not mandated AIS authentication.

G-C107-08 — VOTING SYSTEM VULNERABILITY DISCLOSURE COORDINATION STANDARD
DOMAIN: D1737 (Election Security)
GAP: No established coordinated vulnerability disclosure (CVD) process specific to voting systems. CISA/EAC jurisdiction fragmentation, state-level procurement independence, and vendor NDAs create disclosure barriers not present in commercial software. Defcon Voting Village operates outside formal CVD. Vendors have threatened legal action against researchers (Diebold DMCA, 2003). No national standard for patch deployment timelines given election cycle constraints (systems may not be updateable 90 days before election).

G-C107-09 — GENOMIC DATA RE-IDENTIFICATION RISK THRESHOLD STANDARD
DOMAIN: D1735 (Genomics and Biotech Cybersecurity)
GAP: No regulatory standard for acceptable re-identification risk level for de-identified genomic datasets shared for research. Homer et al. (2008) demonstrated re-identification from aggregate GWAS statistics; NIH subsequently restricted dbGaP access. But no quantitative threshold (e.g., k-anonymity equivalent for genomics) is published or enforced. HIPAA Safe Harbor de-identification does not cover genetic data re-identification risk from summary statistics. Result: research data-sharing decisions made ad hoc without defensible risk standard.

G-C107-10 — AIR-GAP COVERT CHANNEL THREAT MODEL COMPLETENESS
DOMAIN: D1730 (Air-Gap Security)
GAP: No published threat model covering the complete space of known air-gap covert channels for a given facility type (SCIF, nuclear facility, ICS network). Individual channels are published in academic literature (Guri et al. series, Ben-Gurion University 2014-2023: 20+ distinct channels documented), but no synthesis into a coherent threat model with detection countermeasures mapped to each channel type. TEMPEST/EMSEC standards address EM emissions but not acoustic, optical, or thermal channels. Security architects cannot determine what subset of channels is feasible in their physical environment.

A691 — AIS POSITION SPOOFING FOR SANCTIONS EVASION
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
DOMAIN: D1736 (Maritime/Shipping Cybersecurity)
PATTERN INSTANCE: P33.3 (ambient signal exploitation), R11.AMBIENT (AIS broadcast as ambient vessel tracking infrastructure)
ATTACK LAYER:
  Layer 1 — Physical: SDR transmitter ($400 HackRF or RTL-SDR with upconverter) configured to broadcast AIS NMEA sentences on VHF 87B/88B (161.975/162.025 MHz). No authentication field in AIVDM/AIVDO sentence format — receiver accepts any syntactically valid transmission.
  Layer 2 — Protocol: Spoof MMSI (Maritime Mobile Service Identity) of sanctioned vessel with MMSI of compliant vessel. Alternatively, fabricate ghost vessel MMSI not registered in ITU database to create fictional vessel. Transmit false GPS coordinates placing vessel in non-sanctioned sea lane.
  Layer 3 — Operational: Sanctioned vessel activates AIS transponder briefly with legitimate position to establish baseline, then disables transponder (AIS dark) while spoofed signal broadcasts false position. Ship-to-ship transfer occurs at actual dark location while AIS data shows vessel in transit in permitted waters.
  Layer 4 — Cover: Use nearby compliant vessel MMSI for spoofed position (vessel in legitimate transit). Timing coordinated to avoid port state control vessel traffic service (VTS) anomaly detection (spoofed position consistent with reported speed/heading).
DETECTION: Satellite AIS (S-AIS) vs. terrestrial AIS position cross-correlation; vessel speed-over-ground consistency check (teleporting vessel detectable); MMSI registry cross-check for unregistered identifiers; satellite imagery correlation at declared position.
REAL INSTANCE: UN Panel of Experts reports on DPRK sanctions evasion (2019-2023); Iranian oil tanker fleet AIS manipulation documented by TankerTrackers.com and Windward; Ryou-8 vessel MMSI spoofing documented.
R11.AMBIENT LINK: AIS infrastructure exists for safety (collision avoidance), not security. Adversary leverages public maritime tracking ecosystem (MarineTraffic, VesselFinder) as ambient cover for spoofing operations — legitimate vessel data masks anomaly.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A693 — GENOMIC RE-IDENTIFICATION FROM PUBLISHED GWAS SUMMARY STATISTICS
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
DOMAIN: D1735 (Genomics/Biotech Cybersecurity)
ATTACK LAYER:
  Layer 1 — Public Data: Access published GWAS (Genome-Wide Association Study) summary statistics from open repositories (NHGRI GWAS Catalog, UK Biobank derived statistics, dbGaP open-access tier). Summary statistics are aggregate allele frequency differences between case/control groups — not individual genotypes.
  Layer 2 — Statistical Attack (Homer et al. 2008): Given a target individual's genotype (obtained from DTC genomic testing, research participation disclosure, or genetic genealogy database), compute likelihood ratio: probability of target genotype given population frequencies vs. probability given case group frequencies. Sufficient statistical power to determine study membership with high confidence given N~1000 summary statistics and M~500,000 SNPs.
  Layer 3 — Inference Chain: Membership determination reveals phenotype (the case group's condition: HIV status, psychiatric diagnosis, addiction history). Re-identification from phenotype inference rather than identity inference — adversary already has identity, gains medical information.
  Layer 4 — Extended Attack: Genetic genealogy databases (GEDmatch, FamilyTreeDNA) allow reverse: from GWAS membership, identify relatives; from relatives, identify specific individual if not already known. Combined with surname inference from Y-chromosome (Gymrek et al. 2013).
DETECTION: Access logging on summary statistic downloads; query rate limiting on interactive GWAS portals; differential privacy noise injection on published statistics (at cost of statistical power).
REAL INSTANCE: Homer et al. (2008) PLOS Genetics — demonstrated on actual NIH dbGaP data; NIH immediately restricted open access to all GWAS summary statistics. Demonstrated practical re-identification, not theoretical.

A695 — ROS (ROBOT OPERATING SYSTEM) UNAUTHENTICATED MASTER NODE EXPLOITATION
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
DOMAIN: D1719 (Industrial Robotics Security)
ATTACK LAYER:
  Layer 1 — Network Access: Gain access to robot network segment (compromised OT workstation, rogue device on robot LAN, or direct physical connection to robot controller Ethernet port). ROS 1.x (dominant in deployed industrial robots as of 2024) runs rosmaster on TCP port 11311 with no authentication.
  Layer 2 — Master Node Attack: Connect to rosmaster XMLRPC interface. Enumerate all ROS nodes, topics, services, and parameters without credentials. Publish arbitrary messages to control topics (/cmd_vel for mobile robots, joint trajectory controllers for arms). Subscribe to sensor topics for reconnaissance.
  Layer 3 — Physical Consequence: Inject malformed joint trajectory commands exceeding safety-rated limits. Modern collaborative robots (Universal Robots, KUKA LBR) implement software safety limits — command injection may bypass software-layer limits if firmware safety watchdog is separate. Industrial robots (FANUC, ABB, KUKA KR) with safety-rated motion monitoring (ISO 10218) have hardware-level stops — software injection may still cause unintended motion within safety envelope.
  Layer 4 — Production Impact: Robot collision with tooling, workpiece, or personnel in collaborative (cobot) deployment. Production line halt via emergency stop trigger. Teach pendant parameter modification for persistent behavior change.
DETECTION: ROS network traffic baseline; unauthorized node appearance detection; teach pendant physical security; ROS 2.x migration (DDS with SROS2 security plugins — authentication, encryption, access control).
REAL INSTANCE: Alias Robotics (2018-2020): documented ROS vulnerabilities including unauthenticated rosmaster in ABB, Universal Robots, KUKA deployments in production environments. CVE-2019-19625 (ROS master node exposure). Trend Micro (2020): robot cybersecurity research demonstrating production-feasible attacks.

A696 — CRYPTOGRAPHIC PROTOCOL FORMAL VERIFICATION GAP EXPLOITATION (LOGJAM)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
DOMAIN: D1721 (Formal Methods in Security)
PATTERN INSTANCE: P98 (point-in-time assessment gap — formal verification of protocol =/= implementation security)
ATTACK LAYER:
  Layer 1 — Protocol Specification: Diffie-Hellman key exchange as specified in TLS was not formally broken. DH protocol correctness can be verified in ProVerif/Tamarin under standard cryptographic assumptions.
  Layer 2 — Implementation Reality: TLS implementations (OpenSSL, NSS, SChannel) supported DHE_EXPORT cipher suites (512-bit DH for export-controlled cryptography) alongside standard DHE (1024-2048 bit). Downgrade attack: adversary-in-the-middle downgrades negotiation to DHE_EXPORT without triggering alert.
  Layer 3 — Precomputation: 512-bit DH with fixed 'common' primes (specific primes reused across millions of servers) allows precomputation: adversary precomputes discrete log tables for specific prime offline (weeks of compute), enabling real-time session key recovery for any connection using that prime.
  Layer 4 — Mass Exploitation: 8.4% of Alexa Top 1M HTTPS sites, 3.4% of HTTPS browser connections vulnerable at disclosure (May 2015). Nation-state adversary with supercomputer access could decrypt TLS traffic at scale using precomputed tables for 1024-bit primes (NSA inference from Snowden documents — 1024-bit DH factoring).
DETECTION: TLS scanning for DHE_EXPORT support; cipher suite policy enforcement; DHE prime size minimum enforcement (>=2048-bit).
REAL INSTANCE: Adrian et al. (2015) — Logjam attack, CCS 2015. Directly motivated RFC 7919 (Negotiated Finite Field Diffie-Hellman Ephemeral Parameters for TLS, 2016) standardizing safe, known primes. Formal verification of DH protocol did not prevent implementation-layer vulnerability.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A698 — AI SOC CO-PILOT HALLUCINATION EXPLOITATION VIA ALERT CONTEXT POISONING
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
DOMAIN: D1720 (AI-Native Security Operations)
PATTERN INSTANCE: P97 (AI security control vulnerability feedback loop)
ATTACK LAYER:
  Layer 1 — AI SOC Model: Organization deploys LLM-assisted SIEM triage where AI co-pilot summarizes alert context and recommends analyst action (investigate, escalate, close). AI co-pilot ingests alert fields, associated log lines, threat intelligence enrichment, and historical similar alerts.
  Layer 2 — Context Poisoning: Attacker who has achieved initial access (via separate vector) crafts log entries and process names designed to appear in alert context and bias AI co-pilot recommendation. Example: process name 'windows_update_service.exe' (legitimate-appearing) in log context; file path containing 'authorized_maintenance' substring; HTTP User-Agent matching known-benign baseline pattern.
  Layer 3 — Hallucination Trigger: AI co-pilot, lacking ground truth about actual legitimacy, anchors on contextual signals. LLM generates summary: 'This alert appears consistent with routine Windows Update activity based on process name and path. Historical similar alerts were closed as false positives. Recommend: Close.' Analyst following AI recommendation closes alert without manual investigation.
  Layer 4 — Detection Bypass: Actual malicious activity (C2 beacon, lateral movement, data staging) proceeds undetected. Attack leverages AI analyst's efficiency optimization (throughput pressure) and over-trust in AI recommendation to bypass human review that would have caught the anomaly.
DETECTION: Human review sampling of AI-recommended closures (statistical quality control); AI recommendation confidence score thresholds requiring human review below threshold; adversarial robustness testing of AI co-pilot against context poisoning (red team prompt injection for SOC context); AI decision explanation logging for audit.
THEORETICAL BASIS: Prompt injection in agentic AI contexts (Riley Goodside, 2022; Simon Willison ongoing research); MITRE ATLAS AML.T0054 (LLM prompt injection). No confirmed production SOC exploitation published as of 2024 — attack surface established by AI SOC deployment patterns.

A699 — HARDWARE ATTESTATION BYPASS VIA TPM QUOTE REPLAY
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
DOMAIN: D1729 (Hardware Attestation and Trusted Computing)
ATTACK LAYER:
  Layer 1 — Attestation Architecture: Remote attestation using TPM 2.0: verifier sends nonce (challenge); TPM creates Quote (signed PCR values + nonce) using Attestation Key (AK) certified by Privacy CA; verifier validates AK certificate, Quote signature, and PCR values against known-good baseline (golden measurement).
  Layer 2 — Attack Scenario: Attacker compromises system after successful attestation (post-boot persistence, hypervisor escape) without triggering PCR extension (measurements complete at boot). TPM Quote reflects boot-time state (clean); runtime state is compromised. Attacker captures valid Quote from clean system and replays it — nonce prevents direct replay, but nonce freshness window may be exploitable if verifier accepts quotes within time window rather than per-request challenge.
  Layer 3 — Variant Attack: Virtual TPM (vTPM) in cloud environment: hypervisor-provided vTPM does not reflect physical hardware state. Compromised hypervisor can forge vTPM Quote values. Confidential computing (Intel TDX, AMD SEV-SNP) addresses this via hardware-enforced attestation of VM memory encryption, but implementation complexity creates attack surface (firmware version downgrade attacks).
  Layer 4 — Supply Chain Variant: Counterfeit TPM chip with forged Endorsement Key (EK) certificate not in manufacturer's EK certificate database. Privacy CA validation fails; organization accepts self-signed EK cert for internal deployment — bypasses manufacturer-anchored trust chain.
DETECTION: Runtime integrity measurement (IMA/EVM Linux integrity subsystem) for post-boot state; nonce freshness enforcement (single-use, short expiry); EK certificate validation against manufacturer certificate transparency log; hardware TPM physical presence requirement for sensitive operations.
REAL INSTANCE: James Forshaw (Google Project Zero) TPM research; AMD SEV firmware rollback attack (Robert Buhren, 2021); Intel TDX attestation implementation research (USENIX Security 2023). vTPM trust boundary documented in cloud provider shared responsibility models.

R11.AMBIENT CANDIDATE #67 (deferred from C106): Public audit reports as ambient attack design signal.
UPDATE: On further analysis, public audit reports (SOC 2 Type II summary reports, ISO 27001 surveillance audit summaries, NIST CSF assessment results in public filings) reveal which controls are implemented — adversary learns what defenses exist, not what is absent. This is meaningfully distinct from prior confirmed instances which reveal attack surface or defensive gaps. R11.AMBIENT CANDIDATE #68: Public bug bounty program scope as ambient attack roadmap.
EVALUATION: Bug bounty scope documents (HackerOne, Bugcrowd public programs) explicitly define: (a) in-scope assets (subdomains, APIs, mobile apps), (b) out-of-scope assets (production databases, internal systems), (c) reward tier by vulnerability class. Out-of-scope listing is a targeted exclusion map — adversary learns which assets the organization has explicitly chosen not to defend via crowdsourced review. In-scope listing is a high-value asset map. Reward tier reveals which vulnerability classes the organization considers most impactful (and therefore most dangerous to themselves). Passes ambient passive-observability criterion (publicly accessible, no authentication). Passes adversarial utility criterion (directly actionable targeting information). Passes systemic-not-incidental criterion (structural feature of bug bounty programs, not edge case).
STATUS: CONFIRMED.

A703 — DECEPTION TOKEN EXFILTRATION DETECTION EVASION VIA TOKEN INVALIDATION
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
DOMAIN: D1755 (Deception Technology Advanced)
PATTERN INSTANCE: P97 (AI security control vulnerability feedback loop — deception control)
ATTACK LAYER:
  Layer 1 — Deception Infrastructure: Defender deploys deception fabric: honey credentials embedded in legitimate-seeming files (AWS credentials in ~/.aws/credentials on developer workstations), honey tokens in code repositories (GitHub secret scanning alternative), canary Word documents with tracking pixels, decoy network shares with monitoring.
  Layer 2 — Token Discovery and Identification: Attacker with endpoint access (post-initial-compromise) discovers honey credential files. Before using the credential, attacker fingerprints it: (a) check credential format against known honey token patterns (canarytokens.org/Thinkst Canary tokens have characteristic encoding); (b) attempt API call with credential against non-production endpoint not monitored by deception system; (c) compare credential to legitimate credential format from same environment (AWS account ID prefix, IAM role naming convention).
  Layer 3 — Token Invalidation: If token identified as deception with high confidence: invalidate token before use (call AWS STS to confirm token invalidity without triggering alert); discard token without triggering deception alert. Alternatively: use token for one low-value action and observe whether alert fires (canary probe) before using for sensitive action.
  Layer 4 — Arms Race: Defender must make deception tokens indistinguishable from real tokens (fully valid, production-equivalent). Indistinguishable deception tokens require deployment of real infrastructure (real AWS accounts with real but limited permissions) — increasing deception deployment cost and complexity. P97 pattern: published deception token formats enable attacker fingerprinting; more sophisticated deception (real tokens) creates new risk (token misuse beyond intended detection scope).
DETECTION: Use real tokens with limited permissions as honey credentials (not fake tokens); distribute honey tokens across multiple environments with identical format to production credentials; monitor all credential accesses (not just deception system hits); rate-limit sts:GetCallerIdentity calls that could be used for token probing.
THEORETICAL BASIS: Attivo Networks / Illusive Networks deception arms race literature; Canarytokens.org token format published (open source); academic: Fraunhofer SIT deception research.

A706 — PHYSICAL PENETRATION TEST RFID/HID BADGE CLONING FOR ACCESS CONTROL BYPASS
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
DOMAIN: D1757 (Physical Penetration Testing)
ATTACK LAYER:
  Layer 1 — Target: Corporate access control using HID Prox (125kHz LF RFID) or HID iCLASS (13.56MHz HF RFID) credential cards. HID Prox is the most common enterprise badge system globally; approximately 1 billion credentials issued.
  Layer 2 — Card Cloning: Proxmark3 (open-source RFID research tool, ~$400) reads HID Prox card at up to 20cm range (covert reading possible while standing near target in elevator, cafeteria). Captures facility code and card number (no encryption on HID Prox 125kHz). Writes cloned credential to blank T5577 card. Process: <30 seconds total.
  Layer 3 — Physical Access: Present cloned card to reader. Access control system authenticates based on card data alone (no PIN, no biometric in most deployments). Physical access granted to all doors programmed for original card holder's access level. No log anomaly: cloned card presents same credential as original.
  Layer 4 — Expanded Access: Physical access enables: network jack access (802.1X bypass if port authentication not enforced); server room access (server physical console access bypasses all OS-level authentication); USB drop for malware delivery; document theft; laptop theft.
DETECTION: Upgrade to SEOS/iCLASS SE (mutual authentication, cryptographic challenge-response); multi-factor physical access (badge + PIN); anti-passback enforcement (same credential cannot enter before exiting); RFID activity anomaly detection (same badge at two locations simultaneously); physical security audit including covert RFID reading test.
REAL INSTANCE: Defcon Physical Security Village, documented annually. Francis Brown (Bishop Fox): 'RFID Hacking: Live Free or RFID Hard' (2013) — documented mass HID Prox cloning in enterprise environments. SparkFun 'Card Skimmer' product line. Most enterprise physical access control remains on unencrypted 125kHz systems as of 2024.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A709 — INTEL SGX ENCLAVE SIDE-CHANNEL ATTACK VIA FORESHADOW (L1TF)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
DOMAIN: D1756 (Secure Enclave and Confidential Computing Security)
ATTACK LAYER:
  Layer 1 — Confidential Computing Premise: Intel SGX provides hardware-isolated enclaves where code and data are encrypted and protected from the host OS, hypervisor, and other processes. Remote attestation verifies enclave code integrity. Threat model: even a compromised OS cannot read enclave memory.
  Layer 2 — Foreshadow Attack (CVE-2018-3615, Van Bulck et al. 2018): Speculative execution on Intel CPUs fetches enclave memory into L1 cache even when the page table entry marks the memory as not-present (SGX abort-page semantics rely on page fault handling to prevent access). Speculative execution bypasses the fault; data transiently exists in L1 cache. Flush+Reload side-channel reads cached data before architectural rollback.
  Layer 3 — SGX Attestation Key Extraction: Target: SGX EPID (Enhanced Privacy ID) attestation key stored in enclave of Intel's Quoting Enclave. Using Foreshadow: extract EPID private key from Quoting Enclave. With EPID private key: forge SGX attestation quotes for arbitrary (malicious) enclaves. Attestation remote verification accepts forged quotes as genuine. SGX trust model completely broken.
  Layer 4 — Platform-Wide Impact: Single compromised SGX platform can forge attestation for any claimed enclave measurement (MRENCLAVE). Cloud provider SGX attestation service cannot distinguish genuine from forged. All SGX-dependent security properties (confidential cloud compute, private key protection in SGX, DRM) defeated.
DETECTION: Microcode patching (required; Intel released patches Aug 2018 — SGX attestation key revocation and re-provisioning); L1 cache flushing on context switch (performance penalty ~35%); migration to TDX (next-generation, hardware-architecturally different from SGX in isolation model).
REAL INSTANCE: Van Bulck et al. (2018) — 'Foreshadow: Extracting the Keys to the Intel SGX Kingdom with Transient Out-of-Order Execution,' USENIX Security 2018. Intel CVE-2018-3615/3620/3646. Coordinated disclosure with Intel. SGX attestation keys revoked and re-issued globally.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A713 — ENTERPRISE PKI SUBORDINATE CA COMPROMISE FOR MASS CERTIFICATE FORGERY
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
DOMAIN: D1776 (Enterprise PKI Design and Management)
ATTACK LAYER:
  Layer 1 — Target: Enterprise internal PKI with offline root CA and online issuing CA. Issuing CA stores private key in software keystore on Windows Server or HSM. Issuing CA issues certificates for internal TLS, code signing, client authentication, S/MIME.
  Layer 2 — CA Compromise: Gain code execution on issuing CA server (OS vulnerability, domain admin privilege from lateral movement). Extract issuing CA private key from Windows certificate store (certutil export, or from DPAPI-protected PKCS#12 if master key accessible). HSM-protected CA: cannot extract key directly but can issue certificates via CA API while maintaining access.
  Layer 3 — Certificate Forgery: Issue certificates for any subject with full issuing CA trust chain. Applications: (a) forge TLS certificate for any internal domain — MitM all internal HTTPS traffic without TLS alert; (b) forge code signing certificate — sign malware as trusted internal software; (c) forge client auth certificate as any user — authenticate to all certificate-based access controls; (d) forge S/MIME certificate — sign email as any user.
  Layer 4 — Persistence: All forged certificates trusted by entire enterprise PKI. Revocation: if CRL/OCSP not checked by clients (common in internal PKI), revocation is ineffective. Root CA key rotation required to fully remediate — requires re-enrollment of all enterprise devices (days to weeks of operational disruption). High persistence value makes CA a high-value target.
DETECTION: Issuing CA certificate issuance logging with anomaly detection on unexpected subjects; CT log submission for internal CA (internal CT log monitoring); HSM-based CA key storage (prevents key extraction); privileged access to CA server via PAW only; CA server network isolation.
REAL INSTANCE: DigiNotar (2011): external CA compromise, 531 fraudulent certificates including *.google.com; browser trust revocation killed company. Internal enterprise PKI compromise: documented in Mandiant M-Trends (generic) as high-value lateral movement target; ANSSI (French NIST) issued unauthorized *.google.com certificate via internal PKI error (2013) — discovered via CT logs.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A714 — MOBILE CERTIFICATE PINNING BYPASS VIA FRIDA RUNTIME HOOKING
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
DOMAIN: D1767 (Mobile Application Security)
ATTACK LAYER:
  Layer 1 — Target: iOS or Android mobile application implementing SSL/TLS certificate pinning to prevent proxy-based traffic interception. Pinning: application validates server certificate against hardcoded certificate or public key hash (not OS trust store). Intended to prevent Burp Suite/mitmproxy interception even with user-installed CA certificate.
  Layer 2 — Frida Hooking: Install Frida (dynamic instrumentation framework) on jailbroken iOS or rooted Android device. Frida injects JavaScript runtime into target application process. Hook the SSL validation function (iOS: SecTrustEvaluateWithError; Android: X509TrustManager.checkServerTrusted, OkHttp CertificatePinner.check). Replace function implementation with one that always returns success regardless of certificate validation result.
  Layer 3 — Traffic Interception: Configure device proxy to Burp Suite. Certificate pinning function now returns success for any certificate including Burp's CA-signed certificate. All application HTTPS traffic interceptable and modifiable in Burp. API endpoints, authentication flows, and sensitive data visible in plaintext.
  Layer 4 — API Attack Surface Discovery: Intercept all API calls made by application including undocumented internal endpoints not visible in frontend code. Identify authentication token handling, API parameters for business logic testing, privilege escalation opportunities via parameter tampering (IDOR, mass assignment).
DETECTION: Jailbreak/root detection (Frida requires privileged access; detect Frida server process, ptrace anti-attach); runtime integrity verification (detect hooking via function pointer comparison); certificate pinning in native code (harder to hook than Java/Swift layer); application hardening (DexGuard, ProGuard for Android, iXGuard for iOS).
REAL INSTANCE: Standard mobile application security testing technique; documented in OWASP Mobile Security Testing Guide (MSTG); Frida available at frida.re; Objection framework provides automated certificate pinning bypass ('android sslpinning disable', 'ios sslpinning disable' commands).


--- SOURCE LINES 260953–260973 ---
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A717 — CRYPTOGRAPHIC AGILITY FAILURE: HARDCODED DEPRECATED ALGORITHM IN THIRD-PARTY LIBRARY
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
DOMAIN: D1770 (Cryptographic Algorithm Agility)
ATTACK LAYER:
  Layer 1 — Hidden Dependency: Application cryptographic inventory captures explicit cryptographic configurations. Transitive dependency (npm package, Python library, compiled C library bundled in .so) contains hardcoded deprecated algorithm: MD5 for HMAC authentication, SHA-1 for certificate validation, RSA-1024 key generation, DES for legacy compatibility, ECB mode for block cipher.
  Layer 2 — Discovery Failure: Cryptographic inventory tool scans configuration files and explicit code references. Compiled library: algorithm hardcoded in binary, not discoverable by source-level scan. SBOM generation captures library version but not cryptographic algorithm inventory of library internals. PQC migration planning identifies 'all RSA uses' via source scan — misses RSA-1024 in compiled dependency.
  Layer 3 — Exploitation: Adversary with quantum computer (post-2030 timeline) or currently for MD5/SHA-1 collision attacks: exploits deprecated algorithm in library. For MD5 HMAC: collision attack may not directly apply (HMAC-MD5 more resistant than MD5 alone) but MD5 weaknesses compound with usage context. For SHA-1 in certificate validation: SHAttered collision (2017) demonstrates practical collision; forged certificate accepted by library using SHA-1 validation.
  Layer 4 — Remediation Block: Migration requires third-party library update or replacement. Library may be unmaintained (OSS supply chain issue), incompatible with application version, or proprietary with vendor dependency. Cryptographic agility failure: algorithm selection not abstracted from application logic, preventing algorithm substitution without code change.
DETECTION: Binary-level cryptographic scanning (ChaCha20-Poly1305 vs. AES-ECB in compiled libraries via Cryptosense Analyzer, Veracode Binary SCA); dependency update policy enforcement; SBOM with cryptographic annotation (CycloneDX Cryptography Extension — IETF draft); vendor security questionnaire including crypto algorithm inventory.
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A718 — THREAT INTELLIGENCE POISONING VIA INDICATOR FLOODING (DILUTION ATTACK)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
DOMAIN: D1758 (Threat Intelligence Lifecycle)
ATTACK LAYER:
  Layer 1 — TI Ecosystem: Organization subscribes to shared threat intelligence feeds (MISP instance, ISAC sharing, commercial TI). Defense: automated blocking of IPs/domains/hashes matching threat intelligence IOCs. The blocking is automated and immediate (SIEM/SOAR enrichment pipeline).
  Layer 2 — Flooding: Attacker (or attacker-controlled actor) submits large volume of fabricated IOCs to shared TI communities: malicious IPs that are actually legitimate CDN addresses (Cloudflare, Akamai ranges), legitimate FQDN hashes, or competitor/target infrastructure IP addresses. Submitted IOCs appear credible (proper MISP object format, consistent metadata, corroborated by other fabricated indicators).
  Layer 3 — Collateral Damage: Victim organization's automated blocking activates on poisoned IOCs. Cloudflare CDN IPs blocked: organization's own CDN-hosted services become unreachable. Competitor/partner IP blocked: business communications disrupted. Legitimate hash blocked: software update prevented. Attack causes availability impact via TI infrastructure without direct network access to victim.
  Layer 4 — Dilution Variant: Flood TI feed with thousands of low-quality IOCs. Human analyst review capacity overwhelmed. High-fidelity real IOCs buried in noise. Analyst fatigue causes real threats to be dismissed or delayed. TI feed quality degrades; defenders reduce automated blocking confidence threshold. Real attacker infrastructure no longer auto-blocked.
DETECTION: TI indicator quality scoring (source reputation weighting, corroboration requirement from multiple independent sources before auto-blocking); change rate monitoring (sudden IOC volume spike = dilution signal); safe-list for known-good infrastructure (CDN ranges, major cloud providers protected from auto-block regardless of TI); manual review threshold for high-impact blocking actions.
REAL INSTANCE: Academic: Metcalf & Spring (2015) 'Blacklist Ecosystem Analysis' — documented low-quality indicator sharing in public IP reputation feeds. MISP community governance addresses this via trust circle model and endorsement scores. No specific confirmed TI poisoning attack publicly documented at scale; attack surface confirmed by feed architecture analysis.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A722 — ACTIVE DIRECTORY CERTIFICATE SERVICES (ADCS) ABUSE FOR DOMAIN PERSISTENCE (ESC1)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
DOMAIN: D1776 (Enterprise PKI) / Active Directory security
PATTERN INSTANCE: A713 extension — ADCS-specific certificate abuse
ATTACK LAYER:
  Layer 1 — ADCS Environment: Domain has Active Directory Certificate Services (ADCS) deployed — extremely common in enterprise Windows environments. ADCS issues certificates for various purposes: user authentication, computer authentication, code signing, EFS.
  Layer 2 — ESC1 Vulnerability: Certificate template misconfiguration: template allows requester to specify Subject Alternative Name (SAN) in the CSR (ENROLLEE_SUPPLIES_SUBJECT flag enabled); template allows enrollment by standard domain users; template has 'Client Authentication' EKU. This combination allows any domain user to request a certificate for any user (including Domain Admin) by specifying their UPN in the SAN field.
  Layer 3 — Exploitation: Using Certify or Certipy: request certificate from vulnerable template, specify SAN as 'administrator@domain.com'. ADCS issues certificate with administrator UPN. Use certificate to authenticate as Domain Admin via Kerberos PKINIT (PKI-based initial authentication): receive TGT for Domain Admin. Rubeus or Impacket's gettgtpkinit.py performs authentication.
  Layer 4 — Domain Compromise: Domain Admin TGT grants access to all domain systems. Certificate persists for template-defined validity period (often 1-2 years). Even after password reset, certificate remains valid until revoked — high-persistence credential. ADCS compromise more persistent than password compromise.
DETECTION: Certify/Certipy audit (enumerate misconfigured templates — run before attacker does); ENROLLEE_SUPPLIES_SUBJECT flag audit across all templates; CA issuance policy requiring manager approval for SAN override; Defender for Identity alert on PKINIT authentication from unexpected certificate; certificate transparency monitoring for unexpected domain certificates.
REAL INSTANCE: Will Schroeder & Lee Christensen (SpecterOps, 2021): 'Certified Pre-Owned' whitepaper — documented ESC1-ESC12 ADCS vulnerability classes. ESC1 confirmed exploitable in majority of enterprise ADCS deployments (Certipy creator Oliver Lyak estimates >70% of ADCS environments have at least one exploitable template). Mass exploitation documented post-publication.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A724 — ZKP CIRCUIT SOUNDNESS FAILURE (ZCASH COUNTERFEITING VULNERABILITY)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
DOMAIN: D1793 (Zero-Knowledge Proofs in Authentication)
ATTACK LAYER:
  Layer 1 — ZKP Premise: Zcash shielded transactions use zk-SNARKs (Groth16 proving system) to prove transaction validity without revealing transaction details. Core security property: soundness — a proof that verifies must correspond to a valid transaction. Soundness ensures no invalid proofs can be constructed (with overwhelming probability).
  Layer 2 — CVE-2019-7167 (Sapling circuit): Cryptographic subtlety in the Sapling circuit (Zcash upgrade 2018): the verifier's check for a specific algebraic condition (cofactor check on elliptic curve point) was omitted. Result: an attacker could construct a proof that verifies correctly despite corresponding to an invalid transaction (spending non-existent coins). The missing check allowed cofactor manipulation that bypassed the spending constraint.
  Layer 3 — Exploitation Potential: An adversary aware of this vulnerability could create Zcash shielded transactions spending non-existent coins — effectively counterfeiting currency. Because Zcash shielded transactions are zero-knowledge (by design), the counterfeit spending was undetectable by external observers. Only the Zcash company (Electric Coin Company) could detect via privileged view key.
  Layer 4 — Disclosure and Remediation: Electric Coin Company discovered vulnerability internally in January 2019. Sapling circuit deployed October 2018 — vulnerability present for ~3 months without exploitation. Coordinated disclosure: patch deployed (Sapling v2) and vulnerability disclosed after patch deployed to majority of nodes. No confirmed exploitation in production — but exploitability fully confirmed.
DETECTION: Formal verification of ZKP circuits before deployment (Veridise, Trail of Bits ZKP audit methodology); independent cryptographic audit of circuit constraints; test vectors covering boundary cases including cofactor edge cases; trusted setup ceremony audit for Sapling parameters.
REAL INSTANCE: CVE-2019-7167 (Zcash Sapling counterfeiting vulnerability), disclosed April 2019. Daira Hopwood (Electric Coin Company) internal discovery. Academic follow-up: Dao et al. (2023) 'Vulnerable Implementation of Zero-Knowledge Proof in Ethereum Smart Contracts' — documenting systematic ZKP implementation bugs in production systems.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A725 — DRONE SWARM GPS SPOOFING FOR CRITICAL INFRASTRUCTURE PHYSICAL SECURITY DEFEAT
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
DOMAIN: D1796 (Autonomous Systems and Drone Cybersecurity)
PATTERN INSTANCE: D1730 (air-gap covert channel) extended to drone physical security
ATTACK LAYER:
  Layer 1 — Counter-Drone Defense: Facility (nuclear, data center, financial exchange) deploys counter-drone defense: GPS jamming (blocks drone navigation in exclusion zone), RF direction finding, kinetic interception system. Defense assumes drones depend on GPS for navigation.
  Layer 2 — GPS-Independent Navigation: Attack drone uses inertial navigation system (IMU: accelerometer + gyroscope) supplemented by visual odometry (computer vision-based position estimation from camera feed). Does not rely on GPS. GPS jamming ineffective against INS/visual odometry navigation. Drone follows pre-programmed waypoint route using onboard map.
  Layer 3 — Payload Delivery: Swarm of small drones (DJI Mini-class, ~250g below registration threshold) carries lightweight payload (ISR sensor, small IED analog, spray mechanism). Counter-drone detection: RF-based systems detect communication signals — autonomous drone with pre-programmed route emits no RF during approach (radio silence). Radar: small drones have low radar cross section; detection range limited.
  Layer 4 — Physical Security Failure: Drone reaches facility despite counter-drone defenses. Physical security perimeter defeated by air vector. Payload delivered. Physical intrusion without personnel crossing perimeter. Demonstrates convergence of autonomous systems cyber security and physical security — GPS spoofing/jamming counter-countermeasure.
DETECTION: Multi-modal counter-drone: radar (detect low-RCS targets), acoustic (drone acoustic signature identification), optical (camera-based detection and tracking), IR; non-GPS countermeasures: RF jamming alone insufficient against autonomous drones; geofencing at OS level (DJI geofencing) ineffective against custom firmware; Dedicated Short-Range Counter-UAS systems (SRC Inc. GROND, Dedrone, D-Fend Solutions).
REAL INSTANCE: Ukraine conflict (2022-2024): FPV drone swarms using visual guidance for precision strike, GPS-independent navigation documented; Iranian Shahed-136 drones (loitering munitions) with INS navigation; Saudi Aramco attack (2019) attributed to drone/cruise missile combination bypassing air defenses. GPS-independent commercial drone navigation: DJI Obstacle Avoidance + Visual Positioning System (no GPS required indoors).
