A727 — CLOUD SECURITY POSTURE DRIFT VIA TERRAFORM STATE DESYNC
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
DOMAIN: D1784 (Cloud Security Architecture Patterns)
ATTACK LAYER:
  Layer 1 — IaC Security Control: Organization manages cloud infrastructure via Terraform. Security posture is defined in Terraform modules (S3 bucket policy: public access block enabled; security group: port 22 restricted to VPN CIDR; IAM policy: specific resource scope). CSPM tool validates against Terraform-defined intended state.
  Layer 2 — Manual Change (Terraform State Desync): Operations engineer makes emergency change directly in AWS console (bypasses Terraform PR review): opens security group port 22 to 0.0.0.0/0 to debug connectivity issue. Change not reflected in Terraform state. Next 'terraform plan': shows drift; engineer runs 'terraform apply' without reviewing diff carefully — or, engineer runs 'terraform import' of changed resource, updating Terraform state to reflect the misconfigured security group as intended. Terraform state now reflects insecure configuration as desired state.
  Layer 3 — CSPM Detection Gap: CSPM tool compares actual AWS state to Terraform desired state. After state import: both show port 22 open to 0.0.0.0/0. No drift detected. CSPM alert: none. Security review: passes (actual matches intended). The security control (Terraform IaC) has been compromised via state manipulation.
  Layer 4 — Attacker Exploitation: Exposed SSH port discovered via Shodan/Censys scan. Credential brute force or known CVE against SSH version. Server compromise via external SSH access that was blocked before emergency change.
DETECTION: IaC PR review requirement with security-sensitive change approval; Terraform plan output mandatory review with 'security-impacting' change tagging; CSPM cross-reference with independent security baseline (not just Terraform state); detect-drift pipeline (compare actual cloud state to Git-committed IaC, not Terraform state file); emergency change process with mandatory cleanup ticket.
REAL INSTANCE: Capital One breach (2019): WAF misconfiguration enabled SSRF attack on IMDS — not Terraform-specific but IaC drift from intended state. General pattern documented in HashiCorp Terraform operational documentation and cloud security blog posts (Bridgecrew, Snyk). Terraform state desync as attack surface: documented in Terraform security hardening guides.

G-C111-04 | Automotive cybersecurity incident notification threshold
Domain: D1801 (Automotive cybersecurity)
Gap: UNECE WP.29 requires manufacturer CSMS but does not specify incident
  notification thresholds for vehicle cybersecurity incidents to regulatory
  bodies. What constitutes a reportable vehicle cybersecurity incident, to
  whom, and within what timeframe is undefined. Consequence: manufacturers
  self-determine reporting scope; regulatory visibility into fleet-level
  cybersecurity incidents absent.
Closure requirement: UNECE WP.29 or NHTSA must publish vehicle cybersecurity
  incident notification criteria and timeline.

G-C111-05 | Medical device legacy risk acceptance framework
Domain: D1802 (Medical device cybersecurity)
Gap: FDA guidance addresses new device pre-market security requirements;
  legacy medical devices without security update capability in clinical use
  lack a formal risk acceptance framework. Hospitals hold devices that cannot
  be patched and cannot be removed without patient care disruption. Consequence:
  ad-hoc compensating control decisions made without standards basis; risk
  acceptance decisions vary by institution without interoperability.
Closure requirement: FDA, NIST, or HTM (healthcare technology management)
  standards body must publish legacy medical device residual risk acceptance
  framework with compensating control catalog.

A731 | PQC algorithm downgrade via TLS negotiation manipulation
Domain: Post-quantum cryptography migration engineering (D1798)
Tactic: Cryptographic downgrade / HNDL threat exploitation
Mechanism:
  Phase 1 — Reconnaissance: Attacker identifies organization deploying hybrid
    classical/PQC TLS (e.g., X25519+CRYSTALS-Kyber hybrid key agreement) in
    transition mode. Transition mode accepts both classical-only and hybrid
    connections for compatibility.
  Phase 2 — Downgrade: Attacker performs active MitM; strips Kyber key share
    from ClientHello; server falls back to X25519-only; connection proceeds
    with classical cryptography. Hybrid mode intended to prevent downgrade but
    server-side fallback logic accepts classical-only connection when hybrid
    client preference fails negotiation.
  Phase 3 — HNDL collection: Traffic captured with classical-only encryption;
    stored for future CRQC decryption. Long-term value data (classified comms,
    financial transactions, health records) extracted post-CRQC availability.
  Phase 4 — Evasion: Downgrade not detected; hybrid TLS logging records
    negotiated cipher suite as classical (normal for legacy clients); no alert.
Root mechanics: R01 (transition period vulnerability), R06 (compatibility
  requirement creates fallback path), R11.AMBIENT (TLS configuration docs
  reveal fallback behavior)
Pattern refs: P33.3 (PQC transition period as persistent vulnerability window),
  P96-C1 COROLLARY (organizations accepting HNDL risk without PQC migration)
Defense: Enforce hybrid-required mode (no classical fallback) for high-value
  connections; log cipher suite negotiation failures as security events;
  disable TLS 1.2 for sensitive APIs before PQC transition complete.
Severity: CRITICAL (long-term data confidentiality; CRQC timeline 5-15 years)

A734 | CAN bus ECU impersonation via identifier spoofing for vehicle control
Domain: Automotive cybersecurity (D1801)
Tactic: Automotive network protocol abuse
Mechanism:
  Phase 1 — Initial access: Attacker gains access to vehicle CAN bus via
    OBD-II port (physical access), compromised telematics unit (remote), or
    infotainment system (remote via Bluetooth/cellular).
  Phase 2 — ECU impersonation: CAN bus has no authentication; any node can
    send frames with any arbitration ID; attacker replays or crafts frames
    with target ECU arbitration ID; target ECU (braking, steering, powertrain)
    executes spoofed commands.
  Phase 3 — Vehicle control: Attacker disables braking system or forces
    unintended acceleration via spoofed CAN frames; demonstrated by Miller
    & Valasek (Jeep Cherokee 2015); safety-critical control via protocol
    with no authentication.
Root mechanics: R02 (protocol designed without adversarial threat model),
  R08 (physical access requirement removed by telematics exposure)
Pattern refs: P33.3 (automotive as Tier-1 domain; CAN bus as persistent
  structural vulnerability), I8 (impossibility of retrofitting CAN security)
Defense: IDPS for CAN bus (anomaly detection on frame frequency/sequence);
  CAN FD with MAC-based authentication (CAN XL / AUTOSAR SecOC); telematics
  unit isolation from safety-critical ECUs via gateway.
Severity: CRITICAL (physical safety impact)

A747 | Red team finding remediation attestation fraud
Domain: Offensive security program management (D1826)
Tactic: Governance / audit integrity failure
Mechanism:
  Phase 1 — Finding closure pressure: Red team finding marked as high/critical
    creates organizational pressure for rapid closure; remediation owner
    faces performance accountability for open findings.
  Phase 2 — False closure: Remediation owner attests finding as remediated
    without implementing technical fix; superficial change (documentation
    update, architectural diagram revision) submitted as evidence; red team
    does not conduct adversarial retesting due to resource constraint.
  Phase 3 — Persistent vulnerability: Finding closed in tracking system;
    vulnerability persists in production; next red team engagement rediscovers
    same finding; systemic: organizations with poor remediation verification
    show repeated finding recurrence across engagements.
Root mechanics: R03 (governance metric gaming), R04 (accountability
  pressure drives false attestation)
Pattern refs: P98 (remediation metric gaming — 6th context candidate),
  G-C112-10 (remediation verification standard gap), LAW-9 candidate
  (individual metric optimization produces collective security gap)
Defense: Mandatory adversarial retesting for all critical/high findings
  before closure; retest conducted by independent red team member;
  finding closure requires technical evidence artifact (screenshot, config
  diff, scan output), not attestation.
Severity: HIGH (persistent unmitigated vulnerability under false governance
  assurance)

CANDIDATE: Red team finding remediation attestation fraud as collective
  security governance failure (from A747, A1511)

LAW-9 criteria:
  (1) Individually rational: remediation owner attests closure to avoid
      performance accountability consequence; individually rational given
      metric pressure.
  (2) Collectively harmful: vulnerability persists; organization's security
      posture reporting reflects false assurance; security investment decisions
      based on false remediation data.
  (3) No unilateral defection incentive: remediation owner who insists on
      adversarial retesting before closure faces delay and increased scrutiny;
      no individual benefit to maintaining honest attestation under pressure.
  (4) Tractable coordination solution: mandatory adversarial retesting policy
      (D1726) — exists as governance solution; requires CISO mandate.
  (5) Persistent despite awareness: finding recurrence across red team
      engagement cycles is documented industry observation (multiple red team
      practitioners publicly note repeat-finding problem); structural correction
      requires policy intervention rarely implemented.

All 5 criteria met.

LAW-9 INSTANCE #17 CONFIRMED: Red team finding remediation attestation fraud
  — individually rational metric gaming produces collective false security
  assurance; persistent vulnerability masked by governance metric; coordination
  solution (mandatory retesting) exists but requires organizational mandate.

Tactic: Business email compromise via email authentication policy gap
Mechanism:
  Phase 1 — DMARC policy reconnaissance: Attacker queries DNS for target
    organization DMARC record; finds p=none (monitoring mode, no enforcement);
    DMARC p=none logs unauthenticated email but does not reject or quarantine.
  Phase 2 — Domain spoofing: Attacker sends email From: cfo@target-org.com
    without passing SPF or DKIM; receiving mail server delivers email because
    DMARC p=none does not instruct rejection; recipient sees legitimate From
    address.
  Phase 3 — BEC execution: Spoofed CFO email instructs finance team to
    execute wire transfer; social engineering amplified by exact domain
    spoofing (no lookalike domain required); victim verifies email headers
    shows correct From address.
  Prevalence: FBI IC3 2023: BEC losses $2.9B. DMARC p=none represents
    approximately 40% of Fortune 500 companies as of 2023 (Valimail data).
Root mechanics: R09 (DMARC enforcement requires policy progression from
  none → quarantine → reject; organizations stall at none), R04 (fear
  of legitimate email delivery failure blocks enforcement)
Pattern refs: LAW-9 (individual caution about DMARC enforcement produces
  collective BEC vulnerability — same game-theoretic structure as other
  LAW-9 instances)
Defense: DMARC p=reject enforcement with monitoring period; DMARC Analyzer
  or Valimail for enforcement migration; SPF record hardening (all mechanism);
  BIMI for visual brand authentication reinforcement.
Severity: CRITICAL (BEC; direct financial loss)

A757 | SCA false negative via unlisted transitive dependency (phantom
  dependency)
Domain: SCA and open source risk (D1849)
Tactic: Vulnerability detection evasion via dependency opacity
Mechanism:
  Phase 1 — Phantom dependency: Application depends on Package A (declared
    in package.json); Package A depends on Package B (transitive); Package B
    resolved directly from package-lock.json without explicit declaration;
    SCA tool configured to scan declared dependencies only (not lock file);
    Package B's CVE not scanned.
  Phase 2 — Exploitation: Attacker identifies Package B version in target
    (via error messages, HTTP headers, timing); exploits CVE in Package B;
    SCA tool reports clean because Package B is 'phantom' (undeclared
    transitive).
  Root cause: SCA tool scope limited to package manifest vs. lock file;
    organizations often scan manifest only for speed; lock file scanning
    required for complete coverage.
Root mechanics: R05 (transitive dependency opacity), P95 (SCA configuration
  complexity creates coverage gap)
Pattern refs: G-C113-07 (SCA transitive dependency prioritization gap),
  P100 (detection under-investment: lock file scanning deprioritized)
Defense: Configure SCA to scan lock files (package-lock.json, Pipfile.lock,
  Cargo.lock) in addition to manifests; enable reachability analysis in
  SCA tool where available; SBOM generation from lock file not manifest.
Severity: HIGH (known vulnerability undetected by security tooling)

      Proofpoint; structural correction not occurring at industry rate.

A761 | JWT algorithm confusion attack (RS256 to HS256)
Domain: Cryptography implementation auditing (D1871)
Tactic: Cryptographic implementation vulnerability exploitation
Mechanism:
  Phase 1 — Public key extraction: Attacker retrieves JWT signing public key
    from server (often exposed at /.well-known/jwks.json, in API documentation,
    or via error messages).
  Phase 2 — Algorithm confusion: Server configured to accept RS256 (asymmetric)
    tokens; attacker crafts token with alg:HS256 (symmetric HMAC); uses
    server's public key as HMAC secret; library implementation accepts
    HS256 token and verifies signature using public key as HMAC secret—
    which attacker knows.
  Phase 3 — Arbitrary claim forgery: Attacker forges token with any sub, role,
    or scope claim; server verifies signature as valid; authentication and
    authorization bypassed completely.
  Root: Library vulnerability (accepting algorithm from token header rather
    than enforcing configured algorithm); CVE-2015-9235 (jsonwebtoken),
    multiple library instances.
Root mechanics: R02 (JWT design allows algorithm specification in header—
  attacker-controlled input in security-critical field)
Pattern refs: P33.3 (JWT algorithm confusion as Tier-1 auth bypass),
  G-C114 (cryptography implementation auditing gap)
Defense: Enforce algorithm server-side (reject tokens with non-configured
  algorithm); use libraries with strict algorithm enforcement; JWT none
  algorithm rejection; audit JWT implementation at dependency version pinning.
Severity: CRITICAL (authentication and authorization bypass)

A762 | Healthcare FHIR bulk export API misconfiguration enabling mass

Domain: Security in healthcare (D1868)
Tactic: Healthcare data mass exfiltration via API misconfiguration
Mechanism:
  Phase 1 — FHIR endpoint discovery: Attacker identifies healthcare
    organization's FHIR R4 server endpoint (published in provider directory,
    health information exchange, or app registration).
  Phase 2 — Bulk export exploitation: FHIR $export operation (HL7 FHIR
    Bulk Data specification) provides population-level data export; endpoint
    lacks proper authorization enforcement (accepts any OAuth2 token, or

  Phase 3 — Mass PHI export: Attacker exports entire patient population
    data (demographics, diagnoses, medications, lab results); export may
    include millions of patient records; ONC 21st Century Cures Act mandates
    FHIR API exposure, expanding attack surface systematically.

  requirement enforcement), R06 (bulk export operation provides population-

Pattern refs: A710 (FHIR API misconfiguration — cross-cycle persistence;

  as Tier-1 PHI exfiltration surface)

A775 [CONTAINER-RUNTIME] eBPF verifier bypass via JIT compilation edge case
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Domain: Container runtime security / Kernel security
Attack class: Security control bypass via implementation vulnerability
Root mechanics: R03 (implementation complexity), R05 (attack surface at security boundary)

Layer 1 — Mechanism:
eBPF programs run in the Linux kernel with a verifier that statically checks safety properties
(no loops, bounded memory access, no null deref). JIT compilation of verified eBPF bytecode
has historically introduced vulnerabilities where verifier-safe programs produce unsafe native code.
CVE-2021-3490 (eBPF ALU32 bounds tracking), CVE-2022-23222 (pointer arithmetic), CVE-2023-2163
(incorrect verifier pruning) — each allowed privilege escalation from unprivileged eBPF.

Layer 2 — Structural amplification:
eBPF is increasingly used as the foundation for container runtime security (Falco, Cilium, Tetragon).
A bypass of the eBPF verifier defeats the security tool built on top of it simultaneously with
achieving kernel-level code execution. This is a second-order effect: the security tool itself
becomes the attack surface. P95 application #41: eBPF security tool complexity → verifier
bypass attack surface that defeats the security control while enabling exploitation.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A777 [VULN-MGMT-OPS] CVSS score inflation via vendor self-scoring bias
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Domain: Vulnerability management operations
Attack class: Metric integrity failure (passive — systemic)
Root mechanics: R07 (incentive misalignment), R11.AMBIENT (NVD/vendor advisory delta tracking)

Layer 1 — Mechanism:
CVSS base scores are frequently assigned by the vendor disclosing the vulnerability. Research
(Allodi & Massacci 2014, Jacobs et al. 2020) demonstrates systematic downward bias in vendor
self-assigned CVSS scores vs. NVD re-analysis: vendors assign lower severity to their own
product vulnerabilities. Approximately 27% of CVEs show significant score divergence between
vendor advisory and NVD CVSS analysis.

Layer 2 — Structural amplification:
Organizations using vendor-reported CVSS scores for SLA-based remediation prioritization
systematically under-prioritize vendor-downscored vulnerabilities. High-severity vulns scored
Critical by NVD but Medium by vendor advisory are remediated in 90-day SLA instead of 30-day.
This 60-day exposure window gap is directly attributable to metric source selection.
P98 instance #11: CVSS score as remediation priority driver → vendor optimizes score
(downward bias) rather than objective severity assessment.

Layer 3 — EPSS cross-validation:
EPSS (Exploit Prediction Scoring System) is source-independent (based on exploitation evidence)
and partially corrects vendor-bias issue. However G-C115-04 gap: EPSS model version drift
without recalibration creates secondary prioritization failure. Combined CVSS vendor bias +
EPSS model drift produces compound deprioritization of actively exploited vulnerabilities.

Layer 4 — Law resonance:
LAW-9 instance: Vendors rationally minimize disclosed severity (reputational protection) →
collective outcome is systematic under-prioritization of critical vulnerabilities across the
defender ecosystem. P98 structural confirmation: metric drives behavior away from underlying
security outcome.

--- SOURCE LINES 267498–267519 ---
Layer 2 — Structural amplification:
Container escape vulnerabilities have a consistent pattern: kernel features designed before
container isolation was a security requirement create unintended trust boundary crossings.
cgroup v1 was designed for resource accounting; release_agent was designed for cleanup.
Neither was designed with container isolation in mind — they predate the container security
threat model by 5+ years. cgroup v2 (unified hierarchy) does not have this vulnerability;
migration from v1 to v2 is ongoing in Kubernetes clusters.

Layer 3 — Detection:
Falco rule: cgroup release_agent file write by container process.
eBPF: fsnotify event on /sys/fs/cgroup/**/release_agent from container namespace.
Mitigation: Kubernetes security context seccompProfile: RuntimeDefault + non-root + read-only
root filesystem reduces attack surface. cgroup v2 migration eliminates vulnerability class.

Layer 4 — Anatomy milestone context:
A799 is the final anatomy before A800 milestone (800 total anatomies).
A799 represents a class of container escape via kernel legacy feature abuse;
prior instances include: A-prior (CVE-2022-23648 containerd TOCTOU, A-prior docker.sock
privilege, A-prior runc overwrite). The container escape anatomy class is converging:
most escape vectors now require either kernel vulnerability or specific misconfigurations
(privileged mode, host path mounts, dangerous capabilities). Defense-in-depth
via seccomp + AppArmor + non-root + capability drop addresses the class systemically.

Layer 2 — Structural amplification:
Microservices architectures have many internal service-to-service connections with
implicit trust (no authentication between services in the same cluster).
Vulnerability in any one service provides pivot to all internally-trusted services.
Patching is service-specific: patching service A for Log4Shell does not address
service B's Spring4Shell vulnerability. A partial patch state creates chained attack
paths that did not exist before patching began.

Anatomies A811–A820:

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A811: CTI FEED AUTOMATED INGESTION LOOP POISONING
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Domain: Cyber Threat Intelligence Automation (D1958)
Mechanism: Adversary submits crafted indicators to open CTI feeds (MISP communities,
  OTX, VirusTotal) that reference legitimate infrastructure (CDNs, cloud providers,
  government IPs). Automated CTI pipelines ingest and operationalize these indicators.
  SOAR blocks or alerts on legitimate traffic. Analyst investigation time consumed
  by false positives generated by adversary-controlled feed poisoning.

P-linkage: P98 #16 (IOC count as CTI program metric → volume optimization over quality).
Detection: Cross-feed indicator correlation; source reputation scoring; indicator
  age-weighted confidence decay; out-of-band validation before SOAR automation.

R11.AMBIENT CONFIRMATIONS — CYCLE 119
─────────────────────────────────────────

CANDIDATE #90: Federated learning participant gradient updates as training data
  distribution inference signal (source: A1615)
Analysis: In federated learning, each participant's model update (gradient) is
  observable to the aggregation server. Research has demonstrated that gradients
  leak information about the participant's local training data distribution
  (gradient inversion attacks). Participant gradient updates are generated for
  model training purposes — not as security intelligence — but function as an
  inference channel about private training data. This is ambient data generated
  as an operational byproduct of the FL protocol itself.
R11.AMBIENT #90 CONFIRMED: Federated learning participant gradient updates as
  training data distribution inference signal (gradient inversion attack surface).

CANDIDATE: Deception coverage theater (source: A824/A1631)
Mechanism: Deception technology vendors rationally market products on high-precision
  alert quality (when a deception alert fires, it is almost always a true positive).
  Organizations rationally purchase deception for high-precision alerting without
  measuring recall (what fraction of attacker paths trigger any deception alert).
  Security teams rationally report deception program existence without measuring
  coverage. Attacker rationally fingerprints and evades deception coverage.
  No market incentive exists for coverage measurement because it would reveal
  deception gaps that reduce product appeal. Cooperative outcome (adequate deception
  coverage across attack surface) not achieved.
LAW-9 #33 CONFIRMED: Deception coverage theater equilibrium — vendor precision
  marketing, buyer precision focus, and coverage measurement absence produce
  deception deployments that advanced attackers can traverse without triggering.

A841: THREAT MODEL STALENESS EXPLOITATION — UNREVIEWED ARCHITECTURE CHANGE
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Mechanism: Application receives threat model at initial design review. Architecture
  changes (new API endpoints, third-party integrations, cloud service additions)

  coverage false assumption; unmodeled attack surface exploitation.

  → staleness not tracked; coverage assumed from completion date).

  architecture change diff against current threat model; threat model coverage
  measurement including staleness tracking.

--- SOURCE LINES 270999–271031 ---
LAW-9 EVALUATION — CYCLE 122 CANDIDATES
─────────────────────────────────────────

CANDIDATE: Threat model and PIA coverage self-declaration equilibrium
  (source: A841/A850, isomorphic structure)
Mechanism: Organizations implement threat modeling programs and PIA programs with
  coverage obligations. Triggering reviews is the responsibility of the team
  undertaking the work (product teams, development teams). Each team rationally
  minimizes review triggers (reviews cost development time; benefits are shared
  across the security ecosystem). The trigger mechanism (self-declaration of scope)
  is rationally under-applied by each individual team. No coordination mechanism
  ensures systematic trigger application. The cooperative outcome (complete coverage
  of all in-scope processes) is not achieved because no individual team bears the
  cost of another team's under-application. This equilibrium applies identically
  to threat models and PIAs — structural isomorphism confirmed.
LAW-9 #36 CONFIRMED: Design-time analysis coverage self-declaration equilibrium —
  threat model and PIA trigger self-declaration produces systematic under-coverage
  as rational equilibrium; applies universally across design-time security/privacy
  analysis programs.

CANDIDATE: Security champion volunteer bias equilibrium (source: A845)
Mechanism: Security champion programs recruit through voluntary participation.
  Developers with security interest (who are already least likely to introduce
  security vulnerabilities) self-select as champions. Developers in high-risk
  teams with no security interest (most likely to introduce security vulnerabilities)
  do not volunteer. The champion distribution is inversely correlated with team
  security risk. No coordination mechanism allocates champions to highest-risk teams.
  The cooperative outcome (champion coverage proportional to team security risk)
  is not achieved because voluntary selection is biased against the teams that
  need champions most.
LAW-9 #37 CONFIRMED: Security champion volunteer bias equilibrium — voluntary
  selection produces champion coverage inversely correlated with team security risk;
  highest-risk teams are systematically under-championed.

A859: CYBER RESILIENCE INVESTMENT MISALLOCATION — PREVENTION VS. RECOVERY IMBALANCE
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Mechanism: Organization allocates 95% of security budget to breach prevention

--- SOURCE LINES 271679–271709 ---
LAW-9 EVALUATION — CYCLE 123 CANDIDATES
─────────────────────────────────────────

CANDIDATE: Bug bounty scope exclusion cooperative failure (source: A853/A1668)
Mechanism: Organizations rationally exclude sensitive/legacy systems from bug bounty
  scope (availability concerns, system fragility, regulatory sensitivity). Researchers
  rationally do not test out-of-scope systems (no bounty incentive; legal risk).
  The systems most excluded from scope are often those with the highest vulnerability
  density (legacy systems, financial systems, authentication systems) — precisely
  because their security investment has been lowest. Attacker (with no scope
  constraint) targets the excluded systems. The cooperative outcome (all high-risk
  systems covered by bounty scope) is not achieved because each organization's
  rational scope exclusion creates systematic under-testing of highest-risk assets.
LAW-9 #38 CONFIRMED: Bug bounty scope exclusion equilibrium — organizational
  sensitivity concerns and researcher incentive structures produce systematic
  exclusion of highest-risk assets from tested scope; attackers face no scope
  constraints.

CANDIDATE: Cyber resilience under-investment equilibrium (source: A859/A1674)
Mechanism: Prevention investments produce clear, attributable outcomes (vulnerability
  patched, control deployed). Recovery investments produce outcomes visible only
  at recovery time (backup works, IR team knows playbook). Decision-makers rationally
  prefer visible, attributable investments. Recovery investment benefits are invisible
  until they are needed. Each budget cycle, prevention is funded over recovery
  because prevention benefits can be demonstrated; recovery benefits cannot until
  failure occurs. The cooperative outcome (balanced prevention-recovery investment
  portfolio) is not achieved because recovery investment is systematically
  under-attributable to security outcomes in the absence of an actual recovery event.
LAW-9 #39 CONFIRMED: Cyber resilience under-investment equilibrium — prevention
  investment attribution advantage produces systematic under-investment in recovery
  capability until recovery failure demonstrates the deficit.


--- SOURCE LINES 271713–271728 ---

R11.AMBIENT CONFIRMATIONS — CYCLE 123
─────────────────────────────────────────

CANDIDATE #98: Bug bounty submission metadata as vulnerability density heat map
  (source: A853/A1679)
Analysis: Bug bounty platform submission metadata (vulnerability counts by asset,
  submission rates by endpoint, bounty payout concentration) reveals which parts
  of an organization's attack surface have the highest vulnerability density as
  perceived by the researcher community. This data is generated as an operational
  artifact of the bug bounty platform; when analyzed, it functions as an intelligence
  product revealing relative attack surface quality. Notably, zero submissions
  against an in-scope asset may indicate either security quality or researcher
  disinterest in the asset (low payout, low complexity).
R11.AMBIENT #98 CONFIRMED: Bug bounty submission metadata as vulnerability density
  heat map and researcher attention distribution intelligence across attack surface.

A861: SBOM VULNERABILITY CORRELATION FALSE NEGATIVE — TRANSITIVE DEPENDENCY GAP
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Domain: SBOM Operations (D2060)
Mechanism: Application SBOM lists direct dependencies (10 packages). Each direct
  dependency has 5-30 transitive dependencies not listed in the application SBOM.
  Vulnerability scanner correlates CVEs against listed SBOM components. CVE affects
  a transitive dependency (log4j-core pulled 3 levels deep) not in the SBOM.
  Vulnerability is not detected by SBOM-based scanning. Log4Shell-class vulnerability
  in production; SBOM-based assurance reports no known vulnerabilities.
Attack vector: SBOM transitive dependency coverage gap; log4j-class transitive
  vulnerability; SBOM false assurance of completeness.
Structural enabler: G-C124-02 (no SBOM correlation accuracy benchmark).
P-linkage: P100 (detection under-investment — SBOM transitive depth is investment
  decision; shallow SBOM is cheaper; transitive risk is invisible).
Detection: Full transitive dependency enumeration in SBOM generation; depth-N
  SBOM completeness verification; runtime dependency analysis as SBOM complement.

A867: VULNERABILITY PRIORITIZATION GAMING — EPSS SCORE MANIPULATION VIA VENDOR
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Domain: Vulnerability Intelligence Prioritization (D2074)
Mechanism: EPSS (Exploit Prediction Scoring System) model predicts exploitation
  probability based on observable signals (CVE characteristics, PoC publication,
  dark web mentions). Vendor with unpatched critical vulnerability monitors EPSS
  signal inputs. Suppresses PoC publication (takedowns, legal threats); avoids
  dark web mention of vulnerability; delays NVD enrichment. EPSS score remains
  low due to suppressed signals. Organizations using EPSS-prioritized patching
  deprioritize the vulnerability. Window of exploitation opens while EPSS score
  remains suppressed.
Attack vector: EPSS signal suppression; vulnerability disclosure control;
  prioritization model gaming via information control.
Structural enabler: G-C124-08 (no prioritization accuracy measurement).
P-linkage: P98 (EPSS score as vulnerability priority metric → signal suppression
  gaming by parties controlling disclosure information).

--- SOURCE LINES 272382–272402 ---
CANDIDATE: EPSS score suppression by vulnerability disclosure actors (A867)
  Mechanism: EPSS (Exploit Prediction Scoring System) scores reflect observed
             exploitation signals including PoC availability and exploit
             weaponization. Vendors and bug bounty platforms rationally suppress
             disclosure signals (delay CVE publication, embargo PoC repositories,
             restrict NVD enrichment) to manage patch window and reputational
             exposure. Suppression depresses EPSS scores. Organizations using
             EPSS for patch prioritization de-prioritize actively exploited
             vulns. Exploitation window extends.
  Game structure: Each vendor faces dominant strategy — suppress disclosure.
                  Disclosure accelerates patching pressure and adversary
                  weaponization simultaneously; suppression delays both.
                  Collective suppression undermines EPSS signal validity.
  Nash equilibrium: Systematic disclosure suppression. EPSS under-scores
                    actively exploited vulnerabilities. Prioritization tools
                    fail at highest-risk items.
  Cooperative optimum: Timely, complete disclosure with coordinated defender
                       notification. Not individually rational for vendors.
  LAW-9 CONFIRMED — #41: EPSS signal suppression equilibrium
  Pattern: Coordinated disclosure incentive misalignment undermines
           exploit prediction infrastructure

CANDIDATE: Pentest cleanup failure equilibrium (A890)
  Mechanism: Post-engagement cleanup is a cost center with no deliverable value
             for the organization purchasing penetration testing. Pentesters
             face time pressure (fixed-price engagements), and cleanup failures
             are rarely attributed back to them (artifacts discovered later,
             not linked to specific engagement). Organizations do not
             contractually require or verify cleanup completeness. Pentesters
             rationally prioritize findings delivery over cleanup completeness.
             Collectively, persistent test artifacts accumulate across
             organizational environments.
  Nash equilibrium: Incomplete cleanup accepted as industry norm. Organizations
                    accumulate test artifact debt. Threat actors discover and
                    exploit persistent test infrastructure at non-trivial rate.
  Cooperative optimum: Mandatory verified cleanup with escrow holdback.
                       Not individually rational without contractual enforcement.
  LAW-9 CONFIRMED — #45: Penetration test cleanup equilibrium

A900 — Memory-safe language unsafe block concentration attack
  Layer 1 (Migration): Organization migrates codebase to memory-safe
           language (Rust); retains unsafe blocks for FFI and
           performance-critical paths
  Layer 2 (Targeting): Adversary analyzes compiled binary or source
           repository; identifies unsafe block locations and call paths
           leading to unsafe code from external inputs
  Layer 3 (Exploitation): Attacker crafts input traversing call path

G-C129-01 — SIS security assessment has no standardized methodology
  Domain: Safety Instrumented System Security (D2159)
  Gap type: Assessment methodology absence
  Detail: Safety Instrumented Systems protect against process safety events
          (overpressure, overtemperature, runaway reaction). Cyber attack
          against SIS (as demonstrated by Triton/TRISIS) can disable safety
          functions, enabling catastrophic process safety events. No standardized
          cybersecurity assessment methodology exists that accounts for the
          specific convergence risk of SIS-DCS cyber attack paths, SIS logic
          manipulation, and SIS bypass techniques.
  Closure path: IEC 62443 SIS-specific security assessment extension

G-C129-06 — Aviation ADS-B has no mandatory authentication timeline
  Domain: Aviation Cybersecurity (D2173)
  Gap type: Authentication mandate gap
  Detail: ADS-B (Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast) is mandated
          for aircraft position reporting but lacks authentication; any
          transmitter can inject phantom aircraft or suppress real aircraft
          from ATC radar displays. Authenticated ADS-B (ADS-B+) has been
          in research for over a decade with no regulatory mandate for
          authenticated broadcast deployment. GAO has flagged this gap
          repeatedly without regulatory action.
  Closure path: FAA/EASA ADS-B authentication mandate with implementation timeline

G-C129-07 — Nuclear digital I&C cybersecurity has no harmonized international standard

          conflicting requirements. No harmonized international standard

  Closure path: IAEA harmonized nuclear digital I&C cybersecurity standard

--- SOURCE LINES 275099–275116 ---
CANDIDATE: Nuclear supply chain verification under-investment (A920)
  Mechanism: Nuclear facility operators face extreme cost pressure for digital
             I&C component verification. Comprehensive supply chain verification
             (code review, hardware analysis, trusted foundry requirement)
             is orders of magnitude more expensive than standard acceptance
             testing. Regulator cannot enforce verification depth that would
             make facilities economically unviable. Each facility rationally
             applies minimum verification passing regulatory requirements.
             Collectively, nuclear digital I&C supply chain is verified at
             minimum standard insufficient to detect sophisticated supply chain
             implants.
  Nash equilibrium: Minimum viable nuclear supply chain verification. Advanced
                    supply chain implants undetectable by current verification
                    practices. Nuclear facility digital I&C as national security
                    risk concentrated in supply chain gaps.
  Cooperative optimum: Trusted foundry and formal verification requirements.
                       Not individually rational at current economic constraints.
  LAW-9 CONFIRMED — #51: Nuclear supply chain minimum verification equilibrium

--- SOURCE LINES 275914–275939 ---
G-C131-07 — Multimodal AI cross-modal attack surface has no threat
             model framework
  Domain: Multimodal AI Security (D2212)
  Gap type: Threat model framework absence
  Detail: Multimodal AI systems (text + image, text + audio, vision-language
          models) create cross-modal attack surfaces where adversarial inputs
          in one modality affect processing of another. No threat model
          framework exists for multimodal AI attack surface characterization,
          cross-modal injection attack classes, or modality isolation
          requirements.
  Closure path: OWASP multimodal AI threat model framework

G-C131-08 — Cyber resilience measurement has no standardized metric
             independent of cybersecurity control metrics
  Domain: Cyber Resilience Measurement (D2216)
  Gap type: Measurement independence standard absence
  Detail: Cyber resilience (ability to absorb, adapt to, and recover from
          cyber incidents while maintaining mission-essential functions)
          is measured by most frameworks as a function of preventive security
          control implementation. Resilience and security are distinct
          properties: a highly secure but brittle system and a less secure
          but highly resilient system may have identical security metrics
          but vastly different operational outcomes under adversarial conditions.
          No standardized resilience metric exists independent of security
          control metrics.
  Closure path: NIST cyber resilience independent measurement framework

A933 — Visual prompt injection via image payload in multimodal LLM
  Layer 1 (Multimodal processing): System uses vision-language model
           to process images alongside text (document analysis,
           image captioning, visual question answering)
  Layer 2 (Injection payload): Adversary embeds text instructions
           in image (white text on white background, steganographic
           encoding, QR code, adversarial patch visible to model
           but not human) that model processes as instructions
  Layer 3 (Cross-modal execution): Vision-language model processes
           image instructions alongside text context; injected
           instructions override system prompt or user intent
  Layer 4 (Impact): Model executes injected instructions (data
           exfiltration via response, tool call injection,
           response manipulation) without user awareness;
           cross-modal injection evades text-only input filtering
  G-C131-07 instance: Multimodal AI threat model gap
  D2212 instance: Multimodal AI security domain


--- SOURCE LINES 276064–276081 ---
A936 — AI-assisted exploit development acceleration via LLM
  Layer 1 (Vulnerability input): Attacker provides LLM with
           CVE description, vulnerable code snippet, or patch diff
           for target vulnerability
  Layer 2 (Exploit scaffolding): LLM generates initial exploit
           scaffold, identifies exploitation primitive, suggests
           exploitation technique class; significantly reduces
           time-to-working-exploit for n-day vulnerabilities
  Layer 3 (Iteration): Attacker iterates exploit with LLM
           assistance; LLM debugs failed exploit attempts,
           suggests bypass for exploit mitigations (ASLR, stack
           canary, CFI), generates shellcode variants
  Layer 4 (Weaponization): Working exploit produced in fraction
           of traditional development time; lower-skill attackers
           can weaponize vulnerabilities previously requiring
           specialized expertise; exploitation window narrows
  G-C131-10 instance: Responsible AI-assisted offensive research gap
  D2214 instance: AI-assisted vulnerability research domain

LAW-9 INSTANCE #64 — AI Safety Evaluation Cooperative Failure
Context: AI developers know adversarial red-teaming is necessary for safety
verification. Each developer conducts internal red-teaming but does not share
results with competitors — sharing reveals capabilities and vulnerabilities.
Third-party red teams sign NDAs; findings stay confidential. Regulators see
self-reported results. No developer unilaterally publishes full red team findings
without competitive disadvantage. Result: AI safety evaluations are privately
conducted without external verification. Equilibrium: opacity with regulatory
reliance on disclosed findings only.

A1041 — Federated Trust Assertion Injection
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Surface: SAML response with manipulated Attribute element
Vector: XML signature wrapping attack on SP-side validation
Mechanism: Attacker inserts unsigned attribute node adjacent to
  signed assertion block; SP parser reads injected node as authoritative
  when signature validation checks sibling rather than whole document
Depth-1 (Technical): XPath canonicalization inconsistency between
  signature library and parser enables node injection without
  invalidating existing signature
Depth-2 (Systemic): Federation trust model assumes IDP-signed assertion
  is atomic unit; no mechanism for SP to detect partial-document signing
Depth-3 (Structural): SAML specification permits multiple signatures;
  implementation variance creates exploitable ambiguity
Pattern: P12 (trust boundary assumption violation) + P67 (spec optionality
  as implementation attack surface)
Detection: Full-document signature validation; reject assertions with
  multiple or partial signature coverage

A1061 — PAW Bypass via Compromised Jump Server
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Surface: Jump server (RDP gateway, bastion host) mediating PAW to
  target system connections
Vector: Jump server OS or RDP service vulnerability exploitation
Mechanism: PAW architecture routes privileged access through jump server;
  attacker compromises jump server via vulnerability or credential theft;
  jump server is trusted intermediary — compromise grants access to all
  systems PAW users can reach; PAW protects client endpoint but
  jump server becomes new single point of compromise
Depth-1 (Technical): Jump server OS patch cycle, RDP hardening, and
  session recording security are distinct security controls from PAW;
  jump server often less hardened than PAW itself
Depth-2 (Systemic): PAW architecture eliminates endpoint risk but
  concentrates access at jump server; attack surface shifts, not eliminated
Depth-3 (Structural): Defense-in-depth architectures create concentration
  points; each concentration point becomes highest-value target;
  attack adapts to architectural control by targeting control mechanism
Pattern: P6 (trusted intermediary as attack path) + P14 (security
  control creating new concentration risk)
Detection: Jump server behavioral monitoring; privileged session
  recording with integrity protection; jump server isolation
  equivalent to PAW hardening

A1063 — EDR Kernel Driver Exploitation for Sensor Blind
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Surface: EDR vendor kernel driver (Ring 0) on Windows endpoint
Vector: CVE in EDR driver exploited for kernel code execution
Mechanism: EDR kernel driver runs with highest privilege; vulnerability
  in driver (heap overflow, race condition, IOCTL handler flaw);
  attacker exploits driver to achieve kernel code execution;
  unloads or blinds EDR sensor from kernel level; subsequent
  malicious activity invisible to EDR
Depth-1 (Technical): EDR driver in kernel for tamper resistance;
  kernel code execution bypasses all user-mode security controls
  including EDR itself; kernel vulnerability in security product
  more impactful than non-security product kernel vulnerability
Depth-2 (Systemic): EDR vendors patch kernel driver vulnerabilities;
  patch distribution slower than OS vendor patches; enterprise
  EDR update cycles add additional delay
Depth-3 (Structural): Securing endpoints by placing code at kernel
  level increases kernel attack surface; security control expands
  vulnerability surface as side effect
Pattern: P14 (security control as attack surface) + P71 (patch
  latency in security-critical component)
Detection: Kernel integrity monitoring; EDR driver version enforcement;
  kernel patch SLA equivalent to OS patch SLA for EDR vendors

  remains 100% while actual protection approaches zero

Detection: Exception workflow audit; suppression rate anomaly alerting;

A1073 — Stale Threat Model Exploitation
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Surface: Production system evolved beyond documented threat model
Vector: Attack path not in threat model due to system evolution
Mechanism: System threat model documented at initial design;
  system evolves: new API endpoints added, third-party integrations
  added, authentication flows modified; threat model not updated;
  security controls designed for original threat model miss attack
  paths introduced by evolution; attacker exploits security gap
  created by system drift from threat model
Depth-1 (Technical): Threat model is point-in-time documentation;
  system changes introduce new attack surfaces without triggering
  threat model review
Depth-2 (Systemic): Threat modeling treated as design-phase activity;
  no process trigger for threat model update on system change;
  threat model staleness not measured or monitored
Depth-3 (Structural): Security planning tools designed for static
  systems; real systems continuously evolve; security planning
  cadence mismatched to system change rate
Pattern: P71 (static security documentation against dynamic system)
  + P22 (system evolution outpacing security review)
Detection: Automated threat model trigger on significant system change;
  continuous threat model-to-system delta analysis; change management
  security review gate

A1074 — Vehicle OTA Update Rollback for Known Vulnerability Exploitation
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Surface: Vehicle OTA update system without rollback prevention
Vector: Attacker delivers older, vulnerable firmware version as update
Mechanism: Attacker with OTA channel access (compromised OEM backend
  or MitM on update channel) crafts update package with older
  firmware version; vehicle accepts older version if version check
  only validates signature, not version monotonicity; vehicle downgraded
  to version with known CVE; attacker exploits known vulnerability
Depth-1 (Technical): OTA verification validates update authenticity
  (signature) but not freshness (monotonic version counter);
  rollback prevention requires signed version counter or anti-rollback
  counter in secure element
Depth-2 (Systemic): OTA system designed for forward updates;
  rollback scenario considered for failure recovery, not attacker
  exploitation; anti-rollback not in initial threat model
Depth-3 (Structural): Automotive OTA security requirements (UN R156)

  for system time

  shifts system time to date when attacker's expired or not-yet-valid

  certificate that would otherwise be rejected as expired;

  notAfter against system clock; system clock integrity depends on
  NTP; NTP v3 lacks authentication; spoofed time accepted
Depth-2 (Systemic): TLS PKI assumes trustworthy system clock;
  clock integrity not verified by TLS protocol; clock security
  dependency not in TLS threat model
Depth-3 (Structural): PKI certificate validity window assumes
  correct time; time as security dependency creates attack surface
  for entire PKI trust model
Pattern: P6 (infrastructure dependency as attack path) + P3
  (authentication absent at time source)
Detection: NTPsec/NTS deployment; GPS-disciplined time source;
  multiple NTP sources with median time selection;

A1091 — SGX Side-Channel via Cache Timing
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Surface: Intel SGX enclave executing cryptographic operations
Vector: Co-located VM cache timing side-channel analysis
Mechanism: Attacker VM co-located on same physical host as SGX enclave;
  monitors last-level cache (LLC) access patterns via Flush+Reload
  or Prime+Probe technique; cryptographic key schedule operations
  produce cache access patterns correlating with key bits;
  key material extracted from enclave without breaking SGX
  cryptographic attestation
Depth-1 (Technical): SGX isolates enclave memory from hypervisor
  and other VMs; shared hardware resources (LLC, TLB, branch predictor)
  are not isolated; side channels operate on shared hardware
Depth-2 (Systemic): SGX threat model excludes side channels from
  hardware; cloud multi-tenancy creates co-location by design;
  SGX hardware isolation guarantee does not extend to shared cache
Depth-3 (Structural): Confidential computing isolates software
  access but not hardware resource contention; fundamental physical
  sharing of CPU resources creates structural side-channel surface
  that cannot be eliminated by software isolation
Pattern: P12 (trust boundary violation via shared resource) +
  P67 (isolation guarantee violated by out-of-scope attack class)
Detection: SGX-aware constant-time cryptographic implementations;
  cache partitioning (Intel CAT); enclave-to-cache-set exclusivity

A1100 — Cryptographic Agility Negotiation Downgrade
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Surface: Protocol implementing cryptographic algorithm negotiation
  (TLS cipher suite negotiation)
Vector: Downgrade attack forcing negotiation to deprecated algorithm
Mechanism: TLS handshake cipher suite negotiation allows client
  and server to select from supported algorithms; attacker intercepts
  ClientHello; removes strong cipher suites; server selects from
  attacker-permitted set (weak algorithm); connection established
  with deprecated cipher; cryptographic agility implementation
  creates downgrade attack surface that static algorithm
  implementation does not have
Depth-1 (Technical): TLS downgrade attacks (POODLE, DROWN, LOGJAM)
  all exploit cipher suite negotiation; TLS 1.3 eliminated downgrade
  by removing weak cipher suite support; backward compatibility
  with legacy creates ongoing downgrade risk
Depth-2 (Systemic): Cryptographic agility provides future-proofing
  but creates negotiation attack surface; static implementation
  cannot be downgraded but cannot be upgraded; tradeoff is structural
Depth-3 (Structural): Every instance of cryptographic agility
  creates a negotiation protocol; every negotiation protocol
  is a potential downgrade attack surface; agility and downgrade
  resistance are in fundamental tension
Pattern: P8 (downgrade attack via negotiation protocol) + P67
  (cryptographic agility as downgrade attack surface)
Detection: Minimum algorithm enforcement (no weak cipher suites
  in server configuration); TLS 1.3 adoption; downgrade
  sentinel (TLS_FALLBACK_SCSV); MitM detection

G-C148-06 | RASP BYPASS DETECTION GAP
Domain: Runtime Application Self-Protection
Gap: RASP agents detect attack patterns at runtime but have no mechanism to detect their own bypass or disabling. Attackers who exploit vulnerabilities pre-RASP-initialization, or who use reflection/JVM internals to disable RASP agents, proceed without detection. RASP health monitoring (confirming agent is active and unmodified) is not standardized. Gap exists at: RASP integrity attestation, agent liveness verification, bypass technique taxonomy, RASP-aware EDR integration standards.
Delta-trigger: RASP integrity monitoring standard with EDR integration protocol.

G-C148-07 | SOCIAL MEDIA ACCOUNT RECOVERY SECURITY GAP
Domain: Social media account security
Gap: Account recovery mechanisms for high-value social media accounts (executives, brands, government) rely on fallback authentication (phone SMS, backup email, identity document upload) that is systematically weaker than primary authentication. Attackers targeting account takeover specifically target recovery paths rather than primary auth. Platforms provide no enterprise-grade account recovery security tier with hardware token or in-person verification. Gap exists at: tiered recovery security for high-value accounts, enterprise account management APIs, recovery path attack surface reduction, regulatory pressure on platform account security.
Delta-trigger: Platform-enforced high-assurance recovery for verified high-value accounts.

G-C148-08 | ZK PROOF CIRCUIT AUDIT STANDARDIZATION GAP
Domain: Zero-knowledge proof security
Gap: ZK proof systems (Groth16, PLONK, STARKs) require circuit-level audit to verify that the circuit correctly encodes the intended computation and contains no soundness vulnerabilities. No standardized audit methodology, audit firm qualification standard, or circuit audit reporting format exists. ZK circuit audits are conducted by a small number of specialized firms with inconsistent methodology. Deployed ZK systems in production (rollups, privacy protocols) carry unquantified circuit audit risk. Gap exists at: audit methodology standardization, auditor qualification, reporting format, continuous circuit monitoring for deployed systems.
Delta-trigger: Industry consortium standard for ZK circuit audit methodology and reporting.

G-C148-09 | AIR TRAFFIC CONTROL CYBERSECURITY INCIDENT NOTIFICATION GAP
Domain: Air traffic control systems
Gap: ATC cybersecurity incidents affecting safety-critical systems have no standardized rapid notification pathway from cybersecurity responders to aviation safety authorities that operates at the speed required for flight safety decisions. Existing incident reporting frameworks (CISA, FAA) operate on timescales (hours) incompatible with real-time ATC safety requirements (seconds to minutes). Gap exists at: real-time cyber-to-safety notification protocol, joint cyber-safety operations center authority, pilot/crew notification procedures for suspected ATC compromise, continuity of navigation during suspected compromise.
Delta-trigger: ICAO/FAA joint protocol for real-time cybersecurity-to-safety notification in ATC.

G-C148-10 | CYBERSECURITY ECONOMIC INCENTIVE MISALIGNMENT MEASUREMENT GAP
Domain: Cybersecurity economic incentive alignment
Gap: The academic and policy literature on cybersecurity market failures (information asymmetry, externalities, public goods problems) lacks empirical measurement of actual incentive misalignment magnitudes. Theoretical models predict underinvestment and free-riding but the magnitude of underinvestment relative to socially optimal levels is unmeasured. Without measurement, policy interventions (liability regimes, mandatory standards, cyber insurance mandates) cannot be calibrated or evaluated. Gap exists at: empirical economic measurement methodology, firm-level investment data access, counterfactual analysis frameworks, feedback loop between policy intervention and measured outcomes.
Delta-trigger: Large-scale empirical study with regulatory data access measuring cybersecurity investment vs. social optimum.

A1103 | ENTROPY STARVATION AT VM INITIALIZATION
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Surface: Cloud VMs generating cryptographic material immediately after boot with
  insufficient entropy.
Mechanism: VM initialization on shared hypervisor with cloned disk images; /dev/urandom
  seeded from limited hardware entropy pool shared across co-located VMs; cryptographic
  libraries called before entropy pool fully initialized; resulting keys have reduced
  effective entropy despite appearing valid.
Root: R05 (environment assumption violation) — crypto library assumes dedicated hardware
  entropy; operates in shared virtual environment where assumption fails.
Cross-domain: VM clone key collision (CVE-2008-0166 Debian OpenSSL); Dual_EC_DRBG
  backdoor; ROCA vulnerability; weak key generation in embedded devices.
Invariant: Cryptographic libraries that do not verify entropy pool readiness before use
  will produce weak keys in resource-constrained initialization environments.
Closure condition: Mandatory entropy pool readiness check and hardware attestation before
  any cryptographic key generation call.

A1105 | TABLETOP SCENARIO DESIGNER BLIND SPOT BIAS
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Surface: Tabletop exercises systematically miss novel attack scenarios.
Mechanism: Scenario designers draw from organizational memory (past incidents, near-misses,
  industry reports already processed) and from explicit threat model; novel TTPs not
  yet in organizational awareness are invisible to designers; confirmation bias toward
  scenarios organization has partial response for; novelty-averse scenarios provide
  satisfying exercise outcomes reinforcing continued narrow scope.
Root: P31 (availability heuristic in threat modeling) + R08 (unknown unknowns not
  surfaced by internal processes).
Cross-domain: Intelligence community analytic failure (9/11 Commission); financial stress
  test scenario selection; pandemic planning scenario gaps; military wargame assumptions.
Invariant: Any exercise designed entirely by internal teams will systematically exclude
  scenarios outside organizational threat model regardless of exercise quality.

  red team with access to current threat intelligence.

A1108 | ZK CIRCUIT SOUNDNESS VULNERABILITY INVISIBILITY
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Surface: ZK proof system accepts proofs for false statements due to circuit bug.
Mechanism: ZK circuit encodes computation as arithmetic constraint system; constraint
  underspecification allows prover to satisfy constraints without actually computing
  intended function; soundness bug not detectable from external proof verification
  (proofs verify correctly); requires circuit-level code review to detect; few
  auditors have circuit-level expertise; audits are expensive and infrequent.
Root: R05 (abstraction layer violation) — security depends on correct circuit encoding
  of high-level specification, but no formal bridge between specification and circuit.
Cross-domain: Formal verification gap in smart contracts (DAO hack); compiler correctness;
  hardware trojans in chip fabrication; specification-implementation gap in cryptographic
  protocol design.
Invariant: Any system where security proof is valid but implementation encodes incorrect
  constraint system creates accepted-but-false-proof vulnerability invisible to users.
Closure condition: Formal equivalence checking between high-level specification and
  arithmetic circuit with automated soundness verification tools.

  after operational window closes.

Cross-domain: Industrial safety-cybersecurity integration gap; nuclear plant cybersecurity

Invariant: Any safety-critical system where cybersecurity and operational safety chains

Closure condition: Joint cyber-safety operations authority with pre-authorized notification
  protocols and real-time shared situational awareness.

A1111 | MARITIME OT FLAT NETWORK LATERAL MOVEMENT
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Surface: Crew internet access on vessel leads to engine control system compromise.
Mechanism: Crew network connected to vessel OT network via flat or poorly segmented
  topology; crew member phishing delivers malware to crew laptop; malware pivots via
  shared network segment to OT devices (PLCs, SCADA HMIs) with no authentication;
  attacker gains control of engine, propulsion, or cargo systems.

  — crew network as softest entry to OT). R05 (OT environment assumes physical isolation
  that does not exist with connected crew networks).
Cross-domain: Colonial Pipeline (IT-to-OT pivot); Maersk NotPetya (flat IT network);
  Ukraine power grid (IT-to-OT pivot via VPN).
Invariant: Any OT environment reachable from an IT network, however indirectly, inherits
  the full attack surface of that IT network.
Closure condition: Maritime OT network segmentation standard with unidirectional data
  diodes for any IT-to-OT data flow.

A1115 | QKD DETECTOR BLINDING ATTACK
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Surface: Attacker intercepts QKD key exchange without detection.
Mechanism: QKD security proofs assume ideal single-photon detectors; real detectors
  (APD, SNSPD) have classical operating regime at high light intensities; attacker
  blinds detectors with bright illumination, forcing classical operation; intercepts
  qubits classically; resends to receiver with forged quantum states; detector
  blinding eliminates quantum error detection; keys intercepted without triggering
  QBER (Quantum Bit Error Rate) threshold.
Root: R05 (security proof assumes ideal component; real component violates assumption).
  Security proof → implementation gap at detector physics.
Cross-domain: CVE-2018-5407 (Portsmash — side channel in real implementation breaking
  theoretical security); RSA PKCS#1 padding oracle (implementation gap); AES timing
  side channels; HSM physical side channels.
Invariant: Any cryptographic system whose security proof assumes ideal components will
  have implementation vulnerabilities where real components deviate from ideal.
Closure condition: QKD implementations with measurement-device-independent protocols
  (MDI-QKD) removing detector trust assumption entirely.

A1116 | OTA FIRMWARE ROLLBACK TO VULNERABLE VERSION
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Surface: Attacker installs old vulnerable firmware on patched device via OTA channel.
Mechanism: OTA update server compromised or update channel MITM'd; attacker serves
  authenticode-signed but outdated firmware; device verifies signature (valid) and
  version monotonicity (not enforced, or eFuse counter not burned); installs old
  version; device now running previously patched vulnerability; original exploit
  works again; device appears updated (firmware version field could be spoofed
  or simply not checked by fleet management).
Root: R07 (boundary: authentication verifies source identity but not version ordering).
  Authentication necessary but not sufficient for update integrity.
Cross-domain: SSL stripping (downgrade); TLS version downgrade; POODLE (SSLv3
  rollback); FREAK/LOGJAM (export cipher rollback); BIOS rollback attacks.
Invariant: Any update system that authenticates source but does not enforce monotonic
  version progression is vulnerable to rollback regardless of signature strength.
Closure condition: Hardware anti-rollback counter (eFuse/RPMB) incremented on each
  firmware update, enforced in bootloader before any code execution.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Mechanism: DAO uses token-weighted governance with snapshot at block N; attacker
  uses flash loan to borrow large governance token position within block N;
  creates proposal (or votes on existing proposal) with borrowed voting power;
  repays flash loan at end of block; proposal passes or voting snapshot captured
  with attacker’s votes; DAO treasury drained or protocol parameters changed;
  all within single transaction. Real instances: Beanstalk ($182M, 2022).
Root: R01 (temporal gap: governance snapshot and economic ownership diverge within
  block time). Flash loans make token-weighted governance non-binding to genuine
  token holders.
Cross-domain: Corporate vote buying (proxy season); vote by borrowed shares
  (empty voting); electoral fraud via temporary demographic manipulation;
  short-and-distort financial attacks.
Invariant: Any voting system whose snapshot can be manipulated within the same
  transaction that benefits from the vote creates a flash-loan-class attack surface.
Closure condition: Governance token snapshot at block N-K (K > flash loan duration)
  with vote escrow binding voting power to token lock duration.

A1127 | PRESCRIPTION DIGITAL THERAPEUTIC ALGORITHM TAMPERING
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Surface: FDA-regulated DTx therapeutic algorithm modified, causing systematic harm.
Mechanism: Prescription DTx delivers cognitive behavioral therapy, substance abuse
  treatment, or chronic disease management via software; attacker compromises DTx
  backend (update server, algorithm parameter store); modifies therapy parameters
  (session timing, content selection, behavioral reinforcement schedules);
  patients receive systematically subtherapeutic or harmful treatment;
  outcome degradation attributed to patient non-adherence or disease progression
  before statistical analysis identifies systematic pattern.
Root: R05 (clinical environment assumes therapeutic algorithm integrity; compromised
  backend violates assumption). P71 (clinician trust in FDA-cleared DTx reduces
  scrutiny of therapeutic outcomes).
Cross-domain: Pacemaker firmware tampering (medical device software integrity);
  insulin pump attack (therapeutic device compromise); clinical trial data
  manipulation; medical record falsification for insurance fraud.
Invariant: Any therapeutic system whose efficacy is mediated by software parameters
  that can be remotely modified inherits the full attack surface of its
  update/configuration infrastructure.
Closure condition: Runtime integrity monitoring for prescription DTx with cryptographic
  parameter attestation and clinical outcome anomaly correlation.

A1128 | KUBERNETES ADMISSION CONTROLLER SUPPLY CHAIN BYPASS
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Surface: Malicious container deployed in production cluster despite policy enforcement.
Mechanism: Admission controller (OPA/Gatekeeper) enforces pod security policy;
  attacker compromises admission controller OCI image in registry (supply chain);
  malicious admission controller version evaluates all pods as compliant;
  policy enforcement silently disabled; subsequent malicious container deployments
  pass admission unchallenged; cluster security posture degrades invisibly;
  no audit log of admission controller behavior change.
Root: R10 (security control assumes its own integrity; supply chain compromise
  violates assumption). R05 (cluster assumes policy engine is unmodified).
Cross-domain: AV software supply chain (NotPetya via MeDoc); SolarWinds
  (monitoring tool as attack vector); XZ Utils backdoor (build pipeline);
  security tool supply chain as highest-trust attack surface.
Invariant: Any security enforcement component that can be updated via supply chain
  without integrity verification is a high-value supply chain attack target.
Closure condition: Admission controller integrity verification via image digest
  pinning, out-of-band update verification, and runtime behavior monitoring.

A1142 | LLM HALLUCINATED PACKAGE NAME DEPENDENCY CONFUSION
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Surface: Developer installs LLM-hallucinated package name; installs attacker
  malicious package.
Mechanism: LLM code generation suggests import of package that does not exist
  in legitimate registry (hallucinated name plausible-sounding but fictional);
  attacker monitoring for hallucinated package names registers malicious package
  under hallucinated name in npm/PyPI; developer follows LLM suggestion, installs
  malicious package; malware executes in developer environment and in production
  build; supply chain compromise via LLM hallucination.
Root: R05 (developer assumes LLM package suggestions are valid; LLM operates
  in non-adversarial assumption space). LLM confidence in output not correlated
  with factual accuracy of package names.
Cross-domain: Typosquatting (attacker-registered similar name); dependency
  confusion attack (private package name in public registry); TypoSquat of
  npm packages; autocomplete package suggestion hijacking.
Invariant: Any code generation system that suggests package names without
  verifying registry existence creates a supply chain attack surface proportional
  to developer trust in suggestions and attacker monitoring of hallucination
  patterns.
Closure condition: LLM code generation tools verify all suggested package names
  against official registries before presenting to developer; unverified names
  flagged as unverified.

A1146 | SAFETY-CRITICAL EMBEDDED HYPERVISOR GUEST ESCAPE
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Surface: Attacker exploits guest-to-hypervisor vulnerability in automotive
  hypervisor to compromise safety-critical partition.
Mechanism: Automotive system runs mixed-criticality hypervisor (ASIL-D safety
  partition for braking/steering + QoS partition for infotainment); infotainment
  partition exposed to external attack surface (Bluetooth, USB, cellular);
  attacker exploits hypervisor privilege escalation from infotainment guest;
  attacker code executes in hypervisor context; accesses safety-critical
  partition memory and control; safety functions compromised; ISO 26262
  safety certification does not account for adversarial hypervisor escape.
Root: R05 (safety certification assumes non-adversarial environment; adversarial
  infotainment partition violates isolation assumption). Safety and security
  certification frameworks treat orthogonal threat models.
Cross-domain: iOS kernel exploit chain (sandbox escape → kernel → SEP);
  hypervisor escape (Blue Pill, VENOM CVE-2015-3456); Android TrustZone
  exploitation; Jeep Cherokee remote compromise (infotainment to CAN bus).
Invariant: Any mixed-criticality system where a lower-criticality partition
  has external attack surface and shares a hypervisor with higher-criticality
  partitions inherits the security vulnerability of the lower partition in
  its safety-critical functions.
Closure condition: Hardware-enforced partition isolation at IOMMU level;
  physical separation of safety-critical and connected compute where feasible;
  hypervisor security certification co-developed with safety certification.

G-C153-01 | OT ASSET INVENTORY COMPLETENESS VERIFICATION GAP
Domain: Operational technology asset management security
Gap: OT asset inventories are generated by network scanning (passive or active), but passive
scanning misses devices that don't communicate during scan windows (seasonal equipment,
standby redundant systems, infrequently polled sensors). Active scanning can disrupt
legacy PLCs. No standardized OT asset inventory completeness verification methodology
exists — organizations cannot confirm whether their OT asset count represents 70% or 95%
of actual assets. Unknown OT assets represent unpatched, unmonitored attack surface. Gap
exists at: OT inventory completeness metric, non-disruptive completeness verification
methodology, acceptable completeness threshold standards, regulatory requirement for OT
inventory completeness attestation.
Delta-trigger: NERC CIP or IEC 62443 OT inventory completeness attestation standard.


--- SOURCE LINES 287318–287339 ---
G-C153-03 | ML SECURITY TOOL ADVERSARIAL BENCHMARK GAP
Domain: Adversarial ML in cybersecurity tools
Gap: ML-based cybersecurity tools (malware classifiers, UEBA, network anomaly detection)
are evaluated on held-out test sets drawn from same distribution as training data. No
standardized adversarial benchmark exists for cybersecurity ML tools measuring robustness
to adaptive adversarial evasion. Vendors publish detection rates without adversarial
evasion rates. Buyers cannot compare adversarial robustness across vendors. Gap exists
at: adversarial benchmark methodology for cybersecurity ML, independent adversarial
evaluation requirement, vendor disclosure standard for adversarial evasion rates.
Delta-trigger: NIST/MITRE adversarial robustness benchmark for cybersecurity ML tools.

G-C153-04 | CLOUD-NATIVE EBPF SECURITY TOOL PRIVILEGE ESCALATION GAP
Domain: Cloud-native application security
Gap: eBPF-based security tools (Falco, Tetragon, Tracee) require elevated kernel privileges
(CAP_BPF, CAP_PERFMON or root) to load BPF programs and access kernel events. A vulnerability
in the eBPF program itself or the userspace tool processing eBPF output could escalate to
kernel-level compromise. eBPF verifier bypasses have been demonstrated (CVE-2021-3490,
CVE-2022-23222). No standardized security evaluation framework exists for eBPF security
tools assessing their own attack surface. Gap exists at: eBPF security tool security
evaluation standard, privilege minimization architecture for eBPF tools, eBPF program
fuzzing requirements, production deployment security guidance.
Delta-trigger: CNCF security specification for eBPF-based security tools.


--- SOURCE LINES 287353–287363 ---
G-C153-06 | PROCESS SAFETY SYSTEM CYBER-SAFETY INTEGRATION GAP
Domain: Critical safety system security (IEC 61511)
Gap: Process safety systems (SIS) are safety-certified under IEC 61511 and security-
assessed under IEC 62443 but these frameworks address orthogonal threat models. IEC 61511
safety integrity levels (SIL) are calculated for accidental failures; adversarial cyber
attacks are not modeled in SIL calculations. A cyber attack exploiting SIS could simultaneously
compromise all redundant channels (common-mode failure not modeled in SIL analysis). No
integrated cyber-safety analysis methodology exists. Gap exists at: joint SIL/security
analysis methodology, SIS cyber attack failure mode modeling, regulatory harmonization
of IEC 61511 and IEC 62443 at the system level.
Delta-trigger: ISA/IEC joint technical report on cyber-safety co-analysis methodology.

A1151 | OT ASSET INVENTORY COMPLETENESS ILLUSION
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Surface: OT asset inventory shows 1,200 devices; actual environment contains
  1,700; 500 unmonitored devices represent active attack surface.
Mechanism: Passive network monitoring discovers devices that communicate during
  observation window; seasonal equipment (agricultural irrigation controllers,
  cooling systems in off-season), standby redundant systems, infrequently polled
  remote sensors never appear; active scanning deferred or disabled due to
  fragility risk; management assumes inventory is complete because no
  mechanism for detecting unknown unknowns exists.
Root: R08 (unknown unknowns: absent devices are invisible by definition;
  completeness cannot be verified from inventory alone). P98 (device count
  becomes target metric; completeness assumed once count stabilizes).
Cross-domain: Network asset inventory gaps (Heartbleed exposed unknown internet-
  facing systems); software asset management gaps; human HR headcount vs.
  contractor counts; firewall rule inventory vs. actual ruleset.
Invariant: Any inventory built from observing behavior will systematically
  exclude assets whose behavior is below observation threshold, regardless
  of inventory methodology quality.
Closure condition: Physical walk-down inventory cross-referenced against
  network scan; installation records as source of truth; network traffic
  baselining to detect new communicating assets as deviation from baseline.

A1154 | eBPF VERIFIER BYPASS FOR KERNEL PRIVILEGE ESCALATION
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Surface: Exploit in eBPF verifier achieves kernel code execution from
  container context.
Mechanism: Container running eBPF-privileged security tool loads BPF program;
  BPF program crafted to exploit verifier bug (CVE-2021-3490 class — incorrect
  bounds checking in verifier allows out-of-bounds write in kernel memory);
  exploit achieves kernel code execution; container escape with kernel privileges;
  full host system compromise; security tool as exploit delivery mechanism.
Root: R10 (eBPF security tool loaded with kernel privileges assumes BPF verifier
  is correct; verifier bug inverts assumption). Security tool privilege as
  attack escalation path.
Cross-domain: Security software privilege exploitation (AV kernel driver bugs);
  EDR kernel driver privilege escalation; security appliance vulnerabilities;
  firewall RCE (Fortinet, Palo Alto CVE classes).
Invariant: Any security tool requiring elevated kernel privileges to operate
  creates an elevated-privilege attack surface whose compromise achieves
  kernel-level impact.
Closure condition: eBPF security tool architecture with minimal BPF program
  complexity, formal verification of BPF programs, userspace processing
  of events with minimal kernel footprint, eBPF verifier fuzzing.
