A1156 | SIS COMMON-MODE CYBER FAILURE SAFETY ASSUMPTION VIOLATION
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Surface: Cyber attack compromises all redundant channels of safety system
  simultaneously, bypassing SIL calculations.
Mechanism: SIL calculation assumes independent random failure probability
  for each redundant channel; common-mode failures modeled as random but
  low-probability hardware failures; attacker with network access to SIS
  exploits shared vulnerability (same firmware, same network segment,
  same engineering workstation used for all channels) to compromise all
  channels simultaneously; SIL-3 1-of-2 or 2-of-3 redundancy provides
  no protection against coordinated cyber attack affecting all channels.
Root: R05 (SIL calculation assumes failures are independent random events;
  cyber attacks are correlated by shared vulnerability, violating independence
  assumption).
Real precedent: TRITON/TRISIS attack on Triconex Safety System (2017) —
  first known cyber attack targeting safety system.
Cross-domain: Byzantine fault tolerance vs. colluding adversaries; RAID
  failure independence assumption violations; cryptographic multi-party
  collusion threshold.
Invariant: Any redundancy calculation assuming independent failures is
  invalidated by adversaries who can target all redundant instances
  through shared vulnerabilities.
Closure condition: Cybersecurity incorporated into SIL calculations as
  correlated failure mode; heterogeneous SIS architectures (different
  vendors, firmware, network segments) for each redundant channel.

Same EWS used for configuration means same vulnerability, same credentials, same configuration access across all redundant channels. Single EWS compromise yields ability to modify all channels simultaneously — bypassing redundancy. TRITON/TRISIS attack class. Exploits A1156/G-C153-06.

LAW-9 INSTANCE #93:
Domain: SOAR Playbook Security — Collective Adoption Failure
LAW-9: "Security controls protecting control systems are systematically
  underinvested relative to operational risk when adoption requires
  coordinated multi-actor commitment."
Application: SOAR platforms are trusted as force-multiplier infrastructure
  across enterprise SOCs. Playbook integrity verification (cryptographic
  signing of playbook definitions, change-log integrity, execution attestation)
  is technically available but adoption requires: security teams to treat
  their automation as adversarial attack surface (counter-intuitive to the
  efficiency framing), vendors to implement signing natively, and procurement
  to specify integrity requirements. No single actor bears the full cost of
  a Sybil/playbook-tampering incident — the cost diffuses across the incident
  response community after the fact. Collective action failure produces
  systematic under-adoption of playbook integrity controls industry-wide.
LAW-9 instance count: 93 (confirmed).

  equipment conducts IMSI-catching or rogue base station attacks against
  train-borne ETCS (European Train Control System) modems. False Movement
  Authority messages injected cause unintended emergency brake activation
  or, in a more sophisticated variant, suppress legitimate brake commands.
Root mechanics: R01 (GSM-R was a private dedicated network; 5G migration
  to shared infrastructure was not anticipated in original ERTMS threat
  model); R04 (trust assumption: radio channel assumed trustworthy because
  physical access to GSM-R was restricted; 5G public infrastructure
  removes this physical access control).
Pattern trace: P17 (shared infrastructure introduces threat actors
  excluded from dedicated network threat model); P88 (migration from
  dedicated to shared infrastructure without threat model update).
Defense logic: Application-layer cryptographic authentication of Movement
  Authority messages independent of radio channel trust; 5G ERTMS
  profile specifying network slice isolation requirements; onboard
  ETCS anomaly detection for unexpected radio channel transitions.
Closure: Partial. Application-layer auth mitigates injection; 5G slice
  isolation depends on operator implementation quality.

A1169 | GPU CLOUD TENANT ISOLATION FAILURE FOR AI MODEL TRAINING
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Domain: Generative AI Model Hosting Infrastructure (D2711)
Attack vector: Co-located GPU tenant exploits hypervisor or GPU driver
  side-channel (DRAM row-hammer variant adapted for GDDR, shared L2
  cache timing, NVLink bus traffic analysis) to infer gradient updates
  or model weights of adjacent tenant's training workload. GPU
  virtualization (NVIDIA MIG, vGPU) provides performance isolation but
  not cryptographic isolation of memory or bus traffic.
Root mechanics: R05 (common-mode failure: shared physical GPU hardware
  creates side-channel across tenant boundary despite logical isolation);
  R08 (no visibility: tenant cannot detect side-channel observation
  by co-tenant; no GPU-level telemetry for cross-tenant memory access
  pattern monitoring).
Pattern trace: P38 (hardware sharing creates side-channel by physical
  necessity — logical isolation insufficient); P55 (cloud multi-tenancy
  as persistent side-channel attack surface).
Defense logic: Dedicated GPU hardware for sensitive model training
  (eliminates co-tenancy); GPU memory scrubbing between tenant allocations;
  noise injection into training gradients (differential privacy);
  physically isolated GPU clusters for regulated workloads.
Closure: Partial. Dedicated hardware is cost-prohibitive for most;
  side-channel risk is residual for shared GPU clouds.

Ten new anatomies (A1171–A1180). Each traces attack vector through
root mechanics to defense logic. Pattern references stable (P1–P100).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A1171 | BIOMETRIC TEMPLATE DATABASE COMPROMISE AND UNLIMITED FORGERY
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Domain: Biometric Template Protection (D2719)
Attack vector: Adversary compromises biometric template database storing
  fingerprint or iris templates in reference format. Unlike passwords,
  biometric templates cannot be revoked and reissued; compromised templates
  enable indefinite impersonation against any system using the same
  biometric modality for the individual. Reconstruction attacks on
  protected templates succeed when protection scheme is invertible or
  transform is not irreversible under template-database access.
Root mechanics: R01 (biometric system designed assuming template
  confidentiality; database compromise not in threat model for many
  deployments); R06 (central template repository concentrates all
  enrolled individuals' lifetime biometric irrevocability risk).
Pattern trace: P33 (central repository concentrates permanent forgery
  risk across all enrolled individuals simultaneously); P01 (template
  revocability absent because biometric modality was assumed to be
  inherently unforgeable — assumption defeated by template compromise).
Defense logic: Cancelable biometrics (irreversible transform of
  biometric feature; store transformed template only; compromise of
  transformed template does not reveal original; re-enrollment with
  new transform key achieves effective revocation); biometric
  template encryption with per-individual keys in HSM; on-device
  biometric matching (template never leaves device; no central DB).
Closure: Partial. On-device matching eliminates central DB risk;
  cancelable biometrics address database compromise; neither addresses
  physical biometric capture (e.g., high-resolution iris photography).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A1172 | CONFIDENTIAL ENCLAVE ATTESTATION SERVICE COMPROMISE
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Domain: Confidential Computing Enclaves (D2720)
Attack vector: Adversary compromises cloud provider's Intel DCAP
  (Data Center Attestation Primitives) attestation service or the
  certificate chain used by relying parties to verify enclave quotes.
  Compromised attestation service can produce valid attestation for
  non-genuine enclaves; all enclave workloads trusting the compromised
  attestation service are simultaneously vulnerable to data exfiltration
  via fake enclaves accepted as genuine by relying parties.
Root mechanics: R06 (attestation service is concentration point;
  compromise invalidates all trust decisions simultaneously); R04
  (trust assumption: attestation service itself not in threat model
  for enclave relying parties — assumed to be trustworthy cloud
  infrastructure).
Pattern trace: P33 (attestation concentration amplifies single
  compromise to all enclave workloads); P66 (trust transitivity
  failure: enclave trust chain extends to attestation service
  without independent verification of the service itself).
Defense logic: Multi-attestation verification (verify quote against
  multiple independent attestation services; require consensus);
  Intel SGX quote verification caching with anomaly detection on
  quote chain certificate changes; on-premises DCAP infrastructure
  for regulated workloads (eliminates cloud provider attestation
  service from trust chain).
Closure: Partial. Multi-attestation reduces single-point dependency;
  on-premises DCAP adds operational burden incompatible with cloud
  elasticity for most workloads.

A1174 | POSITIVE TRAIN CONTROL RADIO COMMAND INJECTION
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Domain: Freight Rail PTC (D2722)
Attack vector: Adversary with software-defined radio equipment
  transmits crafted I-ETMS (Interoperable Electronic Train Management
  System) messages on PTC radio frequencies targeting a specific
  locomotive. Injected commands: emergency stop activation in
  high-traffic segment causes secondary collision; or false movement
  authority allowing train to exceed speed limit in restricted zone.
  Implementation-specific cryptographic schemes in older I-ETMS
  versions not publicly analyzed for vulnerabilities.

  actor capability); P17 (commodity SDR makes radio protocol
  attacks accessible to actors previously excluded by cost).
Defense logic: Public cryptanalysis of I-ETMS authentication
  schemes (mandate publication for independent review); minimum
  cryptographic standards in FRA regulation update; sequence
  number validation with replay window; received signal strength
  anomaly detection for signals from unexpected directions.
Closure: Partial. Regulatory update path is multi-year; interim
  mitigations limited to anomaly detection on behavioral side.

A1181 | SPACECRAFT ATTITUDE CONTROL COMMAND SPOOFING
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Domain: In-Space Propulsion and Attitude Control (D2737)
Attack vector: State-sponsored adversary with access to ground station
  or orbital radio relay transmits spoofed attitude control commands
  to target spacecraft. Commands alter orientation (pointing away from
  solar panels causes power failure) or initiate unauthorized propulsion
  burns (depletes fuel, alters orbit into collision trajectory). Command
  authentication relies on frequency exclusivity and ranging protocols;
  cryptographic authentication absent or proprietary-and-unanalyzed
  in most commercial and legacy government spacecraft.
Root mechanics: R01 (spacecraft command protocols designed before
  adversarial ground station access became a credible threat model
  for commercial spacecraft; authentication assumed via frequency
  allocation control); R04 (trust assumption: command uplink trusted
  if received on designated frequency and within expected range;
  assumption violated by adversary with licensed or illicit ground
  station access on designated frequency).
Pattern trace: P01 (cryptographic authentication absent because
  frequency control was assumed sufficient at protocol design time);
  P17 (proliferation of commercial ground station infrastructure
  expands access to actors previously excluded by ground station
  infrastructure cost).
Defense logic: CCSDS Spacecraft Onboard Interface Services (SOIS)
  with authenticated command sequences; onboard command authentication
  using pre-shared keys or PKI with key custody in hardware; uplink
  signal anomaly detection (direction of arrival, Doppler signature
  inconsistency); emergency safe mode triggered on authentication
  failure rather than command execution.
Closure: Partial. Onboard authentication requires hardware modification
  for legacy spacecraft; key management across mission lifetime is
  operationally complex for deep-space missions.

A1184 | BLOCKCHAIN VOTING SMART CONTRACT VULNERABILITY EXPLOIT
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Domain: Blockchain-Based Voting Systems (D2745)
Attack vector: Adversary identifies vulnerability in voting smart
  contract (reentrancy in vote tallying, integer overflow in vote
  counting, access control bypass in voter registration function).
  Exploits vulnerability to: cast multiple votes from single
  identity, modify already-cast votes, or alter tally computation
  during counting phase. Blockchain immutability prevents retroactive
  correction; corrupted election results are permanent.
Root mechanics: R01 (smart contract voting system designed by
  election technology team without formal verification background;
  traditional election system threats not mapped to smart contract

  specification); P33 (single authoritative contract concentration
  amplifies single exploit to total election result).
Defense logic: Formal verification of voting contract logic
  (TLA+, K framework for EVM); multiple independent audits before
  deployment; upgradeable proxy pattern with time-locked governance
  for bug fixes; end-to-end verifiability (voter-verified paper
  audit trail as independent election record); smart contract
  result cross-verification against independent off-chain tally.
Closure: Partial. Formal verification reduces known vulnerability
  classes; novel vulnerabilities in complex contracts remain risk;
  immutability makes post-exploit correction impossible without
  election invalidation.

  a research infrastructure component, not treated as
  adversarial attack surface); P61 (legitimate researcher
  account used as insider threat vector against shared facility).
Defense logic: Slurm vulnerability patching on defined schedule
  (CVE response SLA for scheduler components); scheduler
  privilege minimization (run Slurm daemons with least privilege;
  avoid root for all operations not requiring it); file system
  access control enforcement with per-user strict permissions;
  audit logging of privilege escalation events with SIEM integration.
Closure: Partial. Patching reduces known vulnerability exposure;
  zero-day exploitation remains risk; shared parallel file systems
  create inherent data proximity risk.

A1188 | ROBOTIC WAREHOUSE FLEET MANAGEMENT COMMAND INJECTION
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Domain: Robotic Warehouse Systems (D2754)
Attack vector: Adversary compromises warehouse management system
  (WMS) or robot fleet management platform via internet-connected
  interface (supplier portal, ERP integration, remote diagnostics).
  Injects malicious robot motion commands causing: (1) simultaneous
  convergence of multiple robots to same grid location causing
  physical collision; (2) conveyor system speed conflicts causing
  mechanical jam; (3) inventory location falsification causing
  mis-pick cascade destroying order fulfillment pipeline.
Root mechanics: R06 (fleet management system is concentration
  point for all robot coordination; single compromise enables
  fleet-wide command injection); R01 (WMS designed for operational
  efficiency and supplier integration; adversarial command injection
  threat model not addressed in most WMS architectures).
Pattern trace: P33 (fleet management concentration amplifies
  single compromise to fleet-wide physical disruption); P88
  (supplier and ERP integrations added during operational growth
  without security architecture review of command injection risk).
Defense logic: Fleet management command authentication (robots
  validate command signatures; WMS-to-robot commands signed with
  HSM-backed keys); collision avoidance as hardwired onboard
  safety layer independent of fleet management commands;
  network segmentation of robot control network from WMS and
  supplier integration networks; anomaly detection on fleet-wide
  simultaneous command distribution patterns.
Closure: Partial. Hardwired collision avoidance prevents physical
  damage; inventory manipulation and fulfillment disruption
  require application-layer protection.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A1191 | NEURAL IMPLANT WIRELESS COMMAND INJECTION
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Domain: Neurological Implants and BCIs (D2757)
Attack vector: Adversary with software-defined radio within wireless
  range of implanted device (cochlear implant, deep brain stimulator,
  spinal cord stimulator) transmits malicious commands on device's
  RF programming interface. Commands alter therapeutic stimulation
  parameters: increase DBS stimulation amplitude above safe threshold
  (causing seizure or motor dysfunction); disable pain management
  stimulation; drain battery through excessive stimulation cycles.
  Device within range in any public setting; patient has no indication
  of attack in progress.
Root mechanics: R01 (implant RF interface designed for clinician
  programming convenience; authentication deferred or absent to
  minimize battery drain and protocol complexity); R04 (trust
  assumption: RF command trusted because physical proximity assumed
  to imply authorized clinician; assumption violated by any actor
  within RF range in public setting).
Pattern trace: P01 (authentication absent because proximity
  assumption held at device design time — same proximity assumption
  as pacemaker attack surface, persisting across medical device
  generations); P91 (healthcare operational priority: authentication
  adds battery drain and emergency programming latency that clinical
  teams resist for life-critical devices).
Defense logic: Lightweight cryptographic authentication for RF
  programming interface (pre-shared key between device and designated
  programmer; AES-128 command MAC tolerable on modern implant power
  budgets); patient-held access control (patient enables programming
  window via external controller reducing ambient attack window);
  anomaly detection on programming attempts with alert to patient
  and emergency clinic contact.
Closure: Partial. Authentication adds battery and latency overhead;
  legacy deployed devices require hardware replacement for fix;
  emergency programming scenarios create unavoidable authentication
  bypass window.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A1192 | SDN CONTROLLER SOUTHBOUND INTERFACE COMPROMISE
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Domain: SDN Controller Security (D2758)
Attack vector: Adversary compromising SDN controller (via management
  interface vulnerability or control plane lateral movement) uses
  OpenFlow southbound interface to: install malicious flow rules
  redirecting all traffic through adversary-controlled analysis
  node; delete legitimate flow rules causing network-wide forwarding
  failure; inject flow rules creating routing loops consuming all
  switch CPU. Single controller compromise achieves network-fabric-
  wide impact via programmatic control of all connected switches.
Root mechanics: R06 (SDN controller is extreme concentration point;
  all forwarding decisions for entire fabric controlled by single
  system; compromise of one controller instance controls all
  connected data plane devices); R04 (trust assumption: southbound
  interface connections from controller trusted implicitly; OpenFlow
  switch does not validate controller identity or command legitimacy).
Pattern trace: P33 (SDN controller concentration amplifies single
  compromise to network-fabric-wide forwarding control); P66
  (trust transitivity failure: switch trusts controller because it
  connected to it; no independent verification of controller
  authenticity or command legitimacy).
Defense logic: Controller high-availability with Byzantine-fault-
  tolerant consensus (multiple controller instances; commands
  require majority agreement before data plane installation);
  southbound interface TLS with mutual authentication between
  controller and switch; flow rule anomaly detection (new rules
  not matching established network policy flagged for review);
  controller management interface isolation.
Closure: Partial. HA consensus prevents single controller compromise
  from full fabric control; requires majority controller compromise
  to achieve same impact; southbound TLS addresses channel but
  not malicious controller content.

A1194 | AI GOVERNANCE AUDIT LOG RETROACTIVE MANIPULATION
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Domain: AI Governance Audit Trails (D2766)
Attack vector: Following adverse AI decision (loan denial, medical
  triage allocation, criminal justice risk score) subject to
  regulatory review, system operator retroactively modifies AI
  decision audit log to show decision rationale inconsistent with
  actual model output. Modification covers discriminatory decision
  pattern or safety-critical error from regulatory or legal scrutiny.
  Audit log stored in mutable database without integrity controls;
  operator has write access required for legitimate log administration.
Root mechanics: R08 (audit log visibility is the point; mutable
  storage with operator write access means the system designed
  to provide accountability can be modified by the accountable
  party); R03 (trust assumption: operator trusted not to modify
  logs because audit is internal; external regulatory review
  relies on operator-provided log without independent integrity).
Pattern trace: P61 (insider with legitimate write access to
  audit system is the threat; insider threat is the point of the
  control, not an edge case); P44 (administrative control over
  audit log trusted to maintain integrity — administrative
  access is the attack surface).
Defense logic: Append-only audit log with cryptographic hash
  chaining (each entry includes hash of previous; retroactive
  modification detectable by hash chain verification);
  independent audit log archival by regulatory body or trusted
  third party (copy held by party who cannot be compelled
  by operator); log signing with HSM-backed keys at decision time;
  regular audit log integrity verification by automated system.
Closure: Partial. Hash chaining detects modification; requires
  independent verification by party with copy of original hash
  chain state; operator controlling both log and verification
  system can modify both.

A1197 | AGRICULTURAL DRONE GEOFENCE OVERRIDE FOR UNAUTHORIZED AIRSPACE ENTRY
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Domain: Agricultural Drones (D2769)
Attack vector: Adversary with access to agricultural drone fleet
  management platform (via compromised operator credentials or
  fleet management API vulnerability) overrides drone geofencing
  configurations. Drones operate outside approved agricultural
  geofences: entry into airport restricted airspace, overfly
  of restricted facilities, or coordinated swarm operation in
  prohibited areas. FAA UAS remote ID does not prevent operation;
  flight proceeds until physical interception or battery exhaustion.
Root mechanics: R06 (fleet management platform controls geofencing
  for entire agricultural drone fleet; single compromise enables
  fleet-wide geofence override); R04 (trust assumption: geofence
  enforcement assumed to be hardware-enforced on drone; many
  implementations use software geofencing in fleet management
  overridable via platform API).
Pattern trace: P33 (fleet management concentration enables
  fleet-wide simultaneous geofence override from single platform
  compromise); P44 (physical geofence enforcement assumed but
  implemented as software parameter overridable via API).
Defense logic: Hardware-enforced geofencing on drone (geofence
  boundaries stored in tamper-resistant hardware not overridable
  via fleet management API; only updated via authenticated
  secure channel with FAA UAS Service Supplier integration);
  geofence configuration change multi-factor approval;
  drone onboard geofence validation independent of fleet
  management system state.
Closure: Partial. Hardware geofencing requires drone hardware
  update for legacy fleet; FAA USS integration requires
  regulatory mandate not yet in force.

A1198 | ROS2 UNAUTHENTICATED TOPIC COMMAND INJECTION
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Domain: Industrial Robot Firmware (ROS2) (D2770)
Attack vector: Adversary on robot control network (via compromised
  engineering workstation or network intrusion) publishes malicious
  messages to unprotected ROS2 topics. Without SROS2 security
  plugins, ROS2 DDS middleware accepts topic publications from
  any DDS participant in same domain without authentication.
  Malicious joint velocity or force commands injected to robot
  arm control nodes cause unexpected motion in shared workspace;
  physical harm to nearby personnel; damage to tooling or
  workpiece; production line stoppage.
Root mechanics: R01 (ROS2 default configuration has no
  authentication because it was designed for research and
  academic robotics where trusted network assumed; industrial
  deployment inherits research defaults without security
  hardening); R04 (trust assumption: DDS participant trusted
  implicitly if in same DDS domain; domain membership assumed
  to imply authorization).
Pattern trace: P01 (authentication absent because trusted
  network assumed at research-environment design time); P88
  (industrial deployment of research software without security
  posture review for production threat model).
Defense logic: SROS2 security plugin activation (DDS Security
  spec; authentication, access control, and encryption for
  all ROS2 topic publications); node identity certificates
  issued by industrial ROS PKI; topic access control policies
  restricting which nodes may publish to safety-critical
  control topics; robot safety PLC as independent hardwired
  safety layer (validates commanded motion within physical
  safety envelope before actuation).
Closure: Partial. SROS2 activation addresses software injection;
  hardwired safety PLC prevents out-of-envelope actuation
  regardless of software layer.

LAW-9 INSTANCE #97:
Domain: EAS ENDEC Authentication — Collective Adoption Failure
LAW-9: "Security controls protecting control systems are systematically
  underinvested relative to operational risk when adoption requires
  coordinated multi-actor commitment."
Application: CAP digital signature authentication for EAS requires: FEMA and
  NWS to sign all originating CAP messages (cost of PKI management for public
  alert origination), all broadcast ENDECs to be firmware-updated for signature
  verification (cost borne by thousands of independent broadcast stations),
  and downstream relaying stations to enforce authentication before relay
  (cost of false-positive management when authentic alerts are incorrectly
  signed). No single actor bears the cost of a false EAS broadcast — cost
  diffuses to public as mass panic and first responder resource exhaustion.
  FCC lacks technical enforcement authority to mandate ENDEC firmware updates;
  ENDEC manufacturers have no commercial incentive to issue security updates
  to sold equipment without mandate. Collective action failure: no stakeholder
  has sufficient incentive to drive authentication adoption; result is
  decade-plus of known false EAS vulnerability without remedy.
LAW-9 instance count: 97 (confirmed).

A1203 | SD-WAN UNDERLAY BGP HIJACK FOR TRAFFIC INTERCEPTION
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Domain: SD-WAN Security (D2780)
Attack vector: Adversary performs BGP prefix hijacking against IP prefixes
  used by SD-WAN overlay endpoints. SD-WAN traffic rerouted through
  adversary-controlled autonomous system; SD-WAN overlay encryption
  protects payload confidentiality but tunnel establishment phase
  is affected by path change. In implementations without overlay
  endpoint authentication pinning, adversary-in-path position during
  tunnel renegotiation enables MITM against tunnel key exchange;
  subsequent traffic decryptable.
Root mechanics: R04 (trust assumption: SD-WAN overlay endpoint
  authentication relies on PKI; BGP hijack enables adversary-in-path
  position during TLS handshake; PKI trust not verified against
  network path expectation); R01 (SD-WAN design assumes internet
  routing is adversarial at payload layer but not at path layer;
  path integrity not verified as part of overlay security model).
Pattern trace: P44 (overlay encryption trusted to provide security
  against underlay adversary; path integrity not verified as part
  of overlay security model); P66 (trust transitivity: SD-WAN
  trusts PKI trusts internet routing that adversary has compromised).
Defense logic: SD-WAN endpoint certificate pinning (pin expected
  peer certificate at configuration time; BGP hijack routes to
  adversary-controlled endpoint that cannot present pinned certificate);
  path integrity monitoring (compare expected vs. actual BGP path
  to SD-WAN peers; path change triggers alert); RPKI enforcement
  on SD-WAN underlay ISP to reduce BGP hijack attack surface.
Closure: Partial. Certificate pinning effectively blocks BGP hijack
  MITM on tunnel establishment; does not protect against traffic
  analysis by in-path adversary on encrypted SD-WAN flows.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A1204 | MINING AUTONOMOUS HAUL TRUCK REMOTE COMMAND INJECTION
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Domain: Mining Automation Remote Operations (D2781)
Attack vector: Adversary compromising mine site remote operations center
  (ROC) via private LTE network or satellite link injects malicious
  navigation commands to autonomous haul trucks. Commands alter truck
  navigation path to create controlled collision in confined haulage
  road (truck-to-truck or truck-to-infrastructure). Trucks carry
  payloads of hundreds of tonnes at operational speeds; collision
  causes catastrophic physical damage and potential worker fatalities
  in haulage network. Emergency stop command must reach trucks before
  commanded collision path is executed.
Root mechanics: R06 (ROC is concentration point for command authority
  over entire autonomous fleet; ROC compromise enables fleet-wide
  command injection); R01 (mine automation system designed assuming
  ROC network is trusted; adversarial ROC access not modeled as
  primary threat; physical isolation of remote mine site assumed
  to protect ROC connectivity).
Pattern trace: P33 (ROC concentration amplifies single compromise
  to fleet-wide command authority over safety-critical autonomous
  vehicles); P17 (satellite and private LTE connectivity transforms
  physical mine site isolation from protection to attack surface
  extension accessible remotely).
Defense logic: Truck-resident collision avoidance as hardwired
  safety system independent of ROC commands (onboard LiDAR/radar
  with automated emergency stop; not overridable via ROC command);
  ROC command authentication with truck-side signature verification;
  ROC-to-fleet command anomaly detection (simultaneous fleet-wide
  heading change triggers safety halt pending operator confirmation);
  ROC network isolation from internet with dedicated secure comms.
Closure: Partial. Onboard collision avoidance is primary safety
  layer; ROC command authentication protects authorized command
  channel; sophisticated adversary may target onboard safety system
  separately.


--- SOURCE LINES 291505–291571 ---
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A1206 | HVDC TRANSMISSION CONVERTER STATION CONTROL MANIPULATION
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Domain: HVDC Transmission Systems (D2779)
Attack vector: Adversary with access to HVDC converter station
  control system (thyristor or IGBT valve control, DC link voltage
  regulation, reactive power control) manipulates converter firing
  angle parameters. Incorrect firing angles on HVDC converter:
  creates harmonics causing transformer and equipment damage;
  triggers commutation failure causing momentary power interruption;
  causes DC link overvoltage damaging converter valves. HVDC links
  carry GW-scale power over long distances (submarine cables,
  continental interconnections); failure has grid stability impact
  beyond the link itself.
Root mechanics: R06 (HVDC converter station is concentration point
  for power flow on the interconnection; single station compromise
  disrupts entire HVDC link); R01 (HVDC converter control designed
  for power engineering operational requirements; cybersecurity
  threat model not integrated into converter control system design
  for legacy installations).
Pattern trace: P33 (converter station concentration means single
  compromise disrupts entire GW-scale HVDC link); P88 (network
  connectivity added to legacy converter station control without
  threat model update).
Defense logic: Converter control system network isolation (IEC 62443
  zone and conduit model applied to HVDC converter control);
  hardware interlocks on firing angle bounds (protection relays
  not overridable via software for extreme parameter exceedances);
  anomaly detection on converter parameter changes; NERC CIP
  extension to explicitly cover HVDC converter stations.
Closure: Partial. Network isolation reduces remote attack surface;
  hardware interlocks prevent most extreme parameter manipulations;
  subtle parameter manipulation within hardware protection limits
  remains risk.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A1207 | SECURE CONTAINER RUNTIME ESCAPE VIA KERNEL SYSCALL EXPLOIT
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Domain: Secure Container Runtime Isolation (D2784)
Attack vector: Malicious container workload exploits Linux kernel
  vulnerability reachable via container syscall interface. Even with
  seccomp filters, certain syscalls are necessary for container
  operation and may have exploitable kernel bugs. Container escape
  via kernel exploit grants host-level privilege; attacker accesses
  other containers on same host, host filesystem, and potentially
  the orchestration control plane. Kernel-level isolation is the
  last software defense for container multi-tenancy.
Root mechanics: R05 (common-mode failure: all containers on same
  host share kernel; single kernel vulnerability is cross-container
  common-mode failure surface); R08 (container runtime monitoring
  cannot detect kernel exploitation in progress without kernel-level
  instrumentation; exploitation is below runtime visibility layer).
Pattern trace: P38 (shared kernel creates common-mode vulnerability
  across all containers on host by physical necessity of OS design);
  P55 (multi-tenancy on shared kernel as persistent cross-tenant
  attack surface).
Defense logic: VM-based container isolation (gVisor intercepts
  syscalls in user space; Kata Containers uses lightweight VM per
  container; eliminates shared kernel attack surface); seccomp
  profile restricting unnecessary syscalls; runtime security
  monitoring with eBPF for anomalous syscall patterns; kernel
  exploit mitigation technologies (KASLR, SMEP, SMAP, stack
  canaries, shadow call stack).
Closure: Partial. VM-based isolation is most effective; adds
  performance overhead and operational complexity; kernel
  mitigations reduce but don't eliminate kernel vulnerability
  exploitability.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A1209 | LEGAL HOLD PLATFORM EVIDENCE TAMPERING
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Domain: Legal Hold and eDiscovery Platforms (D2790)
Attack vector: Adversary with insider access to eDiscovery platform
  (litigation support team member, IT administrator with platform
  access) modifies or deletes documents collected under court-ordered
  legal hold. Platform's retention custody does not enforce cryptographic
  integrity at collection time; documents stored in mutable database
  accessible to administrator role. Modification leaves no audit trail
  in unprotected platform. Opposing counsel receives modified evidence
  set; spoliation of evidence has legal consequences if discovered
  but modified content may not be detected.
Root mechanics: R08 (no visibility: evidence tampering undetectable
  without cryptographic integrity baseline established at collection);
  R03 (litigation support team trusted with evidence custody; insider
  threat by definition is insider to the custody chain).
Pattern trace: P61 (litigation support insider has legitimate access
  to evidence custody; insider threat is by design of custody
  arrangement); P44 (administrative role over evidence platform
  trusted to maintain integrity; administrative access is the
  attack surface).
Defense logic: Cryptographic hash of collected documents at
  collection time; hash manifest archived with court or neutral
  third party; opposing counsel verifies hash at production;
  WORM storage for legal hold documents (write-once; modification
  physically impossible without WORM media replacement); chain
  of custody log with tamper-evident hash chaining.
Closure: Partial. WORM storage is most effective; cloud-based
  WORM implementation may be administratively overridable by
  provider; neutral third-party hash archival provides independent
  verification.

A1211 — V2X Misbehavior Detection Authority Key Compromise
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
DOMAIN: Automotive V2X / Cooperative ITS
MECHANISM: The Misbehavior Detection Authority (MBDA) holds the certificate
revocation authority for V2X pseudonym certificates. Compromise of MBDA
signing keys allows an attacker to issue fraudulent revocations (denying
legitimate vehicles access to V2X services) or suppress legitimate
revocations (allowing misbehaving vehicles to continue participating).
The attack surface includes HSM compromise at the MBDA, insider threats
among MBDA operators, and API abuse by authorized reporting entities.
PATTERNS: P33 (MBDA concentration makes revocation authority a single
point of failure), P66 (all V2X participants transitively trust MBDA
revocation decisions), P41 (protocol assumes MBDA integrity as invariant).
SEVERITY: Critical — affects safety-critical vehicle coordination at scale.

A1212 — DAO Flash Loan Governance Attack
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
DOMAIN: Decentralized Finance / DAO Governance
MECHANISM: An attacker borrows a massive quantity of governance tokens via
flash loan within a single transaction, uses the temporary voting power to
pass a malicious governance proposal, executes the proposal (draining
treasury or modifying protocol parameters), and repays the loan — all
atomically. No capital is required beyond transaction fees. The attack
exploits the assumption that token holders have economic alignment with
protocol health, which breaks when tokens are transiently borrowed.
PATTERNS: P55 (governance token as multi-tenant attack surface: any holder
can vote regardless of long-term commitment), P44 (governance system trusts
token balance at vote time as proxy for stakeholder alignment).
SEVERITY: Critical — treasury drain and protocol parameter manipulation.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
DOMAIN: Warehouse Automation / Autonomous Mobile Robots
MECHANISM: The AMR fleet management platform authenticates and orchestrates

A1222 — Smart Meter Firmware Rollback Attack
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
DOMAIN: Advanced Metering Infrastructure / Smart Grid
MECHANISM: Smart meters accept firmware updates via RF mesh or PLC network.
An attacker who gains access to the AMI headend or intercepts the update
channel installs an older firmware version with known vulnerabilities,
downgrading the meter's security posture. Once running the vulnerable
firmware, the attacker exploits known issues to gain persistent meter
access, enabling energy theft, false readings, or remote disconnect
command injection across a large meter population.
PATTERNS: P88 (AMI update channel added without rollback prevention),
P33 (AMI headend compromise propagates rollback to entire meter fleet).
SEVERITY: High — energy theft and grid operator visibility loss at scale.

A1223 — Genomic Data Re-identification via Summary Statistics
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
DOMAIN: Biobank Security / Genomic Data Privacy
MECHANISM: Published GWAS summary statistics (allele frequencies, p-values,
effect sizes) can be used to re-identify individuals in the study cohort
using Homer-style membership inference attacks. An attacker with access to
a target individual's genotype data queries publicly available GWAS results
to determine with statistical confidence whether that individual participated
in the study, inferring sensitive phenotype associations from study enrollment.
PATTERNS: P74 (summary statistic as privacy exfiltration channel: aggregate
output leaks individual membership), P55 (open access to GWAS statistics
creates privacy attack surface for entire cohort).
SEVERITY: High — phenotype disclosure for cancer, psychiatric, and rare
disease cohort participants.

A1228 — DePIN Proof-of-Coverage Simulation Attack
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
DOMAIN: Decentralized Physical Infrastructure / Token Economics
MECHANISM: DePIN networks (e.g., Helium) reward node operators for providing
physical coverage verified by proof-of-coverage challenges. Attackers deploy
clusters of nodes that simulate coverage via direct radio communication
with each other rather than providing actual geographic coverage, earning
rewards without contributing real infrastructure. As simulated nodes cluster
in high-reward areas, they crowd out legitimate operators and degrade actual
network coverage while the token reward mechanism continues paying.
PATTERNS: P44 (proof-of-coverage oracle trusts radio challenge response as
proxy for physical coverage without independent geographic verification),
P55 (open participation as multi-tenant attack surface: anyone can deploy
simulated coverage nodes).
SEVERITY: High — network coverage degradation and token reward fraud.

--- SOURCE LINES 294143–294157 ---
DOMAIN: DERMS / Demand Response / Grid Security
INSTANCE: DER Demand Response Program Collective Security Failure

MECHANISM: The security of a demand response program depends on the aggregate
authentication and control integrity of every enrolled DER device, every
utility aggregator, and the DERMS platform itself. No single actor —
utility, aggregator, or device manufacturer — can individually ensure that
the demand response program cannot be weaponized against the grid. A utility
with a secure DERMS platform cannot compensate for poorly authenticated devices
enrolled via third-party aggregators. An aggregator with rigorous IEEE 2030.5
implementation cannot compensate for a DERMS platform vulnerability at a
different aggregator serving the same demand response event. The program's
grid impact at response time is determined by the security posture of every
participant — a collective property that no individual participant can unilaterally
assure.

A1242 — Carbon Credit Double-Counting via Registry Interoperability Gap
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
DOMAIN: Carbon Markets / Environmental Finance
MECHANISM: A carbon credit project developer registers the same emission
reduction activity in multiple registries (e.g., Verra VCS and a national
compliance registry) that do not have real-time interoperability. The developer
sells the credit in both markets before the double-registration is detected
through periodic reconciliation. The delay between registration and
reconciliation — which may be months or years — is the exploitation window.
PATTERNS: P55 (multi-registry carbon market as attack surface: isolation
between registries creates double-counting opportunity), P41 (registry
protocols assume cross-registry deduplication occurs at registration time,
not at reconciliation).
SEVERITY: High — systematic carbon credit fraud; environmental market
integrity damage.

A1246 — Implantable Cardiac Device Unauthorized Command via Clinic Programmer
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
DOMAIN: Implantable Medical Devices / Cardiac Security
MECHANISM: ICD and pacemaker clinic programmers communicate via short-range
RF or NFC. Historically, these communications used proprietary protocols

PATTERNS: P88 (wireless programming capability added to implantable devices

physical proximity as sufficient authentication proxy).
SEVERITY: Critical — direct patient harm; confirmed research demonstration.

A1266 — Telecom Core SS7/Diameter Roaming Attack
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
DOMAIN: Telecommunications Core / Signaling Security
MECHANISM: Attacker with access to a telecom's SS7 or Diameter roaming

visibility into ordered fragment assemblies across multiple providers.
PATTERNS: P55 (multi-provider synthesis market as attack surface: lack of
cross-provider visibility enables fragmentation attack), P41 (screening
protocol evaluates individual sequences assuming attacker cannot assemble
fragments into functional sequences as invariant).
SEVERITY: Critical — pathogen or enhanced select agent synthesis capability;
potential mass casualty risk.

D2917 | QUANTUM INTERNET PROTOCOL STACK SECURITY
  First-mover quantum internet deployments (Dutch QuantumDelta corridor, Chinese

  Classical control channels remain TCP/IP, creating hybrid attack vectors where
  adversaries compromise classical signaling to degrade quantum links without
  touching quantum hardware. Entanglement distribution scheduling algorithms
  introduce timing side-channels. QKD remains quantum; quantum internet requires
  full quantum teleportation — substantially larger trusted-node attack surface.
  Threat actors: nation-state APTs targeting quantum infrastructure; protocol
  researchers discovering zero-days in immature standards. P14, P31, P67.

  hyperparameter data — high-value IP target. Secure aggregation protocols add

A1271 | QUANTUM INTERNET ENTANGLEMENT SCHEDULING TIMING SIDE-CHANNEL
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Domain   : Quantum internet protocol stack (D2917)
Surface  : Entanglement distribution scheduling algorithms in quantum repeater
           networks expose timing side-channels via observable scheduling
           decisions that correlate with traffic volume and routing patterns.
Mechanism: Bell-state measurement retry intervals, entanglement purification
           round counts, and classical control-channel timing all leak
           information about quantum channel utilization even when quantum
           data remains perfectly secret. Adversary with access to classical
           control channel metadata can infer communication graph topology.
P-trace  : P31 (covert channel in timing) → P14 (complexity of quantum
           systems creates unexamined attack surface) → P8 (abstraction
           boundary between quantum and classical creates blind spot).
Anchor   : A1271 confirmed. Resolves to P31/P14/P8 intersection.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A1272 | FEDERATED LEARNING AGGREGATION SERVER SINGLE POINT COMPROMISE
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Domain   : Federated ML infrastructure (D2918)
Surface  : Central aggregation server in federated learning architectures
           holds global model state, participant registry, and aggregation
           logic — compromise yields complete model extraction without
           attacking any participant.
Mechanism: Aggregation server sees all gradient updates; with sufficient
           compute, can perform gradient inversion to reconstruct participant
           training data. Server also controls which updates are accepted,
           enabling silent model poisoning. Secure aggregation protocols
           (cryptographic masking) mitigate gradient visibility but increase
           aggregation server attack surface (homomorphic operations).
P-trace  : P19 (supply chain trust — aggregation server is trusted third
           party) → P5 (centralization creates failure concentration) →
           P44 (ML systems inherit classical infrastructure vulnerabilities).
Anchor   : A1272 confirmed. Resolves to P19/P5/P44 intersection.

A1274 | C2PA METADATA STRIPPING AND CREDENTIAL LAUNDERING ATTACK CHAIN
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Domain   : Generative AI content authentication (D2920)
Surface  : Content authenticity infrastructure assumes metadata integrity
           through media lifecycle — systematic metadata stripping followed
           by re-signing with stolen credentials creates authenticated

Mechanism: Step 1: Strip C2PA metadata from authentic content. Step 2: Modify

A1275 | MALICIOUS PICKLE DESERIALIZATION IN OSS AI MODEL DISTRIBUTION
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A1282 | NUCLEAR I&C COMMON-MODE ATTACK BYPASSING DIVERSITY REQUIREMENT
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Domain   : Nuclear power plant digital I&C (D2943)
Surface  : Software diversity in safety systems assumes independent
           implementations cannot share common vulnerabilities — an attacker
           who understands both diverse implementations may identify shared
           failure modes in the specification rather than code.
Mechanism: Diverse I&C systems share: identical functional specifications
           (same requirements document), same physics models (reactor
           thermal-hydraulics), same sensor inputs (same physical measurements),
           and same human interface designs. Specification-level adversarial
           input crafted to trigger edge case in ALL implementations based
           on shared specification understanding defeats diversity. Examples:
           timing attacks on shared timing requirements; data type boundary
           exploits where specification is ambiguous.
P-trace  : P8 (abstraction — specification layer shared beneath diverse
           implementations) → P27 (independence assumption violated at
           specification level) → P14 (complexity of nuclear systems
           creates unexamined attack paths).
Anchor   : A1282 confirmed. Resolves to P8/P27/P14 intersection.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A1283 | EBPF VERIFIER BYPASS FOR KERNEL CODE EXECUTION
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Domain   : Cloud-native runtime security and eBPF platforms (D2944)
Surface  : Linux eBPF verifier performs static analysis to prevent unsafe
           programs from running in kernel space — verifier bugs have
           historically enabled privilege escalation to arbitrary kernel
           code execution from unprivileged userspace.
Mechanism: eBPF verifier must perform bounded analysis on all possible
           program paths — state explosion, type confusion in verifier,
           and incorrect tracking of pointer arithmetic have produced multiple
           CVEs (CVE-2021-3490, CVE-2022-23222, CVE-2023-2163) allowing
           arbitrary kernel write. Security tools loading eBPF programs have
           CAP_BPF privilege — process compromise plus verifier bypass
           equals full kernel compromise.
P-trace  : P41 (new security infrastructure creates new attack surface) →
           P8 (abstraction — verifier correctness assumed, not proven) →
           P14 (kernel complexity creates unexamined attack paths).
Anchor   : A1283 confirmed. Resolves to P41/P8/P14 intersection.

A1306 | PQC MIGRATION HYBRID MODE DOWNGRADE ATTACK
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

           maintain classical fallback for interoperability — active
           adversary forces downgrade to classical-only negotiation

Collective action structure:
  - OEMs: bear reputational cost of vehicle compromise but control only final
    signing step; third-party component supply chain is opaque
  - Tier-1 suppliers (Bosch, Continental, Harman): provide software components
    integrated into OEM update packages; bear no direct liability for OEM fleet
    compromise resulting from their component vulnerability
  - CDN providers (Akamai, CloudFront): deliver update packages; bear no liability
    for malicious content in signed packages they did not create
  - Telecom carriers: provide connectivity for OTA delivery; bear no liability
    for update content
  - UNECE WP.29: mandates SUMS at OEM level; does not specify supply chain
    security requirements for tier-1 suppliers or CDN providers

Defection incentives:
  - Tier-1 suppliers bear SCA (Software Composition Analysis) cost without
    direct liability for OEM fleet impact of their vulnerabilities
  - CDN providers could sign content delivery but have no contractual obligation
    to verify package integrity beyond OEM signature
  - Each supply chain actor free-rides on adjacent actor's security investment
    while bearing only fraction of fleet compromise cost

--- SOURCE LINES 302626–302640 ---
  P98 APPLICATION #80:
  Domain: CALEA Lawful Intercept Infrastructure Security Compliance
  Context: US telecommunications carriers achieve CALEA compliance through
  implementation of standardized lawful intercept mediation interfaces
  certified by equipment vendors. CALEA compliance metrics measure whether
  the intercept capability works as specified — whether law enforcement can
  access communications through the provisioned interface. The metric does
  not measure whether the LI infrastructure is hardened against adversarial
  access by unauthorized parties. Salt Typhoon demonstrated: CALEA compliance
  metrics confirmed fully operational, adversarial access to the same
  infrastructure confirmed simultaneously. The security metric measured
  intercept capability provisioning. The security outcome — intercept
  infrastructure protected from exploitation by hostile nation-states —
  was never measured and never achieved. CALEA compliance became, in P98
  terms, a certified attack surface standardization.

LAW-9 INSTANCE #113 | CABLE REPAIR VESSEL DP SYSTEM GNSS DEPENDENCY FREE-RIDER
Context: Undersea cable repair operations depend on GPS for DP positioning.
Individual vessel operators benefit from GPS accuracy (civilian P-code) provided
free by U.S. Space Force. Operators bear no cost for GPS disruption risk —
infrastructure is government-provided. GNSS spoofing resilience is a public good
problem: if all vessels had spoofing detection, the attack surface for targeted
vessel disruption decreases for all. But individual vessel operators calculate
that if other vessels have spoofing detection, theirs are less likely to be
targeted; each waits for others to invest.
Free-rider structure: Government provides GPS infrastructure; individual operators
free-ride on public signal without contributing to its resilience; spoofing
detection investment avoided because benefit accrues to fleet not individual.
Confirmation: LAW-9 instance #113. Cumulative: 113 confirmed instances.

G-C174-06 | QKD TRUSTED NODE CLASSICAL CHANNEL COMPROMISE
Domain: Quantum key distribution network infrastructure
Gap: Long-distance QKD requires trusted relay nodes (quantum signal cannot be
amplified). At each relay node, the quantum key is measured and re-encrypted
for the next hop — making each relay node a classical decryption point. The
classical control channels at relay nodes use standard TLS or IPsec. A
compromise of one relay node's classical control infrastructure decrypts all
QKD-secured communications transiting that node. The quantum security guarantee
is entirely voided by classical relay node compromise. Gap exists at: relay
node physical security equivalence to key material, classical channel hardening
for relay infrastructure, relay node threat model specification.

Domain: Industrial robot controllers in precision manufacturing
Gap: Robot controller programs (in robot-manufacturer-specific languages: KRL,
RAPID, Inform, Karel) can be modified via network-connected programming interfaces.
Subtle coordinate modification (fractions of a millimeter) in precision components
causes out-of-tolerance products that pass visual inspection but fail under load.
No runtime integrity check on executed robot programs in most production
environments — program hash verified at upload but not at execution. Gap exists
at: runtime program integrity, execution-time coordinate monitoring, specification-
execution delta detection.

A1366 | QKD RELAY NODE CLASSICAL CHANNEL ATTACK ANATOMY
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Layer 1 — Physical: QKD relay node hardware (quantum detectors, single-photon
  sources, classical control computer), fiber interconnects, site physical security
Layer 2 — Quantum Layer: Relay node receives quantum key from upstream segment;
  measures qubits (destroys quantum state); generates classical key; uses
  classical key to encrypt next-hop quantum key — full classical exposure
Layer 3 — Attack Path: Physical access or remote compromise of relay node
  classical control system → access to in-memory key material — all QKD
  sessions transiting this node decryptable; quantum security guarantee void
Layer 4 — Threat Model Gap: QKD marketed as unconditionally secure; relay
  node vulnerability documented in academic literature but not prominently
  communicated to commercial QKD buyers; trust model mismatch
Layer 5 — Detection: Relay node compromise may be undetectable; quantum
  channel authentication verifies path integrity, not relay node integrity;
  passive key copy leaves no quantum channel anomaly
Layer 6 — Impact: Decryption of all QKD-secured government or financial
  communications transiting compromised relay; security regression vs.
  classical strong encryption at relay nodes
Root mechanic: R04 (trust model mismatch) + R09 (security guarantee boundary)

G-C177-07 | FEDERAL PKI CA COMPROMISE FOR GOVERNMENT DOMAIN MitM
Domain: Federal PKI trust hierarchy and government certificate authorities
Gap: The Federal PKI trust hierarchy (FPKI) has approximately 200 issuing CAs
trusted by government systems. A compromise of any FPKI-trusted intermediate CA
would allow issuance of fraudulent certificates for any .gov or .mil domain.
Certificate transparency logs provide post-issuance detection but the window
between rogue certificate issuance and CT detection (hours to days) allows
real-time MitM against government network communications. Gap exists at:
FPKI intermediate CA compromise detection latency, government domain CT
monitoring with automated revocation, FPKI CA security audit frequency.

A1396 | FPKI INTERMEDIATE CA COMPROMISE FOR GOVERNMENT DOMAIN MitM ANATOMY
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Layer 1 — Physical: Federal PKI intermediate CA (Treasury, DoD, State Dept);
  HSM storing intermediate CA private key; CA issuance infrastructure;
  government network TLS inspection endpoints
Layer 2 — Trust Chain: FPKI root CA → intermediate CA → issuance CA →
  end-entity certificate for gov domain; all government browsers trust
  FPKI root; any certificate issued by FPKI-trusted CA is trusted
Layer 3 — Attack Path: Compromise intermediate CA HSM or signing key via
  CA software vulnerability or insider → issue fraudulent certificate for
  target .gov domain (treasury.gov, irs.gov) → MitM government traffic
Layer 4 — Detection Latency: CT logs receive certificate submission within
  hours; CISA domain monitoring alerts on unexpected certificate; but between
  issuance and CT detection: real-time MitM against government employees
    accessing government services during targeted operation
Layer 5 — CT Monitoring: CISA EINSTEIN monitors TLS for anomalies; but FPKI-
  issued certificate passes validation; CT log anomaly is detection mechanism;
  alert to response gap is the exploitation window
Layer 6 — Impact: Government credential harvest; classified data access via
  intercepted sessions; government network lateral movement via harvested
  credentials; trust in government PKI destroyed if widely discovered
Root mechanic: R07 (CA supply chain) + R03 (CT detection latency gap)

A1408 | VITAL RECORDS DIGITAL CREDENTIAL FORGERY
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
DOMAIN: Vital records / state health statistics / identity document integrity
PATTERN CLUSTER: P31 (foundational identity document compromise), P52 (platform security variability enabling selective attack), P76 (verification service as single point of failure)
ROOT MECHANICS: R03 (trust without standardized verification), R08 (state-level variability as attack surface)

ANATOMY:
Layer 1 — Digital Issuance: State issues cryptographically signed digital birth
  certificate using state-generated signing key. Recipient receives credential
  as PDF with embedded signature or as verifiable credential in digital wallet.
Layer 2 — Platform Compromise: State vital records issuance platform compromised
  through web application vulnerability or supply chain attack. Adversary gains
  access to signing key or signing service without triggering issuance audit.
Layer 3 — Fraudulent Issuance: Adversary issues digital vital records for
  fabricated identities or alters records for existing identities (false date
  of birth, parentage, citizenship status) using legitimate signing key.
  Fraudulent records are cryptographically valid.
Layer 4 — Verification Failure: Relying parties (employers, financial institutions,
  government agencies) verify signature and confirm validity. Fraudulent record
  passes verification. No mechanism exists to distinguish legitimate from
  adversarially issued credentials signed by the same key.
Layer 5 — Revocation Gap: State discovers compromise and revokes signing key.
  Previously issued fraudulent credentials already distributed cannot be recalled.
  Revocation list propagation to relying parties is inconsistent and slow.
CONSEQUENCE: Identity fraud at foundational layer; fraudulent identity documents cryptographically valid
INVARIANT: Key compromise invalidates all issued credentials retroactively but not practically

Layer 5 — No Detection: Officers unaware communications are unencrypted.
  No real-time encryption status monitoring. Operational failure

CONSEQUENCE: Operational security compromise; officer safety risk; counter-surveillance enablement
INVARIANT: Downgrade attack against safety-critical communications exploits protocol fallback without user detection

ANATOMY:
Layer 1 — Fleet Architecture: AV fleet management system issues route commands
  to hundreds to thousands of vehicles simultaneously via cloud backend.
  Vehicles check in continuously and accept route updates from authenticated

Layer 2 — Fleet Management Compromise: Adversary compromises fleet management

--- SOURCE LINES 311039–311059 ---
ANATOMY:
Layer 1 — Detection Architecture: Camera network provides AI-driven smoke
  detection with 2-5 minute notification to CAL FIRE. Cameras transmit
  via cellular or microwave backhaul to management platform.
Layer 2 — Attack Timing: Adversary identifies Red Flag Warning conditions
  (low humidity, high winds, dry fuel): the window where ignition-to-
  conflagration timeline is compressed to 15-30 minutes.
Layer 3 — Feed Suppression: DDoS attack against camera management platform
  backend during Red Flag Warning period. Or targeted physical attack on
  transmission infrastructure serving cameras in target area. Camera
  feeds go offline or show stale frames.
Layer 4 — Detection Blind Spot: Ignition occurs in camera coverage gap.
  No AI smoke detection. Manual reporting (911, observers) delayed 15-30
  minutes versus camera baseline. During Red Flag conditions, this window
  allows fire to transition from ignition to established run.
Layer 5 — Consequence Multiplication: Fire reaches critical size before
  initial attack resources arrive. Containment probability drops sharply.
  Community evacuation warning delayed. Attack converted a detectable fire
  into an uncontrolled wildfire through detection delay alone.
CONSEQUENCE: Wildfire mass destruction; delayed evacuation; detection gap exploited during maximum risk window
INVARIANT: Detection system availability attack timed to vulnerability window multiplies physical consequence

  Output shows lower probable maximum losses and average annual loss than
  unmodified model would produce. Actuary reports model output as valid.
Layer 4 — Regulatory Filing: Reserve adequacy statement filed with state
  insurance department based on manipulated model output. Carrier holds
  reserves below actual expected loss requirement. Reinsurance purchased
  at inadequate limit based on false PML.
Layer 5 — Insolvency Risk: Major catastrophe event causes losses exceeding
  manipulated reserve estimate. Carrier faces insolvency. Policyholders
  impaired. State guarantee fund activated. Manipulation discovered during
  forensic examination of reserve adequacy failure.
CONSEQUENCE: Carrier insolvency; policyholder impairment; false regulatory reserve filing
INVARIANT: Model execution without output integrity attestation enables systematic regulatory falsification

Domain: Offshore oil and gas production cybersecurity
Gap: Offshore production facility ESD (Emergency Shutdown) systems are designed

ANATOMY:
Layer 1 — Drug Library Architecture: Hospital formulary maintained in pump
  management software (Baxter Dose Error Reduction Software, BD Alaris
  Drug Library Manager). Libraries define soft stop (alert) and hard stop
  (prevent) limits by drug and care area. Libraries pushed to pumps via
  hospital network.
Layer 2 — Library Modification: Adversary with pump management software access
  (insider, compromised IT account, or supply chain implant in management
  software) modifies drug library for ICU care area: morphine hard stop
  raised from 20 mg/hr to 40 mg/hr; hydromorphone soft stop removed.
Layer 3 — Library Push: Modified library pushed to pumps in target care area.
  Push appears as routine library update. Nurses acknowledge library
  update notification without clinical review of changed limits.
Layer 4 — Overdose Window: ICU nurse programs morphine infusion at 22 mg/hr
  for post-surgical patient. Rate would have triggered hard stop under
  correct library. Modified library allows programming without alert.
  Patient receives overdose infusion.
Layer 5 — Patient Harm: Patient suffers respiratory depression from opioid
  overdose. Resuscitation required. Incident attributed to programming
  error. Drug library modification discovered only if pharmacy performs
  unexpected version audit against approved library baseline.
CONSEQUENCE: Patient overdose; clinical safety system bypass via configuration; harm without alarm
INVARIANT: Safety configuration without integrity verification converts safety feature into harm enabler

compromise) could enable an adversary to deploy malicious firmware to large
numbers of customer terminals simultaneously, creating a botnet at scale or
disrupting service. The scale of LEO constellations (2+ million terminals)
means a firmware supply chain attack has outsized impact.
Open: No binding security standard for satellite broadband UT firmware
update authentication; no independent security audit requirement for
firmware update supply chain; no anomaly detection for anomalous update
distribution patterns across terminal fleet.

--- SOURCE LINES 318826–318842 ---
LAW-9 INSTANCE #141 — FAERS ADVERSE EVENT SIGNAL SYSTEM (A2633, D2945)
DOMAIN: D3366 (FDA FAERS / VAERS)
TRUST MODEL: FDA's FAERS signal detection system accepts MedWatch submissions —
including anonymous consumer reports — as equivalent data inputs to mandatory
manufacturer expedited reports. No authentication, no reporter identity verification,
no submission rate limit exists at point of entry. The system is designed to aggregate
signal broadly; breadth was a feature to detect rare events missed by healthcare
providers. But the trust model assumes submissions represent real patient experiences.
An adversary who submits synthetic adverse events at volume inverts this trust: the
signal detection algorithm's own operation produces a false regulatory action. The
system's intended sensitivity becomes its attack surface.
TRUST INVERSION SIGNATURE: The same architectural choice (low barrier to submission
for population-level signal detection) that enables detection of rare adverse events
enables adversarial signal injection. The defense requires differentiated trust by
reporter class without eliminating the broad reporting access — a design tension
with no fully satisfying resolution.
LAW-9 INSTANCE #141: CONFIRMED.

INSTANCE #158 — NERC CIP SELF-REPORTED VIOLATION SEVERITY SYSTEM

Regulated system: NERC Critical Infrastructure Protection mandatory reliability standards
Consequential data: CIP violation severity classification and mitigation plan adequacy
Reporting obligation: Registered entities must self-report CIP violations, classify
  by severity, and implement adequate mitigation to remediate the violation
Mechanism of concealment: Entity self-determines violation severity classification
  using regulatory criteria that have interpretive ambiguity; technical violations
  reclassified as procedural under lower severity rubric; mitigation plan describes
  paper procedure updates without technical remediation; NERC CMEP accepts self-report
  with severity classification without field verification for non-High-impact assets;
  actual technical vulnerability persists through paper-compliant mitigation.
Detection apparatus failure: NERC CMEP is primarily document-review based for
  self-reported violations; field verification of technical remediation not routine;
  technical expertise required to identify reclassification fraud exceeds
  CMEP reviewer capacity for all self-reports; penalty structure incentivizes
  low severity classification.
LAW-9 MECHANISM TYPE: Classification manipulation to suppress regulatory consequence

G-C197-08 | OSHA PSM INCIDENT INVESTIGATION ROOT CAUSE ADEQUACY GAP
Domain: OSHA — Process Safety Management (PSM), 29 CFR 1910.119
Gap: PSM requires employers to investigate process safety incidents and
near-misses. OSHA requires that investigations identify root causes and
recommendations be resolved. However, investigation quality is self-
directed: employers write reports, determine root causes, and track
corrective actions. OSHA inspection of investigation adequacy occurs only
following major incidents or scheduled NEP inspections. Employers that
attribute incidents to operator error (proximate cause) rather than
management system deficiencies (root cause) satisfy the paperwork
requirement while leaving systemic vulnerabilities unaddressed. No
mandatory third-party review or independent sign-off on root cause
determination.
Root mechanic: R03 (classification manipulation), R07 (documentation gap)

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A1598 | OSHA PSM PROXIMATE-CAUSE ROOT CAUSE TRUNCATION ANATOMY
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Layer 1 — Surface: Chemical facility experiences process safety incident;
  employer conducts incident investigation and submits report showing
  findings and corrective actions to OSHA during inspection.
Layer 2 — Root cause truncation: Investigation attributes incident to
  'operator error — failed to follow procedure' and stops. No analysis
  of why procedure was not followed (inadequate training, time pressure,
  conflicting instructions, fatigue).
Layer 3 — Systemic gap hidden: Management pressure to complete non-routine
  operation outside normal staffing, inadequate procedure review cycle,
  and deferred maintenance on interlock that would have caught deviation
  — none appear in report.
Layer 4 — Corrective action misdirection: Action item is 'retrain operator'
  rather than 'revise procedure,' 'repair interlock,' or 'review scheduling
  pressure.' Systemic vulnerability persists.
Layer 5 — Repeat incident: Same systemic failure produces second incident
  with different operator; pattern only visible across-incident by OSHA
  analyst reviewing multiple reports — not from single investigation.
Anatomy: classification truncation + corrective action misdirection + repeat risk

D3786 — CISA Cybersecurity Performance Goals (CPG) Voluntary Adoption
  CISA's Cybersecurity Performance Goals are voluntary recommendations
  for critical infrastructure operators. Operators self-assess their
  CPG implementation status and may report adoption through sector
  information sharing mechanisms. The voluntary nature of CPG adoption
  means operators control whether to adopt, which goals to adopt, and
  how to assess their own implementation status. There is no mandatory
  verification of self-reported CPG adoption. An operator that reports
  CPG adoption while not implementing the underlying controls bears
  no regulatory consequence unless the gap is discovered in an incident.
